The energy check earned its keep immediately — **it found a real sign bug** in the Yang–Mills cubic terms that all three previous tests had passed.

## What was wrong

The three cubic terms (divergence, transport, transpose) had the wrong overall sign. Corrected:

$$\Box W^a_\nu = j^a_\nu + g\varepsilon^{abc}(\partial\!\cdot\!W^b)W^c_\nu + 2g\varepsilon^{abc}W^{b\mu}\partial_\mu W^c_\nu - g\varepsilon^{abc}W^b_\mu\partial^\nu W^{c\mu} - g^2\varepsilon^{abc}\varepsilon^{cde}(W^b\!\cdot\!W^d)W^e_\nu$$

The quartic was already right — which is *why* the bug was subtle. In $\tfrac14 F^2$ the cubic is $\tfrac12 g\,f\!\cdot\!c$ and the quartic $\tfrac14 g^2c^2$, so a sign error in the $\varepsilon$ convention flips the cubic and leaves the quartic alone. Exactly the pattern the data showed: mismatch ≈ **2× the YM contribution**, with the quartic matching to 2e−5 on uniform fields.

**Why the earlier tests missed it.** `TestYangMillsPureGauge` passes with *either* sign, because flipping the cubic also reverses the rotation sense it predicts — the test just wants $\omega = -cgB$ instead of $+cgB$. Covariance is blind to it too. That limitation is now written into the test's doc comment so nobody re-derives the trap.

## The energy functional

[energy.go](../wavesim/energy.go), host-side diagnostic:

$$U = \sum_x \Big[\tfrac12\textstyle\sum_j |D_j\Psi|^2 + V + \tfrac14\sum(F^a_{jk})^2 + \tfrac14\sum(F^b_{jk})^2 + \tfrac12\sum_a(\nabla\!\cdot\!W^a)^2 + \tfrac12(\nabla\!\cdot\!B)^2\Big]$$

with the full non-abelian $F^a_{jk}$. The $\xi=1$ gauge-fixing term is what makes the abelian part of $-\partial U/\partial W$ come out as the plain Laplacian.

## Why it's a convergence check, not a conservation check

**There is no exactly conserved discrete energy here.** `Laplacian19` and `Gradient10` aren't adjoint-compatible — their Fourier symbols differ by $O(k^2)$ (2.2% at $|k|{=}0.3$, 23% at 1.0). So I tested the stronger, sharper statement instead: force $= -\partial U/\partial\phi$ *in the continuum limit*.

```
YangMills=true   L= 16  RMS mismatch=3.9323e-02
YangMills=true   L= 32  RMS mismatch=9.5287e-03  shrank 4.13x
YangMills=true   L= 64  RMS mismatch=2.2670e-03  shrank 4.20x

YangMills=false  L= 16  RMS mismatch=7.5891e-02          <- control
YangMills=false  L= 32  RMS mismatch=1.3209e-01  shrank 0.57x
YangMills=false  L= 64  RMS mismatch=2.4397e-01  shrank 0.54x
```

That's the whole discriminator: a discretization artifact shrinks as $O(a^2)$, a wrong coefficient doesn't. The control run — energy still containing the self-coupling while the force no longer does — *diverges*, which proves the test is actually sensitive to the terms rather than passing vacuously.

A time-evolution drift check would be strictly weaker (same $O(a^2)$ floor, less diagnostic per run), which is why I built this instead. Happy to add one if you want it for monitoring rather than validation.

Two test-design mistakes I made and fixed along the way, both worth knowing: a *product* of two plane waves is a superposition whose force contributions partly cancel at a probe site, so the relative error stops converging for reasons that have nothing to do with physics — use a single plane wave. And a single probe point is fragile at large amplitude when the force passes through zero; the check now takes an RMS over 36 probes.

python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p="electroweak.goal"; s=open(p).read()
helpers = r'''// EWBorisRot3 is the Boris rotation for an adjoint 3-vector velocity: the
// EXACT, norm-preserving update for dv/dt = v x Omega over one unit step.
//
//	t = Omega/2 ;  v' = v + v x t ;  v+ = v + v' x (2t / (1 + |t|^2))
//
// The two half-turns compose into a true rotation, which is the whole point:
// the velocity-dependent gauge force does not change |v|, and an explicit
// update gets that wrong at O(Omega^2) EVERY step, which is what makes the
// rotating-frame system blow up.
func EWBorisRot3(v, om math32.Vector3) math32.Vector3 {
	t := om.MulScalar(0.5)
	vp := v.Add(slmath.Cross3(v, t))
	s := t.MulScalar(2.0 / (1.0 + slmath.LengthSquared3(t)))
	return v.Add(slmath.Cross3(vp, s))
}

// EWBorisPhase rotates the Higgs velocity by exp(i theta G_0), the exact
// solution of the velocity-dependent part of the Higgs equation,
//
//	dv/dt = -2c (-i G_0) v = 2ic G_0 v   ->   v(1) = exp(2ic G_0) v(0)
//
// so theta = 2c. For the 2x2 Hermitian gauge matrix this has a closed form:
// splitting G_0 = alpha I + m.sigma, with
//
//	m = (g/2) (W^1_0, W^2_0, W^3_0)   and   alpha = g' Y_Phi B_0
//
// the exponential is exp(i theta alpha) [cos(theta |m|) I + i sin(theta |m|)
// mhat.sigma]. The SU(2) part turns the doublet and the U(1) part is an
// overall phase -- exactly the parallel transport the connection generates.
func EWBorisPhase(w1, w2, w3, b, theta float32, v math32.Vector4) math32.Vector4 {
	hg := 0.5 * Params[0].GW
	m := math32.Vec3(hg*w1, hg*w2, hg*w3)
	al := Params[0].GpW * YPhi * b
	mag := slmath.Length3(m)
	var nx, ny, nz, sn float32
	if mag > 1.0e-12 {
		nx, ny, nz = m.X/mag, m.Y/mag, m.Z/mag
		sn = slmath.Sin(theta * mag)
	}
	cs := slmath.Cos(theta * mag)
	// P = (mhat.sigma) Psi, in real components
	p1r := nz*v.X + nx*v.Z + ny*v.W
	p1i := nz*v.Y + nx*v.W - ny*v.Z
	p2r := nx*v.X - ny*v.Y - nz*v.Z
	p2i := nx*v.Y + ny*v.X - nz*v.W
	// Q = cos Psi + i sin P
	q1r := cs*v.X - sn*p1i
	q1i := cs*v.Y + sn*p1r
	q2r := cs*v.Z - sn*p2i
	q2i := cs*v.W + sn*p2r
	// overall U(1) phase exp(i theta alpha)
	ca := slmath.Cos(theta * al)
	sa := slmath.Sin(theta * al)
	return math32.Vec4(ca*q1r-sa*q1i, ca*q1i+sa*q1r, ca*q2r-sa*q2i, ca*q2i+sa*q2r)
}

'''
s = s.replace("// ElectroweakKernel is the kernel for the SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y electroweak model:",
              helpers + "// ElectroweakKernel is the kernel for the SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y electroweak model:")
open(p,"w").write(s)

package wavesim

import ("math"; "testing")

func TestDbgBoris2(t *testing.T) {
	t.Logf("%-6s %-8s %8s %12s %10s %14s", "case", "Boris", "B", "drift/step", "x4?", "long-run rad")
	for _, kind := range []string{"YM", "Higgs"} {

				ss.Params.Boris.SetBool(bo); ss.Params.Update()
				p := ss.Params
				var om float64; var r float32

					ss.Fill(EWW30s, Both, b); ss.Fill(EWW1Xs, Both, r); ss.Fill(EWW2Xv, Both, float32(om)*r)
				} else {
					om = float64(p.C) * float64(p.GpW) * float64(b) / 2; r = p.HiggsV
					ss.Fill(EWB0s, Both, b); ss.Fill(EWHv0b, Both, float32(om)*r)

			}

	}

}

import math
# rotating-frame system: a = 2w(v2,-v1) + w^2 x   (Coriolis + centrifugal)
# exact: x = r(cos wt, -sin wt), radius constant.
def run(w, n, mode):
    r=1.0; x=[r,0.0]; v=[0.0,-w*r]       # exact initial condition
    W=2*w                                  # Coriolis rotation rate for the velocity
    out=[]
    for i in range(n):
        fp=[w*w*x[0], w*w*x[1]]            # centrifugal (position) part
        if mode=="explicit":
            a=[2*w*v[1]+fp[0], -2*w*v[0]+fp[1]]
            v=[v[0]+a[0], v[1]+a[1]]
        else:                              # Boris split
            vm=[v[0]+0.5*fp[0], v[1]+0.5*fp[1]]
            t=W/2.0; s=2*t/(1+t*t)
            vpx=vm[0]+vm[1]*t; vpy=vm[1]-vm[0]*t     # v + v x t   (t along e3)
            vp=[vm[0]+vpy*s, vm[1]-vpx*s]
            v=[vp[0]+0.5*fp[0], vp[1]+0.5*fp[1]]
        x=[x[0]+v[0], x[1]+v[1]]
        if (i+1)%(n//6)==0: out.append(math.hypot(*x)/r)
    return out

    for m in ("explicit","boris"):
        print(f"   {m:9s} radius: " + " ".join(f"{q:.5f}" for q in run(w, 6*per, m)))

// TestBorisStability measures what the Boris push buys on the configuration
// that previously destroyed the integrator: a uniform W^3_0 large enough that
// the pure-gauge rotation has a 96-step period.
//
// The velocity-dependent (Coriolis) part of the force is a rotation, and Boris
// applies it exactly instead of integrating it explicitly. That is the
// difference between exponential blow-up and a bounded solution.
//
// It does NOT conserve, and cannot. Writing z = W^1 + i W^2, the pure-gauge
// sector obeys
//
//	d2z/dt2 = -2 i w dz/dt + w^2 z   ->   lambda^2 + 2 i w lambda - w^2 = 0
//
// whose discriminant vanishes: lambda = -i w is a DOUBLE root, so the continuum
// general solution is (A + B t) exp(-i w t). The secular branch is there in the
// exact equations, not put there by the discretization -- it is the gauge
// direction, a gauge transformation whose parameter grows linearly in time.
// No integrator removes it; only fixing the gauge does.
//
// (The Higgs sector looks perfectly conserved under the same test, but that is
// partly the Mexican-hat potential supplying a restoring force toward |Phi| = v
// which the pure gauge sector has nothing equivalent to.)
func TestBorisStability(t *testing.T) {
	const nst = 1200 // ~12 rotation periods
	b, r := float32(0.2), float32(0.05)
	var res [2]float64
	for i, bo := range []bool{false, true} {
		ss := ymSim(4)
		ss.Params.Boris.SetBool(bo)
		ss.Params.Update()
		p := ss.Params
		om := float64(p.C) * float64(p.GW) * float64(b)
		ss.Fill(EWW30s, Both, b)
		ss.Fill(EWW1Xs, Both, r)
		ss.Fill(EWW2Xv, Both, float32(om)*r)
		ewWrap()
		r0 := float64(r) * float64(r)
		worst := 1.0
		for range nst {
			ewStep(ss)
			w1, w2 := float64(ewGet(EWW1Xs)), float64(ewGet(EWW2Xs))
			rr := (w1*w1 + w2*w2) / r0
			if math.IsNaN(rr) {
				worst = math.Inf(1)
				break
			}
			worst = math.Max(worst, rr)
		}
		res[i] = worst
		t.Logf("Boris=%-5v  peak radius^2 / initial over %d steps (~%d periods): %.4g",
			bo, nst, int(float64(nst)*om/(2*math.Pi)), worst)
	}
	if !math.IsInf(res[0], 1) && res[0] < 100 {
		t.Errorf("control did not blow up (peak %.3g); the test is not exercising the instability", res[0])
	}
	if res[1] > 4.0 {
		t.Errorf("Boris peak radius^2 grew to %.3g; expected bounded", res[1])
	}
	t.Logf("improvement: unbounded -> bounded at %.3g", res[1])
}

## What the Boris push does

The velocity-dependent forces here are all **gauge connection acting on velocity** — parallel transport — so the exact update is the gauge holonomy over one step. Two representations, one idea:

- **Higgs**: `EWBorisPhase` applies $\exp(2ic\,\mathcal{G}_0)$ to $\dot\Psi$ in closed form. Splitting $\mathcal{G}_0 = \alpha I + \vec m\!\cdot\!\vec\sigma$ with $\vec m = \tfrac{g}{2}\vec W_0$ and $\alpha = g'Y_\Phi B_0$, it's $e^{i\theta\alpha}[\cos(\theta|m|)I + i\sin(\theta|m|)\,\hat m\!\cdot\!\vec\sigma]$ — the SU(2) part turns the doublet, the U(1) part is an overall phase.
- **W**: `EWBorisRot3` is the classic Boris rotation about $\vec\Omega = -2gc\,\vec W_0$, exactly norm-preserving.

Both sit between two half kicks, so the scheme stays second order. Gated by `Params.Boris`.

```
Boris=false  peak radius^2 / initial over 1200 steps (~12 periods): +Inf
Boris=true   peak radius^2 / initial over 1200 steps (~12 periods): 1
```

Unbounded → bounded, on the exact configuration that previously produced `NaN` inside 400 steps.

## But it does not conserve, and can't

The residual decay isn't an integrator defect. Writing $z = W^1 + iW^2$, the pure-gauge sector obeys

$$\ddot z = -2i\omega\dot z + \omega^2 z \;\Longrightarrow\; \lambda^2 + 2i\omega\lambda - \omega^2 = 0$$

whose discriminant is **identically zero** — $\lambda = -i\omega$ is a double root, so the continuum general solution is $(A + Bt)e^{-i\omega t}$. The secular branch is in the exact equations. It's the gauge direction: a gauge transformation whose parameter grows linearly in time. No integrator removes it; only fixing the gauge does.

A standalone model of the split confirms the Go behaviour exactly — explicit grows 207× over 6 periods, Boris decays to 0.54.

One thing I'd flag against over-reading the numbers: the **Higgs sector measures as perfectly conserved** (radius 0.99992–1.00017), but that's partly the Mexican-hat potential supplying a restoring force toward $|\Phi| = v$ that the pure gauge sector has no equivalent of. Boris deserves some of that credit, not all.

## One trap worth knowing

`gosl` silently failed on a tuple assignment (`nx, ny, nz = ...`) — WGSL has no equivalent. It emitted `error: expected assignment or increment/decrement, found ','` in the middle of a long log and **deleted half the shader files**, while `goal build`, `go build` and `go test` all stayed green, because those only exercise the transpiled Go. Same class as the stale-shader trap from earlier: only `go generate` plus a check of the validation count tells you the GPU path is real. Worth grepping `go generate` output for `error:` rather than trusting its exit code.

Good news: the top-level plumbing already works. `Fatal: true` means `cli.Run` calls `os.Exit(1)` itself, so `main()` discarding the return value is harmless. The gaps are further down.

## Answer: yes, `go generate` checks exit codes

Verified empirically:

```
error: something failed
a.go:3: running "sh": exit status 3
=== exit code: 1 ===
```

It reports the failing directive with its file:line, **skips all remaining directives for that package**, and exits 1. Note the second directive never ran — relevant to you, since `wavesim` has two (`core generate -gosl` in [sim.go:21](../wavesim/sim.go:21) and `gosl` in [vars.go:11](../wavesim/vars.go:11)).

## Two places where gosl drops the error

**1. Validation errors are returned but thrown away.** `CompileFile` does the right thing — it runs naga and tint and returns their error:

```go
// gotosl/translate.go:225
out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
fmt.Printf("...naga output for: %s\n%s", fn, out)
if err != nil {
    log.Println(err)
    return err          // correct
}
```

but the one call site discards it:

```go
// gotosl/translate.go:191
WriteFileLines(fn, lines)
st.CompileFile(kfn)      // <- return value dropped
```

So a shader that naga or tint rejects is still written to disk and the run reports success.

**2. Translation errors never become errors at all.** This is the one that bit me — `error: expected assignment or increment/decrement, found ','` from the tuple assignment comes from:

```go
// gotosl/printer.go:127
func (p *printer) userError(err error) {
    fname := fsx.DirAndFile(p.pos.String())
    fmt.Print(fname + ": ")
    fmt.Println(err.Error())     // prints and returns; no error state recorded
}
```

There's no error return and no flag on the printer, so translation continues, emits a truncated shader, and nothing downstream can tell. That's why it silently deleted half the `.wgsl` files while `goal build`, `go build` and `go test` all stayed green.

## Suggested shape of the fix

`userError` needs somewhere to record that it fired — a `p.errs []error` or a simple counter on the printer, surfaced up through the translation call chain so `Run` can return non-zero. `CompileFile`'s error just needs accumulating at line 191 rather than dropping. Accumulating rather than returning on the first failure is probably what you want, so one bad kernel still reports all the others.

Worth doing both: they're independent failure modes, and the translation one is the more dangerous of the two, because it corrupts output rather than merely failing to validate it.

One note for your own benefit while that's outstanding: `go generate` returning 0 is currently not evidence the GPU path is good. Grepping the output for `error:` and checking the validation count (should be 14 here) is the interim check.

// TestMixedBasisPropagation checks the mass-eigenstate views written into the
// Maxwell and Z state variables, and that each carries the right dispersion.
//
// A transverse wave along z is set up directly in the PHYSICAL basis -- the
// photon direction (sin tw, cos tw) or the Z direction (cos tw, -sin tw) in the
// (W^3, B) plane -- and the frequency is then read back out of A0s..AZs / EWZ*,
// which the kernel recomputes from the gauge basis every step. So the test
// exercises the whole round trip: physical -> gauge -> evolve -> physical.
//
//	photon:  omega = c * khat          (massless: phase velocity exactly c)
//	Z:       omega = c * sqrt(khat^2 + m_Z^2)
//
// The photon staying massless at finite k is the sharp part: it is the
// direction Q = T^3 + Y annihilates, and any error in the mixing angle would
// leak Z mass into it and push the phase velocity below c.
func TestMixedBasisPropagation(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 8
	eps := float32(1e-4)
	prof := make([]float32, sz+2)
	kph := 2 * math.Pi / float64(sz)
	for i := range prof {
		prof[i] = float32(math.Cos(kph * float64(i)))
	}
	khat := math.Sqrt(float64(lattice2(kph)))

	fill := func(v EWStates, amp float32) {
		n := sz + 2
		for z := range n {
			for y := range n {
				for x := range n {
					for tt := range 2 {
						State.Set(amp*prof[z], z, y, x, int(v), tt)
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}

	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name  string
		cw3   func(p *Parameters) float32
		cb    func(p *Parameters) float32
		probe EWStates
		want  func(p *Parameters) float64
	}{
		{"photon (A_x)",
			func(p *Parameters) float32 { return p.SinThetaW },
			func(p *Parameters) float32 { return p.CosThetaW },
			AXs,
			func(p *Parameters) float64 { return float64(p.C) * khat }},
		{"Z (Z_x)",
			func(p *Parameters) float32 { return p.CosThetaW },
			func(p *Parameters) float32 { return -p.SinThetaW },
			EWZX,
			func(p *Parameters) float64 {
				return float64(p.C) * math.Sqrt(khat*khat+float64(p.MZ)*float64(p.MZ))
			}},
	} {
		ss := ewSim(sz)
		p := ss.Params
		fill(EWW3Xs, tc.cw3(p)*eps)
		fill(EWBXs, tc.cb(p)*eps)
		ewWrap()
		want := tc.want(p)
		nst := int(10 * 2 * math.Pi / want)
		y := make([]float64, nst)
		for i := range nst {
			ewStep(ss)
			y[i] = float64(State.Value(1, 1, 1, int(tc.probe), int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
		}
		got := freqZC(y)
		t.Logf("%-14s omega = %.6f  want %.6f  ratio %.5f   (khat = %.4f, c = %.2f)",
			tc.name, got, want, got/want, khat, p.C)
		if math.Abs(got/want-1) > 0.01 {
			t.Errorf("%s: omega %g, want %g", tc.name, got, want)
		}
		if tc.probe == AXs {
			v := got / khat
			t.Logf("               phase velocity = omega/khat = %.6f  vs c = %.6f  (ratio %.6f)",
				v, float64(p.C), v/float64(p.C))
			if math.Abs(v/float64(p.C)-1) > 0.01 {
				t.Errorf("photon phase velocity %g, want c = %g", v, p.C)
			}
		}
	}
}

func lattice2(k float64) float32 {
	return float32(4.0 * math.Sin(k/2) * math.Sin(k/2))
}
GOEOF

19 tests green, 14 shaders validated.

## What's in the physical basis now

The kernel rotates the freshly-updated $(W^3, B)$ pair through the weak mixing angle each step and writes:

$$A_\mu = \sin\theta_W\,W^3_\mu + \cos\theta_W B_\mu \;\to\; \texttt{A0s..AZs} \ \text{(+ velocities)}, \qquad Z_\mu = \cos\theta_W\,W^3_\mu - \sin\theta_W B_\mu \;\to\; \texttt{EWZ0..EWZZ}$$

`SinThetaW`/`CosThetaW` are derived in `Params.Update`. Nothing here is *evolved* — the dynamics stays entirely in $(W^1,W^2,W^3,B)$ and these are views recomputed every step.

**One consequence you should know about:** I removed `RunMaxwellKernel` from the `Electroweak` case in [sim.go](../wavesim/sim.go). It was evolving `A0s..AZs` by the free wave equation, which would have fought the kernel writing the mixed photon into the same variables. Side effect: `EX..BZ` are no longer computed in electroweak mode, so the Maxwell view panels that show E and B will be blank. I can add those back — it's one `Gradient10` + one `Curl10` on the previous step's $A$, exactly what `MaxwellKernel` did — but it wasn't part of the ask so I left it.

## On W⁺ / W⁻

Here I made a judgment call worth flagging. $W^\pm_\mu = (W^1_\mu \mp iW^2_\mu)/\sqrt2$, and $W^- = (W^+)^*$ — they are **not two independent fields**. The charged sector has exactly two real degrees of freedom per spacetime index ($W^1$ and $W^2$); the ± basis repackages them into one complex field. So separate `WP` and `WM` real variables would either be identical (magnitudes) or a relabeling.

What I stored instead:
- `EWWPr0..EWWPrZ` = $\mathrm{Re}(W^+_\mu)$, `EWWPi0..EWWPiZ` = $\mathrm{Im}(W^+_\mu)$ — the two real DOF, i.e. the complex $W^+$ in full
- `EWWMag` = $\sum_\mu |W^+_\mu|^2$, the charged amplitude, identical for both charge states

Say the word if you'd rather have literal `WP`/`WM` variables holding the (equal) magnitudes, for view-panel symmetry.

## The test

```
photon -> A_x    omega = 0.385058  want 0.385058  ratio 1.00000   (m = 0.0000, khat = 0.7654)
                 phase velocity = 0.500001 vs c = 0.500000  (ratio 1.000001)  <= massless
Z -> Z_x         omega = 0.490582  want 0.490606  ratio 0.99995   (m = 0.5982, khat = 0.7654)
W+- -> Re(W+_x)  omega = 0.468972  want 0.468996  ratio 0.99995   (m = 0.5273, khat = 0.7654)
```

Phase velocity is $c$ to six digits. Two things I had to get right for that to be meaningful:

- **The leapfrog has its own dispersion.** The discrete frequency is $2\arcsin(\omega/2)$, not $\omega$ — a 0.6% effect here, larger than the tolerance. My first version compared against the continuum value and the photon looked like it was travelling at $1.006c$.
- **The masses had to be raised** so $m_W, m_Z \sim \hat k$. At the default scale all three frequencies agreed to 0.2% and the test couldn't actually tell a massless photon from a massive one.

## The bug this turned up — same family as before

The Z initially read out as ~0 and matched `AXs` exactly. Cause: `EWStatesN` was **60** while my new `EWWMag` sat at index **72**. I'd added the enum values and run `goal build`, but not `go generate`, so `enumgen.go` was stale, `ConfigState` sized the tensor for 60 variables, and every write above 59 silently aliased onto the Maxwell block. No panic, no error — just wrong numbers.

That's the third instance of the same trap in this session (stale WGSL, gosl swallowing a translate error, now stale enumgen). Once your gosl exit-code fix lands, a `go generate` in the loop will catch all three classes.

I repaired those two lines in place rather than restoring from git, because everything else was intact — so the mixed-basis work (which was **not** committed; HEAD stops at the Boris push) survived rather than needing to be redone.

A note on what I checked first, since it mattered: `electroweak.go` was *also* corrupt despite having a newer mtime — `goal build` transpiles before it compiles, so it had written the broken source out and then failed. The `.go` file's `//line` directives point back at `.goal`, which is why `gofmt -e electroweak.go` reported `electroweak.goal:552`. Worth knowing: the transpiled `.go` is never a safe recovery source, because a failed `goal build` will have already overwritten it.

Fixed — warnings gone, 14 validations, all 19 tests pass.

## Cause

My comments, not your code. Goal has to decide per line whether it's Go or a shell command, so a line with an odd number of `"` or unbalanced `[`/`]` looks like a truncated shell command. I'd split two things across line breaks:

```go
// ..."how much charged W          <- one " on this line
// field is here" that...         <- one " on this line

// ...alpha) [cos(theta |m|) I +   <- [ with no ]
// mhat.sigma]. The SU(2)...       <- ] with no [
```

Three warnings, matching exactly: two `": true` (the quote pair) and one `[ true` (the bracket pair).

## Fix

Dropped the quotes from the first, and moved the bracketed expression onto its own indented line using parentheses:

```go
//	exp(i theta alpha) * (cos(theta |m|) I + i sin(theta |m|) mhat.sigma)
```

Then I scanned **all** `.goal` files for the same pattern rather than just the two that reported — zero remaining.

## Worth knowing for the gosl fix

This is a fourth instance of the same theme: the warning printed on every build and `goal build` still reported success, so it was easy to scroll past. Since you're already adding exit codes to gosl, this one's cheap to fold in — and a lint rule is even cheaper. This catches it before the transpiler ever sees the file:

```bash
awk 'FNR{n=gsub(/"/,"&");b=gsub(/\[/,"&")-gsub(/\]/,"&"); if(n%2||b) print FILENAME":"FNR": "$0}' *.goal
```

The underlying constraint is worth stating in a comment somewhere too, since it's non-obvious: **in a `.goal` file, every line must independently balance its quotes and brackets — including inside comments.** Normal Go style of wrapping a quoted phrase across lines is unsafe here.

//	omega = c sqrt(khat^2 + m^2),  khat = 2 sin(k/2)
//
// khat rather than k because that is the wavenumber the discrete Laplacian
// actually sees; using k instead would mistune the packet by a few percent and
// leave a backward-moving remnant.
func ewFreq(ss *Sim, wavelength, mass float32) float32 {
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	khat := 2 * math32.Sin(k/2)
	return ss.Params.C * math32.Sqrt(khat*khat+mass*mass)
}

// ewSlabPacket adds a ONE-WAY travelling wave packet to a gauge potential and
// its velocity: a cosine carrier under a Gaussian envelope along Z, uniform
// across X and Y. A slab rather than a blob so it does not diffract, which
// keeps the propagation speed unambiguous to the eye.
//
// The velocity is the point. For psi = env(z) cos(k z - om t) the initial time
// derivative is om env sin(k z), and dir flips it for the other direction.
// Setting only the position would split the packet into two halves running
// opposite ways at half amplitude each.
func ewSlabPacket(ss *Sim, pos, vel EWStates, ctrZ, wavelength, width, amp, dir, om float32) {
	pi := int(pos.Int64())
	vi := int(vel.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		dz := float32(c.Z) - ctrZ
		g := dz / width
		env := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
		pv := env * math32.Cos(k*dz)
		vv := dir * om * env * math32.Sin(k*dz)
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, cur] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, prv] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, cur] += vv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, prv] += vv
			}
		}
	}
}

// ewNoise adds uniform random noise to a state variable, the seed that lets an
// unstable equilibrium actually fall over.
func ewNoise(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, amp float32, rnd *rand.Rand) {
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				v := amp * (2*rnd.Float32() - 1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, prv] += v
			}
		}
	}
}

// ewWrapEdges re-wraps the edge ring. Every fill above writes only interior
// cells, so without this the stencils see a step at the boundary.
func ewWrapEdges() {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
}

// ewDemoScale raises the electroweak scale so that m_W and m_Z are comparable
// to the wavenumber of a packet a few tens of cubes long. At the Standard Model
// scale the boson Compton wavelengths are about 22 cubes, so a visible packet
// is far above threshold and a Z would travel at 0.97 c, which no one can see.
// Raising the scale is the only way to make the mass do something on screen.
// The couplings g and g' are untouched, so the mixing angle and the m_W to m_Z
// ratio stay at their physical values.
func ewDemoScale(ss *Sim, mu float32) {
	ss.Params.HiggsMu = mu
	ss.Params.Update()
}

//////// configurations

// HiggsSymmetric starts every Higgs component at zero, plus a whisper of noise,
// and lets the field fall off the top of the Mexican hat into the broken vacuum.
//
// Phi = 0 is an exact equilibrium: the force is (mu^2 - lambda |Phi|^2) Phi,
// which vanishes there. It is also the MAXIMUM of the potential, so it is
// unstable, and without a seed the simulation would sit there forever. The
// noise is what lets it fall.
//
// Watch EWHmag climb from 0 to v^2. It will overshoot and ring rather than
// settle, because nothing here dissipates energy: the potential energy released
// on the way down, lambda v^4 / 4 per site, has nowhere to go. In the early
// universe Hubble expansion drained it; there is no equivalent here. Different
// regions also fall in different directions in the internal space, so domains
// with different phases form and their boundaries stay visible.
func HiggsSymmetric(ss *Sim) {
	rnd := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(42, 1))
	amp := 0.02 * ss.Params.HiggsV
	ewNoise(ss, EWHsCa, amp, rnd)
	ewNoise(ss, EWHsCb, amp, rnd)
	ewNoise(ss, EWHs0a, amp, rnd)
	ewNoise(ss, EWHs0b, amp, rnd)
	ewWrapEdges()
}

// PhotonPulse sends a transverse electromagnetic pulse along Z at exactly the
// speed of light.
//
// The packet is written in the PHYSICAL basis: the photon is the combination
// sin(theta_W) W^3 + cos(theta_W) B, which is the direction that Q = T^3 + Y
// annihilates, so the Higgs condensate gives it no mass and it moves at c.
// Watch AXs, which the kernel reconstructs from the gauge fields every step.
func PhotonPulse(ss *Sim) {
	HiggsBroken(ss)
	p := ss.Params
	wl := float32(16)
	om := ewFreq(ss, wl, 0) // massless
	amp := float32(0.02)
	cz := float32(ss.Config.Size.Z) * 0.25
	ewSlabPacket(ss, EWW3Xs, EWW3Xv, cz, wl, 3*wl, p.SinThetaW*amp, 1, om)
	ewSlabPacket(ss, EWBXs, EWBXv, cz, wl, 3*wl, p.CosThetaW*amp, 1, om)
	ewWrapEdges()
}

// ZPulse sends a Z boson pulse along Z, which travels SLOWER than light.
//
// Same construction as PhotonPulse but in the orthogonal combination,
// cos(theta_W) W^3 - sin(theta_W) B. That direction does not annihilate the
// vacuum, so it picks up mass m_Z from the condensate and the packet moves at
// the group velocity
//
//	v_g = c khat / sqrt(khat^2 + m_Z^2)
//
// which for these settings is about 0.7 c. Run this and PhotonPulse one after
// the other and the lag is obvious. Watch EWZX.
//
// Note this raises the Higgs scale, for the reason given in ewDemoScale.
func ZPulse(ss *Sim) {
	ewDemoScale(ss, 0.194)
	HiggsBroken(ss)
	p := ss.Params
	wl := float32(32)
	om := ewFreq(ss, wl, p.MZ)
	amp := float32(0.02)
	cz := float32(ss.Config.Size.Z) * 0.25
	ewSlabPacket(ss, EWW3Xs, EWW3Xv, cz, wl, 2*wl, p.CosThetaW*amp, 1, om)
	ewSlabPacket(ss, EWBXs, EWBXv, cz, wl, 2*wl, -p.SinThetaW*amp, 1, om)
	ewWrapEdges()
}

// WCollision fires two W packets at each other and shows them interact.
//
// They do not bounce like billiard balls -- gauge fields pass through each

	ewWrapEdges()
}

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

// cfgSim builds a sim big enough for a travelling packet, then runs one of the
// ElectroweakConfigs init functions on it.
func cfgSim(sz int32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = Electroweak
	ss.Config.Size.Set(4, 4, sz) // thin in x,y: the packets are Z slabs
	ss.ConfigVars()
	ss.Params = &Params[0]
	ss.Params.Defaults()
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.StateVars = EWStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	State.SetZeros()
	ss.Params.Update()
	init(ss)
	return ss
}

// cfgCentroid returns the energy-weighted Z centroid of a state variable,
// which tracks the packet even as it disperses.
func cfgCentroid(sz int32, vr int32) float64 {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		v := float64(State.Value(int(z), 2, 2, int(vr), cur))
		w := v * v
		num += w * float64(z)
		den += w
	}
	if den == 0 {
		return 0
	}
	return num / den
}

func cfgSumSq(sz int32, vr int32) float64 {
	var s float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		v := float64(State.Value(int(z), 2, 2, int(vr), cur))
		s += v * v
	}
	return s
}

// TestConfigHiggsSymmetric: the field must fall off the unstable maximum and
// reach the vacuum magnitude.
func TestConfigHiggsSymmetric(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 32
	ss := cfgSim(sz, HiggsSymmetric)
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	start := float64(State.Value(8, 2, 2, int(EWHmag), int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
	var peak, last float64
	for i := range 4000 {
		ewStep(ss)
		m := float64(State.Value(8, 2, 2, int(EWHmag), int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
		peak = math.Max(peak, m)
		last = m
		_ = i
	}
	t.Logf("|Phi|^2 at one site: start %.3e -> peak %.4f, final %.4f   (v^2 = %.4f)",
		start, peak, last, v2)
	if start > 0.01*v2 {
		t.Errorf("did not start near the symmetric point: %g vs v^2 = %g", start, v2)
	}
	if peak < 0.5*v2 {
		t.Errorf("never reached the vacuum: peak %g vs v^2 = %g", peak, v2)
	}
	if math.IsNaN(last) {
		t.Errorf("blew up")
	}
}

// TestConfigPulseSpeeds: the photon packet must travel at c and the Z packet
// measurably slower, at its group velocity.
func TestConfigPulseSpeeds(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 96
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name  string
		init  func(*Sim)
		probe int32
		mass  func(p *Parameters) float64
		wl    float64
	}{
		{"photon", PhotonPulse, int32(AXs), func(p *Parameters) float64 { return 0 }, 16},
		{"Z", ZPulse, int32(EWZX), func(p *Parameters) float64 { return float64(p.MZ) }, 32},
	} {
		ss := cfgSim(sz, tc.init)
		p := ss.Params
		c := float64(p.C)
		m := tc.mass(p)
		k := 2 * math.Pi / tc.wl
		khat := 2 * math.Sin(k/2)
		wantV := c * khat / math.Sqrt(khat*khat+m*m)

		nst := 200
		c0 := cfgCentroid(sz, tc.probe)
		for range nst {
			ewStep(ss)
		}
		c1 := cfgCentroid(sz, tc.probe)
		got := (c1 - c0) / float64(nst)
		t.Logf("%-7s centroid %.2f -> %.2f over %d steps: v = %.5f  want %.5f  (v/c = %.4f)",
			tc.name, c0, c1, nst, got, wantV, got/c)
		if math.Abs(got/wantV-1) > 0.08 {
			t.Errorf("%s speed %g, want %g", tc.name, got, wantV)
		}
		if m == 0 && math.Abs(got/c-1) > 0.02 {
			t.Errorf("photon should move at c: %g vs %g", got, c)
		}
		if m > 0 && got/c > 0.9 {
			t.Errorf("Z should be visibly subluminal, got %g c", got/c)
		}
	}
}

// TestConfigWCollision: W^3 must be generated where the two packets overlap,
// and only when the Yang-Mills self-coupling is on.
func TestConfigWCollision(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	var res [2]float64
	for i, ym := range []bool{false, true} {
		ss := cfgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Params.YangMills.SetBool(ym)
			s.Params.Update()
			WCollision(s)
		})
		if s0 := cfgSumSq(sz, int32(EWW3Xs)); s0 > 1e-20 {
			t.Fatalf("W^3 not initially zero: %g", s0)
		}
		peak := 0.0
		for range 600 {
			ewStep(ss)
			peak = math.Max(peak, cfgSumSq(sz, int32(EWW3Xs)))
		}
		res[i] = peak
		t.Logf("YangMills=%-5v  peak sum(W^3_x^2) generated = %.4e", ym, peak)
	}
	if res[1] < 1e4*res[0] {
		t.Errorf("collision generated %g with Yang-Mills vs %g without; expected the "+
			"non-abelian coupling to dominate", res[1], res[0])
	}
}

// unstable equilibrium actually fall over.
func ewNoise(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, amp float32, rnd *rand.Rand) {
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				v := amp * (2*rnd.Float32() - 1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, prv] += v
			}
		}
	}
}''','''// ewNoise seeds a state variable with smooth random fluctuation: a sum of a few
// long-wavelength modes rather than per-site white noise.
//
// White noise would be the obvious choice and is the wrong one. It carries equal
// power at every wavenumber including the lattice cutoff, which is both
// unphysical -- nothing in the continuum theory excites the grid scale -- and
// the fastest way to destabilise a nonlinear solver. Using whole numbers of
// wavelengths per box also keeps the seed periodic, which matters with wrapped
// edges.
func ewNoise(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, amp float32, nmodes int, rnd *rand.Rand) {
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	ma := amp / math32.Sqrt(float32(nmodes))
	for range nmodes {
		nx := float32(rnd.IntN(3) + 1)
		ny := float32(rnd.IntN(3) + 1)
		nz := float32(rnd.IntN(3) + 1)
		ph := TwoPi * rnd.Float32()
		kx := TwoPi * nx / float32(sz.X)
		ky := TwoPi * ny / float32(sz.Y)
		kz := TwoPi * nz / float32(sz.Z)
		var c math32.Vector3i
		for c.Z = range sz.Z {
			for c.Y = range sz.Y {
				for c.X = range sz.X {
					f := c.AddScalar(1)
					v := ma * math32.Sin(kx*float32(c.X)+ky*float32(c.Y)+kz*float32(c.Z)+ph)
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, prv] += v
				}
			}
		}
	}
}''')

## The configs

**Higgs Symmetric** — every component at zero plus smooth noise, then it falls off the top of the hat.

```
|Phi|^2 at one site: start 0.000e+00 -> peak 0.0306, final 0.0039   (v^2 = 0.0151)
```

Peak is **2v²**, exactly the predicted overshoot to $|\Phi| = \sqrt2\,v$ where $V$ returns to zero. It rings rather than settling — nothing dissipates here, and the $\lambda v^4/4$ released on the way down has nowhere to go. Documented, since "settle" is the natural expectation.

**Photon Pulse / Z Pulse** — same carrier wavelength so they're directly comparable:

```
photon  centroid 21.56 -> 68.18 over 100 steps: v = 0.46625  want 0.49039  (v/c = 0.9325)
Z       centroid 21.62 -> 56.14 over 100 steps: v = 0.34519  want 0.34235  (v/c = 0.6904)
```

The Z is at **0.69c**, matching the lattice group velocity $c\,\hat k\cos(k/2)/\sqrt{\hat k^2+m_Z^2}$ to 0.8%. Worth knowing: even the massless packet measures 0.93c, because the lattice itself puts $v_g = c\cos(k/2) = 0.98c$ and a finite packet loses a few percent more to dispersion.

**W Collision** — two packets crossing.

```
YangMills=false  peak sum(W^3^2) = 1.4240e-13
YangMills=true   peak sum(W^3^2) = 5.8455e+00
```

## Three things I had to correct, which are worth knowing

**Watch $W^3_z$, not $W^3_x$.** My first version probed the transverse component and found nothing. With both packets polarised along x travelling along z, $W^{b\mu}\partial_\mu$ vanishes *identically* — nothing varies along the polarisation — so the transport term is silent. What survives is the transpose term, sourcing the **longitudinal** $W^3_z$ (physical for a massive vector: it's the eaten Goldstone).

**It really is the collision.** W³ rises monotonically rather than peaking, which looked like a runaway. The control settles it: a single packet generates **exactly zero**. The rise is accumulation over repeated wrap-around passes.

**`Higgs Symmetric` needed `A0NoWave`.** It blew up to `NaN` — not the Higgs, which broke correctly, but `W10` and `B0` growing 5000×. That's the secular gauge branch from the degenerate eigenvalue we hit earlier. Your `MaxwellKernel` already had the cure, so I wired `Params.A0NoWave` into the electroweak kernel: for the $\nu=0$ components, drive the potential from the force instead of accumulating a velocity. On by default; bounded ever since.

Also switched the seed from white noise to a sum of six long-wavelength modes — white noise puts power at the lattice cutoff, which is both unphysical and the quickest way to destabilise a nonlinear solver, and non-periodic seeds fight wrapped edges.

One caveat on the two massive configs: they call `ewDemoScale` to raise `HiggsMu` to 0.388. At the Standard Model scale the boson Compton wavelengths are ~22 cubes, so a visible packet is far above threshold and the Z would travel at 0.97c — nothing you could see. `g` and `g'` are untouched, so the mixing angle and $m_W/m_Z$ stay physical. It's noted in the Doc strings that surface in the GUI.

I understand that the Higgs field is represented as a doublet complex scalar field, which has two complex numbers at each point, which results in 4 independent degrees of freedom, each updating according to the same Klein-Gordon 2nd order wave equation, with no coupling among them, except when computing the conserved magnitude of the field (multiplying by the complex conjugate), which is what enters in the the Higgs potential. One complex number is associated with charge, labeled with a + sign, and the other neutral, labeled with a 0. It seems that the standard approach is to arbitrarily assign one component, the neutral one, the full weight of this expected magnitude.  My questions are: * doesn't it matter which component gets this expectation value? * some presentations add a $1/\sqrt{2}$ multiplier outside of the Higgs field, while others do not -- is there really no standard, or at least predominantly used form? * likewise, some presentations add factors to the Higgs potential expression, changing the apparent meaning of the constants ($\lambda$ and $\mu$). I would like to do it the most "standard" way.

## 🤖 Assistant - 2026-09-19 11:54:38

*Model: claude-opus-5*

Good questions — all three are real convention traps, and there is a dominant convention for each.

## 1. Does it matter which component gets the VEV?

Three different answers depending on what you've built so far:

**In the model you describe right now (no gauge fields), it genuinely doesn't matter.** Your potential depends only on $\Phi^\dagger\Phi = \sum_{i=1}^{4}\phi_i^2/2$, so the Lagrangian has a full global $O(4)$ symmetry and the vacuum manifold is a 3-sphere of radius $v$ in real-field space. Every point on it is physically identical. If you start from random initial conditions the field will relax to some arbitrary direction, and that's correct behavior, not a bug.

**Once you gauge $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y$, it's a gauge choice.** $SU(2)\times U(1)$ acts transitively on the sphere $\Phi^\dagger\Phi = \text{const}$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$, so any nonzero $\Phi$ can be rotated to $\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}(0, v)^T$. Writing $\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(0,\,v+h)^T$ is *unitary gauge* — you've used the three broken generators to gauge away the three Goldstone components. It's a choice, not an assumption.

**What is *not* arbitrary is that the VEV must sit in the electrically neutral direction** — but only because you've already fixed what "electric charge" means elsewhere. With $Q = T^3 + Y$ and $Y_\Phi = +1/2$, the components have $Q = +1, 0$. Requiring the photon to stay massless means $Q\langle\Phi\rangle = 0$, which picks the lower component. If you instead put the VEV in $\phi^+$, you'd still get an unbroken $U(1)$ (generated by $Y - T^3$) — you'd just have relabeled which generator is the photon. That relabeling is only free until you write down the fermion sector; once the electron has $Q=-1$, the Higgs VEV direction is pinned.

For a numerical implementation the practical consequence is: **don't hard-code the VEV into one component.** Evolve all four real fields and let the dynamics pick the direction. Hard-coding $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(0,v+h)^T$ throws away the three Goldstone modes, which is fine in unitary gauge with gauge fields present, but wrong if you have no gauge fields — there the Goldstones are physical massless particles.

One flag: with only a scalar doublet and no gauge fields, you have spontaneous breaking of a global symmetry, not the Higgs mechanism. The mechanism proper (Goldstones → longitudinal $W/Z$ polarizations) requires the gauge fields.

## 2. The $1/\sqrt2$

Not arbitrary, and there is a clear majority convention. The factor is just the standard conversion between a complex field and two **canonically normalized** real fields: if $\phi = (\phi_1 + i\phi_2)/\sqrt2$ then $|\partial\phi|^2 = \tfrac12(\partial\phi_1)^2 + \tfrac12(\partial\phi_2)^2$, each with the textbook $\tfrac12$ for a real scalar. Drop the $\sqrt2$ and your real components are non-canonically normalized.

The dominant convention (PDG, Peskin & Schwartz, Weinberg, Langacker, essentially all collider phenomenology):

$$\langle\Phi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ v\end{pmatrix},\qquad v = (\sqrt2\,G_F)^{-1/2} = 246.22~\text{GeV}$$

The minority convention absorbs the $\sqrt2$ so that $\langle\phi^0\rangle = v$ with $v \approx 174$ GeV. You'll see it in parts of the SUSY/model-building literature. **Use 246.** The quick discriminator when reading any paper: $m_W = gv/2$ means $v=246$; $m_W = gv/\sqrt2$ means $v=174$.

## 3. The potential

Dominant form (PDG, Peskin, Schwartz):

$$V(\Phi) = \mu^2\,\Phi^\dagger\Phi + \lambda\,(\Phi^\dagger\Phi)^2, \qquad \mu^2 < 0,\ \lambda > 0$$

Many texts write $-\mu^2\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ with $\mu^2>0$ instead; identical theory, just where the sign lives. The variants that actually change the meaning of the constants are $\frac{\lambda}{4}(\Phi^\dagger\Phi)^2$ and the shifted form $\lambda\big(\Phi^\dagger\Phi - \tfrac{v^2}{2}\big)^2$ — those shift $\lambda$ by factors of 2 or 4. Avoid them unless you're following a specific paper.

Self-consistent set for the convention above:

| Quantity | Relation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| VEV | $v^2 = -\mu^2/\lambda$ | $v = 246.22$ GeV |
| Higgs mass | $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2 = -2\mu^2$ | $m_h \approx 125.25$ GeV |
| Quartic | $\lambda = m_h^2/(2v^2)$ | $\lambda \approx 0.129$ |
| Mass parameter | $\mu^2 = -m_h^2/2$ | $\sqrt{-\mu^2} \approx 88.6$ GeV |

The single most useful sanity check on your whole convention stack is $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2$. If your simulated radial-mode oscillation frequency doesn't come out to $\sqrt{2\lambda}\,v$, something in the $\sqrt2$'s is off.

## What to actually code

With $\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\phi_1 + i\phi_2,\ \phi_3 + i\phi_4)^T$, so that $\Phi^\dagger\Phi = \frac12\sum_i \phi_i^2$:

$$\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\sum_i (\partial_\mu\phi_i)^2 - \tfrac12\mu^2\sum_i\phi_i^2 - \tfrac{\lambda}{4}\Big(\sum_i\phi_i^2\Big)^2$$

giving four identical nonlinear Klein–Gordon equations coupled only through $r^2 \equiv \sum_j \phi_j^2$:

$$\partial_t^2\phi_i = \nabla^2\phi_i - \big(\mu^2 + \lambda\, r^2\big)\,\phi_i$$

This confirms your reading — the only coupling is the shared $r^2$ in the effective mass. Two things fall out that are worth using as tests:

- The vacuum manifold is $r = v$ exactly (in real-field units), even though $|\Phi| = v/\sqrt2$. Convenient: your four real fields relax to a 3-sphere of radius 246.
- Near the vacuum, the radial mode has $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2$ and the three tangential modes are exactly massless.

Note $\mu^2 + \lambda r^2 < 0$ near the origin — that's the tachyonic instability driving the roll-off, and it's why a small random perturbation around $\phi_i = 0$ grows rather than oscillates.

On the hypercharge convention, for when you gauge it: $Q = T^3 + Y$ with $Y_\Phi = 1/2$ (Peskin, PDG) and $Q = T^3 + Y/2$ with $Y_\Phi = 1$ (Halzen & Martin) are both common. Nothing physical depends on it, but it changes the coefficient in $D_\mu$, so pick one and stay put.

For units, I'd set $v = 1$ and work with $\lambda = 0.129$, $\mu^2 = -0.129$ — then $m_h = \sqrt{2\lambda} \approx 0.508$ in units of $v$, and you multiply by 246 GeV at the end.

Happy to write the lattice solver (leapfrog/Verlet on the four real fields, with the $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2$ check as a test) if useful, or to add the $SU(2)\times U(1)$ gauge fields so you get the actual mechanism rather than just global symmetry breaking.

## 1. Does it matter which component gets the VEV?

Three different answers depending on what you've built so far.

**In the model you describe right now (no gauge fields), it genuinely doesn't matter.** Your potential depends only on the invariant

$$\Phi^\dagger\Phi = \frac12\sum_{i=1}^{4}\phi_i^2$$

so the Lagrangian has a full global $O(4)$ symmetry and the vacuum manifold is a 3-sphere of radius $v$ in real-field space. Every point on it is physically identical. If you start from random initial conditions the field will relax to some arbitrary direction, and that is correct behavior, not a bug.

**Once you gauge the symmetry, it's a gauge choice.** $SU(2)\times U(1)$ acts transitively on the sphere of constant $\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$, so any nonzero configuration can be rotated into

$$\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ v+h \end{pmatrix}$$

This is *unitary gauge* — you have used the three broken generators to gauge away the three Goldstone components. It's a choice, not an assumption.

**What is not arbitrary is that the VEV must sit in the electrically neutral direction** — but only because you have already fixed what "electric charge" means elsewhere. With $Q = T^3 + Y$ and $Y_\Phi = +1/2$, the components carry $Q = +1$ and $Q = 0$. Keeping the photon massless requires

$$Q\,\langle\Phi\rangle = 0$$

which picks the lower component. If you instead put the VEV in $\phi^+$, you would still get an unbroken $U(1)$, generated by $Y - T^3$ — you would just have relabeled which generator is the photon. That relabeling is free only until you write down the fermion sector; once the electron has $Q = -1$, the VEV direction is pinned.

For a numerical implementation the practical consequence is: **don't hard-code the VEV into one component.** Evolve all four real fields and let the dynamics pick the direction. Hard-coding the unitary-gauge form throws away the three Goldstone modes, which is fine in unitary gauge with gauge fields present, but wrong if you have no gauge fields — there the Goldstones are physical massless particles.

One flag: with only a scalar doublet and no gauge fields you have spontaneous breaking of a *global* symmetry, not the Higgs mechanism. The mechanism proper — Goldstones becoming the longitudinal polarizations of the W and Z — requires the gauge fields.

## 2. The 1/√2 factor

Not arbitrary, and there is a clear majority convention. The factor is the standard conversion between a complex field and two **canonically normalized** real fields: if $\phi = (\phi_1 + i\phi_2)/\sqrt2$ then

$$|\partial_\mu\phi|^2 = \tfrac12(\partial_\mu\phi_1)^2 + \tfrac12(\partial_\mu\phi_2)^2$$

each with the textbook factor of one half for a real scalar. Drop the $\sqrt2$ and your real components are not canonically normalized.

The dominant convention — PDG, Peskin, Schwartz, Weinberg, Langacker, essentially all collider phenomenology — is

$$\langle\Phi\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ v \end{pmatrix}, \qquad v = (\sqrt2\,G_F)^{-1/2} = 246.22~\text{GeV}$$

The minority convention absorbs the $\sqrt2$ so that $\langle\phi^0\rangle = v$ with $v \approx 174$ GeV; you'll see it in parts of the SUSY and model-building literature. **Use 246.** The quick discriminator when reading any paper is the W mass:

$$m_W = \frac{gv}{2} \ \Rightarrow\ v = 246~\text{GeV}, \qquad m_W = \frac{gv}{\sqrt2} \ \Rightarrow\ v = 174~\text{GeV}$$

## 3. The potential

Dominant form (PDG, Peskin, Schwartz):

$$V(\Phi) = \mu^2\,\Phi^\dagger\Phi + \lambda\,(\Phi^\dagger\Phi)^2, \qquad \mu^2 < 0, \quad \lambda > 0$$

Many texts write $-\mu^2\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ with $\mu^2 > 0$ instead — identical theory, just where the sign lives. The variants that actually change the meaning of the constants are

$$\frac{\lambda}{4}\left(\Phi^\dagger\Phi\right)^2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda\left(\Phi^\dagger\Phi - \frac{v^2}{2}\right)^2$$

which shift $\lambda$ by factors of 2 or 4. Avoid them unless you're following a specific paper.

Self-consistent set for the dominant convention:

| Quantity | Relation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| VEV | $v^2 = -\mu^2/\lambda$ | $v = 246.22$ GeV |
| Higgs mass | $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2 = -2\mu^2$ | $m_h \approx 125.25$ GeV |
| Quartic | $\lambda = m_h^2/(2v^2)$ | $\lambda \approx 0.129$ |
| Mass parameter | $\mu^2 = -m_h^2/2$ | $\sqrt{-\mu^2} \approx 88.6$ GeV |

The single most useful sanity check on your whole convention stack is $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2$. If your simulated radial-mode oscillation frequency doesn't come out to $\sqrt{2\lambda}\,v$, something in the $\sqrt2$ factors is off.

## What to actually code

Write the doublet in terms of four real fields:

$$\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} \phi_1 + i\phi_2 \\ \phi_3 + i\phi_4 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Phi^\dagger\Phi = \frac12\sum_{i} \phi_i^2$$

The Lagrangian becomes manifestly $O(4)$-symmetric with all four fields canonically normalized:

$$\mathcal{L} = \frac12\sum_i (\partial_\mu\phi_i)^2 \;-\; \frac12\mu^2\sum_i\phi_i^2 \;-\; \frac{\lambda}{4}\left(\sum_i\phi_i^2\right)^2$$

$$\Box\Phi + \left(\mu^2 + 2\lambda\,\Phi^\dagger\Phi\right)\Phi = 0$$

This confirms your reading — the only coupling between components is the shared magnitude sitting in the effective mass. Two things fall out that are worth using as tests:

- The vacuum manifold is $r = v$ exactly in real-field units, even though the doublet norm is $v/\sqrt2$. Convenient: your four real fields relax to a 3-sphere of radius 246.
- Near the vacuum, the radial mode has $m_h^2 = 2\lambda v^2$ and the three tangential modes are exactly massless.

Note that $\mu^2 + \lambda r^2 < 0$ near the origin. That's the tachyonic instability driving the roll-off, and it's why a small random perturbation around $\phi_i = 0$ grows rather than oscillates.

On hypercharge, for when you gauge it: $Q = T^3 + Y$ with $Y_\Phi = 1/2$ (Peskin, PDG) and $Q = T^3 + Y/2$ with $Y_\Phi = 1$ (Halzen & Martin) are both common. Nothing physical depends on the choice, but it changes the coefficient in $D_\mu$, so pick one and stay put.

## The short answer: you're comparing a free energy to a Lagrangian

In Landau theory of a ferromagnet you write

$$F(M, T) = a\left(T - T_c\right)M^2 + b\,M^4$$

and the temperature is right there. But notice: the *microscopic* Hamiltonian of a ferromagnet — Heisenberg, Ising, whatever — has no temperature in it either. Just spins and exchange couplings. Temperature is not a parameter of the Hamiltonian; it's a property of the statistical *state* you put the system in.

The Landau functional is a **free energy**, $F = E - TS$. It's what you get *after* coarse-graining and integrating out thermal fluctuations. The $T$ appears through that procedure.

So the honest correspondence is:

| Ferromagnet | Higgs |
|---|---|
| Microscopic Hamiltonian (no $T$) | Tree-level $V(\Phi)$ (no $T$) |
| Landau free energy $F(M,T)$ | Finite-$T$ effective potential $V_{\text{eff}}(\Phi, T)$ |

Textbook presentations show you the Landau free energy on the magnet side and the bare Lagrangian on the Higgs side, then draw the same picture twice. That's why it looks like a parameter went missing. It didn't — you were shown two objects at different levels of description.

## Where the temperature actually enters

The SM Lagrangian is a **zero-temperature vacuum** field theory. To get temperature you compute the partition function $Z = \text{Tr}\,e^{-\beta H}$, which in the path integral means putting Euclidean time on a circle of circumference $\beta = 1/T$. The thermal bath of W, Z, top quarks and Higgs quanta then contributes to the Higgs field's effective mass:

$$\mu^2_{\text{eff}}(T) = \mu^2 + c\,T^2, \qquad c \simeq \frac{3g^2 + g'^2}{16} + \frac{y_t^2}{4} + \frac{\lambda}{2}$$

*Now* you have your Landau-style control parameter. At low $T$ the $\mu^2$ wins, the coefficient is negative, Mexican hat. At high $T$ the $cT^2$ term wins, the coefficient turns positive, and the potential becomes a simple bowl with its minimum at the origin — **symmetry restored**. The changeover is at

$$T_c^2 \simeq \frac{-\mu^2}{c} = \frac{\lambda v^2}{c}$$

Numerically $c \approx 0.4$ (the top Yukawa dominates), giving $T_c \sim 140$ GeV from this crude estimate. The full lattice answer for the SM is $T_c = 159.5 \pm 1.5$ GeV.

The more complete high-temperature expansion is

$$V_{\text{eff}}(\varphi, T) = D\left(T^2 - T_0^2\right)\varphi^2 - E\,T\,\varphi^3 + \frac{\lambda_T}{4}\,\varphi^4$$

The cubic term, which comes from bosonic Matsubara zero modes, is what could make the transition first-order with a barrier and bubble nucleation.

## Two things worth knowing about the real SM

**It's a crossover, not a phase transition.** For $m_h = 125$ GeV, that cubic term is far too weak. Lattice work (Kajantie, Laine, Rummukainen, Shaposhnikov) showed the first-order line ends at $m_h \approx 72$ GeV — well below the real Higgs mass. Above that endpoint the electroweak "transition" is a smooth analytic crossover: nothing is discontinuous, there are no bubbles, and strictly speaking there's no sharp symmetry-breaking point at all. This is one of the reasons the SM cannot produce electroweak baryogenesis, and a standard motivation for extending the scalar sector.

**Zero temperature is an outstanding approximation today.** The universe is at $T \approx 2.7$ K, roughly $10^{15}$ times below the electroweak scale. The symmetric phase existed for about the first 10 picoseconds. So yes — the Mexican hat really is always there, for all practical purposes, and 246 GeV really is where the field always sits. You are not missing a knob that matters for anything you can measure in a lab.

## There is an energy-scale parameter — it's just not temperature

You asked about "temperature *or* energy scale," and those are genuinely different things. The vacuum theory does have a scale dependence: $\lambda$ and $\mu^2$ run with renormalization scale. Running $\lambda$ up, it decreases, passing near zero around $10^{10}$–$10^{11}$ GeV — the electroweak vacuum metastability question. That's a real scale-dependence of the shape of the hat, and it has nothing to do with temperature.

## For your simulation

Here's the part I think will actually please you: **the temperature dependence is already in the equation you have.**

Look at your effective mass term, $\mu^2 + \lambda r^2$. Split the field into a mean value plus fluctuations, $\phi_i = \bar\phi_i + \delta\phi_i$. Then

$$\left\langle r^2 \right\rangle = \bar\phi^2 + \left\langle \delta\phi^2 \right\rangle$$

and for a hot field the fluctuation piece grows with temperature. The effective mass becomes

$$m^2_{\text{eff}} = \mu^2 + \lambda\bar\phi^2 + \lambda\left\langle \delta\phi^2\right\rangle$$

That last term is precisely the $cT^2$ thermal mass, arising self-consistently from the quartic coupling you already coded. This is the Hartree approximation, and it means your existing four-field solver will show symmetry restoration with no new physics added — you just have to initialize it hot. Three practical routes:

1. **Cold start near the origin.** Tiny random noise around $\phi_i = 0$, and let the tachyonic instability drive the roll-off. This shows the breaking dynamically and is the easiest to get right. Physically it's spinodal decomposition / tachyonic preheating, not a thermal transition, but it's the clearest demonstration.
2. **Thermal mass by hand.** Replace $\mu^2$ with $\mu^2 + cT^2$ and ramp $T$ downward. This literally reproduces the textbook figure sequence: bowl, flattening, hat. Cheapest way to see the Landau picture.
3. **Genuinely hot initial conditions.** Populate the lattice modes with a thermal spectrum and let the nonlinearity do the rest. The self-generated thermal mass restores the symmetry above $T_c$, and cooling through it gives you the Kibble mechanism with domains and defect formation.

One honest caveat on route 3: classical lattice field theory gets the qualitative behavior right but its thermal mass is linearly cutoff-sensitive (the classical Rayleigh-Jeans spectrum, $\langle\delta\phi^2\rangle \propto T\Lambda$, rather than the quantum $T^2/12$). So $T_c$ will depend on your lattice spacing, and matching to the real quantum theory requires dimensional reduction. Fine for seeing the mechanism, not for extracting a number.

Also note that a pure scalar $O(4)$ model has a much higher $T_c$ than the SM, of order $\sqrt{3}\,v$, because in the real theory the thermal mass is dominated by the gauge boson and top quark loops you haven't included.

The resolution is one line: **the wave equation isn't the potential, it's the** ***derivative*** **of the potential.** Differentiating drops every power by one. That accounts for both shifts you noticed, and nothing else is going on.

## The mechanics

Euler–Lagrange for each real field gives

$$\Box\,\phi_i + \frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi_i} = 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \partial_t^2\phi_i = \nabla^2\phi_i - \frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi_i}$$

So what enters the wave equation is the *gradient of V in field space*, not V. Writing $r^2 = \sum_j \phi_j^2$ and

$$V = \frac{\mu^2}{2}\,r^2 + \frac{\lambda}{4}\,r^4$$

the only thing you need is the chain rule:

$$\frac{\partial\, r^2}{\partial \phi_i} = 2\phi_i$$

Applying it term by term:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_i}\left(\frac{\mu^2}{2}r^2\right) = \frac{\mu^2}{2}\cdot 2\phi_i = \mu^2\phi_i$$

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_i}\left(\frac{\lambda}{4}r^4\right) = \frac{\lambda}{4}\cdot 2r^2\cdot 2\phi_i = \lambda\, r^2\phi_i$$

Adding them gives $(\mu^2 + \lambda r^2)\phi_i$. Tabulating your two observations:

| Term | In $V$ | In the EOM | Power change |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mu^2$ term | $r^2$ (quadratic) | $\mu^2\phi_i$ (linear) | 2 → 1 |
| $\lambda$ term | $r^4$ (quartic) | $\lambda r^2 \phi_i$ (cubic) | 4 → 3 |

Both drop by exactly one power, which is what differentiation does. As a side benefit, this is *why* the conventional $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac14$ are there: they're chosen precisely so the factors of 2 from the chain rule cancel and the EOM comes out clean.

## Why the single component appears alongside the magnitude

This is the part worth internalizing, and it answers your "presumably just the one component" instinct — which is right, but there's a reason the magnitude tags along.

Since $V$ depends only on $r$, write it as $V(r)$. Then

$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi_i} = V'(r)\,\frac{\partial r}{\partial \phi_i} = V'(r)\,\frac{\phi_i}{r}$$

The derivative of a function of the magnitude splits into two pieces: a scalar factor depending only on $r$, and a factor of $\phi_i$ — the specific component you differentiated with respect to. The $\phi_i/r$ is just the unit vector in field space. So the force is **purely radial**: it points along $\hat\phi$ with strength $V'(r)$, and each component gets the same radial pull weighted by its own share of the direction.

Checking against the explicit result, with $V'(r) = \mu^2 r + \lambda r^3 = r(\mu^2 + \lambda r^2)$:

$$V'(r)\frac{\phi_i}{r} = \left(\mu^2 + \lambda r^2\right)\phi_i \quad\checkmark$$

**This is exactly a particle in a central potential in four dimensions.** Newton's law in Cartesian coordinates for a central force reads $\ddot{x}_i = -V'(r)\,x_i/r$ — four identical-looking equations, coupled only through $r$. Your field equations are that, plus the spatial gradient term. If it helps to have a mental picture: a ball rolling on the Mexican hat, where the hat is a surface of revolution, so the slope depends only on how far out you are, while the *direction* of the push depends on where you are around it.

## The complex form, and a factor of 2 to watch

Treating $\Phi$ and $\Phi^\dagger$ as independent:

$$\Box\,\Phi + \frac{\partial V}{\partial \Phi^\dagger} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial V}{\partial \Phi^\dagger} = \mu^2\Phi + 2\lambda\left(\Phi^\dagger\Phi\right)\Phi$$

$$\Box\,\Phi + \left(\mu^2 + 2\lambda\,\Phi^\dagger\Phi\right)\Phi = 0$$

Note the complex form carries $2\lambda\Phi^\dagger\Phi$ while the real form carries $\lambda r^2$. Those agree, because $\Phi^\dagger\Phi = r^2/2$. Worth pinning down given the factor-of-2 bookkeeping you were already wary of — if you ever see the two forms side by side and the 2 looks like a discrepancy, that's the reconciliation.

## One trap this opens up

Two different second-derivative-ish quantities are floating around, and they are not the same:

$$\frac{V'(r)}{r} = \mu^2 + \lambda r^2 \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad V''(r) = \mu^2 + 3\lambda r^2$$

The first is the coefficient in your EOM. The second is the actual curvature. At the vacuum $r = v$, with $\mu^2 = -\lambda v^2$:

$$\frac{V'(v)}{v} = 0, \qquad V''(v) = 2\lambda v^2 = m_h^2$$

So the EOM coefficient **vanishes** at the minimum — no net force, as it must be — while the physical Higgs mass is $2\lambda v^2$. Don't read the EOM coefficient as the mass.

And for free, this gives you Goldstone's theorem geometrically. For a central potential, the curvature in the radial direction is $V''(r)$ and the curvature in each transverse direction is $V'(r)/r$. At the minimum those are $2\lambda v^2$ and $0$ respectively: one massive radial mode, three massless tangential modes. The masslessness of the Goldstones is nothing more than the statement that the EOM coefficient vanishes on the vacuum manifold — the same quantity you were asking about.

Throughout I'll use signature $(+,-,-,-)$ and $\hbar = c = 1$.

## Warm-up: this is just Newton's law

Point particle, one coordinate:

$$L(q, \dot q) = \tfrac12 m\dot q^2 - V(q)$$

Euler–Lagrange, $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$, gives

$$m\ddot q = -V'(q)$$

Nobody finds it surprising that force is *minus the derivative* of the potential. Classical field theory is this, with $q$ promoted to $\phi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ and one extra term for spatial stiffness. The field is the analogue of the **coordinate**, not of the wavefunction. That single identification is the whole conceptual shift.

## The field derivation

$$\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12 (\partial_\mu\phi)(\partial^\mu\phi) - V(\phi) = \tfrac12\dot\phi^2 - \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 - V(\phi)$$

reading as kinetic energy density, gradient (elastic) energy density, potential energy density — so $\mathcal{L} = T - U$ as usual. Now vary the action $S = \int d^4x\,\mathcal{L}$ under $\phi \to \phi + \delta\phi$, with $\delta\phi$ vanishing on the boundary.

**Here is the step you're asking about.** Expanding the potential to first order in the variation:

$$V(\phi + \delta\phi) = V(\phi) + V'(\phi)\,\delta\phi + O(\delta\phi^2)$$

That's it — that's where the derivative comes from, and there's no way around it. The action cares about how $V$ *responds* to a change in the field, and the first-order response of any function is its derivative. So

$$\delta S = \int d^4x \left[(\partial_\mu\phi)(\partial^\mu \delta\phi) - V'(\phi)\,\delta\phi\right]$$

Integrate the first term by parts, $(\partial_\mu\phi)(\partial^\mu\delta\phi) = \partial^\mu\!\left(\delta\phi\,\partial_\mu\phi\right) - (\partial_\mu\partial^\mu\phi)\,\delta\phi$, and drop the total derivative:

$$\delta S = -\int d^4x \left[\Box\phi + V'(\phi)\right]\delta\phi$$

Requiring this to vanish for *arbitrary* $\delta\phi$ forces the bracket to vanish pointwise:

$$\boxed{\;\Box\phi + V'(\phi) = 0\;} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \partial_t^2\phi = \nabla^2\phi - V'(\phi)$$

That's the KG equation for an arbitrary potential. Free KG is the case $V = \tfrac12 m^2\phi^2$, giving $V' = m^2\phi$ and $\Box\phi + m^2\phi = 0$.

## Why it looked like a multiplicative factor

Look at that last line. For a **quadratic** potential, the derivative of the potential *is* a constant times the field:

$$V(\phi) = \tfrac12 m^2\phi^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V'(\phi) = m^2\phi$$

So in the one case everybody meets first, "derivative of the potential" and "potential coefficient times the field" are numerically identical. The distinction is invisible until the potential stops being quadratic — which is exactly when you add $\lambda(\Phi^\dagger\Phi)^2$.

And this is true of the Schrödinger equation too, which I suspect is the real source of the intuition:

$$i\partial_t\psi = -\frac{1}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi$$

That *looks* like a bare multiplicative $V$. But its Lagrangian density contains $V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi^*\psi$, and varying with respect to $\psi^*$ gives

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \psi^*}\Big[V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi^*\psi\Big] = V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi$$

still a derivative. It just doesn't look like one because the term is quadratic in the field. There are two separate things making Schrödinger feel different:

- $V(\mathbf{x})$ depends on **position**, an external landscape the field lives in.
- $V(\phi)$ depends on the **field value itself** — a self-interaction, no external landscape at all.

In the Higgs case there is nothing external. The "hat" is a function of the field's own magnitude at each point, and each point of space carries its own copy.

## The Hamiltonian route, since that's where you're coming from

Conjugate momentum $\pi = \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\dot\phi = \dot\phi$, and

$$H = \int d^3x\left[\tfrac12\pi^2 + \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 + V(\phi)\right]$$

Hamilton's equations in functional form:

$$\dot\phi = \frac{\delta H}{\delta \pi} = \pi, \qquad \dot\pi = -\frac{\delta H}{\delta \phi} = \nabla^2\phi - V'(\phi)$$

Combining gives the same result. This framing may be the most intuitive for you: $-\delta H/\delta\phi$ is manifestly "force equals minus the gradient of the energy," with the gradient taken in field space.

Worth noting how this differs from the route you already know. Starting from $E^2 = p^2 + m^2$ and substituting $E \to i\partial_t$, $p \to -i\nabla$ gets you free KG and nothing else — there's no slot in that procedure for a self-interaction, because it treats $\phi$ as a one-particle wavefunction. The Lagrangian route treats $\phi$ as a classical field, which is what lets you write any $V$ you like, and hands you Noether's theorem and the conserved currents for free. It also matters for your simulation: you're evolving a classical field configuration, not a probability amplitude.

## Back to the doublet

For several fields the derivation is unchanged, one equation per component:

$$\Box\,\phi_i + \frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi_i} = 0$$

and when $V$ depends only on $r^2 = \sum_j \phi_j^2$, the chain rule produces the central-force structure from before, $\partial V/\partial\phi_i = V'(r)\,\phi_i/r$. The components are independent except through that shared magnitude.

Throughout I'll use signature $(+,-,-,-)$ and $\hbar = c = 1$.

## Warm-up: this is just Newton's law

Point particle, one coordinate:

$$L(q, \dot q) = \tfrac12 m\dot q^2 - V(q)$$

The Euler–Lagrange equation

$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$$

then gives

$$m\ddot q = -V'(q)$$

Nobody finds it surprising that force is *minus the derivative* of the potential. Classical field theory is this, with $q$ promoted to $\phi(\mathbf{x}, t)$ and one extra term for spatial stiffness. The field is the analogue of the **coordinate**, not of the wavefunction. That single identification is the whole conceptual shift.

## The field derivation

$$\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12 (\partial_\mu\phi)(\partial^\mu\phi) - V(\phi) = \tfrac12\dot\phi^2 - \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 - V(\phi)$$

reading as kinetic energy density, gradient (elastic) energy density, potential energy density — so $\mathcal{L} = T - U$ as usual. Now vary the action $S = \int d^4x\,\mathcal{L}$ under $\phi \to \phi + \delta\phi$, with $\delta\phi$ vanishing on the boundary.

**Here is the step you're asking about.** Expanding the potential to first order in the variation:

$$V(\phi + \delta\phi) = V(\phi) + V'(\phi)\,\delta\phi + O(\delta\phi^2)$$

That's it — that's where the derivative comes from, and there's no way around it. The action cares about how $V$ *responds* to a change in the field, and the first-order response of any function is its derivative. So

$$\delta S = \int d^4x \left[(\partial_\mu\phi)(\partial^\mu \delta\phi) - V'(\phi)\,\delta\phi\right]$$

Now integrate the first term by parts:

$$(\partial_\mu\phi)(\partial^\mu \delta\phi) = \partial^\mu\!\left(\delta\phi\,\partial_\mu\phi\right) - \left(\Box\phi\right)\delta\phi$$

The total derivative drops out on the boundary, leaving

$$\delta S = -\int d^4x \left[\Box\phi + V'(\phi)\right]\delta\phi$$

Requiring this to vanish for *arbitrary* $\delta\phi$ forces the bracket to vanish pointwise:

$$\boxed{\;\Box\phi + V'(\phi) = 0\;}$$

$$\partial_t^2\phi = \nabla^2\phi - V'(\phi)$$

That's the KG equation for an arbitrary potential. Free KG is the case $V = \tfrac12 m^2\phi^2$, giving $V' = m^2\phi$ and $\Box\phi + m^2\phi = 0$.

## Why it looked like a multiplicative factor

Look at that last line. For a **quadratic** potential, the derivative of the potential *is* a constant times the field:

$$V(\phi) = \tfrac12 m^2\phi^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V'(\phi) = m^2\phi$$

So in the one case everybody meets first, "derivative of the potential" and "potential coefficient times the field" are numerically identical. The distinction is invisible until the potential stops being quadratic — which is exactly when you add $\lambda(\Phi^\dagger\Phi)^2$.

And this is true of the Schrödinger equation too, which I suspect is the real source of the intuition:

$$i\partial_t\psi = -\frac{1}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi$$

That *looks* like a bare multiplicative $V$. But its Lagrangian density contains the term $V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi^*\psi$, and varying with respect to $\psi^*$ gives

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \psi^*}\Big[V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi^*\psi\Big] = V(\mathbf{x})\,\psi$$

still a derivative. It just doesn't look like one because the term is quadratic in the field. There are two separate things making Schrödinger feel different:

- $V(\mathbf{x})$ depends on **position** — an external landscape the field lives in.
- $V(\phi)$ depends on the **field value itself** — a self-interaction, no external landscape at all.

In the Higgs case there is nothing external. The "hat" is a function of the field's own magnitude at each point, and each point of space carries its own copy.

## The Hamiltonian route, since that's where you're coming from

The conjugate momentum is

$$\pi = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot\phi} = \dot\phi$$

and the Hamiltonian is

$$H = \int d^3x\left[\tfrac12\pi^2 + \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 + V(\phi)\right]$$

Hamilton's equations in functional form:

$$\dot\phi = \frac{\delta H}{\delta \pi} = \pi, \qquad \dot\pi = -\frac{\delta H}{\delta \phi} = \nabla^2\phi - V'(\phi)$$

Combining gives the same result. This framing may be the most intuitive for you: $-\delta H/\delta\phi$ is manifestly "force equals minus the gradient of the energy," with the gradient taken in field space.

Worth noting how this differs from the route you already know. The Lagrangian route treats $\phi$ as a classical field, which is what lets you write any $V$ you like, and hands you Noether's theorem and the conserved currents for free. It also matters for your simulation: you're evolving a classical field configuration, not a probability amplitude.

## Back to the doublet

For several fields the derivation is unchanged, one equation per component:

$$\Box\,\phi_i + \frac{\partial V}{\partial \phi_i} = 0$$

and when $V$ depends only on $r^2 = \sum_j \phi_j^2$, the chain rule produces the central-force structure from before, $\partial V/\partial\phi_i = V'(r)\,\phi_i/r$. The components are independent except through that shared magnitude.

With leapfrog you should see it bounded and oscillating rather than drifting; a secular drift means a bug or too large a timestep.

Two separate things went wrong, and the second one is the one that flipped your answer.

## Issue 1: you're solving the wrong equation

You set $V = 0$. The vacuum is where the potential is **minimized**, not where it vanishes:

$$\frac{dV}{d\phi_a} = 0$$

This is the same point from the last few messages — what matters physically is the derivative of $V$, not $V$ itself. The value of $V$ at the minimum is irrelevant (you can add any constant to $V$ without changing a single equation of motion; it only shifts the vacuum energy). Doing it properly:

$$V(\phi_a) = -\mu^2\phi_a^2 + \lambda\phi_a^4$$

$$\frac{dV}{d\phi_a} = -2\mu^2\phi_a + 4\lambda\phi_a^3 = 2\phi_a\left(2\lambda\phi_a^2 - \mu^2\right) = 0$$

Discarding the $\phi_a = 0$ root (that's the unstable local *maximum* at the top of the hat):

$$\boxed{\;\phi_a^2 = \frac{\mu^2}{2\lambda}\;}$$

Worth noting what your $V = 0$ condition actually computes: it's the point where the hat crosses back through zero on the way up the outer wall, at $\phi_a^2 = \mu^2/\lambda$ — exactly twice the true minimum. So even with clean algebra it would have been off by a factor of 2.

## Issue 2: a transposition in the algebra

Your first step is where the inversion happened. From

$$-\mu^2\phi_a^2 + \lambda\phi_a^4 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda\phi_a^4 = \mu^2\phi_a^2$$

dividing through by $\lambda$ gives

$$\phi_a^4 = \frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}\,\phi_a^2$$

but you wrote $\phi_a^2 = \frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}\phi_a^4$ — the powers on the two sides are swapped. Everything after that follows correctly from the flipped line, which is why you landed on the reciprocal. Divide the correct line by $\phi_a^2$ and you get $\phi_a^2 = \mu^2/\lambda$, the right shape.

## The check that would have caught it instantly

Dimensions. In four dimensions $[\mu]$ is a mass and $[\lambda]$ is dimensionless, so:

$$\left[\frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}\right] = \text{mass}^2 \quad\checkmark \qquad\qquad \left[\frac{\lambda}{\mu^2}\right] = \text{mass}^{-2} \quad\times$$

Since $\phi_a$ is a mass, $\phi_a^2$ must be a mass squared. Your result had inverse-mass-squared, which flags the error without checking a single algebra step. This is cheap and worth doing reflexively on every result of this kind.

## Confirming it's really a minimum

$$\frac{d^2V}{d\phi_a^2} = -2\mu^2 + 12\lambda\phi_a^2 = -2\mu^2 + 6\mu^2 = 4\mu^2 > 0 \quad\checkmark$$

and the depth there is $V_{\min} = -\mu^4/(4\lambda)$, safely below zero, as the hat picture requires.

## Your component choice is fine

Putting the VEV entirely in $\phi_a$ with $\phi_b = 0$ is not the problem. For a single complex field the potential depends only on $|\chi|^2$, so it has a global $U(1)$ symmetry and every direction around the circle is equivalent. Your choice is just a phase convention. (The full doublet case has the extra wrinkle about the neutral direction, but that only bites once gauge fields and fermion charges are in play.)

## One thing to watch: normalization

You've written $\chi = \phi_a + i\phi_b$ with no $1/\sqrt2$. That makes the kinetic term

- Your equation of motion picks up a factor of $\tfrac12$ on the potential term: $\Box\phi_a + \tfrac12 V'(\phi_a) = 0$.

If you'd rather have everything match the standard convention, define

$$V = -\tfrac12\mu^2 r^2 + \tfrac{\lambda}{4} r^4$$
