old = """// SlabPacket adds a ONE-WAY travelling wave packet to a gauge potential and
// its velocity: a cosine carrier under a Gaussian envelope along Z, uniform
// across X and Y. A slab rather than a blob, so it does not diffract and the
// propagation speed stays unambiguous to the eye.
//
// The velocity is the point. For psi = env(z) cos(k z - om t) the initial time
// derivative is om env sin(k z), and dir flips it for the other direction.
// Setting only the position would split the packet into two halves running
// opposite ways at half amplitude each.
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacket(pos, vel EWStates, ctrZ, wavelength, width, amp, dir, om float32) {
	pi := int(pos.Int64())
	vi := int(vel.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		dz := float32(c.Z) - ctrZ
		g := dz / width
		env := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
		pv := env * math32.Cos(k*dz)
		vv := dir * om * env * math32.Sin(k*dz)
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, cur] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, prv] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, cur] += vv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, prv] += vv
			}
		}
	}
}

// SlabPacketConfig is a version of [SlabPacket] that takes its
// wavelength and width variables from [Config]
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel EWStates, ctrZ, amp, dir, om float32) {
	ss.SlabPacket(pos, vel, ctrZ, ss.Config.Wavelength, ss.Config.PacketWidth, amp, dir, om)
}"""

new = """// SlabPacket adds a ONE-WAY travelling wave packet to a gauge potential and
// its velocity: a cosine carrier under a Gaussian envelope along dim, centered
// at ctr and uniform across the other two dimensions. A slab rather than a
// blob, so it does not diffract and the propagation speed stays unambiguous to
// the eye.
//
// The velocity is the point. For psi = env(d) cos(k d - om t) the initial time
// derivative is om env sin(k d), and dir flips it for the other direction.
// Setting only the position would split the packet into two halves running
// opposite ways at half amplitude each.
//
// dim is normally [math32.X], since X is the horizontal display axis in every
// view, so the packet then runs across the screen. pos should be a component
// TRANSVERSE to dim, which for an X-Z view means the Y component: [View]
// draws state Y along the vertical, so a Y-polarized wave travelling along X
// is the textbook transverse picture.
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacket(pos, vel EWStates, dim math32.Dims, ctr, wavelength, width, amp, dir, om float32) {
	pi := int(pos.Int64())
	vi := int(vel.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				d := float32(c.Dim(dim)) - ctr
				g := d / width
				env := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
				pv := env * math32.Cos(k*d)
				vv := dir * om * env * math32.Sin(k*d)
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, cur] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, prv] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, cur] += vv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, prv] += vv
			}
		}
	}
}

// SlabPacketConfig is a version of [SlabPacket] that takes its
// wavelength and width variables from [Config]
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel EWStates, dim math32.Dims, ctr, amp, dir, om float32) {
	ss.SlabPacket(pos, vel, dim, ctr, ss.Config.Wavelength, ss.Config.PacketWidth, amp, dir, om)
}"""

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/colors/colormap"
	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

// vwSim builds a state tensor of the given interior size and fills the chosen
// variable with a value that encodes its own coordinates, so that any sampling
// mistake shows up as the wrong cell rather than the wrong number.
func vwSim(size math32.Vector3i, vr EWStates) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = Electroweak
	ss.Config.Size = size
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.StateVars = EWStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	State.SetZeros()
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(0); z < size.Z+2; z++ {
		for y := int32(0); y < size.Y+2; y++ {
			for x := int32(0); x < size.X+2; x++ {
				State.Set(vwCode(x, y, z), int(z), int(y), int(x), int(vr.Int64()), cur)
			}
		}
	}
	return ss
}

// vwCode packs a coordinate into one value, small enough that ValColor's
// fallback (clamp to +-1) leaves it untouched.
func vwCode(x, y, z int32) float32 {
	return 0.001*float32(x) + 0.00001*float32(y) + 0.0000001*float32(z)
}

func vwView(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, depth math32.Dims, slice int32) *View {
	vw := &View{}
	vw.sim = ss
	vw.Settings.Defaults()
	vw.colorMap = colormap.AvailableMaps[string(vw.Settings.ColorMap)]
	vw.Size = ss.Config.Size
	vw.Depth = depth
	vw.Panels[0].Var = vr
	vw.Panels[0].Mode = Plane
	vw.Panels[0].CurPrev = Current
	vw.Start.X = 1
	vw.Start.SetDim(depth, 1)
	vw.Start.SetDim(vw.SliceDim(), slice)
	return vw
}

// TestViewSliceMapping renders the height field directly and checks that every
// vertex carries the value of the state cell it is supposed to: display X is
// always state X, display depth is View.Depth, and the remaining dimension is
// pinned at the slice level.
func TestViewSliceMapping(t *testing.T) {
	// deliberately unequal, so a swapped axis cannot pass by coincidence
	size := math32.Vec3i(7, 5, 3)
	ss := vwSim(size, EWHs0a)
	_ = ss

	for _, tc := range []struct {
		depth math32.Dims
		slice int32
	}{
		{math32.Z, 2}, // X-Z plane at a Y level
		{math32.Y, 2}, // X-Y plane at a Z level
	} {
		vw := vwView(ss, EWHs0a, tc.depth, tc.slice)
		nx := int(vw.Size.X)
		nz := int(vw.DepthSize())
		if nz < 2 {
			t.Fatalf("depth %v gives only %d cells", tc.depth, nz)
		}
		pm := &PlaneMesh{view: vw, panelNo: 0}
		nVtx, nIndex, _ := pm.MeshSize()
		if nVtx != nz*nx {
			t.Errorf("depth %v: MeshSize gave %d vertices, want %d", tc.depth, nVtx, nz*nx)
		}
		vtx := make(math32.ArrayF32, 3*nVtx)
		norm := make(math32.ArrayF32, 3*nVtx)
		tex := make(math32.ArrayF32, 2*nVtx)
		clr := make(math32.ArrayF32, 4*nVtx)
		idx := make(math32.ArrayU32, nIndex)
		pm.SetPlane(vtx, norm, tex, clr, idx)

		for zi := 0; zi < nz; zi++ {
			for xi := 0; xi < nx; xi++ {
				vi := (nz-1-zi)*nx + xi
				var v math32.Vector3
				vtx.GetVector3(vi*3, &v)
				// the plane is laid out with X across and -Z going back
				if int(v.X) != xi || int(-v.Z) != zi {
					t.Fatalf("depth %v: vertex %d at display (%d,%d) placed at (%g,%g)",
						tc.depth, vi, xi, zi, v.X, -v.Z)
				}
				want := vw.StateCoord(vw.Start, int32(xi), int32(zi))
				if want.Dim(vw.SliceDim()) != tc.slice {
					t.Fatalf("slice dim drifted: %v", want)
				}
				if got := 0.5 * vwCode(want.X, want.Y, want.Z); math.Abs(float64(v.Y-got)) > 1e-9 {
					t.Errorf("depth %v display (%d,%d): height %g, want %g for state %v",
						tc.depth, xi, zi, v.Y, got, want)
				}
			}
		}
		t.Logf("depth %v: %d x %d cells, slice %v = %d, all vertices map to the right state cell",
			tc.depth, nx, nz, vw.SliceDim(), tc.slice)
	}
}

// TestViewDisplayVector: a state vector must point along the axis its own
// dimension is drawn on, in either view.
func TestViewDisplayVector(t *testing.T) {
	v := math32.Vec3(1, 2, 3)
	xz := (&View{Depth: math32.Z}).DisplayVector(v)
	if xz != v {
		t.Errorf("X-Z view should pass a vector through unchanged: got %v", xz)
	}
	xy := (&View{Depth: math32.Y}).DisplayVector(v)
	// state Y is drawn going back into the screen (display Z), state Z is up
	if xy != math32.Vec3(1, 3, 2) {
		t.Errorf("X-Y view should swap Y and Z: got %v", xy)
	}
}

// TestViewMoveSlice: the slice level moves within bounds and nothing else does.
func TestViewMoveSlice(t *testing.T) {
	size := math32.Vec3i(7, 5, 3)
	ss := vwSim(size, EWHs0a)
	_ = ss
	vw := vwView(ss, EWHs0a, math32.Z, 2)
	sd := vw.SliceDim()
	if sd != math32.Y {
		t.Fatalf("X-Z view should slice in Y, got %v", sd)
	}
	before := vw.Start
	vw.MoveSlice(1)
	if vw.Start.Dim(sd) != before.Dim(sd)+1 {
		t.Errorf("slice did not move: %v -> %v", before, vw.Start)
	}
	if vw.Start.X != before.X || vw.Start.Dim(vw.Depth) != before.Dim(vw.Depth) {
		t.Errorf("in-plane corner moved: %v -> %v", before, vw.Start)
	}
	for range 100 { // must clamp, not run off the end
		vw.MoveSlice(1)
	}
	if got, mx := vw.Start.Dim(sd), size.Dim(sd)+1; got != mx {
		t.Errorf("slice clamped to %d, want %d", got, mx)
	}
	for range 100 {
		vw.MoveSlice(-1)
	}
	if got := vw.Start.Dim(sd); got != 0 {
		t.Errorf("slice clamped to %d, want 0", got)
	}
}
EOF

Took the stab. Right that I can't see the GUI — but the sampling logic is testable without one, so I wrote tests that drive `PlaneMesh.SetPlane` directly and check every vertex lands on the state cell it should. 25 tests pass.

## What I did

Rather than hardwire XZ, I made the axis mapping explicit, because a blanket switch breaks your 2D sims: they're `Size.Set(100, 100, 1)`, so an XZ slice would be one cell deep and render nothing.

New `View.Depth math32.Dims` — the state dimension drawn going back into the screen. Horizontal is always state X, height is always the value, so `Depth` alone picks the plane, and `SliceDim()` is whatever's left over. Four helpers carry it: `SliceDim`, `DepthSize`, `StateCoord`, `DisplayVector`. Everything that used to hardcode "depth is Y, slice is Z" now goes through those — `planemesh.go` (all three render modes plus `MeshSize`), `ZoomInSize`/`ZoomOutSize`, `MoveStart`, click-picking in `events.go`, `planeScale` and the corner label in `planeobj.go`.

Default in `ConfigGUI`: `Depth = Z` (XZ plane, sliced in Y), falling back to `Y` when `Size.Z <= 1`. So 2D and 1D behave exactly as before, 3D gets what you want. There's a chooser in the viewbar to flip live — it calls `SetDepth`, which re-centers the new slice and rebuilds the mesh, since the depth extent changes.

`MoveStart` was overloaded: `mv.Z != 0` meant "change slice," anything else meant "pan in plane." Split into `MoveSlice(n)` and a `MoveStart` that pans in display terms (X across, Y into the screen). The up/down toolbar buttons now call `MoveSlice`.

## Two things you should look at

**I changed vector-mode rendering.** `SetVectors` drew arrows as `Vec3(vx, vy, vz)` in display space while positioning cells by state X and Y — so a vector's Y component pointed *up* while its Y *position* ran into the screen. Inconsistent either way, but under XZ the naive mapping happens to be correct, and under XY it needs Y and Z swapped. `DisplayVector` does that. This changes how existing 2D vector displays look — a 2D E-field pointing +Y now points into the screen instead of up. Correct, I think, but it's a visible change to something you didn't ask about, so revert it if you preferred the old look.

**`planeScale` has a latent bug I left alone.** It computes `nsc.Z` and, for >2 panels, doubles `sz.Z` — but the mesh scale is `Pose.Scale.Set(nsc.X, ht, nsc.Y)`, so `nsc.Z` feeds nothing and 4-panel layouts never shrink in depth. I set `sz.Y = DepthSize()` and left the rest, so behavior is identical to today. Fixing it would change your 4-panel layout, which you may have tuned by eye.

## Packets now travel along X

Needed either way, as you said. `SlabPacket`/`SlabPacketConfig` take a `math32.Dims` now, matching `MovingWavePacket`'s idiom, and the three configs pass `math32.X` and polarize along **Y** — which `DisplayVector` maps to display-up in an XZ view, so a transverse wave actually looks like the textbook picture.

Speeds are unchanged to five digits, which is a decent isotropy check on the whole kernel:

```
photon  v = 0.46625  want 0.49039  (v/c = 0.9325)
Z       v = 0.34519  want 0.34235  (v/c = 0.6904)
W collision: 1.6573e+01 with Yang-Mills vs 1.8413e-10 without
```

Watch vars moved with them: `AYs`, `EWZY`, and for the collision `EWW3Xs` — the generated mode is longitudinal, so it follows the propagation axis.

One loose end: `ElectroweakViewAll` puts `A0s` in panel 1, which is identically zero for a transverse pulse. `AYs` would make Photon Pulse visible the moment you pick it. Didn't change it since the Higgs configs may be why A0s is there.

Done — 25 tests pass, bindings unchanged, only the pre-existing `wavedata` failure at the root.

**Panel 1 → `AYs`.** Photon Pulse now shows the packet the moment you pick it.

**`Depth` defaults to `Z` unconditionally.** No more size sniffing — the X-Z plane sliced at a Y level is the standard orientation, full stop. I rewrote the field doc to say so and to describe `math32.Y` as the odd case rather than a co-equal option. 1D sims are unaffected either way: `(500,1,1)` has depth 1 under both settings and renders as Bars exactly as before.

The one thing that now differs from before: if a sim ever runs with the bare `Config.Defaults()` size `(100,100,1)` and no per-equation override, Plane mode gets a 1-cell depth and draws nothing until you flip the chooser. Nothing in `waves.go` does that, so it's hypothetical — but it's the reason the auto-fallback existed, and it's gone now.

And you're right that the mechanism is more than today needs. What it did buy, beyond the switch itself, is that the axis assumption is now stated in one place instead of being spread across four files as repeated `Size.Y` / `Start.Z` references — which is what made the vector-arrow inconsistency visible in the first place.

func TestPulseCondensateBackReaction(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 96
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name  string
		init  func(*Sim)
		probe int
		min   float64 // lowest fraction of vacuum |Phi|^2 allowed
		max   float64 // highest fraction allowed

				h := float64(State.Value(2, 2, int(x), int(EWHmag), cur))
				num += a * a * h
				den += a * a
			}
			if den > 0 {
				lo = math.Min(lo, num/den)
			}
		}
		frac := lo / v2
		t.Logf("%-7s lowest |Phi|^2 under the packet %.5f of vacuum %.5f -> %.0f%%",

				tc.name, 100*frac, 100*tc.min, 100*tc.max)
		}
	}
}"""

Fixed — 26 tests pass. But it wasn't a tolerance problem, it was real physics, and I think you'll want to know about it.

## What amplitude 1 actually does

Only the Z broke. At amp 1 it runs at **0.755 c** against a tree-level prediction of 0.685. I traced it by measuring the condensate the packet is sitting in:

```
amp=0.02  |Phi|^2 in packet = 100% of vacuum   v=0.34519   tree +0.8%
amp=0.10                      100%             v=0.34551   tree +0.9%
amp=0.30                       98%             v=0.34827   tree +1.7%
amp=0.60                       91%             v=0.35812   tree +4.6%
amp=1.00                       49%             v=0.37734   tree +10.2%
```

At amp 1 the Z packet is comparable to `v` (0.93 v at the demo scale), so it's not a perturbation on the vacuum — **it partially melts the condensate it's travelling through**, down to 33% at the instantaneous minimum. Less condensate means less mass means a faster Z. The tree-level formula assumes a linear wave on an undisturbed vacuum, so it simply doesn't apply there.

The flip side is the nicest number in this session:

```
photon  lowest |Phi|^2 under the packet = 0.01513 of vacuum 0.01513 -> 100%
Z       lowest |Phi|^2 under the packet = 0.38107 of vacuum 1.16610 ->  33%
```

The photon packet at amp 1 is about **66× the VEV** and leaves `|Phi|^2` unmoved in the fifth decimal. That's exact masslessness demonstrated directly rather than inferred from a speed — Q annihilates ⟨Φ⟩, so the photon direction is flat no matter how far you push along it. Its speed is also bit-identical to the amp 0.02 run.

## The fix

`TestConfigPulseSpeeds` keeps the tight 8% tree-level check on the photon and gives the Z 15%, with the reason written down rather than the number quietly widened. I added the assertion that actually carries the demo's claim and doesn't depend on the packet being small: the Z lags the photon by a clear margin.

New `TestPulseCondensateBackReaction` pins the mechanism — photon must leave the condensate within 1% of vacuum, Z must drive it below 70%. That's what makes the loosened Z tolerance honest: the deviation is explained and measured, not absorbed.

Updated `ZPulse`'s doc to say ~0.75 c and why, since it claimed 0.70.

Worth deciding: the Z demo is now showing a strongly nonlinear excitation that locally restores electroweak symmetry, not a Z boson propagating on the vacuum. Still visibly subluminal, so the demo's point survives — and arguably "watch the Z melt the Higgs as it goes" is the better demo. If you'd rather it be the clean linear case, **amp 0.6 keeps 91% of the condensate and sits within 4.6%**, while still filling most of the display range.

// The cos(k/2) is why even a massless packet comes out slightly subluminal.
func cfgGroupVel(wavelength, mass float64) float64 {
	k := 2 * math.Pi / wavelength
	kh := 2 * math.Sin(k/2)
	return kh * math.Cos(k/2) / math.Sqrt(kh*kh+mass*mass)
}

func TestConfigPulseSpeeds(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 96

	for ti, tc := range []struct {
		name  string
		init  func(*Sim)
		probe int

		m := tc.mass(ss.Params)

			ss = cfgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) { ewDemoScale(s, 0.388) })
			m = tc.mass(ss.Params)
		}
		wantV := cfgGroupVel(wl, m)

		got, hfrac := cfgSpeed(sz, tc.init, tc.probe, amp, 100)
		speed[ti] = got
		t.Logf("%-7s amp %.2f: v = %.5f c, want %.5f c (%+.1f%%), condensate %.0f%% of vacuum",
			tc.name, amp, got, wantV, 100*(got/wantV-1), 100*hfrac)
		if math.Abs(got/wantV-1) > 0.08 {
			t.Errorf("%s speed %g c, want %g c", tc.name, got, wantV)
		}
		// The lattice already puts a massless packet at cos(k/2) = 0.98 c, and
		// the finite packet loses a few percent more to dispersion; the point
		// is that it is near c and far above the Z.
		if m == 0 && got < 0.9 {
			t.Errorf("photon should move at essentially c: %g c", got)
		}
		if m > 0 && got > 0.85 {
			t.Errorf("Z should be visibly subluminal, got %g c", got)
		}
	}
	// the claim the demo makes, and the one that holds at any amplitude
	if speed[1] > speed[0]-0.1 {
		t.Errorf("Z at %.4f c should lag the photon at %.4f c by a clear margin",
			speed[1], speed[0])
	}
}

// TestPulseCondensateBackReaction measures what the pulses do to the Higgs
// condensate they travel through, which at the default amplitude is the
// difference between a linear wave and a strongly nonlinear one.
//
// The photon direction is the combination that Q = T^3 + Y annihilates, so it
// costs the condensate nothing no matter how large it gets -- at amplitude 1
// the packet is many times v and |Phi|^2 does not move, and its speed is the
// same as in the linear regime. That is exact masslessness shown directly,
// rather than inferred from a propagation speed.

// partially restores the symmetry underneath itself. The local mass falls with
// the condensate and the packet speeds up, which is why the tree-level group
// velocity only applies to a small Z.
func TestPulseCondensateBackReaction(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 96
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name    string
		init    func(*Sim)
		probe   int
		minDrop float64 // how far below vacuum the condensate must go at amp 1
		maxDrop float64
	}{
		{"photon", PhotonPulse, int(AYs), 0.99, 1.01},
		{"Z", ZPulse, int(EWZY), 0.0, 0.70},
	} {
		vLin, hLin := cfgSpeed(sz, tc.init, tc.probe, 0.02, 100)
		vBig, hBig := cfgSpeed(sz, tc.init, tc.probe, 1, 100)
		t.Logf("%-7s amp 0.02: v = %.5f c, condensate %3.0f%%   |   amp 1: v = %.5f c, condensate %3.0f%%  (%+.1f%% faster)",
			tc.name, vLin, 100*hLin, vBig, 100*hBig, 100*(vBig/vLin-1))
		if hBig < tc.minDrop || hBig > tc.maxDrop {
			t.Errorf("%s left the condensate at %.0f%% of vacuum, want %.0f-%.0f%%",
				tc.name, 100*hBig, 100*tc.minDrop, 100*tc.maxDrop)
		}
		if tc.name == "photon" && math.Abs(vBig/vLin-1) > 0.01 {
			t.Errorf("photon speed moved %.1f%% between amplitudes: it should not "+
				"care, since it does not couple to the condensate", 100*(vBig/vLin-1))
		}
		if tc.name == "Z" && vBig <= vLin {
			t.Errorf("Z at amplitude 1 (%g c) should outrun the linear Z (%g c): "+
				"it has melted its own mass down", vBig, vLin)
		}
	}
}

## Does the melting correspond to real physics?

Yes, to several things, and the mechanism you're seeing is the standard one — but with an important caveat about which of them your sim is actually doing.

**Symmetry restoration by a field condensate.** The Higgs effective potential picks up a term from whatever else is around: a background of gauge field contributes $+\frac{g^2}{4}\langle W^2\rangle |\Phi|^2$, which adds to $\mu^2$ and pushes the minimum inward. When it exceeds $|\mu^2|$ the minimum goes to zero and the symmetry is restored. That is exactly the algebra of your $|D_\mu\Phi|^2$ term — the coupling that gives the Z its mass is the same one that lets the Z push back. Mass generation and back-reaction are two readings of one vertex, which is why the photon can't do it: no coupling, no mass, no back-reaction.

**The thermal version is the electroweak phase transition.** Replace the coherent packet with a thermal bath and $\langle W^2\rangle \to cT^2$, giving $\mu^2_{\rm eff} = \mu^2 + cT^2$ and restoration above $T_c \sim 160$ GeV. Your `HiggsSymmetric` config is the cooling side of that same story; this is the heating side, driven by one coherent mode instead of a thermal ensemble. (That's the "add a thermal mass by hand" suggestion at the bottom of the `electroweak_py` README — you've stumbled into it from the other direction.)

**Non-thermal restoration after inflation** is the closest literature match: coherent oscillating fields with amplitude comparable to $v$ restoring symmetry through exactly this induced-mass term, without anything being in equilibrium. That's the regime your amp-1 packet is in — a single coherent mode, not a bath.

**Sphalerons** are the other place a large gauge-field configuration sits on top of a suppressed condensate — $|\Phi| \to 0$ at the center — and they matter for baryogenesis.

Two honest caveats. First, this is classical: a real Z boson is a quantum excitation whose amplitude isn't a free dial, and the perturbative single-Z state can't do this. What you have is a coherent state of enormous occupation number, which is the right classical limit for the early-universe phenomena above and the wrong picture for collider physics. Second, per the `electroweak_py` README's scope notes, your gauge fields are non-compact with $O(a^2)$ gauge invariance and no exact Gauss law — fine for this, but sphaleron/Chern-Simons work would want compact links.

So: a real effect, correctly reproduced, and the same physics as the electroweak phase transition — read in reverse. With `Amplitude` now in the GUI you can sweep it and watch $|\Phi|^2$ under the packet cross over from 100% to 33%, which is a genuinely nice demo in its own right.

s=open(p).read()

# --- new editable params after HiggsLambda
old = """	// HiggsLambda is the Higgs potential weight factor that determines
	// effectively how strongly the complex magnitude minus mu_H contributes.
	HiggsLambda float32
"""
new = """	// HiggsLambda is the Higgs potential weight factor that determines
	// effectively how strongly the complex magnitude minus mu_H contributes.
	HiggsLambda float32

	// Temp is the temperature T of the thermal bath the Higgs sits in, in the
	// same 1/cube units as HiggsMu. Everything else in this simulator is at
	// zero temperature; this one term stands in for a bath of all the other
	// particles, which contribute an effective mass
	//	mu^2 -> mu^2 - ThermalC * Temp^2
	// to the Higgs. It is a real effect (the leading term of the finite
	// temperature effective potential) added by hand, not something the
	// lattice generates: there is no bath here, and nothing thermalizes.
	//
	// Raise Temp through TempCrit and the broken minimum closes up: HiggsV,
	// MW and MZ all go to zero and the symmetry is restored, which is the
	// electroweak phase transition of the early universe run backwards.
	// Lower it back through TempCrit and the field has to pick a direction
	// again. Zero by default, which leaves everything else untouched.
	Temp float32

	// ThermalC is the coefficient c in the thermal mass mu^2 -> mu^2 - c T^2.
	// In the Standard Model it comes from the particles in the bath:
	//	c = (3 g^2 + g'^2 + 4 y_t^2 + 8 lambda) / 16
	// which is about 0.397, dominated by the top Yukawa y_t. That is the
	// default. There are no fermions in this simulator, so it cannot be
	// derived from the other parameters here; dropping the top term would
	// give 0.152 instead, and a correspondingly higher TempCrit.
	ThermalC float32
"""
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)

# --- derived fields: make visible read-only, add TempCrit
old = """	// HiggsMuSq = HiggsMu*HiggsMu, in 1/cube^2 -- the Higgs equivalent of
	// MOverHSq, occupying the same slot in the update.
	HiggsMuSq float32 `display:"-"`

	// HiggsV = HiggsMu / sqrt(HiggsLambda) is the Higgs vacuum expectation
	// value: the radius of the minimum of the potential, in 1/cube. The
	// neutral (lower) doublet component is initialized to this.
	HiggsV float32 `display:"-"`

	// MW = GW * HiggsV / 2 is the W boson mass in 1/cube. Nothing in the
	// kernel uses it -- the mass is generated dynamically by the Higgs
	// current. It is here to check that against.
	MW float32 `display:"-"`

	// MZ = HiggsV * sqrt(GW^2 + GpW^2) / 2 is the Z boson mass in 1/cube,
	// likewise for reference only. The photon mass is zero.
	MZ float32 `display:"-"`"""
new = """	// HiggsMuSq is the EFFECTIVE mu^2 that the kernel actually uses, in
	// 1/cube^2: HiggsMu^2 - ThermalC * Temp^2. The Higgs equivalent of
	// MOverHSq, occupying the same slot in the update. It goes negative
	// above TempCrit, at which point the origin becomes the minimum.
	HiggsMuSq float32 `display:"-"`

	// TempCrit is the critical temperature, HiggsMu / sqrt(ThermalC), where
	// the thermal mass exactly cancels mu^2 and the broken minimum closes up.
	// Above it the symmetry is restored and the gauge bosons are massless.
	TempCrit float32 `edit:"-"`

	// HiggsV = sqrt(HiggsMuSq / HiggsLambda) is the Higgs vacuum expectation
	// value: the radius of the minimum of the potential, in 1/cube. The
	// neutral (lower) doublet component is initialized to this. It is the
	// THERMAL VEV v(T), equal to HiggsMu/sqrt(HiggsLambda) at Temp = 0 and
	// falling to zero at TempCrit.
	HiggsV float32 `edit:"-"`

	// MW = GW * HiggsV / 2 is the W boson mass in 1/cube. Nothing in the
	// kernel uses it -- the mass is generated dynamically by the Higgs
	// current. It is here to check that against. Since it follows HiggsV it
	// is likewise the thermal mass, and vanishes above TempCrit.
	MW float32 `edit:"-"`

	// MZ = HiggsV * sqrt(GW^2 + GpW^2) / 2 is the Z boson mass in 1/cube,
	// likewise for reference only. The photon mass is zero at any temperature.
	MZ float32 `edit:"-"`"""
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)

# --- Update
old = """	pr.HiggsMuSq = pr.HiggsMu * pr.HiggsMu
	if pr.HiggsLambda > 0 {
		pr.HiggsV = pr.HiggsMu / math32.Sqrt(pr.HiggsLambda)
	}"""
new = """	// the thermal mass adds to mu^2 with the opposite sign, so raising Temp
	// closes the broken minimum; above TempCrit it is negative and the only
	// minimum is the origin, where v(T) = 0.
	pr.HiggsMuSq = pr.HiggsMu*pr.HiggsMu - pr.ThermalC*pr.Temp*pr.Temp

	if pr.HiggsLambda > 0 && pr.HiggsMuSq > 0 {

assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)

# helper next to ewDemoScale
old = """//////// configurations"""
new = """// ewVZero returns the ZERO-temperature vacuum value, mu/sqrt(lambda). That
// stays the natural scale for field amplitudes even when Params.Temp has driven
// the actual HiggsV to zero, which is why the configs size their noise and
// their packets against it rather than against HiggsV.
func ewVZero(ss *Sim) float32 {
	p := ss.Params
	if p.HiggsLambda <= 0 {
		return 0
	}
	return p.HiggsMu / math32.Sqrt(p.HiggsLambda)
}

// Params.Temp adds -ThermalC*Temp^2 to mu^2, so above Params.TempCrit the

// top of a hat: the field sits at zero and stays there, the W and Z are
// massless, and the whole electroweak symmetry is intact. That is the state of
// the universe before about a picosecond.
//
// The demonstration is interactive. Run it, then drag Temp down through

// MZ come off zero together, the field rolls out to v(T), and different
// regions pick different directions in the internal space, leaving domain

// with far more violent ringing and more domains that survive.

// Unlike HiggsSymmetric, which sits on an unstable maximum at Temp = 0 and

	p.Update()

	ss.SmoothNoise(EWHs0b, amp, 6)
}

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

// thSetTemp sets the temperature on a running sim and recomputes the derived
// values, which is exactly what the GUI form does when you drag Temp.
func thSetTemp(ss *Sim, t float32) {
	ss.Params.Temp = t
	ss.Params.Update()
}

// thMag returns the mean |Phi|^2 over the interior.
func thMag(sz int32) float64 {
	var s float64
	var n int
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				s += float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(EWHmag), cur))
				n++
			}
		}
	}
	return s / float64(n)
}

// TestThermalVEV checks the thermal parameters against the algebra they stand
// for: mu^2 -> mu^2 - c T^2, v(T) = sqrt(mu^2(T)/lambda), and the gauge boson
// masses following v(T) down to zero at TempCrit.
func TestThermalVEV(t *testing.T) {
	ss := ewSim(4)
	p := ss.Params
	mu, lam, c := float64(p.HiggsMu), float64(p.HiggsLambda), float64(p.ThermalC)
	tc := mu / math.Sqrt(c)
	if math.Abs(float64(p.TempCrit)-tc) > 1e-6 {
		t.Errorf("TempCrit = %g, want mu/sqrt(c) = %g", p.TempCrit, tc)
	}
	for _, f := range []float64{0, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0, 1.2, 2.0} {
		thSetTemp(ss, float32(f*tc))
		musq := mu*mu - c*float64(p.Temp)*float64(p.Temp)
		want := 0.0
		if musq > 0 {
			want = math.Sqrt(musq / lam)
		}
		got := float64(p.HiggsV)
		if math.Abs(got-want) > 1e-6+1e-4*want {
			t.Errorf("T = %.2f Tc: v(T) = %g, want %g", f, got, want)
		}
		wantMW := float64(p.GW) * want / 2
		if math.Abs(float64(p.MW)-wantMW) > 1e-6+1e-4*wantMW {
			t.Errorf("T = %.2f Tc: m_W = %g, want %g", f, p.MW, wantMW)
		}
		t.Logf("T = %.2f Tc: mu^2(T) = %+.3e  v(T) = %.5f  m_W = %.5f  m_Z = %.5f",
			f, musq, p.HiggsV, p.MW, p.MZ)
	}
	thSetTemp(ss, 0)
}

// TestThermalVEVStatic: v(T) must be an actual fixed point of the kernel, not
// just of the formula -- the same check as TestHiggsVacuumStatic but with the
// thermal term carrying part of mu^2.
func TestThermalVEVStatic(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	ss := ewSim(sz)
	defer thSetTemp(ss, 0)
	for _, f := range []float32{0.5, 0.9} {
		thSetTemp(ss, f*ss.Params.TempCrit)
		v := ss.Params.HiggsV
		State.SetZeros()
		ss.Fill(EWHs0a, Both, v)
		WrapEdges()
		for range 500 {
			ewStep(ss)
		}
		drift := math.Abs(float64(ewGet(EWHs0a) - v))
		vel := math.Abs(float64(ewGet(EWHv0a)))
		t.Logf("T = %.1f Tc: v(T) = %.5f, drift after 500 steps %.3e, velocity %.3e", f, v, drift, vel)
		if drift > 1e-5 || vel > 1e-6 {
			t.Errorf("T = %.1f Tc: thermal vacuum not stationary: drift %g vel %g", f, drift, vel)
		}
	}
}

// TestThermalRestoration: heated above TempCrit, a field sitting in the old
// broken vacuum is no longer in a minimum at all, and must fall back to zero.
func TestThermalRestoration(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 6
	ss := ewSim(sz)
	defer thSetTemp(ss, 0)
	v0 := ss.Params.HiggsV // the cold VEV, where ewSim leaves the field
	start := thMag(sz)
	thSetTemp(ss, 1.5*ss.Params.TempCrit)
	if ss.Params.HiggsV != 0 {
		t.Fatalf("above TempCrit the VEV should be zero, got %g", ss.Params.HiggsV)
	}
	if ss.Params.MW != 0 || ss.Params.MZ != 0 {
		t.Errorf("above TempCrit the gauge bosons should be massless, got m_W %g m_Z %g",
			ss.Params.MW, ss.Params.MZ)
	}
	var low float64 = math.Inf(1)
	for range 4000 {
		ewStep(ss)
		low = math.Min(low, thMag(sz))
	}
	t.Logf("heated to 1.5 Tc from v = %.5f: |Phi|^2 %.3e -> %.3e at its lowest (started %.3e)",
		v0, start, low, float64(v0)*float64(v0))
	if low > 0.05*start {
		t.Errorf("symmetry not restored: |Phi|^2 only fell from %g to %g", start, low)
	}
}

// TestThermalQuench runs the config the way the GUI does: start hot, where the
// symmetric point is genuinely stable, then cool through TempCrit and watch the
// field break out to the new vacuum.
func TestThermalQuench(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 16
	ss := cfgSim(sz, ThermalQuench)
	defer thSetTemp(ss, 0)
	if ss.Params.Temp <= ss.Params.TempCrit {
		t.Fatalf("ThermalQuench should start above TempCrit: %g vs %g",
			ss.Params.Temp, ss.Params.TempCrit)
	}
	hot := thMag(sz)
	for range 1000 { // hot: must stay put, this is a real minimum
		ewStep(ss)
	}
	held := thMag(sz)
	t.Logf("hot at %.2f Tc: |Phi|^2 %.3e -> %.3e after 1000 steps", ss.Params.Temp/ss.Params.TempCrit, hot, held)
	if held > 4*hot+1e-12 {
		t.Errorf("symmetric phase should be stable above TempCrit: |Phi|^2 grew %g -> %g", hot, held)
	}

	thSetTemp(ss, 0) // quench all the way down
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	var peak float64
	for range 4000 {
		ewStep(ss)
		peak = math.Max(peak, thMag(sz))
	}
	final := thMag(sz)
	t.Logf("quenched to T = 0: |Phi|^2 peak %.5f, final %.5f  (v^2 = %.5f)", peak, final, v2)
	if peak < 0.5*v2 {
		t.Errorf("quench did not reach the broken vacuum: peak %g vs v^2 = %g", peak, v2)
	}
	if math.IsNaN(final) {
		t.Errorf("quench blew up")
	}
}
EOF

Thermal mass term added — yes, entirely by hand, one term. 30 tests pass, bindings regenerated.

## The term

Two editable params, `Temp` and `ThermalC`, feeding the existing hook:

```go
pr.HiggsMuSq = pr.HiggsMu*pr.HiggsMu - pr.ThermalC*pr.Temp*pr.Temp
```

The kernel already reads `Params[0].HiggsMuSq`, so **the kernel needed no change at all** — the thermal correction enters exactly where it belongs, as a shift in μ². `ThermalC` defaults to the Standard Model value 0.3973, from $(3g^2+g'^2+4y_t^2+8\lambda)/16$. It can't be derived from your params since there are no fermions here and the top Yukawa dominates; without it you'd get 0.152 and a much higher $T_c$. Documented in the field.

I made `HiggsV` the **thermal** VEV, $\sqrt{\mu^2(T)/\lambda}$, which falls out nicely: `MW` and `MZ` already derive from it, so they follow $v(T)$ to zero on their own.

```
T = 0.00 Tc: mu^2(T) = +1.953e-03  v(T) = 0.12300  m_W = 0.04018  m_Z = 0.04558
T = 0.50 Tc:             +1.465e-03         0.10652         0.03479         0.03947
T = 0.90 Tc:             +3.711e-04         0.05361         0.01751         0.01987
T = 0.99 Tc:             +3.887e-05         0.01735         0.00567         0.00643
T = 1.01 Tc:             -3.926e-05         0.00000         0.00000         0.00000
```

## Display

`ElectroweakDisplay` now has `Temp`, `ThermalC` in the editable group and `TempCrit`, `HiggsV`, `MW`, `MZ` after `Boris` as readouts. Those last three were tagged `display:"-"`, so the list alone wouldn't have shown them — `ShouldDisplay` is a filter on top of the struct tags, not a substitute. Changed them to `edit:"-"` so they render read-only and update live as you drag `Temp`. That's the whole point here: you watch $m_W$ and $m_Z$ collapse as you approach $T_c$.

## Ramping

The ramp is just the GUI — drag `Temp` while running and `Params.Update()` fires. `TempCrit` is right there to aim at.

New **Thermal Quench** config starts at $1.25\,T_c$ with zero field plus noise. Unlike `HiggsSymmetric`, which balances on an unstable maximum and falls the moment it's nudged, this one is genuinely stable — the origin is a real minimum up there. It waits for you to cool it.

Four tests: the $v(T)$ algebra; that $v(T)$ is a true fixed point of the *kernel* (drift 0.0, velocity 4e-10 after 500 steps — the thermal vacuum is as exact as the cold one); restoration, where a field left in the cold vacuum and heated to $1.5\,T_c$ falls from $1.5\times10^{-2}$ to $3\times10^{-10}$; and the full quench cycle:

```
hot at 1.25 Tc: |Phi|^2 1.105e-05 -> 2.790e-06 after 1000 steps   (stable, noise decaying)
quenched to T = 0: |Phi|^2 peak 0.02914, final 0.00965  (v^2 = 0.01513)
```

Peak ≈ 2v² again — same $\sqrt2 v$ overshoot as `HiggsSymmetric`, since nothing dissipates.

One caveat worth stating plainly: this is the leading-order thermal correction only. It gives a smooth second-order transition. The real SM transition gets a $-ET^3\phi^3$ cubic term from the gauge boson Matsubara modes, which would make it first-order with a barrier, bubble nucleation and latent heat — and at the physical Higgs mass the true answer is a crossover, not a transition at all. Adding the cubic is another one-line term in the same place if you ever want the bubbles.

// it breaks out to the new vacuum.
func TestThermalQuench(t *testing.T) {
	ss := cfgSim(16, func(s *Sim) {
		s.Params.Temp = 1.25 * s.Params.TempCrit
		s.Params.Update()
		HiggsSymmetric(s)
	})
	defer thSetTemp(ss, 0)
	ewStep(ss) // EWHmag is kernel-written: step once to fill it
	hot := thMag()
	for range 1000 { // above TempCrit this is a real minimum: must stay put
		ewStep(ss)
	}
	held := thMag()
	t.Logf("hot at %.2f Tc: |Phi|^2 %.3e -> %.3e after 1000 steps",
		ss.Params.Temp/ss.Params.TempCrit, hot, held)
	if held > 4*hot+1e-12 {
		t.Errorf("symmetric phase should be stable above TempCrit: %g -> %g", hot, held)
	}

	thSetTemp(ss, 0) // quench
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	var peak float64
	for range 4000 {
		ewStep(ss)
		peak = math.Max(peak, thMag())
	}
	final := thMag()
	t.Logf("quenched to T = 0: |Phi|^2 peak %.5f, final %.5f  (v^2 = %.5f)", peak, final, v2)
	if peak < 0.5*v2 {
		t.Errorf("quench did not reach the broken vacuum: peak %g vs v^2 %g", peak, v2)
	}
	if math.IsNaN(final) {
		t.Errorf("quench blew up")
	}
}
"""

  // neutral (lower) component: that is what makes Q = T^3 + Y annihilate the
  // vacuum and leaves the photon massless.

  // EWGaugeAct returns -i * G * Psi in real components, where G is the Hermitian
  // 2x2 gauge matrix that the covariant derivative is built from:
  //
  //	G = g W^a T^a + g' Y_Phi B,   T^a = sigma^a / 2
  //	  = [[ du, or + i oi ], [ or - i oi, dd ]]
  //	du = (g/2) W3 + g' Y B      or = (g/2) W1
  //	dd = -(g/2) W3 + g' Y B     oi = -(g/2) W2
  //
  // The opposite sign of W3 on the two diagonal entries is T^3 = +-1/2, and it
  // is the whole reason the upper and lower doublet components feel W3
  // oppositely while feeling B identically. Solving for the combination that
  // annihilates the vacuum is what picks out Q = T^3 + Y and leaves one
  // massless direction.
  //
  // This single operation is the entire content of the gauge coupling. The
  // covariant derivative is
  //
  //	D_mu Psi = d_mu Psi + EWGaugeAct(W_mu, B_mu, Psi)
  //
  // and the covariant Laplacian composes out of it (see the kernel).

  // ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear sums the energy over the 27 sites centred on
  // (x,y,z). Every stencil here reaches at most one cube, so the energy at a site
  // depends on the field only within +-1 of it: the derivative of the TOTAL
  // energy with respect to one site's value therefore lives entirely inside this
  // block. Summing locally makes the numerical-gradient check independent of the
  // boundary, so the test field does not have to be lattice-periodic.
  func ElectroweakStaticEnergyNear(x, y, z int32) float64 {
  === params MOverHSq ===
  	// MOverHSq = (Mass * C / Hbar)^2 is the mass drag factor in KleinGordon
  	// and related equations: the INVERSE REDUCED COMPTON WAVELENGTH squared,
  	// in units of 1/cube^2. The update applies it as
  	//	vel += CSq * (Laplacian + ... - MOverHSq*psi)
  	// which matches Klein-Gordon written as
  	//	d2psi/dt2 = c^2 [ Laplacian(psi) - (m c / hbar)^2 psi ]
  	// so the C^2 inside MOverHSq is required and is NOT the same as the outer
  	// CSq factor -- one converts mass to inverse length, the other converts
  	// the whole bracket to an acceleration.
  	MOverHSq float32 `display:"-"`

// StateMean computes the mean of given variable over the non-edge interior.
func StateMean(sz math32.Vector3i, vr enums.Enum, curPrv int32) float64 {
	n := int(sz.X) * int(sz.Y) * int(sz.Z)
	if n == 0 {
		return 0
	}
	return StateSum(sz, vr, curPrv) / float64(n)
}

// StateCentroids computes the intensity-weighted (value squared) centroid
// along dim for each of the given variables, in cube coordinates, in ONE pass
// over the state. Variables that are everywhere zero get the box center.
// One pass because a full scan is the expensive part of any stat: at 100^3
// that is a million cells, so do not add more passes than you need.
func StateCentroids(sz math32.Vector3i, dim math32.Dims, curPrv int32, vrs []enums.Enum, ctrs []float64) {
	nv := len(vrs)
	vris := make([]int, nv)
	num := make([]float64, nv)
	den := make([]float64, nv)
	for i, vr := range vrs {
		vris[i] = int(vr.Int64())
	}
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				d := float64(c.Dim(dim))
				for i := range nv {
					v := float64(State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vris[i], curPrv])
					w := v * v
					num[i] += w * d
					den[i] += w
				}
			}
		}
	}
	for i := range nv {
		if den[i] == 0 {
			ctrs[i] = float64(sz.Dim(dim)) / 2
		} else {
			ctrs[i] = num[i] / den[i]
		}
	}
}

// StatCentroidName is the stat name for the centroid of vr along dim.
func StatCentroidName(vr enums.Enum, dim math32.Dims) string {
	return "Ctr" + vr.String() + dim.String()
}

// StatGroupVelName is the stat name for the group velocity of vr along dim.
func StatGroupVelName(vr enums.Enum, dim math32.Dims) string {
	return "Vg" + vr.String() + dim.String()
}

// StatGroupVel records, for each of the given variables, the intensity
// centroid along dim and the speed of that centroid in units of C: the group
// velocity of a wave packet. Both are recorded; only the velocity is plotted
// by default.
//
// A packet crossing a wrapped edge is taken the short way round the box, so it
// does not register as a jump. Uniform fields sit at the box center and read
// zero. All variables share one pass over the state, so pass them together.
func (ss *Sim) StatGroupVel(dim math32.Dims, vrs ...enums.Enum) func(init bool) {
	prev := make([]float64, len(vrs))
	ctrs := make([]float64, len(vrs))
	var prevStep int
	var have bool
	return func(init bool) {
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		if init {
			have = false
			for i, vr := range vrs {
				ct := ss.Stats.Float64(StatCentroidName(vr, dim))
				vt := ss.Stats.Float64(StatGroupVelName(vr, dim))
				ct.SetNumRows(0)
				vt.SetNumRows(0)
				plot.SetFirstStyler(ct, func(s *plot.Style) {
					s.On = false
				})
				plot.SetFirstStyler(vt, func(s *plot.Style) {
					s.On = true
				})
				metadata.SetDoc(ct, "Intensity centroid of "+vr.String()+" along "+dim.String()+", in cubes")
				metadata.SetDoc(vt, "Group velocity of "+vr.String()+" along "+dim.String()+", in units of C")
				_ = i
			}
			return
		}
		sz := ss.Config.Size
		ln := float64(sz.Dim(dim))
		StateCentroids(sz, dim, ctx.CurState, vrs, ctrs)
		ds := float64(int(ctx.Step) - prevStep)
		for i, vr := range vrs {
			vg := 0.0
			if have && ds > 0 && ss.Params.C > 0 {
				d := ctrs[i] - prev[i]
				if d > ln/2 {
					d -= ln
				} else if d < -ln/2 {
					d += ln
				}
				vg = d / ds / float64(ss.Params.C)
			}
			prev[i] = ctrs[i]
			ss.Stats.Float64(StatCentroidName(vr, dim)).AppendRowFloat(ctrs[i])
			ss.Stats.Float64(StatGroupVelName(vr, dim)).AppendRowFloat(vg)
		}
		prevStep = int(ctx.Step)
		have = true
	}
}

// StatMean is a stats function that records the mean of given variable over
// the interior, which for |Phi|^2 is directly comparable to v^2.
func (ss *Sim) StatMean(vr enums.Enum) func(init bool) {
	return func(init bool) {
		name := "Mean" + vr.String()
		tsr := ss.Stats.Float64(name)
		if init {
			tsr.SetNumRows(0)
			plot.SetFirstStyler(tsr, func(s *plot.Style) {
				s.On = true
			})
			metadata.SetDoc(tsr, "Mean of "+vr.String()+" over the interior")
			return
		}
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		tsr.AppendRowFloat(StateMean(ss.Config.Size, vr, ctx.CurState))
	}
}

// StatSumSq records the summed squares of the given variables under the given
// name: the total power in a multi-component field.
func (ss *Sim) StatSumSq(name string, vrs ...enums.Enum) func(init bool) {
	return func(init bool) {
		tsr := ss.Stats.Float64(name)
		if init {
			tsr.SetNumRows(0)
			plot.SetFirstStyler(tsr, func(s *plot.Style) {
				s.On = false
			})
			metadata.SetDoc(tsr, "Summed squares of "+name)
			return
		}
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		cur := ctx.CurState
		sz := ss.Config.Size
		vris := make([]int, len(vrs))
		for i, vr := range vrs {
			vris[i] = int(vr.Int64())
		}
		sum := 0.0
		var c math32.Vector3i
		for c.Z = range sz.Z {
			for c.Y = range sz.Y {
				for c.X = range sz.X {
					f := c.AddScalar(1)
					for i := range vris {
						v := float64(State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vris[i], cur])
						sum += v * v
					}
				}
			}
		}
		tsr.AppendRowFloat(sum)
	}
}

// StatWeightedMean records the mean of vr weighted by the intensity of wtVr:
// what a wtVr wave packet sees as it passes, rather than the box average.
func (ss *Sim) StatWeightedMean(name string, vr, wtVr enums.Enum) func(init bool) {
	return func(init bool) {
		tsr := ss.Stats.Float64(name)
		if init {
			tsr.SetNumRows(0)
			plot.SetFirstStyler(tsr, func(s *plot.Style) {
				s.On = false
			})
			metadata.SetDoc(tsr, "Mean of "+vr.String()+" weighted by the intensity of "+wtVr.String())
			return
		}
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		cur := ctx.CurState
		sz := ss.Config.Size
		vri := int(vr.Int64())
		wti := int(wtVr.Int64())
		num, den := 0.0, 0.0
		var c math32.Vector3i
		for c.Z = range sz.Z {
			for c.Y = range sz.Y {
				for c.X = range sz.X {
					f := c.AddScalar(1)
					w := float64(State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, wti, cur])
					w *= w
					num += w * float64(State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur])
					den += w
				}
			}
		}
		if den > 0 {
			num /= den
		}
		tsr.AppendRowFloat(num)
	}
}

// StatVals returns the values recorded so far for the named stat,
// nil if there is no such stat.
func (ss *Sim) StatVals(name string) []float64 {
	tsrs, err := ss.Stats.Values(name)
	if err != nil || len(tsrs) != 1 {
		return nil
	}
	tsr := tsrs[0]
	n := tsr.Len()
	vals := make([]float64, n)
	for i := range n {
		vals[i] = tsr.Float1D(i)
	}
	return vals
}

// cfgHmagName is the stat holding |Phi|^2 as weighted by the given packet.
func cfgHmagName(vr enums.Enum) string {
	return "Hmag" + vr.String()
}

// cfgStep advances one step and records the stats, as StepRun does.
func cfgStep(ss *Sim) {
	ewStep(ss)
}

// cfgMean is the mean of vals, skipping the first: the first group velocity
// sample has no previous centroid to difference against and reads zero.
func cfgMean(vals []float64) float64 {
	if len(vals) < 2 {
		return 0
	}
	tot := 0.0
	for _, v := range vals[1:] {
		tot += v
	}
	return tot / float64(len(vals)-1)
}"""

// fraction of vacuum |Phi|^2 seen under the packet.
func cfgSpeed(sz int32, init func(*Sim), probe enums.Enum, amp float32, nst int) (vc, hfrac float64) {
	ss := cfgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
		s.Config.Amplitude = amp
		init(s)
	}, probe)
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	for range nst {
		cfgStep(ss)
	}
	vc = cfgMean(ss.StatVals(StatGroupVelName(probe, math32.X)))
	hfrac = math.Inf(1)
	for _, h := range ss.StatVals(cfgHmagName(probe)) {
		hfrac = math.Min(hfrac, h/v2)
	}
	return
}

func TestConfigHiggsSymmetric(t *testing.T) {
	ss := cfgSim(32, HiggsSymmetric)
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	for range 4000 {

		start, peak, last, v2)
	// the overshoot goes to |Phi| = sqrt(2) v, where V returns to zero: with no
	// dissipation the field rings between there and the origin forever.
	if peak < 1.5*v2 || peak > 2.5*v2 {
		t.Errorf("overshoot %g, expected about 2 v^2 = %g", peak, 2*v2)
	}
	if start > 0.01*v2 {
		t.Errorf("did not start near the symmetric point: %g vs v^2 = %g", start, v2)
	}
	if math.IsNaN(last) {
		t.Errorf("blew up")
	}
}

	var res [2]float64

			s.Params.Update()

	}
}

var thMag = "Mean" + EWHmag.String()

// thTail returns the values of the named stat recorded since index from.
func thTail(ss *Sim, name string, from int) []float64 {
	v := ss.StatVals(name)
	if from >= len(v) {
		return nil
	}
	return v[from:]
}

func thMin(v []float64) float64 {
	m := math.Inf(1)
	for _, x := range v {
		m = math.Min(m, x)
	}
	return m
}

func thMax(v []float64) float64 {
	m := math.Inf(-1)
	for _, x := range v {
		m = math.Max(m, x)
	}
	return m
}

'''

	ss := ewSim(6)
	defer thSetTemp(ss, 0)
	v0 := ss.Params.HiggsV // the cold VEV, where ewSim leaves the field
	ewStep(ss)             // EWHmag is kernel-written: step once to fill it
	start := ss.StatVals(thMag)[0]
	thSetTemp(ss, 1.5*ss.Params.TempCrit)
	if ss.Params.HiggsV != 0 {
		t.Fatalf("above TempCrit the VEV should be zero, got %g", ss.Params.HiggsV)
	}
	if ss.Params.MW != 0 || ss.Params.MZ != 0 {
		t.Errorf("above TempCrit the gauge bosons should be massless, got m_W %g m_Z %g",
			ss.Params.MW, ss.Params.MZ)
	}
	from := len(ss.StatVals(thMag))
	for range 4000 {
		ewStep(ss)
	}
	low := thMin(thTail(ss, thMag, from))
	t.Logf("heated to 1.5 Tc from v = %.5f: |Phi|^2 %.3e -> %.3e at its lowest (started %.3e)",
		v0, start, low, float64(v0)*float64(v0))
	if low > 0.05*start {
		t.Errorf("symmetry not restored: |Phi|^2 only fell from %g to %g", start, low)
	}
}

'''

n = '''func TestThermalQuench(t *testing.T) {
	ss := cfgSim(16, func(s *Sim) {
		s.Params.Temp = 1.25 * s.Params.TempCrit
		s.Params.Update()
		HiggsSymmetric(s)
	})
	defer thSetTemp(ss, 0)
	ewStep(ss) // EWHmag is kernel-written: step once to fill it
	hot := ss.StatVals(thMag)[0]
	for range 1000 { // above TempCrit this is a real minimum: must stay put
		ewStep(ss)
	}
	held := ss.StatVals(thMag)
	t.Logf("hot at %.2f Tc: |Phi|^2 %.3e -> %.3e after 1000 steps",
		ss.Params.Temp/ss.Params.TempCrit, hot, held[len(held)-1])
	if held[len(held)-1] > 4*hot+1e-12 {
		t.Errorf("symmetric phase should be stable above TempCrit: %g -> %g",
			hot, held[len(held)-1])
	}

	thSetTemp(ss, 0) // quench
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	from := len(held)
	for range 4000 {
		ewStep(ss)
	}
	cold := thTail(ss, thMag, from)
	peak, final := thMax(cold), cold[len(cold)-1]
	t.Logf("quenched to T = 0: |Phi|^2 peak %.5f, final %.5f  (v^2 = %.5f)", peak, final, v2)
	if peak < 0.5*v2 {
		t.Errorf("quench did not reach the broken vacuum: peak %g vs v^2 %g", peak, v2)
	}
	if math.IsNaN(final) {
		t.Errorf("quench blew up")
	}
}
'''

n = '''// StatGroupVel records, for each of the given variables, the intensity
// centroid along dim and the speed of that centroid in units of C: the group
// velocity of a wave packet. Both are recorded; only the velocity is plotted
// by default.
//
// The shift is measured over [StatGroupVelWindow] samples, so the first that
// many read zero. A packet crossing a wrapped edge is taken the short way
// round the box, so it does not register as a jump.
//
// A variable carrying a negligible share of the intensity in the group reads
// zero rather than the centroid of its own roundoff, which would otherwise be
// pure noise: in a Z pulse, for instance, the photon field is not excited at
// all. That is why these belong in one call rather than several -- besides
// sharing the one pass over the state, they calibrate each other.
func (ss *Sim) StatGroupVel(dim math32.Dims, vrs ...enums.Enum) func(init bool) {
	nv := len(vrs)
	ctrs := make([]float64, nv)
	wts := make([]float64, nv)
	var hist []float64
	var steps []int
	var n, win int
	return func(init bool) {
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		if init {
			win = max(StatGroupVelWindow, 1)
			hist = make([]float64, win*nv)
			steps = make([]int, win)
			n = 0
			for _, vr := range vrs {
				ct := ss.Stats.Float64(StatCentroidName(vr, dim))
				vt := ss.Stats.Float64(StatGroupVelName(vr, dim))
				ct.SetNumRows(0)
				vt.SetNumRows(0)
				plot.SetFirstStyler(ct, func(s *plot.Style) {
					s.On = false
				})
				plot.SetFirstStyler(vt, func(s *plot.Style) {
					s.On = true
				})
				metadata.SetDoc(ct, "Intensity centroid of "+vr.String()+" along "+dim.String()+", in cubes")
				metadata.SetDoc(vt, "Group velocity of "+vr.String()+" along "+dim.String()+", in units of C")
			}
			return
		}
		sz := ss.Config.Size
		ln := float64(sz.Dim(dim))
		StateCentroids(sz, dim, ctx.CurState, vrs, ctrs, wts)
		mx := 0.0
		for i := range nv {
			if wts[i] > mx {
				mx = wts[i]
			}
		}
		// the window slot about to be overwritten holds the oldest sample
		old := n % win
		have := n >= win
		ds := float64(int(ctx.Step) - steps[old])
		for i, vr := range vrs {
			vg := 0.0
			if have && ds > 0 && ss.Params.C > 0 && wts[i] > 1.0e-6*mx {
				d := ctrs[i] - hist[old*nv+i]
				if d > ln/2 {
					d -= ln
				} else if d < -ln/2 {
					d += ln
				}
				vg = d / ds / float64(ss.Params.C)
			}
			hist[old*nv+i] = ctrs[i]
			ss.Stats.Float64(StatCentroidName(vr, dim)).AppendRowFloat(ctrs[i])
			ss.Stats.Float64(StatGroupVelName(vr, dim)).AppendRowFloat(vg)
		}
		steps[old] = int(ctx.Step)
		n++
	}
}

	}

Done — 30 tests pass, all reading from the Stats data now.

## New stats methods in `stats.goal`

`StatGroupVel(dim, vrs...)` is the main one: intensity centroid along `dim` plus its speed in units of C, for any set of vars in one pass. Also `StatMean`, `StatSumSq`, `StatWeightedMean`, the `StateMean`/`StateCentroids` helpers, and `StatVals(name)` so tests (and anything else) can read a stat back.

`ElectroweakStats` now records `MeanHmag`, `SumHV`, group velocities for **AYs, ZY, BYs, W3Ys** along X, `W3Sq` (all four W³ components), and `HmagZY` (|Φ|² weighted by the Z packet). Also added group velocity to `WaveStats` and `SchrodingerStats` — for a matter wave that's the one that isn't the phase velocity.

## Two things the plot exposed that I had to fix

**A velocity read off consecutive samples is mostly carrier wobble.** |A|² for a carrier under an envelope has a term oscillating at 2ω, so the centroid jitters at the phase velocity. Raw per-step values swung ±0.3 around 0.7. `StatGroupVel` now differences over `StatGroupVelWindow` (20) samples — an exact moving-average velocity, not a filter, so it's unbiased. Wobble dropped to ±0.07.

That made the test *more* accurate than my hand-rolled probe:

```
Z       v = 0.68454 c, want 0.68470 c  (-0.0%)     was +0.8%
photon  v = 0.94878 c, want 0.98079 c  (-3.3%)     was -4.9%
```

**An unexcited field's centroid is pure roundoff.** In a Z pulse, `AYs` is ~zero, and its "velocity" came out as `13.3, -1.9, -0.4, ...` — noise that would wreck the plot scale. A variable now reads zero when it carries under 1e-6 of the intensity in its group. That's an argument for passing the four together rather than separately: they calibrate each other.

Which gives exactly the comparison you asked for:

```
Z pulse:       VgAYsX  0.000    VgZYX 0.711   VgBYsX 0.711   VgW3YsX 0.711
photon pulse:  VgAYsX  1.094    VgZYX 0.000   VgBYsX 1.094   VgW3YsX 1.094
```

B and W³ track whichever combination is excited and are *identical* to it — correct, since both configs write them as fixed multiples of one profile. A and Z are the ones that separate.

## Notes

Tests now use `ewStep`, which records stats, and `ewSim`/`cfgSim` register `ElectroweakStats`. I dropped `cfgCentroid`/`cfgSumSq`/`thMag` — superseded.

I also dropped the "W³ starts at zero" guard in the collision test: the stat's first sample is after one step, by which time the coupling has already produced some. The `YangMills=false` control subsumes it — if `WCollision` wrote W³ directly, that run would show it too.

Each stat is a full pass over the state, so on a 100³ box with `ViewInterval = 1` the six passes are a real cost. Noted in the `ElectroweakStats` doc; raising `ViewInterval` is the lever.

// StateAt returns the value of the given variable at the cell nearest to pos,
// in non-edge coordinates, clamped to the interior.
func StateAt(sz math32.Vector3i, vri int, pos math32.Vector3, curPrv int32) float32 {
	c := CoordToInt(pos)
	c.X = min(max(c.X, 0), sz.X-1)
	c.Y = min(max(c.Y, 0), sz.Y-1)
	c.Z = min(max(c.Z, 0), sz.Z-1)
	f := c.AddScalar(1)
	return State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, curPrv]
}

// Direction labels for [StatRadialName].
const (
	// StatRadialAxis is the +X direction, along a face axis of the stencil.
	StatRadialAxis = "X"

	// StatRadialDiag is the (1,1,1) direction, through a corner of the stencil.
	StatRadialDiag = "D"
)

// StatRadialName is the stat name for a radial sample: name, direction label
// and radius index.
func StatRadialName(name, dir string, i int) string {
	return name + dir + strconv.Itoa(i)
}

// StatRadial records the given variable sampled at radii of
// [Config.Wavelength], twice that and so on out to nrad, from [Config.Source],
// along +X and along the (1,1,1) diagonal.
//
// The two directions at the same radius are the point: a field that should be
// spherical reads the same both ways only if the discretization is isotropic,
// so the pair measures the anisotropy directly.
func (ss *Sim) StatRadial(name string, vr enums.Enum, nrad int) func(init bool) {
	return ss.statRadial(name, vr, nrad, false)
}

// StatRadialVec is [Sim.StatRadial] for the MAGNITUDE of the three-vector
// whose X component is vr, such as E or B.
func (ss *Sim) StatRadialVec(name string, vr enums.Enum, nrad int) func(init bool) {
	return ss.statRadial(name, vr, nrad, true)
}

func (ss *Sim) statRadial(name string, vr enums.Enum, nrad int, vec bool) func(init bool) {
	dirs := []string{StatRadialAxis, StatRadialDiag}
	unit := []math32.Vector3{{1, 0, 0}, {InvSqrt3, InvSqrt3, InvSqrt3}}
	return func(init bool) {
		what := "Value of " + vr.String()
		if vec {
			what = "Magnitude of the vector at " + vr.String()
		}
		for d, dir := range dirs {
			for i := 1; i <= nrad; i++ {
				tsr := ss.Stats.Float64(StatRadialName(name, dir, i))
				if init {
					tsr.SetNumRows(0)
					plot.SetFirstStyler(tsr, func(s *plot.Style) {
						s.On = !vec
					})
					metadata.SetDoc(tsr, what+" at "+strconv.Itoa(i)+
						" x Config.Wavelength from Config.Source, along "+dir)
					continue
				}
				ctx := GetCtx(0)
				sz := ss.Config.Size
				ctr := CenterF(ss.Config.Source)
				pos := ctr.Add(unit[d].MulScalar(float32(i) * ss.Config.Wavelength))
				vri := int(vr.Int64())
				v := float64(StateAt(sz, vri, pos, ctx.CurState))
				if vec {
					vy := float64(StateAt(sz, vri+1, pos, ctx.CurState))
					vz := float64(StateAt(sz, vri+2, pos, ctx.CurState))
					v = math.Sqrt(v*v + vy*vy + vz*vz)
				}
				tsr.AppendRowFloat(v)
			}
		}
	}
}

// wave of given carrier wavelength and mass, both in cube units:
//
//	omega = c sqrt(khat^2 + m^2),  khat = 2 sin(k/2)
//
// khat, not k: that is what the discrete Laplacian sees. Using k mistunes the
// packet and leaves a backward-moving remnant.
func (ss *Sim) LatticeFreq(wavelength, mass float32) float32 {
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	khat := 2 * math32.Sin(k/2)
	return ss.Params.C * math32.Sqrt(khat*khat+mass*mass)
}

// SlabPacket adds a ONE-WAY travelling wave packet"""
assert o in s

//////// initialization helpers

// emSourceI returns the integer cell of [Config.Source], where negatives mean
// the center.
func emSourceI(ss *Sim) math32.Vector3i {
	return CoordToInt(ss.Config.Source)
}

// emTransverse returns the potential and velocity variables for the transverse
// direction [Config.Polarization], and the orthogonal pair. A wave running
// along X can be polarized along Y or Z, and nothing else.
func emTransverse(ss *Sim) (pos, vel, orthoPos, orthoVel EMStates) {
	if ss.Config.Polarization == math32.Z {
		return AZs, AZv, AYs, AYv
	}
	return AYs, AYv, AZs, AZv
}

//////// configurations

// ElectricPotential puts a point charge at [Config.Source] and lets the scalar
// potential build up around it: A0 falls off as 1/r, and E = -grad A0 as 1/r^2.
//
// With Params.A0NoWave on (the default) the A0 update sets velocity from force
// rather than accumulating it, which makes it Jacobi relaxation of Poisson's
// equation instead of a wave. The potential fills in from the charge outward
// and settles. It is not quick: relaxation is diffusive, so reaching the far
// wall takes on the order of (L/pi)^2 / C^2 steps.
//
// Edges are damped, not wrapped. A net charge in a periodic box has an image
// in every neighboring copy and the potential never settles.
//
// Watch the A0 radial stats: the X and diagonal samples at the same radius
// should agree, which is what makes the 19-point stencil worth having, and
// successive radii should fall as 1/r.
func ElectricPotential(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesDamp
	ss.Params.A0NoWave.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.Point(Charge, Both, emSourceI(ss), ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// ChargeDipole is two opposite charges, one [Config.Wavelength] either side of
// [Config.Source] along X.
//
// The far field is the dipole one, falling as 1/r^3 rather than 1/r^2, because
// the two potentials cancel to leading order. Along the axis between them E is
// strongest and points from positive to negative; on the perpendicular bisector
// it is half the strength and points the other way.
func ChargeDipole(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesDamp
	ss.Params.A0NoWave.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Update()
	d := int32(ss.Config.Wavelength)
	c := emSourceI(ss)
	ss.Point(Charge, Both, math32.Vec3i(c.X-d, c.Y, c.Z), ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.Point(Charge, Both, math32.Vec3i(c.X+d, c.Y, c.Z), -ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// PolarizedPhoton sends a linearly polarized electromagnetic packet along X.
//
// Only the vector potential is set, in the single transverse component
// [Config.Polarization]. Everything else follows from the kernel: E = -dA/dt
// is along that same component, and B = curl A is along the OTHER transverse
// one. So with Y polarization you get E along Y and B along Z, and with Z
// polarization E along Z and B along -Y. E, B and the direction of travel are
// mutually perpendicular, and there is nothing along X: that is what makes it
// a transverse wave, and it is the whole content of "polarization" for a plane
// wave -- which of the two transverse directions E points along.
//
// A longitudinal wave is not available to pick, and that is not an omission:
// setting AX instead would be pure gauge, giving E = B = 0.
func PolarizedPhoton(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	pos, vel, _, _ := emTransverse(ss)
	om := ss.LatticeFreq(ss.Config.Wavelength, 0)
	cx := float32(ss.Config.Size.X) * 0.25
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel, math32.X, cx, 1, 1, om, 0)
}

// CircularPolarization sends a circularly polarized packet along X: both
// transverse components at once, a quarter cycle out of step.
//
// A_pol goes as cos(kx - wt) and the orthogonal component as sin(kx - wt), so
// their sum has constant magnitude and a direction that turns. At a fixed
// point E rotates in the transverse plane once per period; at a fixed time it
// traces a helix along X. Neither component is doing anything a linear wave
// does not do -- circular polarization is not a third kind of wave, it is two
// linear ones added with a phase offset, which is why any polarization can be
// written in either basis.
//
// [Config.Polarization] picks which component leads, and that is the
// handedness: Y leading Z turns one way, Z leading Y the other.
func CircularPolarization(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	pos, vel, opos, ovel := emTransverse(ss)
	om := ss.LatticeFreq(ss.Config.Wavelength, 0)
	cx := float32(ss.Config.Size.X) * 0.25
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel, math32.X, cx, 1, 1, om, 0)
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(opos, ovel, math32.X, cx, 1, 1, om, -PiOver2)
}

// StandingWave is two identical polarized packets sent at each other along X.
//
// Where they overlap E and B are both standing rather than travelling, and
// their nodes are a quarter wavelength apart: E vanishes where B is largest.
// That offset is the whole reason a standing wave stores energy without
// transporting it -- the Poynting vector E x B averages to zero.
func StandingWave(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	pos, vel, _, _ := emTransverse(ss)
	om := ss.LatticeFreq(ss.Config.Wavelength, 0)
	xl := float32(ss.Config.Size.X)
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel, math32.X, xl*0.3, 1, 1, om, 0)
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel, math32.X, xl*0.7, 1, -1, om, 0)
}

// MovingCharge shows the magnetic field that moving charge produces: a
// uniformly charged line along X, moving along its own length at
// [Config.Velocity].X, which is a current.
//
// A line rather than a blob, because this kernel has no advection: charge and
// current are set once and stay put. A line of charge sliding along itself is
// the one moving-charge configuration for which that is exactly right, since
// the density it leaves behind is the density it had. Anything localized would
// need the charge to actually move, and would violate continuity.
//
// The result is E pointing radially away from the line and B circling around
// it, with |B|/|E| = v/c^2. Set the velocity to zero and B disappears while E
// stays: magnetism is what electric charge looks like when it moves.
func MovingCharge(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesDamp
	ss.Params.A0NoWave.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Update()
	v := ss.Config.Velocity.X
	if v == 0 {
		v = 0.5 * ss.Params.C
	}
	c := CenterFull(emSourceI(ss))
	q := ss.Config.Amplitude
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	for x := int32(1); x <= sz.X; x++ {
		State[c.Z, c.Y, x, Charge, cur] += q
		State[c.Z, c.Y, x, Charge, prv] += q
		State[c.Z, c.Y, x, CurrentX, cur] += q * v
		State[c.Z, c.Y, x, CurrentX, prv] += q * v
	}
}

// MaxwellConfigs are the initialization options offered in the GUI.
var MaxwellConfigs = []InitFunc{
	InitFunc{Name: "Electric Potential", Doc: "A point charge at Config.Source: A0 relaxes to 1/r and E to 1/r^2; watch the A0 radial stats", Func: ElectricPotential, Current: true},
	InitFunc{Name: "Charge Dipole", Doc: "Two opposite charges: the far field falls as 1/r^3 because the potentials cancel to leading order", Func: ChargeDipole},
	InitFunc{Name: "Polarized Photon", Doc: "A linearly polarized packet along X, in the Config.Polarization transverse direction; E along it, B along the other", Func: PolarizedPhoton},
	InitFunc{Name: "Circular Polarization", Doc: "Both transverse components a quarter cycle apart, so E turns as it travels; Config.Polarization picks the handedness", Func: CircularPolarization},
	InitFunc{Name: "Standing Wave", Doc: "Two packets sent at each other: E and B stand still with nodes a quarter wavelength apart", Func: StandingWave},
	InitFunc{Name: "Moving Charge", Doc: "A charged line moving along itself at Config.Velocity.X: E radial, B circling, with |B|/|E| = v/c^2", Func: MovingCharge},
}

// MaxwellStats adds the stats plotted over time in the GUI.
func (ss *Sim) MaxwellStats() {
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatStep())
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatRadial("A0", A0s, EMNRadii))
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatRadialVec("Emag", EX, EMNRadii))
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatRadialVec("Bmag", BX, EMNRadii))
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatGroupVel(math32.X, AYs, AZs))
}

// EMNRadii is how many Config.Wavelength steps out the radial stats sample.
const EMNRadii = 4
GOALEOF

// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

// emSim builds a 3D Maxwell sim and runs one of the MaxwellConfigs on it.
func emSim(sz int32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = Maxwell
	ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, sz, sz)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.StateVars = EMStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	ss.MaxwellStats()
	ss.InitFunc = init
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

func emStep(ss *Sim) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	ctx.StepInc()
	ns := int(ctx.Size.X * ctx.Size.Y * ctx.Size.Z)
	RunMaxwellKernel(ns)
	switch ss.Params.Edges {
	case EdgesWrap:
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	case EdgesDamp:
		RunMaxwellDampKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	ss.RunStats(false)
}

// emLast is the most recent value of the named stat.
func emLast(ss *Sim, name string) float64 {
	v := ss.StatVals(name)
	if len(v) == 0 {
		return math.NaN()
	}
	return v[len(v)-1]
}

// TestElectricPotential: A0 must relax to 1/r and E to 1/r^2, the same in both
// directions sampled.
func TestElectricPotential(t *testing.T) {
	ss := emSim(40, ElectricPotential)
	ss.Config.Wavelength = 4 // radii 4, 8, 12, 16 inside a 40 box
	for range 6000 {
		emStep(ss)
	}
	for _, dir := range []string{StatRadialAxis, StatRadialDiag} {
		for i := 1; i < EMNRadii; i++ {
			r0, r1 := float64(i), float64(i+1)
			a0, a1 := emLast(ss, StatRadialName("A0", dir, i)), emLast(ss, StatRadialName("A0", dir, i+1))
			e0, e1 := emLast(ss, StatRadialName("Emag", dir, i)), emLast(ss, StatRadialName("Emag", dir, i+1))
			t.Logf("%s r=%.0f->%.0f: A0 %.5f -> %.5f (ratio %.3f want %.3f)  |E| %.3e -> %.3e (ratio %.3f want %.3f)",
				dir, r0, r1, a0, a1, a0/a1, r1/r0, e0, e1, e0/e1, (r1/r0)*(r1/r0))
		}
	}
	for i := 1; i <= EMNRadii; i++ {
		ax := emLast(ss, StatRadialName("A0", StatRadialAxis, i))
		dg := emLast(ss, StatRadialName("A0", StatRadialDiag, i))
		t.Logf("anisotropy at r=%d: axis %.5f diag %.5f  ratio %.4f", i, ax, dg, ax/dg)
	}
}

		ElectricPotential(s)

			a[i] = emLast(ss, StatRadialName("A0", dir, i))

		// R is where the potential reaches zero: solve from the two ends
		// A0(r) = k(1/r - 1/R)
		r1, rn := wl, wl*float64(EMNRadii)
		k := (a[1] - a[EMNRadii]) / (1/r1 - 1/rn)

				dir, r, a[i], want, 100*(a[i]/want-1))

}

Found it — my sampling truncates coordinates, so the diagonal samples sit at shorter radii than intended. That's a measurement bug, not anisotropy:

<details>
<summary>Tool Calls (8)</summary>

- **Bash**: `Ran `cd /Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim && python3 - <<'PYEOF'
p='stats.goal'
s=open(p).read()
o = """// Direction labels for [StatRadialName]."""
n = """// StateAtInterp returns the trilinearly interpolated value of the given
// variable at pos, in non-edge coordinates, clamped to the interior.
//
// Interpolated rather than nearest-cell because the radial stats compare an
// axis against a diagonal: [CoordToInt] truncates, which along a diagonal
// shortens the radius by up to 13% and reads as an anisotropy that is not
// there.
func StateAtInterp(sz math32.Vector3i, vri int, pos math32.Vector3, curPrv int32) float32 {
	b := math32.Vec3i(int32(math32.Floor(pos.X)), int32(math32.Floor(pos.Y)), int32(math32.Floor(pos.Z)))
	f := pos.Sub(CoordToFloat(b))
	tot := float32(0)
	for k := range 2 {
		wz := f.Z
		if k == 0 {
			wz = 1 - f.Z
		}
		for j := range 2 {
			wy := f.Y
			if j == 0 {
				wy = 1 - f.Y
			}
			for i := range 2 {
				wx := f.X
				if i == 0 {
					wx = 1 - f.X
				}
				c := math32.Vec3i(b.X+int32(i), b.Y+int32(j), b.Z+int32(k))
				c.X = min(max(c.X, 0), sz.X-1)
				c.Y = min(max(c.Y, 0), sz.Y-1)
				c.Z = min(max(c.Z, 0), sz.Z-1)
				g := c.AddScalar(1)
				tot += wx * wy * wz * State[g.Z, g.Y, g.X, vri, curPrv]
			}
		}
	}
	return tot
}

// Direction labels for [StatRadialName]."""
assert o in s
s = s.replace(o, n, 1)
s = s.replace("""				v := float64(StateAt(sz, vri, pos, ctx.CurState))
				if vec {
					vy := float64(StateAt(sz, vri+1, pos, ctx.CurState))
					vz := float64(StateAt(sz, vri+2, pos, ctx.CurState))""",
"""				v := float64(StateAtInterp(sz, vri, pos, ctx.CurState))
				if vec {
					vy := float64(StateAtInterp(sz, vri+1, pos, ctx.CurState))
					vz := float64(StateAtInterp(sz, vri+2, pos, ctx.CurState))""")
open(p,'w').write(s)

// emRMS is the root mean square of a variable over the interior.
func emRMS(sz int32, vr EMStates) float64 {
	var s float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	n := 0
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(vr), cur))
				s += v * v
				n++
			}
		}
	}
	return math.Sqrt(s / float64(n))
}

// emLine samples a variable along X at fixed y, z.
func emLine(sz int32, vr EMStates, y, z int32) []float64 {
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	v := make([]float64, sz)
	for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
		v[x-1] = float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(vr), cur))
	}
	return v
}

// TestPolarizedPhoton: only the vector potential is set, and everything else
// follows. E must come out along the polarization, B along the other
// transverse direction, nothing along the direction of travel, and |E|/|B| = c.
func TestPolarizedPhoton(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 32
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name          string
		pol           math32.Dims
		wantE, wantB  EMStates
		otherE, otherB EMStates
	}{
		{"Y", math32.Y, EY, BZ, EZ, BY},
		{"Z", math32.Z, EZ, BY, EY, BZ},
	} {
		ss := emSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Polarization = tc.pol
			s.Config.Wavelength = 8
			s.Config.PacketWidth = 12
			PolarizedPhoton(s)
		})
		for range 20 {
			emStep(ss)
		}
		e := emRMS(sz, tc.wantE)
		b := emRMS(sz, tc.wantB)
		eo := emRMS(sz, tc.otherE)
		bo := emRMS(sz, tc.otherB)
		ex := emRMS(sz, EX)
		bx := emRMS(sz, BX)
		c := float64(ss.Params.C)
		t.Logf("%s-polarized: |%v|=%.4f |%v|=%.4f  E/B=%.4f (c=%.2f)   other transverse %.1e/%.1e  along travel %.1e/%.1e",
			tc.name, tc.wantE, e, tc.wantB, b, e/b, c, eo, bo, ex, bx)
		if math.Abs(e/b/c-1) > 0.05 {
			t.Errorf("%s: |E|/|B| = %g, want c = %g", tc.name, e/b, c)
		}
		if eo > 1e-6*e || bo > 1e-6*b {
			t.Errorf("%s: the other transverse direction is not empty: E %g B %g", tc.name, eo, bo)
		}
		if ex > 1e-6*e || bx > 1e-6*b {
			t.Errorf("%s: something along the direction of travel: E %g B %g", tc.name, ex, bx)
		}
	}
}

// TestCircularPolarization: adding the two transverse components a quarter
// cycle apart must give a transverse |E| that barely varies along the packet,
// where a linear wave swings to zero twice a wavelength.
func TestCircularPolarization(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 32
	ripple := func(init func(*Sim)) (float64, *Sim) {
		ss := emSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Wavelength = 8
			s.Config.PacketWidth = 16
			init(s)
		})
		for range 20 {
			emStep(ss)
		}
		ey := emLine(sz, EY, sz/2, sz/2)
		ez := emLine(sz, EZ, sz/2, sz/2)
		// over one wavelength at the packet center, where the envelope is flat
		lo, hi := math.Inf(1), 0.0
		ctr := int(float32(sz) * 0.25)
		for x := ctr - 4; x <= ctr+4; x++ {
			m := ey[x]*ey[x] + ez[x]*ez[x]
			lo = math.Min(lo, m)
			hi = math.Max(hi, m)
		}
		return (hi - lo) / (hi + lo), ss
	}
	lin, _ := ripple(PolarizedPhoton)
	cir, _ := ripple(CircularPolarization)
	t.Logf("|E_transverse|^2 ripple over one wavelength: linear %.3f, circular %.3f", lin, cir)
	if lin < 0.9 {
		t.Errorf("a linear wave should swing to zero: ripple %g", lin)
	}
	if cir > 0.1 {
		t.Errorf("a circular wave should have near-constant |E|: ripple %g", cir)
	}
}

// TestStandingWave: in a travelling wave E and B rise and fall together; in a
// standing one their nodes are a quarter wavelength apart, so they are
// anti-correlated.
func TestStandingWave(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 48
	corr := func(init func(*Sim), nst int) float64 {
		ss := emSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Wavelength = 8
			s.Config.PacketWidth = 24
			init(s)
		})
		for range nst {
			emStep(ss)
		}
		e := emLine(sz, EY, sz/2, sz/2)
		b := emLine(sz, BZ, sz/2, sz/2)
		// correlate the magnitudes over the middle of the box, where the two
		// packets of the standing case overlap
		var se, sb, see, sbb, seb float64
		n := 0.0
		for x := sz/4 - 1; x < 3*sz/4; x++ {
			ea, ba := math.Abs(e[x]), math.Abs(b[x])
			se += ea
			sb += ba
			see += ea * ea
			sbb += ba * ba
			seb += ea * ba
			n++
		}
		cov := seb/n - (se/n)*(sb/n)
		return cov / math.Sqrt((see/n-(se/n)*(se/n))*(sbb/n-(sb/n)*(sb/n)))
	}
	trav := corr(PolarizedPhoton, 20)
	stand := corr(StandingWave, 60)
	t.Logf("correlation of |E| with |B| along X: travelling %+.3f, standing %+.3f", trav, stand)
	if trav < 0.9 {
		t.Errorf("travelling wave: |E| and |B| should move together, got %g", trav)
	}
	if stand > -0.3 {
		t.Errorf("standing wave: |E| and |B| nodes should be a quarter wave apart, got %g", stand)
	}
}

// TestMovingCharge: a charged line moving along itself makes B circle it, with
// |B|/|E| = v/c^2. At rest there is no B at all.
func TestMovingCharge(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 24
	run := func(v float32) (eRMS, bRMS, bz float64, ss *Sim) {
		ss = emSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Velocity.X = v
			MovingCharge(s)
		})
		for range 1500 {
			emStep(ss)
		}
		cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
		// a point offset in +Y from the wire: B should be along +Z there,
		// since the current is along +X and x_hat cross y_hat is z_hat
		c := sz / 2
		bz = float64(State.Value(int(c), int(c+4), int(c), int(BZ), cur))
		return emRMS(sz, EY), emRMS(sz, BZ), bz, ss
	}
	e0, b0, _, _ := run(0)
	t.Logf("at rest:  |E_y| = %.4e, |B_z| = %.4e", e0, b0)
	if b0 > 1e-8*e0 {
		t.Errorf("a charge at rest should make no magnetic field: %g vs E %g", b0, e0)
	}
	v := float32(0.25)
	e1, b1, bz, ss := run(v)
	c := float64(ss.Params.C)
	want := float64(v) / (c * c)
	t.Logf("moving at v=%.2f (c=%.2f): |E_y| = %.4e, |B_z| = %.4e, ratio %.4f, want v/c^2 = %.4f",
		v, c, e1, b1, b1/e1, want)
	t.Logf("B_z 4 cubes in +Y from the wire: %+.4e (positive = circulating as x cross y)", bz)
	if bz <= 0 {
		t.Errorf("B should circulate the other way: B_z = %g at +Y", bz)
	}
	if math.Abs(b1/e1/want-1) > 0.15 {
		t.Errorf("|B|/|E| = %g, want v/c^2 = %g", b1/e1, want)
	}
}

  // Sine adds sine wave values along given dimension, to given variable.
  func (ss *Sim) Sine(vr enums.Enum, dim math32.Dims, wavelength, phase, amp, off float32) {
  	vri := int(vr.Int64())
  	ctx := GetCtx(0)
  	cur := ctx.CurState
  	sz := ss.Config.Size
  	var c math32.Vector3i
  	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
  		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
  			for c.X = range sz.X {
  				f := c.AddScalar(1)
  				dv := float32(c.Dim(dim))
  				v := off + amp*math32.Sin(TwoPi*((dv+phase)/wavelength))
  				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
  			}
  		}
  	}
  }
