// TestMovingWavePacket: the rewritten packet must actually travel, at the
// lattice group velocity, instead of splitting into two halves going opposite
// ways. A split packet has a centroid that barely moves, so the speed is a
// decisive test of it.
func TestMovingWavePacket(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	ss := drSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
		s.Config.Wavelength = 16
		s.Config.PacketWidth = 16
		s.MovingWavePacketConfig(Dirac1As, Dirac1Av, math32.X, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), 1, 0, 1)
	})
	p := ss.Params
	k := 2 * math.Pi / float64(ss.Config.Wavelength)
	kh := 2 * math.Sin(k/2)
	m := math.Sqrt(float64(p.MOverHSq))
	want := kh * math.Cos(k/2) / math.Sqrt(kh*kh+m*m) // in units of c
	ctr := func() float64 {
		var num, den float64
		cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
		c := int(sz / 2)
		for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
			v := float64(State.Value(c, c, int(x), int(Dirac1As), cur))
			num += v * v * float64(x)
			den += v * v
		}
		return num / den
	}
	drStepExt(ss)
	c0 := ctr()
	nst := 60
	for range nst {
		drStepExt(ss)
	}
	got := (ctr() - c0) / float64(nst) / float64(p.C)
	t.Logf("packet centroid %.2f -> %.2f over %d steps: v = %.4f c, group velocity %.4f c",
		c0, ctr(), nst, got, want)
	if math.Abs(got/want-1) > 0.15 {
		t.Errorf("packet speed %g c, want %g c: a split packet barely moves", got, want)
	}
}

## MovingWavePacket, properly

All the fitted constants are gone — `vamp`, `vwavelength`, `vwidth`, `vphase`, `veloff`, the `wavelength > 20` regime switch, and the `0.996`/`0.997` fudges on the previous-step velocity. The whole thing is now the two lines it should have been:

```go
pv := WavePacket(dd, dl, wavelength, width, phase, amp)
vv := dir * om * WavePacket(dd, dl, wavelength, width, phase-0.25, amp)
```

For $\psi = \text{env}\cos(kx + \phi - \text{dir}\,\omega t)$ the time derivative is $\text{dir}\,\omega\,\text{env}\sin(kx+\phi)$, and a quarter cycle of the carrier turns the cosine into the sine — so the velocity is the same packet shifted by −¼ and scaled by $\text{dir}\cdot\omega$. No spatial-translation trick, no fitting.

The frequency comes from a new `Sim.PacketFreq(wavelength)`, which picks the **lattice** dispersion for whichever equation is running: massless for Wave and Maxwell, $c\sqrt{\hat k^2 + m^2}$ where there's a mass. That's what the old version couldn't know, and using continuum $k$ instead is exactly what leaves a counter-propagating remnant.

```
packet centroid 33.04 -> 45.87 over 30 steps: v = 0.8557 c, group velocity 0.9684 c
```

It travels. (The 12% shortfall is real dispersion: a Gaussian envelope is a spread of wavenumbers, and at width 16 that's a broad spread. Wider packets tighten it — same effect as in the photon test.)

**One thing that caught me:** my first run measured 0.12 c and I nearly went hunting for a bug. The packet had simply wrapped around the box and straddled both edges, breaking the centroid. Profile dump settled it. Test now runs 30 steps instead of 60.

**Schrödinger was misusing this API** — `waves.go` passed `CabAs, CabBs` as *posVar, velVar*, i.e. using the velocity slot for the imaginary component. That worked by accident with the old fudge and would have been wrong by a factor of ω with the correct version. Added `ComplexPacket`/`ComplexPacketConfig` for first-order complex waves, where both components get the same amplitude a quarter cycle apart, and pointed `waves.go` at it.

## SpinInPotential

An electron lump offset from a fixed 1/r well, pulled in:

```
lump centroid 25.00 -> 20.56 (well at 16.0), A0 probe 0.00255 -> 0.00255
```

Getting the external field to stay external needed a new parameter. The Dirac kernel **overwrites `Charge` every step** with the wave's own charge, so a nucleus left in that variable is erased on the first step — and with Maxwell running, A₀ relaxes away from whatever you put there. So the potential goes straight into `A0s`, and `Params.SelfField` (default off) now gates whether `MaxwellKernel` runs at all:

> SelfField determines whether the wave sources its own electromagnetic field. Off, the field is whatever was put there at init and stays fixed: an EXTERNAL potential.

The test asserts A₀ doesn't budge (0.00255 → 0.00255), which is the thing that would silently break.

`ChargeSelfField` opts in; `SpinPrecession` explicitly opts out, since its uniform `BZ` has to stay put too. Well depth is scaled to 20% of the rest energy, for the `kgSelfScale` reason — past that you're in the Klein regime. Edges damped so the unbound part can leave instead of wrapping back.

p='schrodinger.goal'; s=open(p).read()
a = s.index("// SchrodingerKernel is the kernel")

n = '''// SchrodingerKernel is the kernel for Schrodinger's equation, as a staggered
// leapfrog on the real and imaginary parts.
//
// Splitting i hbar d(chi)/dt = H chi into chi = a + ib gives
//
//	da/dt = -(hbar/2m) Lap b + (V/hbar) b
//	db/dt = +(hbar/2m) Lap a - (V/hbar) a
//
// so each part is driven entirely by the other. Updating both from the same
// old values is unstable -- it is a rotation being integrated by a method that
// does not rotate, the same failure the complex Klein-Gordon equation has
// without Params.Boris. The fix is to stagger them: advance a using the old b,
// then advance b using the NEW a. That is Visscher's scheme, and it is
// explicitly stable, second order, and conserves a modified norm exactly.
//
// It is also the only form this can take in a cellular automaton. Advancing b
// with the new a means reading the new a at the NEIGHBORS, which one local
// pass cannot see -- so the update has to alternate between steps, a on even
// and b on odd, with the other carried forward. The alternation is not a hack
// around the instability; it is what makes the stable scheme local. Two sim
// steps make one full leapfrog step, so time runs at half rate here compared
// with the second-order equations.
//
// Stability needs (hbar / 2m) < about 1: the Laplacian's extreme eigenvalue is
// near 2 and the leapfrog tolerates a product under 2. SchrodingerConfig sets
// a mass that satisfies it, which the Klein-Gordon default does NOT.
func SchrodingerKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	pposA := State[z, y, x, CabAs, prv]
	pposB := State[z, y, x, CabBs, prv]
	pvelA := State[z, y, x, CabAv, prv]
	pvelB := State[z, y, x, CabBv, prv]
	vpot := State[z, y, x, CabV, prv]

	hbar := Params[0].Hbar
	hm := Params[0].HSqOver2M / hbar // hbar / 2m
	voh := vpot / hbar

	var velA, posA, velB, posB float32
	if cur == 0 { // a moves, driven by b
		var lap float32
		if Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue() {
			lap = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(CabBs), prv, pposB)
		} else {
			lap = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(CabBs), prv, pposB)
		}
		velA = -hm*lap + voh*pposB // first order: velocity IS the derivative
		posA = pposA + velA
		velB = pvelB // b carried forward, to move on the next step
		posB = pposB
	} else { // b moves, driven by the a that just moved
		var lap float32
		if Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue() {
			lap = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(CabAs), prv, pposA)
		} else {
			lap = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(CabAs), prv, pposA)
		}
		velB = hm*lap - voh*pposA
		posB = pposB + velB
		velA = pvelA
		posA = pposA
	}

	State[z, y, x, CabAv, cur] = velA
	State[z, y, x, CabAs, cur] = posA

	State[z, y, x, CabBv, cur] = velB
	State[z, y, x, CabBs, cur] = posB

	State[z, y, x, CabMag, cur] = posA*posA + posB*posB
}

'''

func (ss *Sim) Quadratic(vr enums.Enum, ctr math32.Vector3, coef float32) {
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	ctr = CenterF(ctr)
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				d := CoordToFloat(c).Sub(ctr).Length()
				v := coef * d * d
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, prv] += v
			}
		}
	}
}

// Expo adds amp * exp(-r / decay) centered at ctr: the shape of a bound state
// in a Coulomb potential, as opposed to the gaussian of a harmonic one.
func (ss *Sim) Expo(vr enums.Enum, curPrev CurPrevBoth, ctr math32.Vector3, decay, amp float32) {
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	ctr = CenterF(ctr)
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				d := CoordToFloat(c).Sub(ctr).Length()
				v := amp * math32.FastExp(-d/decay)
				if curPrev == CurOnly || curPrev == Both {
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
				}
				if curPrev == PrevOnly || curPrev == Both {
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, prv] += v
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

// SineBox adds the product of half-sine waves that vanish on the walls, which
// is the ground state of a particle in a box: sin(n pi x / L) in each
// dimension that is more than one cube deep, with L the wall separation.
// Use with EdgesFixed, which is what holds the walls at zero.
func (ss *Sim) SineBox(vr enums.Enum, curPrev CurPrevBoth, n int32, amp float32) {
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	fn := float32(n)
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				v := amp
				for d := math32.X; d <= math32.Z; d++ {
					ln := sz.Dim(d)
					if ln <= 1 {
						continue
					}
					// walls sit at 0 and ln+1, so the separation is ln+1
					v *= math32.Sin(fn * math32.Pi * float32(c.Dim(d)+1) / float32(ln+1))
				}
				if curPrev == CurOnly || curPrev == Both {
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, cur] += v
				}
				if curPrev == PrevOnly || curPrev == Both {
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vri, prv] += v
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

// InvR adds 1/r values radiating from given center point,'''

// schrodOmega returns the angular frequency of the harmonic well, in radians
// per LEAPFROG step. A sim step advances half of one, so the period you count
// on screen is twice 2 pi / omega.
func schrodOmega(ss *Sim) float32 {
	return 2 * math32.Pi / SchrodPeriod
}

// SchrodPeriod is the harmonic oscillator period in leapfrog steps.
const SchrodPeriod = 320

// HarmonicOscillator is the classic: a particle in a parabolic well
// V = (1/2) m omega^2 r^2, started as its own ground state pushed off center.
//
// That displaced ground state is a coherent state, and it is the one quantum
// state that behaves exactly like a classical particle: it swings back and
// forth at omega and does NOT spread, because the well squeezes it back
// together as fast as dispersion pulls it apart. Any other starting width
// breathes as well as swinging.
//
// The ground state width is sqrt(hbar / m omega), which is set from the period
// rather than chosen, so the two are not free to disagree.
func HarmonicOscillator(ss *Sim) {
	p := ss.Params
	om := schrodOmega(ss)
	ss.Quadratic(CabV, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), 0.5*p.Mass*om*om)
	w := math32.Sqrt(p.Hbar / (p.Mass * om)) // ground state width
	ctr := math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)
	ctr.X = float32(ss.Config.Size.X)*0.5 + 2*w
	ss.Gauss(CabAs, Both, ctr, w, ss.Config.Amplitude, 0)
}

// BoxStandingWave is a particle in a box: the walls hold the wave at zero, and
// the state is the lowest standing wave that fits between them.
//
// It is an energy eigenstate, so nothing about |chi|^2 moves at all -- the two
// components turn into each other at the rate E / hbar and their squares add
// to a constant. Stationary states being genuinely stationary is the whole
// content of "energy level", and it is worth seeing that it is not an
// approximation here.
func BoxStandingWave(ss *Sim) {
	ss.SineBox(CabAs, Both, 1, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// BoxTwoStates is the same box holding the lowest two standing waves at once.
//
// Neither one moves on its own, but they turn at different rates, E1/hbar and
// E2/hbar, so their sum beats: |chi|^2 sloshes from one side to the other and
// back at the DIFFERENCE frequency. Every visible motion in a bound quantum
// system is a beat between levels like this one.
func BoxTwoStates(ss *Sim) {
	a := ss.Config.Amplitude
	ss.SineBox(CabAs, Both, 1, a)
	ss.SineBox(CabAs, Both, 2, a)
}

// HydrogenGround is as close to a hydrogen atom as this equation gets: an
// attractive 1/r well with the electron in its ground state, exp(-r/a).
//

// well depth is set from the Bohr radius here rather than picked, which is
// what makes the state actually stationary. Watch Mag sit still.
//
// Two caveats worth knowing. The 1/r singularity is softened to its value one
// cube out, since a lattice cannot hold an infinity; that shifts the true
// ground state slightly, so the wave breathes a little rather than sitting
// perfectly still. And this is one electron in a fixed external potential, not
// a nucleus and an electron finding each other -- there is no back-reaction,
// and no second electron, so no chemistry.
func HydrogenGround(ss *Sim) {
	p := ss.Params
	a := SchrodBohr
	k := p.Hbar * p.Hbar / (p.Mass * a)
	ss.InvR(CabV, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), -k)
	ss.Expo(CabAs, Both, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), a, ss.Config.Amplitude)

}

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

func scSim(sz int32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = Schrodinger
	ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, sz, sz)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.StateVars = CabStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	ss.InitFunc = init
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

func scStep(ss *Sim) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	ctx.StepInc()
	RunSchrodingerKernel(int(ctx.Size.X * ctx.Size.Y * ctx.Size.Z))
	ss.RunStats(false)
}

func scNorm(sz int32) float64 {
	return StateSum(GetCtx(0).Size.V(), CabMag, GetCtx(0).CurState)
}

// scCtrX is the |chi|^2 weighted X centroid.
func scCtrX(sz int32) float64 {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(CabMag), cur))
				num += v * float64(x)
				den += v
			}
		}
	}
	return num / den
}

// TestSchrodNorm: the staggered scheme must hold the norm. Visscher's scheme
// conserves a modified norm exactly, so the drift should be tiny and bounded
// rather than growing -- which is what the naive simultaneous update does.
func TestSchrodNorm(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 24
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name string
		init func(*Sim)
	}{
		{"BoxStandingWave", BoxStandingWave},
		{"HarmonicOscillator", HarmonicOscillator},
		{"HydrogenGround", HydrogenGround},
	} {
		ss := scSim(sz, tc.init)
		scStep(ss)
		n0 := scNorm(sz)
		lo, hi := n0, n0
		for range 2000 {
			scStep(ss)
			n := scNorm(sz)
			lo, hi = math.Min(lo, n), math.Max(hi, n)
		}
		t.Logf("%-19s norm %.5f, varies by %.2e (%.3f%%) over 2000 steps",
			tc.name, n0, hi-lo, 100*(hi-lo)/n0)
		if math.IsNaN(hi) {
			t.Errorf("%s blew up", tc.name)
		}
		if (hi-lo)/n0 > 0.02 {
			t.Errorf("%s: norm varies by %.1f%%", tc.name, 100*(hi-lo)/n0)
		}
	}
}

// TestSchrodBoxStationary: an energy eigenstate must be stationary -- the two
// components turn into each other and their squares add to a constant.
func TestSchrodBoxStationary(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 16
	ss := scSim(sz, BoxStandingWave)
	scStep(ss)
	c := int(sz / 2)
	cur := func() float64 {
		return float64(State.Value(c, c, c, int(CabMag), int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
	}
	m0 := cur()
	lo, hi := m0, m0
	for range 2000 {
		scStep(ss)
		lo, hi = math.Min(lo, cur()), math.Max(hi, cur())
	}
	t.Logf("box ground state |chi|^2 at center: %.5f, varies by %.2e (%.3f%%)",
		m0, hi-lo, 100*(hi-lo)/m0)
	if (hi-lo)/m0 > 0.02 {
		t.Errorf("an eigenstate should not move: |chi|^2 varies by %.1f%%", 100*(hi-lo)/m0)
	}
}

// TestSchrodCoherent: a displaced ground state in a harmonic well swings at
// omega and does not spread. The period is the one the well was built from,
// doubled because a sim step is half a leapfrog step.
func TestSchrodCoherent(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 40
	ss := scSim(sz, HarmonicOscillator)
	want := 2 * float64(SchrodPeriod) // sim steps per swing
	scStep(ss)
	mid := float64(sz) / 2
	// count zero crossings of (centroid - center) to get the period
	prev := scCtrX(sz) - mid
	first, last, n := -1, -1, 0
	nst := int(3 * want)
	for i := range nst {
		scStep(ss)
		c := scCtrX(sz) - mid
		if prev < 0 && c >= 0 {
			if first < 0 {
				first = i
			}
			last = i
			n++
		}
		prev = c
	}
	if n < 2 {
		t.Fatalf("only %d crossings in %d steps: the packet is not swinging", n, nst)
	}
	got := float64(last-first) / float64(n-1)
	t.Logf("coherent state period %.1f sim steps, want %.1f (%+.1f%%)", got, want, 100*(got/want-1))
	if math.Abs(got/want-1) > 0.1 {
		t.Errorf("period %g, want %g", got, want)
	}
}
EOF

For now I'm settling on a pragmatic path: keep the simple a²+b² display quantity, but loosen tolerance thresholds slightly and note in the docs that this ripple is an inherent feature of the leapfrog scheme rather than a bug, while still trying to compute the true staggered norm cheaply by carrying forward the b value from the previous half-step.

Schrödinger is done — 49 tests pass, 13 validations, everything builds.

## The alternation is not a hack — keep it

It's **Visscher's scheme**, the standard explicit method for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation: real and imaginary parts staggered by half a time step. Advance `a` using the old `b`, then `b` using the *new* `a`. It's explicitly stable, second order, and conserves a modified norm exactly.

And it has to be an alternation *here specifically*, because advancing `b` with the new `a` means reading the new `a` at the **neighbours** — which one local pass can't see. So the update alternates between steps, `a` on even, `b` on odd, with the other carried forward. The locality constraint forces it. Two sim steps make one leapfrog step, so time runs at half rate compared with the second-order equations.

Your instinct that something was wrong was right, though — just not about the alternation.

## Three real bugs

**1. The potential was being multiplied into the Laplacian.** `forceA *= -HSqOver2M + vpot*pposB` computes `Lap(b) × (-ħ²/2m + V·b)`. It should be `-(ħ/2m)Lap(b) + (V/ħ)b` — added, not multiplied. The `// todo: not sure about this!!` on the B branch was pointing right at it. Also the `1/ħ` was missing from both terms.

**2. The default mass makes it unconditionally unstable.** Stability needs `ħ/2m ≲ 1`; the shared default `Mass = 0.125` at `ħ = 1` puts it at **4**. `SchrodingerConfig` now sets `Mass = 2` (giving 0.25) and says why. I suspect this is most of what you were fighting.

**3. `CabMag` was measuring the wrong thing.** `a² + b²` is *not* what a staggered scheme conserves — `a` and `b` sit half a step apart, so squaring `b` compares it with itself at the wrong time. The exactly conserved quantity is `a² + b(t−½)b(t+½)`, which is available on the step `b` moves. That one change:

```
BoxStandingWave     norm varies by 1.180%  ->  0.000%  (9.51e-05)
HarmonicOscillator            6.949%  ->  0.000%  (1.32e-05)
box eigenstate at center      2.538%  ->  0.000%  (3.40e-06)
```

## Configs

**Harmonic Oscillator** (default) — a coherent state: the ground state displaced off center. It swings and does *not* spread, the one quantum state that behaves classically. Period comes out at **649 sim steps against 640 predicted (+1.4%)**, and the width is derived from the period rather than chosen, so the two can't disagree.

**Box Standing Wave** — the lowest standing wave between hard walls (`EdgesFixed` is the walls). A genuine eigenstate: |χ|² doesn't move to 6 digits.

**Box Two States** — the lowest two together. Neither moves alone, but they turn at different rates and beat, so the probability sloshes side to side. Every visible motion in a bound system is a beat like this.

**Hydrogen Ground** — yes, it works. An attractive 1/r well with the electron in exp(−r/a); the well depth is *derived* from the Bohr radius ($a = \hbar^2/mk$), which is what makes it actually stationary. Two caveats in the doc: the singularity is softened to its value one cube out, so it breathes slightly; and it's one electron in a fixed external potential — no back-reaction, no second electron, no chemistry.

**Free Packet** — travels and spreads, with damped edges so it leaves rather than bouncing.

New helpers in `init.goal`: `Quadratic`, `Expo`, `SineBox`.

## One trap worth knowing

`HydrogenGround` initially blew up to 7.65e10. `InvR` writes **cur only** — so the potential was present on one step and absent the next, which pumps the wave straight to infinity. Fixed with `CopyCurToPrev`, same as `SpinInPotential` already does. `Gauss` and my new `Quadratic` write both, so this only bites with `InvR`; might be worth making it consistent.

  ```
  $$
  {\phi_b}_i^{t+1} = {\phi_b}_i^t + \dot {\phi_b}_i^{t+1}
  $$
  
  So, in the end, Schrödinger's equation really just boils down to two very simple differential equations. Interestingly, these equations are *coupled*, in the sense that it is the curvature of $\phi_a$ that drives the change in $\phi_b$, and vice-versa. This is the rotational aspect of the equation mentioned earlier, which is caused by the presence of the $i$ in the equation.
  
  When you actually implement Schrödinger's equation on a computer using the update rules given above, the resulting system is numerically unstable. In other words, the resulting numbers quickly blow up to infinity. This is not due to any kind of numerical roundoff error from limited precision floating point numbers on the computer, but rather due to the way that changes in state values reverberate back and forth across the two scalar values. However, it is possible to overcome it relatively simply by just alternating the update: on one time step you compute one value, and on the next you update the other. This is what is done for illustrative purposes in the computer explorations.
  
  The basic phenomenology of Schrödinger's equation is that wave packets propagate through space, with a speed that is proportional to $\nabla^2 \psi$, which in turn is proportional to the frequency of the wave. In other words, it describes exactly the same behavior as the KG equation, where particle speed is proportional to frequency.
  
  One critical property of Schrödinger's equation (which the scalar [[Klein-Gordon]] equation does not have) is that it preserves the overall magnitude of the $\psi$ state values across all of space, for all time. This is to say, if you compute the sum of $\psi \psi^*$ for each point in space, this sum will remain the same across time under the Schrödinger equation. This conserved value is interpreted as a probability in standard quantum mechanics.

This is not due to any kind of numerical roundoff error from limited precision floating point numbers on the computer, but rather due to the way that changes in state values reverberate back and forth across the two scalar values. However, it is possible to overcome it relatively simply by just alternating the update: on one time step you compute one value, and on the next you update the other. This is what is done for illustrative purposes in the computer explorations."
new = "When you actually implement Schr\u00f6dinger's equation on a computer using the update rules given above, the resulting system is numerically unstable. In other words, the resulting numbers quickly blow up to infinity. This is not due to any kind of numerical roundoff error from limited precision floating point numbers on the computer, but rather due to the way that changes in state values reverberate back and forth across the two scalar values: it is a rotation being integrated by a method that does not rotate. The fix is to alternate the update: advance $\\phi_a$ using the old $\\phi_b$, then advance $\\phi_b$ using the *new* $\\phi_a$. Far from being a hack, this is the standard method for this equation ([[@Visscher91]]; [[@AskarCakmak78]]): it is explicitly stable and second-order accurate, and it is the only form the scheme can take in a [[cellular automaton]], because advancing $\\phi_b$ from the new $\\phi_a$ means reading that new value at the *neighboring* cells, which a single local pass cannot see. Two update steps make one step of time."
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new)

old2 = "This conserved value is interpreted as a probability in standard quantum mechanics."
new2 = "This conserved value is interpreted as a probability in standard quantum mechanics. The alternating update conserves it too, but in a staggered form: because $\\phi_a$ and $\\phi_b$ are half a step apart in time, what is exactly constant is $\\phi_a^2 + \\phi_b(t-1/2) \\phi_b(t+1/2)$, rather than $\\phi_a^2 + \\phi_b^2$."
assert old2 in s
s = s.replace(old2, new2)

// TestSchrodGroupVel: a free packet must travel at the de Broglie group
// velocity hbar k / m, with the lattice correction k -> sin(k). This also
// pins down Sim.TimePerStep: the staggered update takes two sim steps per
// step of time, so a stat that counted steps would report half this speed.
func TestSchrodGroupVel(t *testing.T) {
	sz := int32(48)
	ss := scSim(sz, FreePacket)
	for range 4 { // CabMag is written by the kernel, so let it fill in
		scStep(ss)
	}
	c0 := scCtrX(sz)

	if math.Abs(sv-vg)/vg > 0.1 {
		t.Errorf("StatGroupVel %.5f, but the packet moved at %.5f", sv, vg)
	}
	t.Logf("group velocity %.5f, hbar sin(k) / m = %.5f, stat %.5f", vg, want, sv)
}
EOF

## 1. Visscher for KG instead of Boris? No — they solve different problems

The two schemes look similar but attack different couplings:

| | what couples a and b | locality |
|---|---|---|
| **Schrödinger** | the **Laplacian** of the other component | non-local → must stagger over steps |
| **Complex KG** | the A₀ term acting on the **velocity** | purely on-site → one pass can do it |

In Schrödinger, `da/dt` is driven by `Lap(b)`. To use the *new* `b` you'd have to read it at the neighbours, which a cell can't do in the same pass — hence the alternation. It's forced by locality.

In KG the Laplacian acts on the **same** component (each of a, b satisfies its own real wave equation; the second-order operator doesn't mix them). The only thing that mixes velocities is the A₀ rotation, `d(vₐ + i v_b)/dt = −iω(vₐ + i v_b)`, and ω is read **at the cell**. No neighbour access, so there's nothing a stagger would buy you.

And Boris is strictly better at that job anyway. Boris applies the *exact* rotation by ω (half kick, rotate, half kick) — norm-preserving by construction, at any ω. A stagger would give you the semi-implicit rotation, which only approximately preserves the magnitude and degrades as ω grows. You'd trade an exact method for an approximate one *and* halve the time rate.

There's also a structural reason it doesn't fit: Schrödinger is first order in time, so a and b are naturally half-step-offset — that's the whole premise. KG is genuinely second order; a and b each carry their own position *and* velocity, and there's no half-step to stagger into. You'd be inventing an offset the equation doesn't have.

The `A·∇χ` gauge term *does* mix a and b through a spatial derivative, but it's an explicit force from the current positions, exactly like the Laplacian. It's fine where it is.

## 2. The half-step and C — you were right that it mattered, and there was a bug

Your instinct "it doesn't even have a C" is correct: **C does not appear anywhere in the Schrödinger kernel**. It's the non-relativistic limit; the only rate in it is ħ/2m, and a wave moves at ħk/m, not at a fraction of some light speed the equation never mentions. Nothing in the *physics* needs rescaling, and `SchrodPeriod` was already documented in leapfrog steps with the test expecting 2× that in sim steps — so the coherent-state result was right.

But the **stats** were wrong, and I hadn't caught it. `StatGroupVel` divides the centroid displacement by elapsed *steps*, so Schrödinger read half its true speed. Fixed with a `Sim.TimePerStep` field — 1 for the second-order equations, 0.5 for Schrödinger, set in `SchrodingerConfig`.

While verifying it I found a second stat bug: the Schrödinger group velocity was measured on `CabAs`. The centroid weights by value², and a² carries a ripple at **twice** the wavenumber that drags the centroid toward the *phase* velocity — the wrong quantity for a matter wave, and exactly the one you'd notice being wrong. Switched to `CabMag`, which is the real |χ|² envelope.

New `TestSchrodGroupVel` pins both down:

```
group velocity 0.34895, hbar sin(k) / m = 0.35355, stat 0.37007
```

1.3% off the lattice de Broglie relation ħ·sin(k)/m (the residual is the isotropic 19-point stencil differing slightly from the 1D one). Before the fix it would have read 0.17.

Unrelated, but `go generate` was **broken at HEAD** — `bce643f` dropped fields from `Parameters`, leaving it at 184 bytes, and gosl needs a multiple of 16. Added `pad, pad1 float32`. Also fixed an unbalanced quote in a `dirac.goal` comment that was tripping the goal line parser.

## 3. The reference

> Visscher, P. B. (1991). A fast explicit algorithm for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. *Computers in Physics, 5*, 596–598. doi:10.1063/1.168415

Building on the explicit second-order method of:

> Askar, A., & Cakmak, A. S. (1978). Explicit integration method for the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for collision problems. *The Journal of Chemical Physics, 68*, 2794–2798. doi:10.1063/1.436072

Both added to `references.md`, and cited in the kernel comment. I also revised the paragraph in `schrodinger.md` that called the alternation something done "for illustrative purposes" — it now names the scheme, cites it, and gives the locality argument. And I added a sentence to the conservation paragraph noting that what's exactly constant is the staggered $\phi_a^2 + \phi_b(t-\tfrac12)\phi_b(t+\tfrac12)$, not $\phi_a^2 + \phi_b^2$. Both are in the `web` repo, so they're separate commits from the code.

Sources: [Visscher 1991 (AIP)](https://pubs.aip.org/aip/cip/article/5/6/596/279764/A-fast-explicit-algorithm-for-the-time-dependent), [Askar & Cakmak 1978 (AIP)](https://pubs.aip.org/aip/jcp/article-abstract/68/6/2794/767213/Explicit-integration-method-for-the-time-dependent)

  131:When you actually implement Schrödinger's equation on a computer using the update rules given above, the resulting system is numerically unstable. In other words, the resulting numbers quickly blow up to infinity. This is not due to any kind of numerical roundoff error from limited precision floating point numbers on the computer, but rather due to the way that changes in state values reverberate back and forth across the two scalar values: it is a rotation being integrated by a method that does not rotate. The fix is to alternate the update: advance $\phi_a$ using the old $\phi_b$, then advance $\phi_b$ using the *new* $\phi_a$. Far from being a hack, this is the standard method for this equation ([[@Visscher91]]; [[@AskarCakmak78]]): it is explicitly stable and second-order accurate, and it is the only form the scheme can take in a [[cellular automaton]], because advancing $\phi_b$ from the new $\phi_a$ means reading that new value at the *neighboring* cells, which a single local pass cannot see. Two update steps make one step of time.

  The paper "Why is Boris algorithm so good?" was authored by H. Qin, S. Zhang, J. Xiao, J. Liu, Y. Sun, and W. M. Tang, published in Physics of Plasmas, volume 20, issue 8, article 084503 (2013).
  
  Due to its excellent long term accuracy, the Boris algorithm is the de facto standard for advancing a charged particle. Despite its popularity, there has been no convincing explanation why the Boris algorithm has this advantageous feature. The paper provides an answer by showing that the Boris algorithm conserves phase space volume, even though it is not symplectic.
  
  The paper is available from multiple sources including the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and can be accessed via the DOI: 10.1063/1.4818428.

  web/content/complex-kg.md:376:When you actually simulate these equations on the computer, the self-coupling interactions between these two fields has a tendency to result in positive feedback loops that quickly go to infinity. There is an important numerical integration fix, known as the _Boris push_, which deals with the fact that the electromagnetic potentials drive a rotation through the $\phi_a$ and $\phi_b$ variables, which is evident in the fact that they subtract from $\phi_b$ but add to $\phi_a$ --- these opposite signs are the signature of a rotation (and are caused by the presence of the imaginary $i$ numbers in the equations). The Boris push implements this rotation explicitly, instead of using discrete integration steps, and helps manage the numerical issues ([[@BORISCITES]]). It is also important to ensure that the numerical values do not exceed critical thresholds, which are within the constraints of the known physical parameters.

## Boris

> Boris, J. P. (1970). Relativistic plasma simulation — optimization of a hybrid code. In J. P. Boris & R. A. Shanny (Eds.), *Proceedings of the Fourth Conference on Numerical Simulation of Plasmas* (pp. 3–67). Naval Research Laboratory.

No DOI — it's a 1970 NRL conference proceedings. The volume is on DTIC: [apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/ADA023511](https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/ADA023511)

Worth pairing with the paper that explains *why* it works, which is the more citable one and directly supports your "implements the rotation explicitly" sentence:

> Qin, H., Zhang, S., Xiao, J., Liu, J., Sun, Y., & Tang, W. M. (2013). Why is Boris algorithm so good? *Physics of Plasmas, 20*(8), 084503. doi:[10.1063/1.4818428](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4818428)

It shows Boris conserves phase-space volume despite not being symplectic — which is exactly the property you're relying on (the rotation doesn't pump amplitude over long runs).

Free copy if you want the PDF into Zotero: [PPPL-4872](https://bp-pub.pppl.gov/pub_report//2013/PPPL-4872.pdf)

// TestSchrodingerBigBox: the harmonic well grows as r^2, so it runs past what
// the staggered leapfrog can carry once the box is big enough -- at the
// defaults, past 48^3. Quadratic clamps at SchrodingerVMax, which is why this
// stays finite instead of blowing in from the edges.
func TestSchrodingerBigBox(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	ss := scSim(sz, HarmonicOscillator)
	vmax := float64(ss.SchrodingerVMax())
	om := float64(schrodOmega(ss))
	corner := 0.5 * float64(ss.Params.Mass) * om * om * 3 * (sz / 2) * (sz / 2)
	if corner <= vmax {
		t.Fatalf("box too small to test the clamp: corner V %.3f <= %.3f", corner, vmax)
	}
	if v := float64(StateMax(GetCtx(0).Size.V(), CabV, GetCtx(0).CurState)); v > vmax {
		t.Errorf("V reaches %.3f, over the %.3f the integrator can carry", v, vmax)
	}
	scStep(ss)
	n0 := scNorm(sz)
	lo, hi := n0, n0
	for range 300 {
		scStep(ss)
		n := scNorm(sz)
		lo, hi = math.Min(lo, n), math.Max(hi, n)
	}
	if (hi-lo)/n0 > 1e-3 {
		t.Errorf("norm %.5f varies by %.2e (%.3f%%) -- unstable", n0, hi-lo, 100*(hi-lo)/n0)
	}
	t.Logf("uncapped corner V would be %.3f, clamped to %.3f; norm %.5f varies by %.2e (%.3f%%)",
		corner, vmax, n0, hi-lo, 100*(hi-lo)/n0)
}

Yes — 1.5 is too high, and the size is exactly why.

## The bound

The staggered leapfrog is stable only while every eigenvalue of H satisfies |E|/ħ < 2. The kinetic term already spends part of that budget:

$$\frac{\hbar}{2m}\lambda_{\max} = 0.25 \times \tfrac{16}{3} = 1.333$$

(16/3 being the spectral radius of `Laplacian19` — the same number that caps `C` at √3/2.) That leaves **V ≤ 0.667**. Your ~1.5 is more than double it.

## Why size is the whole story

V = ½mω²r², and ω is fixed by `SchrodingerPeriod` — so V at the walls scales as the **square of the box**. The center is at N/2, so the corner sits at √3·N/2:

| size | face | edge | corner | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24³ | 0.056 | 0.111 | 0.167 | fine, 4× margin |
| 48³ | 0.222 | 0.444 | 0.666 | right at the limit |
| 64³ | 0.395 | 0.790 | 1.184 | blows |
| 100³ | 0.964 | **1.928** | 2.891 | blows |

Your measured ~1.5 at the edges of a 100³ box lands right between the face and edge values. And "coming in from the edges" is the signature — the violation is largest where V is largest, i.e. at the boundary, worst in the corners.

Unlucky that 24³ is stable and the cutover is at 48³, so the default test size hid it.

## Fix

Clamped the bowl rather than weakening it. The wave function is a Gaussian of width √(ħ/mω) ≈ 5 cubes; the clamp first bites around r ≈ 39, nearly 8σ out, where the amplitude is ~10⁻¹⁴. The well is untouched everywhere it does anything.

- `Laplacian19Radius` — named the 16/3 in [funcs.goal](wavesim/funcs.goal), since it now sets two different stability limits
- `Sim.SchrodingerVMax()` — `2ħ − (ħ²/2m)·Laplacian19Radius`, with the size-dependence noted
- `Quadratic` takes a `vmax` (capped when positive, 0 = uncapped); `HarmonicOscillator` passes the bound
- `StateMax` in `stats.goal`

`TestSchrodingerBigBox` runs `HarmonicOscillator` at 64³ and checks both that V stays under the bound and that the norm holds. I verified it actually catches the bug — with the clamp removed it fails with the norm going NaN, exactly what you saw.

50 tests pass, generate/gofmt/build clean, and all the 24³ numbers are bit-identical (the clamp never triggers there).

Worth knowing: this bound applies to **any** potential you add, not just the harmonic one. `HydrogenGround` is well inside it (depth 0.1), but if you build a new config with a steep or deep well, `SchrodingerVMax()` is the number to check against.

func (ss *Sim) ExpoP(vr enums.Enum, curPrev CurPrevBoth, ctr math32.Vector3, dim math32.Dims, decay, amp float32) {

				}
			}
		}
	}
}

//	omega = E / hbar,  E = m c^2 - hbar^2 / (2 m a^2 n^2)
//
// This charge has V = -e A0, so an attractive well is a POSITIVE A0, giving
// V = -k/r with k = hbar^2 / m a. Params.SelfField must be off, or
// MaxwellKernel overwrites A0 on the first step.
func (ss *Sim) HydrogenWell(a, n float32) float32 {
	p := ss.Params
	k := p.Hbar * p.Hbar / (p.Mass * a)
	ss.InvR(A0s, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), k/p.E)
	ss.CopyCurToPrev() // InvR writes cur only
	return p.Omega0 - p.Hbar/(2*p.Mass*a*a*n*n)
}

'''
s = s.replace(anchor, blk + anchor, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")

//
// It is an eigenstate of the same 1/r well, so |chi|^2 sits just as still as

// times deeper than HydrogenGround's, so that the n = 2 orbital, which decays
// over 2a rather than a, comes out the same size and fits the same box.
//
// The node is why a p electron feels the nucleus less than an s one, and the
// lobes are why bonds built from them point in particular directions.
func HydrogenP(ss *Sim) {
	p := ss.Params
	a := HydrogenRadius / 2 // n = 2 decays over 2a, so halve a to keep the size
	k := p.Hbar * p.Hbar / (p.Mass * a)
	ctr := math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)
	ss.InvR(CabV, ctr, -k)
	ss.CopyCurToPrev()
	ss.ExpoP(CabAs, Both, ctr, math32.Z, 2*a, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}"""

func scalarAtom(ss *Sim, a, n float32) float32 {
	p := ss.Params
	p.EM.SetBool(true)
	p.SelfField.SetBool(false) // the well is EXTERNAL and must stay as set
	p.Mass = HydrogenMass
	p.Edges = EdgesDamp
	p.Update()
	return ss.HydrogenWell(a, n)
}

// ScalarHydrogen is the same atom as HydrogenGround, but from the relativistic
// wave equation: a spin-0 particle bound in a Coulomb well, which is what a
// pionic atom actually is.
//
// The shape is the nonrelativistic exp(-r/a), which is an eigenstate only to
// order (Z alpha)^2 -- the true Klein-Gordon Coulomb state carries an extra
// r^s with s = -(Z alpha)^2 near the origin. At Z alpha = 0.2 that is a few
// percent, so the state stays put but breathes slightly rather than sitting
// perfectly still. The breathing IS the relativistic correction.
//
// The uniform phase rate is what makes it a bound state at all: one frequency
// everywhere, E = m c^2 + binding. Compare Charge At Rest, which uses the local
// rate and is not an eigenstate of anything.
func ScalarHydrogen(ss *Sim) {
	a := HydrogenRadius
	om := scalarAtom(ss, a, 1)
	ss.Expo(CabAs, Both, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), a, ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.ChargedBound(1, om)
}

// ScalarHydrogenP is the 2p orbital of the same equation: two lobes of
// opposite phase with a node between them, held by a well four times deeper so
// that it comes out the size of the ground state above.
//
// A spin-0 particle can sit in an l = 1 orbital and this is what it looks like.
// The deeper well puts it at Z alpha = 0.4, which for l = 0 would be close to
// the Z alpha = 1/2 where the Klein-Gordon Coulomb ground state stops existing
// at all; l = 1 is safe until 3/2, so the p state tolerates a far heavier
// nucleus than the s state does.
func ScalarHydrogenP(ss *Sim) {
	a := HydrogenRadius / 2
	om := scalarAtom(ss, a, 2)
	ss.ExpoP(CabAs, Both, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), math32.Z, 2*a, ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.ChargedBound(1, om)
}

'''

// scalarAtom is for the complex Klein-Gordon ones.
func diracAtom(ss *Sim, a, n float32) float32 {
	p := ss.Params
	p.EM.SetBool(true)
	p.SelfField.SetBool(false) // the well is EXTERNAL and must stay as set
	p.Mass = HydrogenMass
	p.Edges = EdgesDamp
	p.Update()
	return ss.HydrogenWell(a, n)
}

// DiracHydrogen is a spin-1/2 electron bound in a Coulomb well: the closest
// this gets to a real hydrogen atom, since the electron is now a fermion with
// spin rather than the scalar of ScalarHydrogen.
//
// The shape is the nonrelativistic exp(-r/a) in the spin-up component alone,
// which is an eigenstate to order (Z alpha)^2. What the Dirac equation adds
// over the scalar case is the sigma . (cB + iE) term: the nucleus has a radial
// E field, so the spin now feels the orbit it is in. That is spin-orbit
// coupling, and it is the origin of fine structure -- the reason the levels of
// a real atom split by spin rather than depending only on n.
//
// Watch SigZ: it holds, because an s state has no orbital angular momentum for
// the spin to couple to. DiracHydrogenP is where that changes.
func DiracHydrogen(ss *Sim) {
	a := HydrogenRadius
	om := diracAtom(ss, a, 1)
	ss.Expo(Dirac1As, Both, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), a, ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.DiracBound(1, om)
}

// DiracHydrogenP is the 2p orbital with spin: two lobes of opposite phase,
// spin up, in a well four times deeper so it comes out the size of the ground
// state above.
//
// This one has both spin and orbital angular momentum, so the sigma . (cB + iE)
// term genuinely acts and the state is not quite stationary: what is conserved
// is the total j, not the two separately. The p orbital of a real atom splits
// into j = 1/2 and j = 3/2 for exactly this reason, and a spin-up l = 1 state
// is a mixture of the two, so it evolves rather than sitting still.
func DiracHydrogenP(ss *Sim) {
	a := HydrogenRadius / 2
	om := diracAtom(ss, a, 2)
	ss.ExpoP(Dirac1As, Both, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), math32.Z, 2*a, ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.DiracBound(1, om)
}

'''

open(p,'w').write(s)
print("dirac ok")

package wavesim

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"testing"

// rms radius weighted by mag
func rmsRad(sz int32, mag enums.Enum) (float64, float64) {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	c := float64(sz) / 2
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(mag), cur))
				dx, dy, dz := float64(x-1)-c, float64(y-1)-c, float64(z-1)-c
				num += v * (dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz)
				den += v
			}
		}
	}
	return math.Sqrt(num / den), den
}

// EFromA0 fills E from the static potential already in A0, E = -grad A0,
// using the same stencil MaxwellKernel does.
//
// An external field needs this. MaxwellKernel is what normally derives E and B
// from the potentials, and it does not run when Params.SelfField is off -- so
// a potential written straight into A0 otherwise carries no E field at all,
// and every term that reads one is silently zero. That includes the Dirac
// sigma . (cB + iE) term, which is the entire difference between the Dirac
// equation and a pair of Klein-Gordon ones.
func (ss *Sim) EFromA0() {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	threeD := ss.Params.ThreeD.IsTrue()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				var g math32.Vector3
				if threeD {
					g = Gradient10(f.X, f.Y, f.Z, int32(A0s), cur)
				} else {
					g = Gradient1D(f.X, f.Y, f.Z, int32(A0s), cur)
				}
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, EX, cur] += -g.X
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, EY, cur] += -g.Y
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, EZ, cur] += -g.Z
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, EX, prv] += -g.X
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, EY, prv] += -g.Y
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, EZ, prv] += -g.Z
			}
		}
	}
}"""

// atomRMS is the |wave|^2 weighted rms radius about the center, in cubes: how
// spread out the state is, which is what says whether it is bound.
func atomRMS(sz int32, mag enums.Enum) float64 {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	mid := float64(sz) / 2
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(mag.Int64()), cur))
				dx, dy, dz := float64(x-1)-mid, float64(y-1)-mid, float64(z-1)-mid
				num += v * (dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz)
				den += v
			}
		}
	}
	return math.Sqrt(num / den)
}

// scalarUnbound is ScalarHydrogen with the well removed: the control that says
// the binding in TestScalarHydrogenBound is doing the work, not the damping.
func scalarUnbound(ss *Sim) {
	p := ss.Params
	p.EM.SetBool(false)
	p.SelfField.SetBool(false)
	p.Mass = HydrogenMass
	p.Edges = EdgesDamp
	p.Update()
	ss.Expo(CabAs, Both, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), HydrogenRadius, ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.ChargedBound(1, p.Omega0)
}

// TestScalarHydrogenBound: a spin-0 particle in a Coulomb well stays put. The
// initial shape is the nonrelativistic exp(-r/a), an eigenstate only to order
// (Z alpha)^2, so it breathes -- but it must stay the size of an atom, while
// the same wave with no well to hold it runs away.
func TestScalarHydrogenBound(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name  string
		init  func(*Sim)
		bound bool
	}{
		{"ScalarHydrogen", ScalarHydrogen, true},
		{"ScalarHydrogenP", ScalarHydrogenP, true},
		{"unbound control", scalarUnbound, false},
	} {
		ss := kgSim(sz, tc.init)
		kgStepExt(ss)
		r0 := atomRMS(sz, CabMag)
		for range 300 {
			kgStepExt(ss)
		}
		grow := atomRMS(sz, CabMag)/r0 - 1
		if tc.bound && grow > 0.15 {
			t.Errorf("%s spread by %.1f%%, not bound", tc.name, 100*grow)
		}
		if !tc.bound && grow < 0.5 {
			t.Errorf("%s spread by only %.1f%%, so the control is not a control", tc.name, 100*grow)
		}
		t.Logf("%-16s rms %6.3f -> %6.3f (%+.1f%%)", tc.name, r0, r0*(1+grow), 100*grow)
	}
}
EOF

// spin term is actually live while it does.

// and the Dirac equation collapses into two independent Klein-Gordon ones.
func TestDiracHydrogenBound(t *testing.T) {

}

## Six new configs

| equation | 1s | 2p |
|---|---|---|
| Schrödinger | `HydrogenGround` (existing) | **`HydrogenP`** |
| complex KG | **`ScalarHydrogen`** | **`ScalarHydrogenP`** |
| Dirac | **`DiracHydrogen`** | **`DiracHydrogenP`** |

All three use one atom, sized by a shared `HydrogenRadius = 5`. The n=2 configs use a well four times deeper so the 2p comes out the same size as the 1s and fits the same box — and the binding energy works out identical either way, ħ²/2mR².

I renamed `SchrodingerBohr` → `HydrogenRadius` and moved it to `init.goal`, since it's now shared by all three.

## The p orbital

Textbook, and exact where it matters:

```
dz  -8  0.10435     lobes peak at dz = ±5, which is the n=2
dz  -5  0.13533     decay length 2a
dz  -1  0.02681
dz  +0  0.00000  <- node
dz  +5  0.13533
```

The node is fixed by symmetry, not by getting the radial function right, so it stays exact — under 0.8% of the lobe peak after 1000 steps. The lobes are opposite-signed in `CabAs`, which is invisible in |χ|² and is precisely what keeps them from merging into one lump.

## A bug this turned up

`SpinInPotential` — your existing config — has no spin term acting. The Dirac kernel reads `EX/EY/EZ` and `BX/BY/BZ` as **state**, and `MaxwellKernel` is what fills them from the potentials. With `SelfField` off it never runs, so a well written straight into `A0s` carries no E field, `σ·(cB + iE)` is identically zero, and the Dirac equation quietly collapses into two independent Klein-Gordon ones.

I caught it because `DiracHydrogen` and `ScalarHydrogen` came out **bit-identical**. New `EFromA0()` fills E = −∇A0 with the same stencil Maxwell uses, and `HydrogenWell` calls it. After that they diverge properly, and `TestDiracHydrogenBound` asserts the E field is nonzero so this can't come back silently.

Worth deciding separately whether `SpinInPotential` should call it too — I left your config alone.

## Results, honestly

Binding is real and the control proves it isn't just edge damping:

```
ScalarHydrogen    rms  8.654 ->  8.915  (+3.0%)
ScalarHydrogenP   rms 13.639 -> 13.100  (-4.0%)
unbound control   rms  8.654 -> 20.163  (+133.0%)
```

Both rms values match theory exactly — √3·a = 8.66 for the 1s, 13.69 for the 2p.

These states **breathe rather than sit still**, and I updated the docs to say so with real numbers instead of "a little":

- The initial shape is the non-relativistic exp(−r/a), an eigenstate only to O((Zα)²), and `HydrogenRadius` puts you at Zα = 0.2 for n=1 and 0.4 for the deeper n=2 well. Those are real atoms — 0.2 is around iron — so the corrections are visibly not small. The breathing *is* the relativistic correction.
- `DiracHydrogen` swings widest (rms up ~25% then back down to ~10% by step 800 — bounded, oscillating, not diverging). It has the σ·E term the scalar case lacks.
- Even the Schrödinger `HydrogenGround` you already had breathes ~40% at the peak, which I hadn't measured before. It's the cusp: exp(−r/a) is non-smooth exactly at the softened core, so the peak relaxes immediately and then oscillates. The shape away from the core barely moves.

`HydrogenMass = 2` is forced — a = Compton/Zα, so a light particle makes an atom far too big for the lattice. At C = 0.5 this puts the Compton wavelength at one cube.

If you want these genuinely stationary, the fix is imaginary-time relaxation to find the true lattice eigenstate rather than initializing from the continuum formula. Say the word and I'll add it.

Also removed a duplicate `KleinGordonCStats()` call in `kgSim` — `ConfigSim` already registers them, so the test harness was appending two rows per step, the same bug you hit with the electroweak stats.

## `Config.HydrogenRadius`

Now a Config field, default 5, added to the Schrödinger, KGC and Dirac `ShouldDisplay` lists so it's tunable in the GUI. All six configs read `ss.Config.HydrogenRadius`; the constant is gone.

**Mass = 2 stays fine as a constant** — in fact it has to be. The radius and the mass aren't independent knobs: a = Compton/Zα, and at C = 0.5 the Compton wavelength is exactly one cube, so **Zα = 1/R** falls out. Growing R just makes the well shallower and the atom more non-relativistic, which is the direction you want. Verified at R = 10 in a 100³ box:

```
R  5  box  50^3  Z*alpha 0.200  omega 0.49000  rms  8.619
R 10  box 100^3  Z*alpha 0.100  omega 0.49750  rms 17.240
```

rms scales exactly 2×, still bound, still stable.

## Bigger does help — but as 1/R, not fast

You're right, and I measured it. Schrödinger ground state, each radius run for the same *physics* time (the binding period goes as R²):

| R | box | peak swing |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 40³ | 50.6% |
| 5 | 50³ | 41.9% |
| 8 | 80³ | 28.0% |

That's roughly 1/R, which is what you'd expect: the softened core is one cube out of R, so it's a 1/R fraction of the atom. It shrinks steadily but you'd need R ≈ 40 to get under 5%.

For KG and Dirac there are **two** error sources and they die at different rates — the relativistic one (starting from the non-relativistic shape) goes as (Zα)² = 1/R², so it's gone quickly; the core one goes as 1/R and is what's left. So on the GPU at R = 20–30 these should look distinctly cleaner, dominated by the core. Agreed that's enough without the lattice eigenstate — and if you ever want it exact, imaginary-time relaxation is still the answer.

I put all of this in the `Config.HydrogenRadius` doc comment so the trade-off is visible where you set it.

## The cur/prev fix

Audited every function in `init.goal` for the asymmetry. Three offenders, now all writing both:

- **`InvR`** — the one that bit us
- **`InvRDrive`** — same pattern, spinfield drive
- **`Sine`** — used by `StandingWave`

Six now-redundant `CopyCurToPrev()` calls removed from `HydrogenWell`, `HydrogenGround`, `HydrogenP`, `SpinInPotential`, `StandingWave` and a KG test. Everything else in `init.goal` was already symmetric.

`InvR`'s doc now says why, since it's the trap: a value that's there on one step and gone the next isn't a well, it's a drive, and it pumps whatever sits in it to infinity.

`CopyCurToPrev` itself has no callers left. I left it exported — it's a reasonable thing for an outside config to want — but say the word if you'd rather drop it.

// corrections are not small -- which is the point of running these at all.
// Raise the radius to make them smaller.
const BoundStateMass float32 = 2

// HarmonicWell puts a harmonic well of angular frequency om into vr, the
// SCALAR potential of a second-order equation, and returns the phase rate of a
// coherent state displaced by d from the center.
//
// Scalar, not electric. The kernel adds vpot to the MASS term, so this is a
// position-dependent mass and confinement means getting heavier with distance.
// That is the coupling a relativistic equation needs in order to confine at
// all: a well that grows without bound in the ENERGY runs past 2 m c^2, where
// the bound states dissolve into pairs and the single-particle equation stops
// meaning anything. A scalar well has no such ceiling, which is why the quark
// models use one.
//

// 1/2 m om^2 r^2 needs vpot = -(m om / hbar)^2 r^2 -- negative, which is the
// mass rising. The returned rate is the MEAN energy of the coherent state,
// 3/2 hbar om for the ground state plus 1/2 m om^2 d^2 from the displacement.
func (ss *Sim) HarmonicWell(vr enums.Enum, om, d, vmax float32) float32 {
	p := ss.Params
	mo := p.Mass * om / p.Hbar
	ss.Quadratic(vr, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), -mo*mo, vmax)
	e := 1.5*p.Hbar*om + 0.5*p.Mass*om*om*d*d
	return p.Omega0 + e/p.Hbar
}"""

package wavesim

import (
	"fmt"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/enums"
)

func ctrX(sz int32, mag enums.Enum) float64 {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(mag.Int64()), cur))
				num += v * float64(x)
				den += v
			}
		}
	}
	return num / den
}

func TestScratchOsc(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 48
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name string
		mag  enums.Enum
		init func(*Sim)
		mk   func(int32, func(*Sim)) *Sim
		step func(*Sim)
	}{
		{"ScalarOscillator", CabMag, ScalarOscillator, kgSim, kgStepExt},
		{"DiracOscillator", DiracMag, DiracOscillator, drSim, drStepExt},
	} {
		ss := tc.mk(sz, tc.init)
		tc.step(ss)
		c0 := ctrX(sz, tc.mag)
		mid := float64(sz) / 2
		var crossings []int
		prev := c0 - mid
		lo, hi := c0, c0
		for i := range 800 {
			tc.step(ss)
			c := ctrX(sz, tc.mag)
			if c < lo {
				lo = c
			}
			if c > hi {
				hi = c
			}
			d := c - mid
			if prev > 0 && d <= 0 {
				crossings = append(crossings, i)
			}
			prev = d
		}
		per := 0.0
		if len(crossings) >= 2 {
			per = float64(crossings[len(crossings)-1]-crossings[0]) / float64(len(crossings)-1)
		}
		fmt.Printf("%-17s start %.2f, swings %.2f..%.2f, period %.1f steps (want %.0f)\n",
			tc.name, c0, lo, hi, per, ss.Config.OscillatorPeriod)
	}
}

// TestScalarOscillator: the relativistic coherent state swings at the well
// frequency slowed by E / m c^2, because the level spacing is
// hbar omega (m c^2 / E) rather than hbar omega. Dirac must agree exactly:
// with no EM field its spin term is zero and it is two copies of this.
func TestScalarOscillator(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 48
	var period [2]float64
	for i, tc := range []struct {
		name string
		mag  enums.Enum
		init func(*Sim)
		mk   func(int32, func(*Sim)) *Sim
		step func(*Sim)
	}{
		{"ScalarOscillator", CabMag, ScalarOscillator, kgSim, kgStepExt},
		{"DiracOscillator", DiracMag, DiracOscillator, drSim, drStepExt},
	} {
		ss := tc.mk(sz, tc.init)
		tc.step(ss)
		mid := float64(sz)/2 + 1
		p := ss.Params
		om := 2 * math.Pi / float64(ss.Config.OscillatorPeriod)
		w := math.Sqrt(float64(p.Hbar) / (float64(p.Mass) * om))
		mc2 := float64(p.Mass) * float64(p.CSq)
		e := 1.5*float64(p.Hbar)*om + 0.5*float64(p.Mass)*om*om*4*w*w
		want := float64(ss.Config.OscillatorPeriod) * (mc2 + e) / mc2
		var first, last, n int
		prev := atomCtrX(sz, tc.mag) - mid
		for s := range 800 {
			tc.step(ss)
			d := atomCtrX(sz, tc.mag) - mid
			if prev > 0 && d <= 0 { // downward zero crossing: one per swing
				if n == 0 {
					first = s
				}
				last, n = s, n+1
			}
			prev = d
		}
		if n < 2 {
			t.Fatalf("%s: only %d crossings, it is not swinging", tc.name, n)
		}
		period[i] = float64(last-first) / float64(n-1)
		if math.Abs(period[i]-want)/want > 0.05 {
			t.Errorf("%s period %.1f steps, want %.1f (well period x E / m c^2)", tc.name, period[i], want)
		}
		t.Logf("%-17s period %.1f steps, want %.1f (well says %.0f, slowed by E / m c^2 = %.3f)",
			tc.name, period[i], want, ss.Config.OscillatorPeriod, (mc2+e)/mc2)
	}
	if period[0] != period[1] {
		t.Errorf("Dirac period %.1f but scalar %.1f: with no field the spin term must do nothing",
			period[1], period[0])
	}
}

## The well had to be a *scalar* potential

This is the interesting part. For hydrogen I used `A0` — an electric potential, coupling to the energy. That's fine for 1/r because it dies away. A harmonic well doesn't: it grows without bound, so it inevitably runs past 2mc², where bound states dissolve into pairs and the single-particle equation stops meaning anything. **The relativistic oscillator can't be built from an electric potential.**

The fix is a Lorentz scalar potential, which adds to the *mass* term instead — confinement becomes "the particle gets heavier as it goes out", which has no such ceiling. Same reason quark models use scalar confinement.

The KG kernel already had the slot (`CabV` enters as `(vpot − M²)`). Dirac didn't, so I added `DiracV` and the matching term. Two lines in the kernel, and now Dirac has external-scalar-potential capability generally, symmetric with KG. New `Sim.HarmonicWell` works out the coefficient: `vpot = −(mω/ħ)²r²`, negative because it's the mass rising.

## It swings slow, and that's the physics

```
ScalarOscillator  period 357.0 steps, want 364.0 (well says 320, slowed by E/mc² = 1.137)
DiracOscillator   period 357.0 steps, want 364.0
```

The levels go as √(m²c⁴ + 2mc²ħω(n+3/2)), so the spacing is ħω·(mc²/E), not ħω — **the energy the particle carries dilates its own clock.** 14% at the default period, and it falls as 44/`OscillatorPeriod`, so a longer period is a more Newtonian one. Prediction lands within 2% of measurement, and the test checks against the derived value rather than a magic number.

Those levels are also unevenly spaced, so unlike the Schrödinger coherent state this one slowly dephases and smears. The state that moves like a classical particle *forever* is a non-relativistic idea.

## Dirac is identical to scalar here — on purpose

Both come out at exactly 357.0, and the test asserts that equality. With no EM field, `σ·(cB + iE)` is identically zero and the Dirac equation genuinely *is* two Klein-Gordon equations. Spin needs a field to do anything; `SpinPrecession` is where it wakes up. I'd rather the demo make that explicit than have it look like a redundant config.

- **`Quadratic`'s clamp now works on magnitude**, so a negative (confining scalar) coefficient clamps the same way a positive one does. New `KleinGordonVMax()` gives the bound: `4/c² − Laplacian19Radius − M²` = 9.67 at defaults, which the corners of a 100³ box would otherwise exceed. Dirac shares it, since the mass term is the same.

## "The electron is 2 Weyl waves bound by mass"

Write the Dirac equation in the chiral basis, where the 4-spinor splits into two 2-spinors ψ_L and ψ_R:

$$i\hbar\,\partial_t \psi_L = -c\,(\sigma\!\cdot\!p)\,\psi_L + Mc^2\,\psi_R$$
$$i\hbar\,\partial_t \psi_R = +c\,(\sigma\!\cdot\!p)\,\psi_R + Mc^2\,\psi_L$$

Set M = 0 and they **completely decouple**. Each is then a self-contained massless field — a Weyl wave — moving at exactly c, with fixed helicity: spin anti-parallel to momentum for L (from the −σ·p), parallel for R. Two independent particles.

Turn M on and the *only* thing that appears is the off-diagonal term. Each wave is now continuously converting into the other, at rate Mc²/ħ. That's the whole content of "bound by mass."

And it's a genuinely mechanical picture of where mass comes from: both pieces always travel at c, but they keep turning into each other and reversing, so the *average* motion is slower than c. The rest mass is literally the frequency of that L↔R flipping — and the flipping is zitterbewegung, at 2Mc²/ħ. A particle at rest isn't sitting still; it's two lightspeed waves trading places.

## Why the neutrino is left only — and why that makes it massless

Weak SU(2) acts **only on left-chiral fields**. That's the experimental fact the model encodes, not something derived. So:

- (ν_L, e_L) form a doublet — W bosons rotate one into the other
- e_R is a **singlet** — W's don't touch it at all
- there is no ν_R in the minimal Standard Model

Now look back at the mass term. It couples L to R. **No ν_R means no partner to bind to, so no mass term can exist** — the neutrino stays a pure Weyl wave at c forever. It isn't that the neutrino's mass is small; in the minimal SM there's nothing to write down. (Real neutrinos do have mass, which is exactly why it's evidence for physics beyond this model.)

## Your third question: not a gauge coupling

Your suspicion is right — it really is "Yukawa × Higgs stuck into the mass slot," and it is **not** a gauge coupling. Gauge couplings come out of covariant derivatives with strengths fixed by the group; the Yukawa y_e is a free parameter bolted on. That's precisely why the SM can't predict fermion masses.

But two things make it less arbitrary than it sounds:

**Gauge invariance dictates the form completely.** You cannot write a bare mass term. m·ē_L e_R isn't gauge invariant — e_L sits in a doublet with hypercharge −½, e_R is a singlet with −1, so the product carries leftover SU(2) and hypercharge. The only Lorentz-scalar, gauge-singlet combination available is

$$-y_e\,(\bar L\cdot\Phi)\,e_R = -y_e(\bar\nu_L\phi^+ + \bar e_L\phi^0)e_R$$

which works because Φ carries exactly the hypercharge needed to cancel. The Higgs isn't decoration — without it there's no way to write a mass at all.

**The mass becomes a field, not a constant.** After the VEV, ⟨φ⁰⟩ = v/√2, giving m_e = y_e v/√2 — and the neutrino term drops out because ⟨φ⁺⟩ = 0. But off the vacuum the mass is y_eΦ(x), so **where the Higgs is small the electron is light**. That's directly visible here: ramp T through T_c with your thermal mass term and the electron should go massless, with L and R decoupling into free Weyl waves. That's the payoff demo.

(Nice detail: φ⁺ couples ν_L to e_R. It's zero in the vacuum, but not in a dynamical simulation.)

## The problem this creates for the second-order framework

This is the bit that matters for implementation, and it's bad news: **the second-order form does not survive chiral gauge couplings.**

The second-order Dirac equation exists because you can eliminate one chirality — ψ_L = (iħ/Mc)σ·D ψ_R — and substitute. Three separate things break that here:

1. **It requires dividing by M**, which is now a field that vanishes. It's singular exactly where the Higgs is small — above T_c and inside vortex cores, the regime you most want to explore.
2. **The neutrino has M ≡ 0.** There's nothing to divide by. A Weyl field has no second-order form with a mass slot, full stop.
3. **L and R have different covariant derivatives.** You get σ̄·D_L σ·D_R instead of D² + σ·F, so the clean structure that made g = 2 fall out is gone.

The second-order trick works precisely when both chiralities are the same field with the same interactions. Chiral gauge theory is the definition of when they aren't.

**The good news:** the first-order system above is iħ∂_tΨ = HΨ with H Hermitian — *exactly the Schrödinger structure*. So Visscher's staggered scheme applies directly, and the work we just finished carries straight over. Running the two passes within one sim step (two kernels instead of one) keeps fermions and bosons on the same clock, avoiding Schrödinger's half-rate.

Cost estimate: ~12 state variables (ν_L, e_L, e_R as 2-spinors, 4 reals each — first-order needs no velocities), two kernels, and the gauge/Yukawa couplings. EW is at 73 vars now, so ~85.

	State[z, y, x, DiracL2As, cur] = l2a
	State[z, y, x, DiracL2Bs, cur] = l2b
	State[z, y, x, DiracLMag, cur] = l1a*l1a + l1b*l1b + l2a*l2a + l2b*l2b

	State[z, y, x, DiracMag, cur] = mag"""
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s); print("kernel ok")

// drChiralUniform is a proper rest state on a uniform field: the control for
// TestDiracChirality, which must come out an exact 50/50 of the chiralities.
func drChiralUniform(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.EM.SetBool(false)
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.Fill(Dirac1As, Both, ss.Config.Amplitude)
	ss.DiracRest(1)
}

// TestDiracChirality checks the left-chiral spinor the kernel recovers, and
// with it the claim that an electron is two massless waves bound by mass.
//
// Two things have to hold. A particle AT REST is an exact 50/50 mixture, since
// chirality is not helicity. And a state started purely right-chiral converts
// ENTIRELY into the left one and back, at the rest mass frequency, with the
// sum conserved -- which is what the mass term does and all it does.
func TestDiracChirality(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 16
	sums := func() (l, r float64) {
		c := GetCtx(0)
		return StateSum(c.Size.V(), DiracLMag, c.CurState), StateSum(c.Size.V(), DiracMag, c.CurState)
	}

	rs := drSim(sz, drChiralUniform)
	drStepExt(rs)
	l, r := sums()
	if math.Abs(l/r-1) > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("at rest |psi_L|^2 / |psi_R|^2 = %.5f, want 1: chirality is not helicity", l/r)
	}
	t.Logf("at rest  |psi_L|^2 / |psi_R|^2 = %.5f", l/r)

	ss := drSim(sz, ChiralOscillation)
	drStepExt(ss)
	l, r = sums()
	tot := l + r
	if l/tot > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("starts %.2f%% left-chiral, should be purely right", 100*l/tot)
	}
	// half a period of |psi|^2 is where the right half has gone entirely away
	want := math.Pi / float64(ss.Params.Omega0)
	lo, hi, rmin, at := tot, tot, r, 0
	for i := range int(1.2 * want) {
		drStepExt(ss)
		l, r = sums()
		lo, hi = math.Min(lo, l+r), math.Max(hi, l+r)
		if r < rmin {
			rmin, at = r, i+1
		}
	}
	if rmin/tot > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("right half only ever falls to %.2f%%, so it does not fully convert", 100*rmin/tot)
	}
	if got := 2 * float64(at); math.Abs(got-want)/want > 0.05 {
		t.Errorf("conversion period %.1f steps, want pi hbar / m c^2 = %.1f", got, want)
	}
	if (hi-lo)/tot > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("total varies by %.3f%%, but |psi_L|^2 + |psi_R|^2 must be conserved", 100*(hi-lo)/tot)
	}
	t.Logf("right half falls to %.3f%% at step %d, so the period is %d vs pi hbar / m c^2 = %.1f; total varies %.4f%%",
		100*rmin/tot, at, 2*at, want, 100*(hi-lo)/tot)
}
EOF

## What the kernel now does

ψ_L is **recovered, not evolved** — solving the second chiral equation for it costs nothing, because the velocity and the gradients are already in hand:

$$\psi_L = \frac{i\hbar}{mc^2}\left(\partial_t + c\,\sigma\!\cdot\!\nabla\right)\psi_R$$

New state: `DiracL1As/L1Bs/L2As/L2Bs` and `DiracLMag`, plus a stat. The view now shows `DiracMag` and `DiracLMag` side by side, so you watch the two halves directly.

I also corrected `DiracMag`'s doc — it's |ψ_R|², *not* the probability. The conserved quantity is |ψ_L|² + |ψ_R|²; `Charge` is the conserved current.

## `ChiralOscillation`, and it's exact

```
at rest  |psi_L|^2 / |psi_R|^2 = 1.00024
right half falls to 0.005% at step 50, period 100 vs pi*hbar/mc^2 = 100.5; total varies 0.0244%
```

Both claims confirmed to 4 digits:

**At rest it's an exact 50/50.** Chirality is not helicity, and a particle at rest is half of each. That's the control.

**Started purely right-chiral, it converts *entirely* — to 0.005% — and comes back**, at exactly the predicted π ħ/mc², with the sum flat. Set `Mass` to zero and the trading stops dead, which is the neutrino.

That's "two Weyl waves bound by mass" as a measurement rather than a slogan.

## One thing worth knowing, which I got wrong first

My first version used a Gaussian packet and it didn't start right-chiral at all — it was ~80% left immediately.

**Chirality isn't local.** ψ_L depends on σ·∇ψ_R, so any localized lump carries a spread of momentum and is already a mixture before the mass does anything. A packet narrower than the Compton wavelength is mostly the *wrong* chirality from the start — and at the default Dirac mass the Compton wavelength is 16 cubes while `PacketWidth` is 12, so the default packet is well into that regime.

Hence the uniform field, with wrapped edges so the boundary doesn't reintroduce a gradient. Dull to look at, exact to measure. It's the same reason `ChargeUniform` exists on the KG side.

This also sharpens the answer to your third question: it's why the mass term can't be thought of as a local property of the wave. It's a *rate* — the rate at which two things that only exist globally turn into each other.

## Where this leaves the electroweak build

The diagnostic confirms the picture but also confirms the obstruction: here ψ_L is derivable from ψ_R only because they share one covariant derivative and one constant mass. In the electroweak sector neither holds — ψ_L carries SU(2) that ψ_R doesn't, and the mass is y·Φ(x) which vanishes above T_c. So ν_L, e_L, e_R have to become three independent first-order Weyl fields.

That's the next stage whenever you want it. The Visscher machinery from the Schrödinger work is what it runs on.

p='/Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim/schrodinger.goal'; s=open(p).read()
start = s.index("// SchrodingerKernel is the kernel")
end = s.index("//gosl:end")
new = '''// Schrodinger's equation runs as TWO kernels, a then b, both within one sim
// step. RunSchrodinger dispatches them; nothing else needs to know.
//
// Splitting i hbar d(chi)/dt = H chi into chi = a + ib gives
//
//	da/dt = -(hbar/2m) Lap b + (V/hbar) b
//	db/dt = +(hbar/2m) Lap a - (V/hbar) a
//
// so each part is driven entirely by the other. Updating both from the same
// old values is unstable -- it is a rotation being integrated by a method that
// does not rotate, the same failure the complex Klein-Gordon equation has
// without Params.Boris. The fix is to stagger them: advance a using the old b,
// then advance b using the NEW a. That is Visscher's scheme -- see Visscher
// 1991, building on Askar & Cakmak 1978 -- which is explicitly stable, second
// order, and conserves a modified norm exactly.
//
// Advancing b from the new a means reading that new a at the NEIGHBORS, which
// one pass cannot do. Two kernel dispatches can: the barrier between them is
// what makes the neighbors visible. CurState does NOT advance in between, so
// both write cur and one sim step is one whole leapfrog step. The two kernels
// touch disjoint variables -- A writes CabAs and CabAv, B writes CabBs, CabBv
// and CabMag -- so the only thing crossing between them is the new a, which is
// the dependency the split exists to satisfy.
//
// Note there is no C here at all. This is the nonrelativistic limit, and the
// only rate in it is hbar / 2m; a wave moves at hbar k / m, not at some
// fraction of a light speed the equation never mentions.
//
// Stability needs (hbar / 2m) < about 1: the Laplacian's extreme eigenvalue is
// near 2 and the leapfrog tolerates a product under 2. SchrodingerConfig sets
// a mass that satisfies it, which the Klein-Gordon default does NOT.
func SchrodingerAKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	pposA := State[z, y, x, CabAs, prv]
	pposB := State[z, y, x, CabBs, prv]

	hbar := Params[0].Hbar
	hm := Params[0].HSqOver2M / hbar // hbar / 2m
	voh := State[z, y, x, CabV, prv] / hbar

	var lap float32
	if Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue() {
		lap = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(CabBs), prv, pposB)
	} else {
		lap = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(CabBs), prv, pposB)
	}
	velA := -hm*lap + voh*pposB // first order: the velocity IS the derivative
	State[z, y, x, CabAv, cur] = velA
	State[z, y, x, CabAs, cur] = pposA + velA
}

// SchrodingerBKernel advances b from the a that SchrodingerAKernel just wrote,
// reading it at cur. See that kernel for the scheme.
func SchrodingerBKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	pposB := State[z, y, x, CabBs, prv]
	posA := State[z, y, x, CabAs, cur] // the new a: this is the whole point

	hbar := Params[0].Hbar
	hm := Params[0].HSqOver2M / hbar
	voh := State[z, y, x, CabV, prv] / hbar

	var lap float32
	if Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue() {
		lap = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(CabAs), cur, posA)
	} else {
		lap = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(CabAs), cur, posA)
	}
	velB := hm*lap - voh*posA
	posB := pposB + velB
	State[z, y, x, CabBv, cur] = velB
	State[z, y, x, CabBs, cur] = posB

	// the norm a^2 + b^2 is NOT what a staggered scheme conserves: a and b sit
	// half a step apart, so squaring b compares it with itself at the wrong
	// time and the total ripples at the level rate. What is exactly conserved
	// is a^2 + b(t-1/2) b(t+1/2), and this kernel holds all three.
	State[z, y, x, CabMag, cur] = posA*posA + pposB*posB
}

'''
s = s[:start] + new + s[end:]

# CPU-side wrapper, after gosl:end
old = "//gosl:end\n\nfunc (ss *Sim) SchrodingerConfig() {"
new2 = '''//gosl:end

// RunSchrodinger runs one whole step of Schrodinger's equation: the a kernel
// then the b kernel, with CurState held fixed across both.
func RunSchrodinger(n int) {
	RunSchrodingerAKernel(n)
	RunSchrodingerBKernel(n)
}

func (ss *Sim) SchrodingerConfig() {'''
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new2,1)

open(p,'w').write(s); print("kernels split")
