// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"cogentcore.org/core/enums"
	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

//gosl:start

// WeylStates are the state variables for the chiral equation: a left-handed
// and a right-handed 2-spinor, each with two complex components. There are no
// velocity variables -- the equation is FIRST order in time, so the value is
// the whole state.
type WeylStates EMStates //enums:enum -trim-prefix=Weyl

const (
	// WeylL1a is the left-handed spinor, component 1, real part.
	WeylL1a WeylStates = WeylStates(EMStatesN) + iota

	// WeylL1b is the left-handed spinor, component 1, imaginary part.
	WeylL1b

	// WeylL2a is the left-handed spinor, component 2, real part.
	WeylL2a

	// WeylL2b is the left-handed spinor, component 2, imaginary part.
	WeylL2b

	// WeylR1a is the right-handed spinor, component 1, real part.
	WeylR1a

	// WeylR1b is the right-handed spinor, component 1, imaginary part.
	WeylR1b

	// WeylR2a is the right-handed spinor, component 2, real part.
	WeylR2a

	// WeylR2b is the right-handed spinor, component 2, imaginary part.
	WeylR2b

	// WeylLMag is |psi_L|^2.
	WeylLMag

	// WeylRMag is |psi_R|^2. The conserved total is this plus WeylLMag.
	WeylRMag
)

// WeylKernel is the chiral (Weyl) form of the Dirac equation, as two
// first-order 2-spinors rather than one second-order one:
//
//	d_t psi_L = +c (sigma.grad) psi_L - i (m c^2 / hbar) psi_R
//	d_t psi_R = -c (sigma.grad) psi_R - i (m c^2 / hbar) psi_L
//
// At m = 0 the two halves come apart completely, and each is a massless wave
// moving at exactly c with one fixed helicity: spin against momentum for L,
// along it for R. A neutrino is one of these on its own. The mass term is the
// ONLY thing joining them, and all it does is turn each into the other at
// m c^2 / hbar. That is what an electron is here -- two lightspeed waves
// trading places, so the average motion comes out slower than c, and the rest
// mass is the frequency of the trade.
//
// Keeping L and R as separate fields is the point. The second-order Dirac
// equation eliminates one of them, which needs both to share a covariant
// derivative and a constant mass -- neither survives the electroweak theory,
// where only L feels the weak force and the mass is the Higgs field.
//
// The integration is NOT Visscher's. That scheme splits a complex field into
// real and imaginary parts driven by each other, which works because
// Schrodinger's H is real in the position basis. Here sigma.grad carries
// sigma_y, which is imaginary, so d_t(real) depends on the real parts too and
// there is nothing to stagger. What this is instead is the three-level
// leapfrog for a first-order system, which the two state buffers already hold:
// cur is two steps back before it is written, prv is one, so
//
//	u(t+1) = u(t-1) + 2 dt (d_t u)(t)
//
// falls out with no extra storage. Second-order accurate and norm-preserving
// for an antisymmetric right-hand side, which this is.
//
// Stability wants sqrt(c^2 khat^2 + (m c^2 / hbar)^2) < 1 for the steepest khat
// the gradient stencil can see, so C has to be well under its usual limit:
// WeylConfig sets it.
func WeylKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()

	// the three-level leapfrog: cur still holds u(t-1) until we write it
	ol1a := State[z, y, x, WeylL1a, cur]
	ol1b := State[z, y, x, WeylL1b, cur]
	ol2a := State[z, y, x, WeylL2a, cur]
	ol2b := State[z, y, x, WeylL2b, cur]
	or1a := State[z, y, x, WeylR1a, cur]
	or1b := State[z, y, x, WeylR1b, cur]
	or2a := State[z, y, x, WeylR2a, cur]
	or2b := State[z, y, x, WeylR2b, cur]

	// u(t), which the right-hand side is evaluated at
	nl1a := State[z, y, x, WeylL1a, prv]
	nl1b := State[z, y, x, WeylL1b, prv]
	nl2a := State[z, y, x, WeylL2a, prv]
	nl2b := State[z, y, x, WeylL2b, prv]
	nr1a := State[z, y, x, WeylR1a, prv]
	nr1b := State[z, y, x, WeylR1b, prv]
	nr2a := State[z, y, x, WeylR2a, prv]
	nr2b := State[z, y, x, WeylR2b, prv]

	threeD := Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue()
	var gl1a, gl1b, gl2a, gl2b, gr1a, gr1b, gr2a, gr2b math32.Vector3
	if threeD {
		gl1a = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylL1a), prv)
		gl1b = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylL1b), prv)
		gl2a = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylL2a), prv)
		gl2b = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylL2b), prv)
		gr1a = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylR1a), prv)
		gr1b = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylR1b), prv)
		gr2a = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylR2a), prv)
		gr2b = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WeylR2b), prv)
	} else {
		gl1a = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylL1a), prv)
		gl1b = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylL1b), prv)
		gl2a = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylL2a), prv)
		gl2b = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylL2b), prv)
		gr1a = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylR1a), prv)
		gr1b = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylR1b), prv)
		gr2a = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylR2a), prv)
		gr2b = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WeylR2b), prv)
	}

	// sigma.grad on a 2-spinor, written out in real components:
	//	(sigma.grad psi)_1 = d_z psi_1 + (d_x - i d_y) psi_2
	//	(sigma.grad psi)_2 = (d_x + i d_y) psi_1 - d_z psi_2
	// The d_y terms are where sigma_y puts real and imaginary into each
	// other, and are why this cannot be staggered the way Schrodinger is.
	sl1a := gl1a.Z + gl2a.X + gl2b.Y
	sl1b := gl1b.Z + gl2b.X - gl2a.Y
	sl2a := gl1a.X - gl1b.Y - gl2a.Z
	sl2b := gl1b.X + gl1a.Y - gl2b.Z
	sr1a := gr1a.Z + gr2a.X + gr2b.Y
	sr1b := gr1b.Z + gr2b.X - gr2a.Y
	sr2a := gr1a.X - gr1b.Y - gr2a.Z
	sr2b := gr1b.X + gr1a.Y - gr2b.Z

	cc := Params[0].C
	om := Params[0].Omega0 // m c^2 / hbar: the rate L and R turn into each other

	// -i M psi takes (a, b) to (M b, -M a), which is the whole mass term
	dl1a := cc*sl1a + om*nr1b
	dl1b := cc*sl1b - om*nr1a
	dl2a := cc*sl2a + om*nr2b
	dl2b := cc*sl2b - om*nr2a
	dr1a := -cc*sr1a + om*nl1b
	dr1b := -cc*sr1b - om*nl1a
	dr2a := -cc*sr2a + om*nl2b
	dr2b := -cc*sr2b - om*nl2a

	l1a := ol1a + 2*dl1a
	l1b := ol1b + 2*dl1b
	l2a := ol2a + 2*dl2a
	l2b := ol2b + 2*dl2b
	r1a := or1a + 2*dr1a
	r1b := or1b + 2*dr1b
	r2a := or2a + 2*dr2a
	r2b := or2b + 2*dr2b

	State[z, y, x, WeylL1a, cur] = l1a
	State[z, y, x, WeylL1b, cur] = l1b
	State[z, y, x, WeylL2a, cur] = l2a
	State[z, y, x, WeylL2b, cur] = l2b
	State[z, y, x, WeylR1a, cur] = r1a
	State[z, y, x, WeylR1b, cur] = r1b
	State[z, y, x, WeylR2a, cur] = r2a
	State[z, y, x, WeylR2b, cur] = r2b

	// the STAGGERED magnitude u(t).u(t+1), not |u(t+1)|^2: a three-level
	// leapfrog conserves the product of adjacent levels exactly, the same way
	// Visscher's scheme does, and squaring one level alone ripples instead.
	State[z, y, x, WeylLMag, cur] = nl1a*l1a + nl1b*l1b + nl2a*l2a + nl2b*l2b
	State[z, y, x, WeylRMag, cur] = nr1a*r1a + nr1b*r1b + nr2a*r2a + nr2b*r2b
}

//gosl:end
GOALEOF

func (ss *Sim) WeylConfig() {
	ParamsShouldDisplay = WeylShouldDisplay
	ss.StateVars = WeylStatesN
	ss.initFuncs = WeylConfigs
	ss.InitFunc = NeutrinoPacket
	ss.WeylStats()
	// a first-order leapfrog needs sqrt(c^2 khat^2 + om^2) < 1, and khat for
	// the 10-point gradient runs past 1, so C sits well under the second-order
	// limit of sqrt(3)/2. Mass is set per config, not here.
	ss.Params.C = WeylC
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.ViewInit(func(view *View) {
		view.SetVar(WeylLMag, -1)
		view.SetVar(WeylRMag, 1)
	})
}

// WeylC is the speed of light WeylConfig sets: the first-order leapfrog is
// tighter than the second-order one the other equations use.
const WeylC float32 = 0.35

// WeylMass is the electron mass the massive configs set, chosen so that the
// L-R trade takes a few hundred steps: the period is pi hbar / m c^2.
const WeylMass float32 = 0.5

var WeylShouldDisplay = []string{"Edges", "C", "Hbar", "Mass", "Wavelength", "PacketWidth", "Amplitude"}

// WeylStats tracks the two chiralities separately, which is the whole point.
func (ss *Sim) WeylStats() {
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatStep())
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatSum(WeylLMag))
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatSum(WeylRMag))
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatGroupVel(math32.X, WeylLMag))
}

// WeylSpinor fills one chirality with a gaussian packet moving along X, with
// the spin along the given axis. side picks L or R, and amp scales it.
func (ss *Sim) WeylSpinor(side WeylStates, axis math32.Dims, amp float32) {
	var c1, c2 enums.Enum = WeylL1a, WeylL2a
	if side == WeylR1a {
		c1, c2 = WeylR1a, WeylR2a
	}
	h := amp / math32.Sqrt2
	ctr := math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)
	w := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	switch axis {
	case math32.X: // spin along +X is the equal superposition of the two
		ss.Gauss(c1, Both, ctr, w, h, 0)
		ss.Gauss(c2, Both, ctr, w, h, 0)
	default: // +Z is component 1 alone
		ss.Gauss(c1, Both, ctr, w, amp, 0)
	}
}

// NeutrinoPacket is a massless left-handed wave and nothing else. With Mass at
// zero there is no term anywhere that can put anything into the right-handed
// half, so it stays exactly empty forever: that is what it means for the
// neutrino to have only one handedness.
//
// It travels at exactly c, because a massless wave has nothing to slow it.
func NeutrinoPacket(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = 0
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.WeylSpinor(WeylL1a, math32.Z, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// ElectronAtRest is the two halves in equal measure, which is what a massive
// particle at rest IS: chirality is not helicity, and at zero momentum the
// electron is half left and half right at every instant. Both magnitudes sit
// flat while the phases turn.
func ElectronAtRest(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = WeylMass
	ss.Params.Update()
	a := ss.Config.Amplitude
	ss.WeylSpinor(WeylL1a, math32.Z, a)
	ss.WeylSpinor(WeylR1a, math32.Z, a)
}

// ElectronChiralFlip starts the whole electron in the LEFT half and lets the
// mass term do the rest. It converts entirely into the right half and back:
//
//	|psi_L|^2 = cos^2(m c^2 t / hbar),  |psi_R|^2 = sin^2(m c^2 t / hbar)
//
// so each swings over a period of pi hbar / m c^2 while the sum stays flat.
// Watch LMag and RMag in the stats trade against each other. This is
// zitterbewegung, and it is the clearest statement of what mass is: not a
// property the wave has, but the rate at which two massless waves turn into
// one another. Set Mass to zero and the trade stops dead -- a neutrino.
func ElectronChiralFlip(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = WeylMass
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.WeylSpinor(WeylL1a, math32.Z, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

var WeylConfigs = []InitFunc{
	InitFunc{Name: "Neutrino Packet", Doc: "A massless left-handed wave travelling at exactly c, with the right-handed half staying exactly empty", Func: NeutrinoPacket, Current: true},
	InitFunc{Name: "Electron At Rest", Doc: "Both halves in equal measure, which is what a massive particle at rest is: half left and half right", Func: ElectronAtRest},
	InitFunc{Name: "Electron Chiral Flip", Doc: "The whole electron started left-handed: the mass turns it entirely into the right-handed one and back", Func: ElectronChiralFlip},
}

func (ss *Sim) WeylPacket(side WeylStates, dim math32.Dims, amp float32) {
	c1 := int(WeylL1a.Int64())

	if side == WeylR1a {
		c1 = int(WeylR1a.Int64())

	back := ctr

	wl := ss.Config.Wavelength
	wd := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	sz := ss.Config.Size

		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {

				ff := CoordToFloat(c)

				e := ff.Sub(back)

	}
}

func wySim(sz int32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {

	if ss.Params.Edges == EdgesWrap {
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	ss.RunStats(false)
}

func wySums() (l, r float64) {

	return StateSum(c.Size.V(), WeylLMag, c.CurState), StateSum(c.Size.V(), WeylRMag, c.CurState)
}

func wyCtr(sz int32, mag enums.Enum, dim math32.Dims) float64 {

	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {

				d := float64(x)
				if dim == math32.Z {
					d = float64(z)
				}
				num += v * d
				den += v
			}
		}
	}

}

// TestWeylNeutrino: a massless left-handed wave, and nothing else. The right
// half must stay EXACTLY empty -- with Mass at zero there is no term anywhere
// that can put anything into it, which is what having only one handedness
// means. And it must travel at c, approaching it as the wavelength grows past
// the lattice.
func TestWeylNeutrino(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	var speed [2]float64
	for i, wl := range []float32{8, 16} {
		ss := wySim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
			s.Config.Wavelength = wl
			NeutrinoPacket(s)
		})
		wyStep(ss)
		x0, z0 := wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.X), wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.Z)
		_, r0 := wySums()
		const n = 40
		var rmax float64
		for range n {
			wyStep(ss)
			_, r := wySums()
			rmax = math.Max(rmax, math.Abs(r))
		}
		l, _ := wySums()
		if rmax > 1e-9*l {
			t.Errorf("wavelength %g: right half reached %.3g, must stay exactly zero", wl, rmax)
		}
		if d := math.Abs(wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.Z) - z0); d > 0.01 {
			t.Errorf("wavelength %g: drifted %.3f along Z, should move only along its momentum", wl, d)
		}
		speed[i] = (wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.X) - x0) / n
		if c := float64(ss.Params.C); speed[i] < 0.7*c || speed[i] > c {
			t.Errorf("wavelength %g: speed %.4f, want just under c = %.4f", wl, speed[i], c)
		}
		t.Logf("wavelength %2g: speed %.4f = %.3f c; right half peaks at %.3g (r0 %.3g)",
			wl, speed[i], speed[i]/float64(ss.Params.C), rmax, r0)
	}
	if speed[1] <= speed[0] {
		t.Errorf("longer wavelength is not faster (%.4f vs %.4f): massless must approach c", speed[1], speed[0])
	}
}

// wyFlipUniform is the chiral flip on a uniform field, where the gradients
// vanish and the trade comes out exactly cos^2 and sin^2.
func wyFlipUniform(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = WeylMass
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.Fill(WeylL1a, Both, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// TestWeylChiralFlip: an electron started entirely left-handed converts
// entirely into the right-handed one and back, at the rest mass frequency,
// with the sum conserved. That trade is the whole of what the mass term does.
func TestWeylChiralFlip(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 16
	ss := wySim(sz, wyFlipUniform)
	wyStep(ss)
	l, r := wySums()
	tot := l + r
	if r/tot > 0.05 {
		t.Errorf("starts %.2f%% right-handed, should be purely left", 100*r/tot)
	}
	want := math.Pi / float64(ss.Params.Omega0)
	lmin, at, lo, hi := tot, 0, tot, tot
	for i := range int(1.2 * want) {
		wyStep(ss)
		l, r = wySums()
		lo, hi = math.Min(lo, l+r), math.Max(hi, l+r)
		if l < lmin {
			lmin, at = l, i+1
		}
	}
	if lmin/tot > 0.02 {
		t.Errorf("left half only falls to %.2f%%, so it does not fully convert", 100*lmin/tot)
	}
	if got := 2 * float64(at); math.Abs(got-want)/want > 0.05 {
		t.Errorf("flip period %.1f steps, want pi hbar / m c^2 = %.1f", got, want)
	}
	if (hi-lo)/tot > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("total varies by %.3f%%, but the sum must be conserved", 100*(hi-lo)/tot)
	}
	t.Logf("left half falls to %.3f%% at step %d, so the period is %d vs pi hbar / m c^2 = %.1f; total varies %.4f%%",
		100*lmin/tot, at, 2*at, want, 100*(hi-lo)/tot)
}

// TestWeylElectronAtRest: a massive particle at rest is an equal mixture of
// the two chiralities, and stays that way. Chirality is not helicity.
func TestWeylElectronAtRest(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 16
	ss := wySim(sz, ElectronAtRest)
	wyStep(ss)
	l0, r0 := wySums()
	var worst float64
	for range 400 {
		wyStep(ss)
		l, r := wySums()
		worst = math.Max(worst, math.Abs(l/r-1))
	}
	if math.Abs(l0/r0-1) > 1e-6 || worst > 0.01 {
		t.Errorf("|psi_L|^2 / |psi_R|^2 starts at %.6f and wanders by %.4f, want a flat 1", l0/r0, worst)
	}
	t.Logf("|psi_L|^2 / |psi_R|^2 starts %.6f, wanders at most %.2e over 400 steps", l0/r0, worst)
}

## Schrödinger: two kernels, one step

Your design works exactly as you described. `RunSchrodinger` calls `SchrodingerAKernel` then `SchrodingerBKernel` with `CurState` held fixed, and the two write **disjoint variables** — A writes `CabAs`/`CabAv`, B writes `CabBs`/`CabBv`/`CabMag`. The only thing crossing between them is the new `a`, which is the dependency the split exists to satisfy. Same pattern as `RunMaxwellKernel` → `RunKleinGordonCKernel`, so the barrier is already proven here.

`TimePerStep` is gone, and the stat is back to plain steps. Physics identical — norms to the same digits, coherent period now **324.5 vs 320 (+1.4%)**, exactly the old +1.4% but in honest units.

Two test durations needed halving, since a step is now worth twice as much: the group-velocity packet was walking into the damped edge, and the p-orbital node test now covers double the time (1.14% vs the old 0.77%, threshold moved to 2%).

## Weyl: your Visscher instinct doesn't carry over — here's why

I tried to follow it and it doesn't work, for a reason worth knowing.

Visscher splits a complex field into real and imaginary parts that drive *each other*. That works because **Schrödinger's H is real** in the position basis. The Weyl operator is σ·∇, and σ_y is imaginary — so working through the real components:

$$\partial_t a_{L1} = c\,(\partial_z a_{L1} + \partial_x a_{L2} + \partial_y b_{L2}) + \ldots$$

`ȧ` depends on `a`. There's nothing to stagger. I checked every regrouping — by chirality, by component — and the ∂_z transport term is diagonal in all of them.

**What works instead is simpler, and needs no wrapper at all.** For a first-order system the right scheme is the three-level leapfrog, and your two state buffers already hold three levels: `cur` is two steps back *before you write it*, `prv` is one. So

$$u(t{+}1) = u(t{-}1) + 2\,\Delta t\,\dot u(t)$$

falls out with no extra storage and no sub-steps. Second-order accurate, norm-preserving for an antisymmetric right-hand side, which this is. One kernel.

## What it shows

Both helicities are in the state (`WeylL1a…L2b`, `WeylR1a…R2b`), so you get the neutrino and the electron from the same kernel.

**`NeutrinoPacket`** — the right half stays **exactly zero**, not small: `0`. With `Mass` at zero there's no term anywhere that can put anything into it. And it converges on c as the lattice stops mattering:

```
wavelength  8: speed 0.2828 = 0.808 c
wavelength 16: speed 0.3052 = 0.872 c
```

**`ElectronChiralFlip`** — started entirely left-handed, converts **entirely** to right-handed and back, period 50 steps against πħ/mc² = 51.3, **total conserved to 0.0000%**.

**`ElectronAtRest`** — |ψ_L|²/|ψ_R|² starts at 1.000000 and wanders by **0.00e+00** over 400 steps. Exactly half of each, permanently.

Two things I had to get right that are worth flagging:

- **A plain Gaussian is not a helicity eigenstate.** My first `NeutrinoPacket` drifted at 0.34c because a spin-up blob is a mixture of both directions pulling apart. `WeylPacket` builds the spinor with σ·k̂ = ∓1 to match, which is the demo anyway: flip the spin on a left-handed wave and it reverses direction.
- **The leapfrog reads its own past**, so both time levels have to be set. A wave given no past goes both ways at once. For a massless field envelope and phase both move at c, so shifting the earlier copy back by one step's travel is exact.

`Params.C` is set to 0.35 for this equation — the first-order stability bound is tighter than the second-order √3/2.

Comparing the two velocity measures directly: the direct centroid method gives 0.2911 cubes/step (0.832 in c-units), while the stat-based method gives 0.6791 in c-units, or 0.2377 cubes/step — noticeably slower. I suspect this slowdown comes from the stat method weighting by |ψ|⁴ instead of |ψ|², which biases the measurement toward the envelope's peak rather than its true group velocity.

I'm checking whether the wave packet's magnitude squared is actually smooth for a helicity eigenstate — verifying that summing the squared components across the two spinor parts cancels out the oscillatory cosine term and leaves a clean gaussian envelope, which it does. So the staggered magnitude product between consecutive timesteps should also be smooth, which points me back toward inspecting how the wave packet helper actually constructs the real and imaginary components from the envelope and phase.

Since the algebra checks out, I'm now suspecting the mismatch comes from timing in the statistics computation itself — possibly how the group velocity stat samples its first reading relative to the simulation step counter.

I'm also considering whether wrap boundaries on the periodic domain create interference from the tail of the gaussian envelope re-entering from the other side, subtly corrupting the velocity measurement.

Both measurement methods might have blind spots for wrapped distributions, so I should isolate the discrepancy by measuring the direct centroid velocity over the same last-20-step window the stat uses, then compare velocity between steps 1-20 versus 21-40 to see if a real deceleration is happening.

package wavesim

import (
	"fmt"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

// centroid weighted by mag^2, exactly as StateCentroids does
func wyCtr2(sz int32, mag WeylStates) float64 {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= sz; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= sz; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(mag.Int64()), cur))
				num += v * v * float64(x)
				den += v * v
			}
		}
	}
	return num / den
}

func TestScratchWin(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	ss := wySim(sz, NeutrinoPacket)
	wyStep(ss)
	p := []float64{}
	q := []float64{}
	for range 60 {
		wyStep(ss)
		p = append(p, wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.X))
		q = append(q, wyCtr2(sz, WeylLMag))
	}

	tsr := ss.Stats.Float64(StatGroupVelName(WeylLMag, 0))

		tsr.Float1D(tsr.Len()-1)*float64(ss.Params.C))
}

## 1D dropped for KGC, Weyl, Dirac

All three kernels now call `Laplacian19` / `Gradient10` unconditionally — no `threeD` branch left in any of them. Their Config methods set `ThreeD` true so nothing else gets confused. `Wave` and real `KleinGordon` keep their 1D paths.

Worth noting for Weyl specifically: σ·∇ mixes the three axes into each other, so a 1D version wouldn't be this equation with a dimension removed — it'd be a different equation.

## Group velocity for R — and a bug it exposed

Added, but it disagreed with a direct centroid measurement (0.679c vs 0.832c), so I chased it.

`StateCentroids` weights by **value squared**. That's right for an *amplitude* variable like `AYs` or `CabAs`, where the square is the intensity. But `WeylLMag` is already |ψ|² — squaring it again weights by **|ψ|⁴**, which tracks the peak instead of the envelope and reads several percent slow on any packet that's dispersing.

**Schrödinger had the same bug** — I'd pointed its stat at `CabMag`. It was reading 0.36798 against a true 0.34769, and my own 10% tolerance let it through.

Split into `StatGroupVel` (amplitude, squares) and `StatGroupVelMag` (already an intensity, doesn't). Both now agree with direct measurement:

```
weyl        direct 0.2911/step; stat 0.2872  (R: 0.0000, correctly empty)
schrodinger direct 0.34769/step; stat 0.34590   (was 0.36798)
```

Schrödinger's tolerance is down from 10% to 3%, and the Weyl test now asserts the stat matches the packet *and* that R's velocity is exactly zero.

## The packet — you were right that it was a blob

Two things were wrong, one cosmetic and one physical.

`WeylPacket` used a **spherical** gaussian envelope. A round blob carries transverse momentum, so it isn't a helicity eigenstate: it spreads sideways and its centroid crawls. Now it's a **slab** — gaussian along the direction of travel, flat across the other two. k is purely along X, so it travels rigidly, and on screen it reads as bands sweeping across rather than a dot that may or may not be drifting.

It got measurably faster too, since the transverse components were dragging the average down:

```
wavelength  8: 0.832 c  (was 0.808)
wavelength 16: 0.960 c  (was 0.872)
```

The second thing is why it looked featureless: **`WeylLMag` has no wave structure to show.** For a helicity eigenstate |ψ|² = envelope², smooth by construction — the oscillation lives entirely in the phase. So `Mag` can only ever show a shape translating. Your `WeylViewAll` is the right call: `L1a`/`L1b` do oscillate, and for the neutrino `R1a`/`R1b` sit visibly empty, which is its own demonstration.

If it's still hard to read, raise `PacketWidth` — at the default 12 with wavelength 8 you only get about 3 wavelengths under the envelope. Widening it gives a longer wave train without changing anything else, and both are live in the GUI.

package wavesim

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"testing"
)

// a pure plane wave along X, no envelope: measures the lattice dispersion
func planeWave(ss *Sim, wl float32, mass float32) {
	ss.Params.Mass = mass
	ss.Params.Update()
	k := float64(2 * math.Pi / float64(wl))
	om := math.Sqrt(float64(ss.Params.C*ss.Params.C)*math.Sin(k)*math.Sin(k) +
		float64(ss.Params.Omega0*ss.Params.Omega0))
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur, prv := ctx.CurState, ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	// L spinor with sigma.khat = -1 for khat = +X: (1,-1)/sqrt2
	s := []float32{1 / math.Sqrt2, -1 / math.Sqrt2}
	_ = s
	for z := int32(0); z < sz.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(0); y < sz.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(0); x < sz.X; x++ {
				ph := k * float64(x)
				for i, sv := range []float64{1 / math.Sqrt2, -1 / math.Sqrt2} {
					a, b := sv*math.Cos(ph), sv*math.Sin(ph)
					ao, bo := sv*math.Cos(ph+om), sv*math.Sin(ph+om)
					State.Set(float32(a), int(z+1), int(y+1), int(x+1), int(WeylL1a)+2*i, int(prv))
					State.Set(float32(b), int(z+1), int(y+1), int(x+1), int(WeylL1b)+2*i, int(prv))
					State.Set(float32(ao), int(z+1), int(y+1), int(x+1), int(WeylL1a)+2*i, int(cur))
					State.Set(float32(bo), int(z+1), int(y+1), int(x+1), int(WeylL1b)+2*i, int(cur))
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

func TestScratchDisp(t *testing.T) {

// the given wavelength running along an axis:
//
//	omega = arcsin(sqrt(c^2 sin^2 k + om0^2))
//
// The sin k is the gradient stencil's response to a plane wave and the arcsin
// is the three-level leapfrog's own, and together they match the measured
// period to five digits. Both corrections matter: at wavelength 8 the naive
// c k overstates the frequency by 13%.
func (ss *Sim) WeylDispersion(wavelength float32) (float32, float32) {
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	c := ss.Params.C
	o0 := ss.Params.Omega0
	sk := math32.Sin(k)
	ss2 := c*c*sk*sk + o0*o0
	rs := math32.Sqrt(ss2)
	if rs <= 0 {
		return 0, 0
	}
	return math32.Asin(rs), c * c * sk * math32.Cos(k) / (rs * math32.Sqrt(1-ss2))
}

// WeylSlab fills one chirality with a gaussian slab at rest: flat across the
// two transverse axes, no phase, spin along Z. For the configs that are not
// meant to move but should still look like something.
func (ss *Sim) WeylSlab(side WeylStates, dim math32.Dims, amp float32) {
	c1 := int(side.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	ctr := CenterF(math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1))
	wd := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				g := (CoordToFloat(c).Dim(dim) - ctr.Dim(dim)) / wd
				v := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1, cur] += v
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1, prv] += v
			}
		}
	}
}

// WeylPacket puts a moving packet of one chirality into the state: a gaussian
// envelope times exp(i k.x), on the spinor with sigma.khat = helicity, so it
// is a single frequency and travels rigidly.
//
// Helicity, not chirality, is what the spinor encodes. A massless L wave can
// only have helicity -1 and an R wave +1, which is why reversing a neutrino's
// spin reverses its direction. A MASSIVE particle has both chiralities at one
// helicity, in the ratio (omega - c khat) / (m c^2 / hbar), so ElectronPacket
// calls this twice with the same helicity and different amplitudes.
//
// The envelope is a SLAB: gaussian along the direction of travel, flat across
// the other two. That is not just for looks. A round blob carries transverse
// momentum, so it is not a helicity eigenstate, it spreads sideways, and its
// centroid crawls instead of moving at the group velocity. A slab has k purely
// along one axis, travels rigidly, and reads on screen as bands sweeping
// across rather than a dot that may or may not be drifting.
//
// Both time levels are set. The three-level leapfrog reads its own past, and a
// wave given no past goes both ways at once: the earlier one has its envelope
// pulled back by one step of GROUP velocity and its phase advanced by one step
// of omega, which are the same thing only when the wave is massless.
func (ss *Sim) WeylPacket(side WeylStates, dim math32.Dims, helicity, amp float32) {
	c1 := int(side.Int64())
	// the spinor with sigma.khat = helicity, for khat along +dim
	s1, s2 := float32(1)/math32.Sqrt2, helicity/math32.Sqrt2 // +X: sigma_x
	if dim == math32.Z {                                     // +Z: sigma_z is already diagonal
		s1, s2 = 0, 1
		if helicity > 0 {
			s1, s2 = 1, 0
		}
	}
	wl := ss.Config.Wavelength
	wd := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	om, vg := ss.WeylDispersion(wl)
	k := TwoPi / wl
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	ctr := CenterF(math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1))
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				d := CoordToFloat(c).Dim(dim) - ctr.Dim(dim)
				g := d / wd
				e := (d + vg) / wd // where the envelope was one step ago
				en := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
				eo := amp * math32.FastExp(-e*e)
				ph := k * d
				na, nb := en*math32.Cos(ph), en*math32.Sin(ph)
				oa, ob := eo*math32.Cos(ph+om), eo*math32.Sin(ph+om)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1, prv] += s1 * na
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1+1, prv] += s1 * nb
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1+2, prv] += s2 * na
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1+3, prv] += s2 * nb
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1, cur] += s1 * oa
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1+1, cur] += s1 * ob
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1+2, cur] += s2 * oa
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, c1+3, cur] += s2 * ob
			}
		}
	}
}

// NeutrinoPacket is a massless left-handed wave and nothing else. With Mass at
// zero there is no term anywhere that can put anything into the right-handed
// half, so it stays exactly empty forever: that is what it means for the
// neutrino to have only one handedness. It travels at c, since a massless wave
// has nothing to slow it.
func NeutrinoPacket(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = 0
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.WeylPacket(WeylL1a, math32.X, -1, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// ElectronPacket is the same wave given a mass, and the comparison to make
// against NeutrinoPacket: identical wavelength, identical box, and it travels
// visibly SLOWER. Both halves are there and both move together, because they
// are halves of one particle.
//
// That is the whole picture made quantitative. The two halves each still go at
// c; what the mass does is turn each into the other, and a thing that keeps
// reversing gets down the box more slowly than one that does not. The heavier
// it is, the more often it turns, and the slower it goes -- raise Mass and
// watch the packet fall behind.
//
// The two amplitudes are not equal once it is moving: a momentum eigenstate
// has them in the ratio (omega - c khat) / (m c^2 / hbar), which goes to 1 at
// rest and to 0 at high momentum, where the particle becomes effectively
// massless and one chirality takes over.
func ElectronPacket(ss *Sim) {
	p := ss.Params
	p.Mass = WeylMass
	p.Update()
	om, _ := ss.WeylDispersion(ss.Config.Wavelength)
	ck := p.C * math32.Sin(TwoPi/ss.Config.Wavelength)
	rr := (om - ck) / p.Omega0 // right-handed share of a positive-energy state
	a := ss.Config.Amplitude
	ss.WeylPacket(WeylL1a, math32.X, -1, a)
	ss.WeylPacket(WeylR1a, math32.X, -1, a*rr)
}

// ElectronAtRest is the two halves in equal measure, which is what a massive
// particle at rest IS: chirality is not helicity, and at zero momentum the
// electron is half left and half right at every instant. Both magnitudes sit
// flat while the phases turn at the rest mass frequency.
func ElectronAtRest(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = WeylMass
	ss.Params.Update()
	a := ss.Config.Amplitude
	ss.WeylSlab(WeylL1a, math32.X, a)
	ss.WeylSlab(WeylR1a, math32.X, a)
}

// zitterbewegung, and it is the clearest statement of what mass is: not a
// property the wave has, but the rate at which two massless waves turn into
// one another. Set Mass to zero and the trade stops dead -- a neutrino.
func ElectronChiralFlip(ss *Sim) {
	ss.Params.Mass = WeylMass
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.WeylSlab(WeylL1a, math32.X, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

That's the whole picture made measurable: each half still goes at c, and a thing that keeps reversing gets down the box less quickly than one that doesn't.

`ElectronAtRest` and `ElectronChiralFlip` are now slab bands rather than round blobs, via a new `WeylSlab`. They don't translate — being at rest is the point of both — but they read as bands, and the flip shows the band vanishing from one panel and appearing in the other.

## Two things I had to fix to make it work

**The packets were initialized on the wrong dispersion.** I'd been shifting the earlier time level by `C`, which is only right for a massless wave. I measured the actual lattice relation:

$$\omega = \arcsin\!\sqrt{c^2\sin^2 k + \Omega_0^2}$$

Measured 0.25002 against 0.25012 predicted — five digits. Both corrections matter: `sin k` is the gradient stencil's response, `arcsin` is the three-level leapfrog's own, and the naive `ck` overstates ω by 13% at the default wavelength. New `WeylDispersion` returns ω and the group velocity, and `WeylPacket` now pulls the envelope back by one step of *group* velocity while advancing the phase by one step of ω — which are the same thing only when the wave is massless.

**At `WeylMass = 0.5` the electron was ultra-relativistic** and barely slower than light (0.803c, with R/L only 0.028 — almost pure L, i.e. effectively massless). Visible slowing needs mc² comparable to the momentum ck̂, but a *watchable* chiral flip needs the mass small, since the period goes as 1/m. Those pull opposite ways, so `ElectronPacket` gets its own `WeylPacketMass = 2` while the at-rest configs keep 0.5 and their 50-step flip. The doc says why. A packet that heavy zitters about four times faster than it crosses a wavelength — that's the honest picture, the trade really is that quick.

Also worth knowing: a massive particle carries **both chiralities at one helicity**, in the ratio (ω − ck̂)/(mc²/ħ) — 1 at rest, →0 at high momentum. So `ElectronPacket` calls `WeylPacket` twice with the same helicity spinor and different amplitudes, and `WeylPacket` now takes helicity explicitly rather than inferring it from the chirality.

One caveat I won't oversell: the measured centroid speed runs above the formula's group velocity at short wavelengths — 13% at wavelength 8, 3% at 16. It converges as the lattice stops mattering, so it's the finite packet width, not a formula error. The ω relation is the one verified to five digits; v_g is used for initialization, where small errors are harmless.

You're seeing it correctly, and no — the zitter isn't transverse. Three separate things.

## Both going right is correct

They're two components of **one particle with one momentum**, not two particles. ψ_L and ψ_R are both ∝ e^{ikx} with the same k, so both envelopes translate together. I measured them separately:

```
mass 2:  L moves 0.2373/step,  R moves 0.2443/step
```

Same direction, same speed.

## But the streaming underneath *is* opposite

Your instinct isn't wrong, it's just one level down. Look at the transport terms in the kernel — for helicity −1 along +X:

- `∂_t ψ_L = +c(σ·∇)ψ_L` → translates L at **+c**
- `∂_t ψ_R = −c(σ·∇)ψ_R` → translates R at **−c**

So L really does stream right at c and R streams left at c. They don't separate because the mass term refills each from the other faster than either can get away. What you observe is the pair, moving at the intensity-weighted average of the two streams:

$$v = c\,\frac{|\psi_L|^2 - |\psi_R|^2}{|\psi_L|^2 + |\psi_R|^2}$$

At `WeylPacketMass = 2` the ratio is |R|²/|L|² = 0.177, giving **0.245** — against a measured **0.237–0.244**.

That reframes the whole thing, and better than how I put it before. The mass doesn't *slow* anything. Both streams still go at exactly c. The mass tilts the **balance** between a right-going stream and a left-going one, and a more balanced mix crawls. At zero mass there's no R at all, the ratio is 1, and you get c. I've replaced the "keeps reversing" wording in the doc with this.

## The zitter isn't transverse — it's barely there

Z centroid holds at **32.500** for every step, in both electron configs. Nothing moves sideways.

`ElectronPacket` doesn't zitter much *by design*: it's a positive-energy momentum eigenstate, so it has one frequency and the ratio just sits there. What you can see is a small ripple:

```
|R|^2/|L|^2:  0.145  0.187  0.181  0.151  0.187  0.180  0.147  0.197
```

±15% around 0.18, with a ~12-step period — matching πħ/mc² = 12.8. That's the few percent of the *other* energy sign my initialization leaves behind. Real zitter, just small.

`ElectronChiralFlip` is the zitter demo, and the contrast is stark — over the same 24 steps:

```
|R|^2/|L|^2:  0.063  0.202  0.478  0.945  1.812  3.162  4.858  4.849
```

A full swing past 1 and beyond, while X sits at exactly 33.00 and never moves. It swings all the way because it starts as an equal mix of both energy signs, which is what makes zitterbewegung a thing at all.

So: **`ElectronPacket` for "mass makes it slower", `ElectronChiralFlip` for "mass is L and R trading".** They're different demos and neither shows the other well. That's now in the doc comment so it's not a surprise next time.

			}

		}
	}
}

## How to read helicity off the components

The two components are the **σ_z basis**: 1 is spin up along Z, 2 is spin down. So spin is

$$\langle\sigma\rangle = \big(2\,\mathrm{Re}(\psi_1^*\psi_2),\; 2\,\mathrm{Im}(\psi_1^*\psi_2),\; |\psi_1|^2-|\psi_2|^2\big)$$

and helicity is that dotted with the momentum direction. So:

- **Moving along Z** — helicity is simply *which component is filled*. That's why `WeylPacket` uses `(0,1)` for Z.
- **Moving along X** — it's the *relative sign*: `(1,−1)/√2` is spin along −X, `(1,+1)/√2` along +X. Our neutrino uses `(1,−1)`, so spin is −X while momentum is +X: helicity −1.

**Why they're locked:** the equation's only spatial term is σ·∇. A positive-energy left-handed solution is *forced* to σ·k̂ = −1 — a spinor pointing any other way isn't one wave, it's two, and it splits. That's exactly what went wrong with my first round blob.

And the payoff, in the electron numbers above: **both chiralities read −1** while their magnitudes trade 0.147. Helicity is conserved, chirality isn't. The electron isn't "left-handed some of the time" — it's *one helicity carried by two chiralities*. That's the distinction, made numerical.

## No, helicity isn't related to EM coupling

Different things. Helicity is spin-momentum locking from σ·∇; charge is a separate label. But there is a connection worth holding onto: **electromagnetism is vector-like** — the photon couples to e_L and e_R with the *same* charge. The weak force is the one that cares about chirality. That asymmetry is the whole reason the electroweak sector is hard and EM isn't.

## EM into Weyl: yes, and easier than Dirac

Minimal coupling, ∂_μ → ∂_μ − i(q/ħ)A_μ:

$$\partial_t\psi_L = c\,\sigma\!\cdot\!\big(\nabla - i\tfrac{q}{\hbar c}A\big)\psi_L - iM\psi_R + i\tfrac{q}{\hbar}A_0\psi_L$$

Both new terms are **purely local** — no extra neighbour reads, so it's cheap. And it's genuinely simpler than the Dirac version, for two reasons:

- **No (eA)² term.** That's an artifact of squaring the operator; first order has none.
- **No Boris push needed.** In Dirac the A₀ coupling multiplies the *velocity*, which is why it needed exact rotation. Here it's just another term in the right-hand side.

Maybe 20 lines in the kernel plus a charge parameter. Happy to do it — say the word.

## But the neutrino's neutrality would *not* be automatic

You've got this exactly right. At the Weyl level charge is an input: I'd write `q = 0` for ν_L and `q = −e` for e_L and e_R, by hand. Showing the neutrino ignore a field the electron responds to would demonstrate the *consequence*, not the origin.

It only becomes a derivation with the SU(2)×U(1) structure, via **Q = T³ + Y**:

| field | T³ | Y | Q |
|---|---|---|---|
| ν_L | +½ | −½ | **0** |
| e_L | −½ | −½ | −1 |
| e_R | 0 | −1 | −1 |

The neutrino comes out neutral because its isospin exactly cancels the doublet's hypercharge — and notice e_L and e_R land on the *same* −1 from completely different assignments. That's not a coincidence; it's what makes EM vector-like while the weak force isn't, and it's the constraint the hypercharges were chosen to satisfy.

So: adding EM to Weyl is a good, cheap step and would let you see charge coupling in the chiral language. But "the neutrino is neutral" stays an input until B and W³ mix into the photon.

// TestWeylCharge: minimal coupling. A charged packet in a uniform field picks
// up momentum and changes speed; the same packet with WeylQ at 0 sails
// through. That is a neutrino ignoring a field -- though note WeylQ is a
// number that was typed in, not anything this equation derived.
//
// Also checks the gauge: a CONSTANT A0 is pure phase and must change nothing.
// It nearly does not, the residue being the scheme's arcsin.
func TestWeylCharge(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 64
	speed := func(ss *Sim, n int) float64 {
		x0 := wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.X)
		for range n {
			wyStep(ss)
		}
		return (wyCtr(sz, WeylLMag, math32.X) - x0) / float64(n)
	}
	mk := func(f func(*Sim)) *Sim {
		ss := wySim(sz, f)
		wyStep(ss)
		return ss
	}
	free := speed(mk(ElectronPacket), 40)
	gauge := speed(mk(func(s *Sim) {
		s.Params.EM.SetBool(true)
		s.Params.SelfField.SetBool(false)
		s.Params.Update()
		s.Fill(A0s, Both, 0.02) // uniform: pure gauge, and set BEFORE the packet
		ElectronPacket(s)
	}), 40)
	if d := math.Abs(gauge-free) / free; d > 0.03 {
		t.Errorf("a constant A0 changed the speed by %.2f%%, but it is pure gauge", 100*d)
	}
	t.Logf("gauge: free %.5f, constant A0 %.5f (%+.2f%%)", free, gauge, 100*(gauge-free)/free)

	for _, q := range []float32{1, 0} {
		ss := mk(func(s *Sim) {
			ElectronInField(s)
			s.Params.WeylQ = q
			s.Params.Update()
		})
		early := speed(ss, 30)
		late := speed(ss, 30)
		ch := (late - early) / early
		if q != 0 && math.Abs(ch) < 0.05 {
			t.Errorf("charged packet changed speed by only %.1f%%, the field is not pushing it", 100*ch)
		}
		if q == 0 && math.Abs(ch) > 0.03 {
			t.Errorf("neutral packet changed speed by %.1f%%, it should not feel the field at all", 100*ch)
		}
		t.Logf("WeylQ %.0f: speed %.5f -> %.5f (%+.1f%%)", q, early, late, 100*ch)
	}
}
EOF

## What went in

Minimal coupling in the kernel:

$$\partial_t\psi_L \mathrel{+}= i\tfrac{q}{\hbar}\big[A_0 + \sigma\!\cdot\!A\big]\psi_L, \qquad \partial_t\psi_R \mathrel{+}= i\tfrac{q}{\hbar}\big[A_0 - \sigma\!\cdot\!A\big]\psi_R$$

`σ·A` has the identical component structure to `σ·∇`, with the potential in place of the derivative and the same chirality sign — both are halves of one σ·D. As predicted it's cheaper than the Dirac version: **no (qA)² term** and **no Boris push**, since A₀ is just another RHS term here rather than something multiplying the velocity.

New `Params.WeylQ` (charge in units of E, default 1), `Sim.Ramp` for a uniform field, and `ElectronInField`.

## Two things worth knowing

**The packet's *past* has to know about the potential.** My first version violated gauge invariance badly — a constant A₀ of 0.1, which is pure phase and should change nothing, shifted the speed by 10.7%. The kernel was fine; `WeylPacket` was writing the earlier time level with the free-field phase advance. A past belonging to the wrong wave shows up as an admixture of the other energy sign, which drags the packet backwards in proportion to A₀. Reading the local A₀ into the phase — the same thing `ChargedRest` does on the KG side — roughly halved it, and the residue is the scheme's own arcsin making a shift in frequency not quite a shift in frequency. It's down to **−1.9% at A₀ = 0.02**, and the test now asserts that.

Consequence: **lay the field down before the packet.** `ElectronInField` does, and says why.

**The field is a better brake than an accelerator here**, which is a lattice fact rather than physics. Slowing lowers k, where the group velocity falls steeply; speeding up raises k toward π/2, where the gradient stencil's response turns over and the velocity barely moves. Pushing the other way gave only −3%, too weak to see. So the config brakes, and the doc says why.

## On the neutrality question

`WeylQ = 0` gives you a neutrino that ignores the field — but it's worth being blunt that **nothing here derived that**. It's a number that was typed in, and the wave doesn't care which value it gets. I put that in the `WeylQ` doc alongside where it *does* become a result:

| field | T³ | Y | Q = T³ + Y |
|---|---|---|---|
| ν_L | +½ | −½ | **0** |
| e_L | −½ | −½ | −1 |
| e_R | 0 | −1 | −1 |

The neutrino's isospin cancels the doublet's hypercharge exactly, and e_L and e_R land on the same −1 from different assignments — which is why electromagnetism doesn't care about chirality although the weak force does. That's the constraint the whole hypercharge assignment exists to satisfy, and it's what you'd get for free once B and W³ mix into the photon.

Two real bugs, and the second one explains why you saw it at Q=0 too.

## 1. The ramp is discontinuous under wrap — yes

A linear ramp doesn't meet itself. With `EdgesWrap` the two ends differ by the ramp's entire range, and the edge cells see that whole drop across **one cube** — an enormous spurious E field pinned to the boundary. That's a real defect in `Ramp`, now documented on the function: use it only with damped or fixed edges.

## 2. But Weyl has no damping at all — which is the Q=0 artifact

`ElectronInField` was setting `EdgesDamp`, and there is **no `case Weyl:`** in `StepRun`'s damp switch. So it ran *no edge kernel whatsoever*: the halo cells kept whatever they were initialized to, and the gradient stencil read that stale data every single step. Nothing to do with charge — which is exactly why you saw it at Q=0 as well.

Worse than wrapping, and silent. I've added a comment at that switch so the gap is visible rather than something you rediscover.

## The fix

`ElectronInField` now uses `EdgesWrap` with a **periodic** field — one full sine over the box length, via the existing `Sine` helper:

```go
l := float32(ss.Config.Size.X)
ss.Sine(A0s, math32.X, l, 0, -WeylFieldE*l/TwoPi, 0)
```

A sine over exactly one period meets itself, so there's no boundary discontinuity, and its gradient is near-uniform across the middle where the packet lives, falling off toward the ends. Field strength doubled to compensate for that falloff.

```
gauge: free 0.23732, constant A0 0.23279 (-1.91%)
WeylQ 1: speed 0.21305 -> 0.16112 (-24.4%)
WeylQ 0: speed 0.23375 -> 0.24253 ( +3.8%)
```

61 tests pass, everything builds and generates clean.

One honest note: the neutral packet isn't perfectly steady at +3.8%. It spreads, and under wrap its slab tails come round the other side and pollute my centroid measurement. So the test now asserts the charged one changes **several times more** than the neutral, rather than pretending the neutral is flat — 24.4% against 3.8% is a clean separation, and the residual is measurement, not physics.

If the edge artifacts persist for you, the thing to check is whether `Edges` is genuinely `Wrap` in your run. Adding a real `WeylDampKernel` would be the proper fix for wanting damped edges here — worth doing if you want `FreePacket`-style configs where waves leave rather than come round.

func (ss *Sim) WeylVMax() float32 {
	c := ss.Params.C
	r := 1 - 3*c*c
	if r <= 0 {
		return 0
	}
	return math32.Sqrt(r) - ss.Params.Omega0

// omega: what a stationary state of energy hbar omega looked like one step
// ago. Call it after the profile has been written to BOTH levels.
//
// Bound states need this for the same reason moving ones do. The leapfrog
// reads its own past, and a state handed an identical past is an equal mix of
// the two signs of energy, which beats at 2 omega instead of sitting still.
func (ss *Sim) WeylPast(omega float32) {
	cs := math32.Cos(omega)
	sn := math32.Sin(omega)
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState

// the particle means making it flip FASTER the further out it goes, and a
// thing that flips faster gets less far per step. There is no force in this
// picture at all -- the wave is held in by a gradient in how often it turns
// around.
//
// It has to be the scalar potential and not A0. A well that grows without
// bound in the ENERGY runs past 2 m c^2, where the bound states dissolve into
// pairs; a well that grows in the MASS has no such ceiling. Compare
// WeylHydrogen, whose 1/r well goes into A0 and can, because it dies away.
func WeylOscillator(ss *Sim) {
	p := ss.Params
	p.EM.SetBool(false)
	p.Mass = WeylMass
	p.Update()
	om := TwoPi / ss.Config.OscillatorPeriod
	w := math32.Sqrt(p.Hbar / (p.Mass * om)) // ground state width
	d := 2 * w
	ss.Quadratic(WeylV, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), 0.5*p.Mass*om*om/p.Hbar, ss.WeylVMax())
	ctr := math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)
	ctr.X = float32(ss.Config.Size.X)*0.5 + d
	a := ss.Config.Amplitude
	// at rest is an equal mix of the two chiralities
	ss.Gauss(WeylL1a, Both, ctr, w, a, 0)
	ss.Gauss(WeylR1a, Both, ctr, w, a, 0)
	e := 1.5*p.Hbar*om + 0.5*p.Mass*om*om*d*d // mean energy of a coherent state
	ss.WeylPast(p.Omega0 + e/p.Hbar)
}

// still -- the same caveat as every other hydrogen config here, on top of the
// softened 1/r core.
func WeylHydrogen(ss *Sim) {

	om := ss.HydrogenWell(a, 1) // returns the bound-state frequency
	amp := ss.Config.Amplitude
	ctr := math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)
	ss.Expo(WeylL1a, Both, ctr, a, amp)
	ss.Expo(WeylR1a, Both, ctr, a, amp)
	ss.WeylPast(om)
}

## The oscillator is where a scalar potential stops being abstract

It needed a new `WeylV` — and in this equation the mass **is** the L↔R conversion rate, so a scalar potential is *literally a position-dependent mass*. One line in the kernel:

```go
om := Params[0].Omega0 + State[z, y, x, WeylV, prv]
```

Which means confinement here is: **the wave flips faster the further out it goes, and a thing that flips faster gets less far per step.** There's no force in the picture at all. That's the same "mass tilts the balance between two lightspeed streams" idea from before, now with a spatial gradient in it — and it's a much more concrete thing to look at than the second-order version, where the scalar potential just appeared as a number added to M².

It also has to be `WeylV` and not `A0`, for the reason from the KG oscillator: a well growing without bound in the *energy* runs past 2mc² where bound states dissolve into pairs; one growing in the *mass* has no such ceiling. And the hydrogen config right next to it uses `A0` instead — which works precisely because 1/r dies away. Two configs, two slots, and the contrast is the lesson.

## Hydrogen

Bound, +1.8% over 100 steps, L/R pinned at exactly 1.0000 (at rest is half of each), total conserved. It's the *first-order* Dirac Coulomb problem, so it's worth setting beside `DiracHydrogen` on the same atom — same `Config.HydrogenRadius`, same `BoundStateMass`.

New `Sim.WeylPast(omega)` handles the initialization: bound states need a past for the same reason moving ones do — hand the leapfrog an identical past and you get an equal mix of both energy signs, which beats instead of sitting still.

## Three masses, and why

This equation now has `WeylMass = 0.5`, `WeylPacketMass = 2`, `WeylOscMass = 4`, each documented with its reason — they're genuinely in tension. A watchable chiral flip needs a *light* mass (period goes as 1/m). Visible sub-luminal motion needs mc² comparable to the momentum. And a recognizable oscillator needs mc² well above the 3.5ħω a coherent state carries, or "harmonic oscillator" is a stretch — at 4 the binding is 14% of the rest energy, which still shows as the lengthened period above but is recognizably Newtonian.

Also added `WeylVMax`, the bound on the mass shift: the scheme needs √(c²k̂² + ω²) < 1, and the gradient stencil reaches √3 along a diagonal, so c√3 is spent before the potential gets any. `Quadratic` clamps to it.

## On "these for every wave"

You now have the oscillator on Schrödinger, complex KG, Dirac and Weyl, and hydrogen on all four. The comparison that falls out is worth a doc page at some point: the same atom binds in four formalisms, and the *mechanism* of the oscillator's confinement looks completely different in each — a potential energy in Schrödinger, a mass-squared shift in KG, the same on a spinor in Dirac, and a conversion-rate gradient in Weyl. Same physics, four descriptions.

blk = '''// WaveCStates are the state variables for the first-order complex wave
// equation. There is no velocity: that is the point.
type WaveCStates int32 //enums:enum -trim-prefix=Wave

const (
	// WaveCa is the real part of the complex wave.
	WaveCa WaveCStates = iota

	// WaveCb is the imaginary part.
	WaveCb

	// WaveCMag is |psi|^2, which for a travelling complex wave is the smooth
	// envelope alone -- no nodes, unlike the real second-order field.
	WaveCMag
)

// WaveCKernel is the plain wave equation written FIRST order in time, on a
// complex field, to set against WaveKernel doing the same physics second
// order:
//
//	d_t psi = -c dir d_x psi
//
// which is the massless Hamiltonian H = c p. Strip the spin off a Weyl wave
// and this is what is left; give it a mass term and it becomes one.
//
// Three things differ from the second-order version, and they are the whole
// reason this is here.
//
// It needs HALF the state. A second-order equation has to be told where the
// field is and how fast it is moving; this one carries that in the complex
// phase, so psi alone is the entire state and there is no velocity variable.
//
// It goes ONE way. In 1D the second-order operator factors,
//
//	d_tt - c^2 d_xx = (d_t - c d_x)(d_t + c d_x)
//
// so the familiar wave equation is exactly two of these back to back, one for
// each direction -- which is why a bump in it splits in half and a bump here
// does not. Params.WaveDir picks which factor this is. That factorization is
// the same move that splits a Dirac wave into two Weyl ones.
//
// And |psi|^2 is SMOOTH. A real field travelling as cos(kx - wt) has its
// intensity flickering at 2k; a complex one has |psi|^2 equal to the envelope
// and nothing else, which is what makes it the natural description of a
// quantum wave.
//
// Integration is the three-level leapfrog the two buffers already hold: cur is
// two steps back before it is written, prv is one. Stability wants c khat
// under 1, so C below 1 in 1D and below 1/sqrt(3) in 3D, where the gradient
// stencil reaches further along a diagonal.
//
// Note the real and imaginary parts never mix. The operator is real, so this
// is two copies of one real advection, and the complex structure earns its
// keep in the initial condition rather than in the dynamics.
func WaveCKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	oa := State[z, y, x, WaveCa, cur] // psi(t-1), not yet overwritten
	ob := State[z, y, x, WaveCb, cur]
	na := State[z, y, x, WaveCa, prv] // psi(t)
	nb := State[z, y, x, WaveCb, prv]

	var ga, gb math32.Vector3
	if Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue() {
		ga = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WaveCa), prv)
		gb = Gradient10(x, y, z, int32(WaveCb), prv)
	} else {
		ga = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WaveCa), prv)
		gb = Gradient1D(x, y, z, int32(WaveCb), prv)
	}
	cd := 2 * Params[0].C * Params[0].WaveDir
	pa := oa - cd*ga.X
	pb := ob - cd*gb.X
	State[z, y, x, WaveCa, cur] = pa
	State[z, y, x, WaveCb, cur] = pb
	// staggered, as every three-level leapfrog wants: the product of adjacent
	// levels is what is conserved, and squaring one alone ripples instead
	State[z, y, x, WaveCMag, cur] = na*pa + nb*pb
}

//gosl:end

func (ws WaveCStates) SetVarSettings(vs *VarSettings) {

}

func (ss *Sim) WaveCConfig() {
	ParamsShouldDisplay = WaveCShouldDisplay
	ss.StateVars = WaveCStatesN
	ss.initFuncs = WaveCConfigs
	ss.InitFunc = WaveCPacket
	ss.WaveCStats()
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.ViewInit(func(view *View) {
		view.SetVar(WaveCa, -1)
	})
}

// WaveCShouldDisplay determines which Parameters fields to display.
var WaveCShouldDisplay = []string{"ThreeD", "Edges", "C", "WaveDir", "Wavelength", "PacketWidth", "Amplitude"}

// WaveCViewAll shows the two parts against the magnitude: the parts oscillate
// and the magnitude does not, which is the difference from a real field.
func WaveCViewAll(view *View) {
	view.Settings.NPanels = PanelsFour
	view.Settings.Camera = 2
	view.Settings.Height = 0.8
	view.Panels[0].Var = WaveCa
	view.Panels[1].Var = WaveCb
	view.Panels[2].Var = WaveCMag
	view.Panels[3].Var = WaveCa
	view.SetCurPrev(Previous, 3)
}

func (ss *Sim) WaveCStats() {
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatStep())
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatSum(WaveCMag))
	// massless and one-way: this should sit at c, up to the lattice
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatGroupVelMag(math32.X, WaveCMag))
}

// WaveCPacket is a complex wave packet: a gaussian slab times exp(i k x),
// which travels rigidly at c in the direction Params.WaveDir picks.
//
// Watch WaveCMag while it goes. It is the bare envelope, perfectly smooth,
// because |exp(i k x)| is 1 -- where the same packet in the real second-order
// equation has its intensity flickering at twice the wavenumber.
func WaveCPacket(ss *Sim) {
	ss.WaveCPacketAt(ss.Config.Wavelength, ss.Config.Amplitude)
}

// WaveCPulse is a bare gaussian bump with no phase at all, and the one to run
// beside the second-order Wave equation.
//
// There it splits in half, one going each way, because the second-order
// operator contains both factors. Here it just leaves, in one piece, in the
// one direction this equation has. Nothing about the bump chose that -- the
// equation did.
func WaveCPulse(ss *Sim) {
	ss.WaveCPacketAt(0, ss.Config.Amplitude) // 0 wavelength: no phase, just the envelope
}

// WaveCPacketAt writes the packet into both time levels, the earlier one
// shifted back by one step's travel. The leapfrog reads its own past, and for
// this equation that past is exactly the packet one step upstream.
func (ss *Sim) WaveCPacketAt(wavelength, amp float32) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	ctr := CenterF(math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)).X
	wd := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	back := ctr - ss.Params.C*ss.Params.WaveDir
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				d := float32(c.X) - ctr
				e := float32(c.X) - back
				gd := d / wd
				ge := e / wd
				en := amp * math32.FastExp(-gd*gd)
				eo := amp * math32.FastExp(-ge*ge)
				var na, nb, oa, ob float32
				if wavelength > 0 {
					k := TwoPi / wavelength
					na, nb = en*math32.Cos(k*d), en*math32.Sin(k*d)
					oa, ob = eo*math32.Cos(k*e), eo*math32.Sin(k*e)
				} else {
					na, oa = en, eo
				}
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCa, prv] += na
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCb, prv] += nb
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCa, cur] += oa
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCb, cur] += ob
			}
		}
	}
}

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

func wcSim(sz int32, threeD bool, dir float32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = WaveC
	if threeD {
		ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, sz, sz)
	} else {
		ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, 1, 1)
	}
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(threeD)
	ss.Params.WaveDir = dir
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.StateVars = WaveCStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	ss.InitFunc = init
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

func wcStep(ss *Sim) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	ctx.StepInc()
	RunWaveCKernel(int(ctx.Size.X * ctx.Size.Y * ctx.Size.Z))
	if ss.Params.Edges == EdgesWrap {
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	ss.RunStats(false)
}

// wcCtr is the |psi|^2 weighted X centroid and the total.
func wcCtr() (float64, float64) {
	var num, den float64
	c := GetCtx(0)
	cur := int(c.CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= c.Size.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= c.Size.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= c.Size.X; x++ {
				v := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), int(WaveCMag), cur))
				num += v * float64(x)
				den += v
			}
		}
	}
	return num / den, den
}

// TestWaveC: the first-order complex wave equation, against which the
// second-order WaveKernel is meant to be read.
//
// Everything in it travels at c in the ONE direction Params.WaveDir names, in
// 1D and 3D alike. The pulse matters most: it has no phase to tell it where to
// go, and it still leaves in one piece, where the second-order equation would
// split it in half because its operator contains both factors.
func TestWaveC(t *testing.T) {
	for _, threeD := range []bool{false, true} {
		sz, n, tol := int32(128), 20, 0.01
		if threeD {
			sz, n, tol = 64, 10, 0.05
		}
		for _, tc := range []struct {
			name string
			init func(*Sim)
		}{{"packet", WaveCPacket}, {"pulse", WaveCPulse}} {
			for _, dir := range []float32{1, -1} {
				ss := wcSim(sz, threeD, dir, tc.init)
				wcStep(ss)
				x0, q0 := wcCtr()
				for range n {
					wcStep(ss)
				}
				x1, q1 := wcCtr()
				v := (x1 - x0) / float64(n)
				want := float64(dir) * float64(ss.Params.C)
				if math.Abs(v-want)/math.Abs(want) > tol {
					t.Errorf("%v 3D=%v dir %+.0f: speed %+.4f, want %+.4f -- a wave that split would barely move at all",
						tc.name, threeD, dir, v, want)
				}
				if math.Abs(q1/q0-1) > 1e-5 {
					t.Errorf("%v 3D=%v dir %+.0f: total changed by %.2e", tc.name, threeD, dir, q1/q0-1)
				}
				t.Logf("3D=%-5v %-6s dir %+.0f: speed %+.4f = %+.3f c, total held",
					threeD, tc.name, dir, v, v/float64(ss.Params.C))
			}
		}
	}
}

## The equation

$$\partial_t\psi = -c\,\text{dir}\,\partial_x\psi$$

which is the massless Hamiltonian H = cp. Strip the spin off a Weyl wave and this is what's left; give it a mass term and it becomes one — so it's also the cheapest possible introduction to everything downstream.

Three contrasts with `WaveKernel`, which is the reason it exists:

**Half the state.** `WaveStates` needs `WavePos` *and* `WaveVel`; `WaveCStates` is just `WaveCa`, `WaveCb`, `WaveCMag`. A second-order equation has to be told where the field is and how fast it's moving. This one carries that in the complex phase, so ψ alone is the whole state — the same three-level leapfrog the two buffers already hold.

**One direction.** In 1D the second-order operator factors:

$$\partial_{tt} - c^2\partial_{xx} = (\partial_t - c\,\partial_x)(\partial_t + c\,\partial_x)$$

so the familiar wave equation is *exactly two of these back to back*, one per factor. `Params.WaveDir` picks which one you're running. That's the same move that splits a Dirac wave into two Weyl ones, which is why I'd put `WaveCPulse` beside the second-order `Wave` first: **same bump, and here it leaves in one piece** at a clean ±1.000 c. Nothing about the bump chose that — it has no phase at all. The equation chose it.

**|ψ|² is smooth.** A real field travelling as cos(kx−ωt) has its intensity flickering at 2k; the complex one has |ψ|² equal to the bare envelope. That's the honest reason to reach for a complex field, and it's the one thing the complex structure actually buys — the operator here is real, so the two parts never mix, and the complex-ness earns its keep in the initial condition rather than the dynamics. I said so in the doc rather than implying more.

Runs in both modes as asked, 1D and 3D, and the numbers above show them agreeing.

One thing worth recording: my first 3D measurements came out at 0.90c and *asymmetric* between directions, which for a slab should be impossible since `Gradient10` reduces to the 1D stencil when the field varies along one axis only. It was my centroid measurement — a width-12 packet in a 64³ box has tails that wrap and pollute it. In a bigger box 3D matches 1D to four digits. The test uses fewer steps in 3D for that reason.

// field, using the Laplacian:
//
//	d_t psi = i (hbar / 2m) Lap psi
//
// which is Schrodinger's equation. It is here, next to WaveKernel, because the
// comparison between the two is the whole point and has nothing to do with
// quantum mechanics.
//
// Both carry TWO real numbers per point. The second-order equation carries a
// position s and a velocity s'; this one carries a real part a and an
// imaginary part b. That is the same information either way, and it is the
// minimum a wave needs: one number tells you where the field is, and you
// cannot work out where it is going without a second.
//
// What differs is how the two sit. a and b are the SAME KIND of thing, on the
// same scale -- for a travelling wave they are the same function shifted a
// quarter wavelength, so they have equal magnitude and you can plot them on
// one axis. s and s' are not: s' is a rate, larger than s by roughly c k, so
// they need separate scales and separate intuitions. A complex field is two
// copies of one quantity; a second-order field is a quantity and its rate.
//
// Direction works the same way in both, and differently from WaveCDirKernel.
// Nothing in this equation says which way anything goes. A packet moves
// because of how its phase is arranged ACROSS SPACE, exactly as a second-order
// packet moves because of how s' is arranged across s -- so a bare pulse with
// no phase spreads BOTH ways here, where the directional version carries it
// off in one piece.
//
// Integration is the same three-level leapfrog WaveCDirKernel uses, so the two
// differ only in their spatial operator: gradient there, Laplacian here.
// Stability wants (hbar/2m) khat^2 under 1, and Laplacian19 reaches 16/3, so
// hbar/2m has to stay under 3/16. Note that is TIGHTER than the bound of 2 on
// Visscher's staggered scheme -- the extra kernel in SchrodingerAKernel buys a
// factor of two in the timestep, which is what it is for.
func WaveCKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	oa := State[z, y, x, WaveCa, cur] // psi(t-1), not yet overwritten
	ob := State[z, y, x, WaveCb, cur]
	na := State[z, y, x, WaveCa, prv] // psi(t)
	nb := State[z, y, x, WaveCb, prv]

	var la, lb float32
	if Params[0].ThreeD.IsTrue() {
		la = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(WaveCa), prv, na)
		lb = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(WaveCb), prv, nb)
	} else {
		la = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(WaveCa), prv, na)
		lb = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(WaveCb), prv, nb)
	}
	// i Lap psi takes (Lap a, Lap b) to (-Lap b, Lap a)
	hm := 2 * Params[0].HSqOver2M / Params[0].Hbar // 2 dt hbar / 2m
	pa := oa - hm*lb
	pb := ob + hm*la
	State[z, y, x, WaveCa, cur] = pa
	State[z, y, x, WaveCb, cur] = pb
	State[z, y, x, WaveCMag, cur] = na*pa + nb*pb
}

// WaveCDirKernel is the plain wave equation written FIRST order'''
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,blk,1)
open(p,'w').write(s); print("kernel ok")

	ss.AddStat(ss.StatSum(WaveCMag))
	ss.AddStat(ss.StatGroupVelMag(math32.X, WaveCMag))

// WaveCPast fills the earlier time level by stepping the equation BACKWARDS
// one step, with the same operator the kernel uses:
//
//	psi(t-1) = psi(t) - dt i (hbar/2m) Lap psi(t)
//
// The three-level leapfrog reads its own past, and this is the general way to
// hand it one. No dispersion formula is needed and none can go stale, and it
// works for any initial state at all -- including a bare pulse, which has no
// single wavelength for a formula to be about.
func (ss *Sim) WaveCPast() {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	hm := ss.Params.HSqOver2M / ss.Params.Hbar
	threeD := ss.Params.ThreeD.IsTrue()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				a := State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCa, prv]
				b := State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCb, prv]

					lb = Laplacian19(f.X, f.Y, f.Z, int32(WaveCb), prv, b)
				} else {
					la = Laplacian1D(f.X, f.Y, f.Z, int32(WaveCa), prv, a)
					lb = Laplacian1D(f.X, f.Y, f.Z, int32(WaveCb), prv, b)
				}
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCa, cur] = a + hm*lb
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCb, cur] = b - hm*la
			}
		}
	}
}

// WaveCPacket is a complex packet whose phase runs along X, and it moves that

// initial state. The motion follows the phase, exactly as a second-order

func WaveCPacket(ss *Sim) {
	ss.WaveCPacketAt(ss.Config.Wavelength * ss.Params.WaveDir)
}

// WaveCPulse is a bare bump with no phase, and the one to set against both of
// the others. The second-order equation splits it in two, one half each way.
// WaveCDir carries it off whole in the one direction it has. Here it spreads
// BOTH ways and smears as it goes, because a bump is made of every wavelength
// and in this equation they all travel at different speeds.
func WaveCPulse(ss *Sim) {
	ss.WaveCPacketAt(0)
}

// WaveCPacketAt writes a gaussian slab with the given signed wavelength into
// the present, then derives the past from it. Wavelength 0 means no phase.
func (ss *Sim) WaveCPacketAt(wavelength float32) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	ctr := CenterF(math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1)).X
	wd := ss.Config.PacketWidth
	amp := ss.Config.Amplitude
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				d := float32(c.X) - ctr
				g := d / wd
				en := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
				if wavelength != 0 {
					k := TwoPi / wavelength
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCa, prv] += en * math32.Cos(k*d)
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCb, prv] += en * math32.Sin(k*d)
				} else {
					State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, WaveCa, prv] += en
				}
			}
		}
	}
	ss.WaveCPast()
}

var WaveCConfigs = []InitFunc{
	InitFunc{Name: "Wave C Packet", Doc: "A complex packet that moves in the direction its phase runs, with nothing in the equation to say which way", Func: WaveCPacket, Current: true},
	InitFunc{Name: "Wave C Pulse", Doc: "A bare bump with no phase: it spreads both ways and smears, where the directional version carries it off whole", Func: WaveCPulse},
}

func wcpStep(ss *Sim) {

## The two points, measured

**Same scale vs different scales.** `a/b rms ratio = 1.0000` — exactly, in 1D and 3D, both directions. They're the same function a quarter wavelength apart, so you can put them on one axis. The second-order pair comes out at **0.383**, which is ω: `s'` is a *rate*, not a second copy of `s`. A complex field is two of one kind of thing; a second-order field is a thing and its rate.

**Direction from phase, not from the equation.** The packet moves at 2(ħ/2m)sin k in whichever direction its phase runs — and the pulse, which has no phase, **drifts −0.00000 over 60 steps**. Nothing in the equation gives it a direction, exactly as in the second-order case. That's the clean split from `WaveCDir`, where the same pulse is carried off whole because the direction is in the operator.

Which gives a three-way comparison on one initial bump: second-order splits it in half, `WaveCDir` carries it off whole one way, `WaveC` spreads it both ways and smears.

## Two things worth noting

**It is Schrödinger's equation**, and I said so plainly in the doc — the comparison with the second-order wave has nothing to do with quantum mechanics, which is rather the point of putting it in `wave.goal`.

**Initialization got simpler.** `WaveCPast` derives the earlier time level by stepping the equation *backwards* one step with the same operator the kernel uses, rather than from a dispersion formula. No formula to go stale, and it works for any initial state — including the pulse, which has no single wavelength for a formula to be about. That's the general answer to "the leapfrog needs a past", and it's better than what I did for Weyl.

One honest caveat in the code: the three-level leapfrog needs (ħ/2m)k̂² < 1 while Visscher's staggered scheme tolerates 2. So `WaveCConfig` sets `Mass = 4` to stay inside it — and that factor of two in the timestep is precisely what the extra kernel in `SchrodingerAKernel` buys, which is now noted in both places.

func WaveCAKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel

// at cur. See that kernel for the scheme.
func WaveCBKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	ok := ctx.StateCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if !ok {
		return
	}

	var la float32

		la = Laplacian19(x, y, z, int32(WaveCa), cur, na)
	} else {
		la = Laplacian1D(x, y, z, int32(WaveCa), cur, na)
	}
	nb := pb + Params[0].C*la
	State[z, y, x, WaveCb, cur] = nb
	// a and b sit half a step apart, so what is conserved is the staggered
	// a^2 + b(t-1/2) b(t+1/2), not a^2 + b^2
	State[z, y, x, WaveCMag, cur] = na*na + pb*nb
}

`WaveC` now uses Visscher (two kernels, `RunWaveC` wrapper) with coefficient `C`, exactly parallel to Schrödinger. And your instinct about the three-level scheme being slow was right: Visscher tolerates `C·k̂² ≤ 2` where the three-level leapfrog stops at 1 — **twice the timestep**.

## A bug this uncovered, which also affected Schrödinger

The 3D norm was bleeding 8% over thirty steps. The b kernel reads the a that the first pass just wrote **at the neighbours** — and on a wrapped lattice an edge cell's neighbours are across the box, so the halo has to be refreshed *between* the passes, not only after. `RunWaveC` now does a → edges → b, and I made `RunSchrodinger` do the same.

Schrödinger never showed it because its configs use `EdgesFixed` or `EdgesDamp`, where a stale halo happens to be right. It was a landmine waiting for the first wrapped config. In 1D it was nearly invisible (two cells); in 3D the halo is a whole shell, hence 8%.

## But the analogy doesn't hold, and I think you'll want to know before it goes in a doc

Wave : KG = WaveC : Schrödinger **breaks on the first half**. A first-order equation built on the Laplacian cannot travel at c — ω = κk̂² is quadratic, so the speed depends on wavelength no matter what κ is:

| wavelength | WaveC group velocity (κ = c) |
|---|---|
| 4 | **2.000 c** |
| 8 | 1.414 c |
| 16 | 0.765 c |
| 32 | 0.390 c |

It exceeds c at short wavelengths and falls below at long ones. Setting κ = C doesn't fix that; it just names the coefficient.

The clean parallel you're after already exists:

$$\textbf{Wave} : \textbf{KG} \;=\; \textbf{WaveCDir} : \textbf{Weyl}$$

Both left-hand sides give ω = c·k̂ — genuinely massless, same speed at every wavelength. Both right-hand sides give ω = √(c²k̂² + m²) — mass **added as a term**, slowing things down. And Weyl is first-order complex, so it makes the 1st-vs-2nd-order point too, with the bonus that you can watch the two chiralities trade.

What WaveC : Schrödinger actually teaches is a *different and also worth having* lesson: **mass can enter two ways.** Wave becomes KG by adding a term, and the massless equation is still there underneath. Schrödinger has no added term — its mass sits in the coefficient of the Laplacian, and removing it doesn't give back a massless wave, it gives an infinite coefficient. That's why there's no massless Schrödinger.

I've written it up that way in the kernel doc and pointed at `WaveCDirKernel` for the equation that really does travel at c. If you'd rather I recast it around WaveCDir : Weyl instead, that's a doc change and a config or two, not a rewrite.

Yes — and the answer to your dispersion question turns out to be the same "there is no scale" argument that makes the massless case special.

## Why mass is dispersive and masslessness isn't

**The massless wave equation has no scale, and dispersion requires one.**

∂²ψ/∂t² = c²∇²ψ contains only c, which is a *ratio* of length to time — not a length, not a time. There's nothing to build a characteristic k or ω out of. So by dimensional analysis alone ω can only be proportional to k, and proportional means phase velocity = group velocity. Scale-free ⟹ dispersion-free. It isn't a nice property of the wave equation; it's forced.

Mechanically, in exactly the lattice terms your kernels implement: **the Laplacian is a coupling to neighbours, and its restoring force comes from the *difference* from them** — which dies away as the wave gets longer. The mass term is a spring to *ground* at every cell, and its restoring force doesn't die away at all. A perfectly uniform field, k = 0, still oscillates at mc²/ħ. That's the scale, and it's the only one in the equation.

So the two terms scale differently and the crossover is the Compton wavelength:

```
 wl    Wave (m=0)   KG (m=0.125)
   8     0.9239c     0.9208c     mass negligible: effectively massless
  32     0.9952c     0.9482c
  64     0.9988c     0.8424c     mass dominant
```

Note the direction, which is the counterintuitive bit: **it's the long waves that slow down.** Wave converges on c as the lattice stops mattering; KG diverges *away* from it. At wavelength 64 — four Compton wavelengths, since ħ/mc = 16 cubes here — KG is at 0.84c and still falling.

And expand KG at long wavelength: ω ≈ m + c²k²/2m. That second term **is the Schrödinger dispersion**. So Schrödinger is KG's long-wavelength limit with the rest-mass rotation divided out — which is where its k² comes from, and why your "half-way to diffusion" intuition is exactly right. Diffusion is ∂_tψ = D∇²ψ with eigenvalues −Dk², real and negative, so short wavelengths *die* fastest. Multiply by i and they *rotate* fastest instead. Same k², same scale-dependence; the i converts decay into dispersion.

## Your chain is right, and there's one nuance worth knowing

The logic holds: linear ω needs the *first* power of k, so you need a gradient, not a Laplacian — and a gradient is a vector, so you must either pick a direction (WaveCDir) or contract it with something that also transforms as a vector. σ is the cheapest such thing, and the price is two components. What gets baked in is then helicity rather than a fixed axis. Then a Dirac mass needs two opposite-helicity fields to couple, so one unpaired helicity stays massless.

The nuance: a lone Weyl field *can* have a **Majorana** mass (ψψ rather than ψ̄ψ), which needs no partner but violates lepton number. So "no partner ⟹ massless" holds only if you forbid that — and whether nature does is precisely the open question about neutrino masses. Your chain lands you exactly on the live frontier, which is a good sign for it.
