**Penrose's zigzag** is your "two Weyl waves bound by mass", by that name — *The Road to Reality* ch. 25. A massive electron as two massless components, the *zig* (left-handed) and *zag* (right-handed), continually interchanging, with the coupling strength being the mass. Each travels luminally; the zigzagging gives an apparent subluminal velocity, and Penrose reads the interchange as zitterbewegung. That is your `ElectronPacket` measurement, in words, from 2004.

**Feynman's checkerboard** (Feynman & Hibbs 1965, problem 2-6) is the 1D version as a path integral, and it's essentially `WaveCDir` → `Weyl`. Paths are zigzags of null segments — the particle always moves at ±c — and a path with R reversals carries amplitude (imε)^R. **Mass is literally the amplitude to reverse.** At m = 0 it only goes one way, and the two directions are the two chiralities in 1+1D. There's [a 3+1D extension from 2023](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2023.1286030/full), and [Feynman's 1947 letter](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.15070v1) on where it came from.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"

// wvSim builds Wave or KleinGordon on the same state with the same config, in
// 1D and in a box big enough that the packet never approaches the edges.
func wvSim(sz int32, eq Equations, wl, width float32) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = eq
	ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, 1, 1)
	ss.Config.Wavelength = wl
	ss.Config.PacketWidth = width
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.ConfigState()
	ss.InitFunc = WavePacket
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

func wvStep(ss *Sim) {
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	ctx.StepInc()
	n := int(ctx.Size.X * ctx.Size.Y * ctx.Size.Z)
	if ss.Config.Equation == Wave {
		RunWaveKernel(n)
	} else {
		RunKleinGordonKernel(n)
	}
	RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
}

// wvCtr is the intensity-weighted X centroid of the second-order field.
func wvCtr(sz int32) float64 {
	var num, den float64
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
		v := float64(State.Value(1, 1, int(x), int(WavePos), cur))
		v *= v
		num += v * float64(x)
		den += v
	}
	return num / den
}

// TestWaveDispersion is what the mass term costs, measured: the same packet,
// the same box, the same config, run under Wave and under KleinGordon at two
// wavelengths.
//
// Wave travels at c whatever the wavelength, because its equation has no
// scale in it -- c is a ratio, not a length, so nothing can make omega
// anything but proportional to k. The mass term supplies the one scale there
// is, the Compton wavelength, and after that omega cannot be proportional to
// anything.
//
// Note WHICH waves it slows. The Laplacian is a coupling to neighbours and its
// restoring force comes from the difference with them, which dies away as the
// wave gets longer; the mass is a spring to ground, and its does not. So short
// waves barely notice the mass and long ones are dominated by it -- the
// opposite of the usual lattice error, which spoils SHORT waves.
func TestWaveDispersion(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 2048
	const short, long float32 = 16, 64
	speed := map[Equations]map[float32]float64{}
	for _, eq := range []Equations{Wave, KleinGordon} {
		speed[eq] = map[float32]float64{}
		for _, wl := range []float32{short, long} {
			ss := wvSim(sz, eq, wl, 2*wl)
			wvStep(ss)
			x0 := wvCtr(sz)
			const n = 100
			for range n {
				wvStep(ss)
			}
			speed[eq][wl] = (wvCtr(sz) - x0) / n / float64(ss.Params.C)
			t.Logf("%-12v wavelength %2.0f: %.4f c", eq, wl, speed[eq][wl])
		}
	}
	// massless: the same speed at both, and that speed is c
	for _, wl := range []float32{short, long} {
		if math.Abs(speed[Wave][wl]-1) > 0.03 {
			t.Errorf("Wave at wavelength %.0f runs at %.4f c, but a massless wave has no scale to disperse about",
				wl, speed[Wave][wl])
		}
	}
	// massive: distinctly slower at the LONG wavelength, where the mass wins
	drop := speed[KleinGordon][short] - speed[KleinGordon][long]
	if drop < 0.08 {
		t.Errorf("KleinGordon only slowed by %.4f c between the two wavelengths: the mass term should disperse it", drop)
	}
	if speed[KleinGordon][long] >= speed[Wave][long]-0.05 {
		t.Errorf("at wavelength %.0f KleinGordon runs at %.4f c against Wave's %.4f c -- the mass is not costing anything",
			long, speed[KleinGordon][long], speed[Wave][long])
	}
	t.Logf("mass costs %.4f c at wavelength %.0f and %.4f c at wavelength %.0f: the LONG waves are the ones it slows",
		speed[Wave][short]-speed[KleinGordon][short], short,
		speed[Wave][long]-speed[KleinGordon][long], long)
}
EOF

  ## Nielsen-Ninomiya No-Go Theorem and Fermion Doubling
  
  The Nielsen-Ninomiya no-go theorem states that the doubling problem of lattice fermions is inevitable if the bilinear free-field action satisfies the conditions of reflection positivity, locality, global axial symmetry, and translational invariance at a fixed scale.
  
  The theorem states that there can be no net chirality under a set of relatively general conditions, namely the lattice Hamiltonian of a fermion being local, quadratic in the fields and invariant under both lattice translations as well as under a change of the phase of the fields, meaning that the number of left-handed and right-handed states must be equal.
  
  ## First-Order Derivatives and Fermion Doubling
  
  The core of the problem is that the first-derivative structure of the Dirac equation yields aliasing where the numerical, first-derivative with central difference skips a lattice site and therefore causes a doubling of the expected spectrum.

## The comparison set

`Wave` and `KleinGordon` now share the **same two configs**, `WavePacket` and `WavePulse`, on the same state variables — so you pick the same config under each equation and the only difference is the mass term. `MovingWavePacketConfig` gets its initial velocity from `PacketFreq`, which already knows whether the equation has a mass, so both get a genuine travelling packet.

That gives you `Packet` + `Pulse` across all four basic equations. The pulse is the sharp one:

| | bare bump, no velocity |
|---|---|
| `Wave` | splits in half, ±c |
| `KleinGordon` | splits, and disperses |
| `WaveC` | spreads both ways, smears |
| `WaveCDir` | leaves whole, one way |

## The lattice literature — your insight is known, but framed as a problem

The first-order/second-order distinction is **the** central structural fact in lattice fermion theory, and the mechanism is literally your chain read backwards:

> *the first-order derivative operator decouples even and odd sites of the lattice, leading to a doubling of the number of degrees of freedom* … *bosons are healthy because the second derivative has no doubling problem*

That's the [Nielsen–Ninomiya theorem](https://mcgreevy.physics.ucsd.edu/s13/final-papers/2013S-215C-Kadakia-Nirag.pdf): no local, translation-invariant, chirally-symmetric lattice fermion action can avoid equal numbers of left- and right-handed species. So "you need a gradient, and a gradient behaves completely differently from a Laplacian on a lattice" is thoroughly known — but as an *obstruction* to be worked around (Wilson terms, staggered fermions, domain wall), not as a route to why fermions must be what they are. There's also a [second-order formalism for lattice fermions](https://arxiv.org/pdf/hep-th/9301072) literature bearing directly on your Dirac kernel.

**The closest thing to your actual chain** is D'Ariano & Perinotti, *Derivation of the Dirac equation from principles of information processing*, PRA **90**, 062106 (2014), [arXiv:1306.1934](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1306.1934). They derive the **Weyl** equation from minimal cellular-automaton axioms — unitarity, locality, homogeneity, discrete isotropy — and get Dirac by coupling two Weyl automata with a mass. Same destination, same order of construction. Follow-up: Bisio, D'Ariano, Perinotti & Tosini, *Weyl, Dirac and Maxwell quantum cellular automata*, Found. Phys. (2015).

Worth noting you already cite **Bialynicki-Birula (1994)**, *Weyl, Dirac, and Maxwell equations on a lattice as unitary cellular automata* — that's the ancestor of this whole line, sitting in your references already.

So: **the destination is not novel, and neither are the pieces.** What I still don't find is the *entry point*. Everyone else starts from an equation (Dirac, or the QCA axioms) and derives structure. You start from an ordinary question about wave dynamics — does the spatial operator drive the velocity or the acceleration? — and let dispersion force the gradient, the gradient force the spinor, and the mass force the pair. D'Ariano & Perinotti's axioms are information-theoretic; yours are what you'd ask after playing with a wave equation. That's a genuinely different road to the same place, and the fact that it's all runnable is not nothing.

My honest read: pitch it as exposition, not as a new result, and cite D'Ariano–Perinotti and Nielsen–Ninomiya up front so a physicist reader knows you know where the ground is. The value is the road, and the fact that a reader can watch each step.

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"
)

// TestEquationSwitch cycles the Equation through every case the way the GUI
// does -- set the field, call Update -- and checks that each one comes up
// clean rather than inheriting the last one's stats, init options or state.
//
// Twice round, because the failure this guards against is accumulation: a
// second pass that registers each stat again would silently double every row.
func TestEquationSwitch(t *testing.T) {
	eqs := []Equations{Wave, WaveC, WaveCDir, KleinGordon, KleinGordonC,
		Schrodinger, Maxwell, Dirac, Weyl, Electroweak}
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = Wave
	ss.Config.Size.Set(16, 16, 16)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(true)

	nstats := map[Equations]int{}
	nvars := map[Equations]int64{}
	for pass := range 2 {
		for _, eq := range eqs {
			ss.Config.Equation = eq
			ss.Config.Update() // the GUI path
			if ss.Config.curEquation != eq {
				t.Fatalf("%v: Update did not reconfigure", eq)
			}
			if ss.StateVars == nil || ss.StateVars.Int64() == 0 {
				t.Errorf("%v: no state variables", eq)
				continue
			}
			// ThreeD must survive a switch: it is not something an equation owns
			if ss.Params.ThreeD.IsFalse() {
				t.Errorf("%v: ThreeD was reset by the switch", eq)
			}
			if pass == 0 {
				nstats[eq], nvars[eq] = len(ss.StatFuncs), ss.StateVars.Int64()
			} else {
				if len(ss.StatFuncs) != nstats[eq] {
					t.Errorf("%v: %d stats on the second pass, %d on the first -- Reset is not clearing",
						eq, len(ss.StatFuncs), nstats[eq])
				}
				if ss.StateVars.Int64() != nvars[eq] {
					t.Errorf("%v: state vars changed between passes", eq)
				}
			}
			// and it has to actually run
			for range 3 {
				ss.StepRun()
			}
			v := float64(State.Value(1, 1, 1, 0, int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
			if math.IsNaN(v) || math.IsInf(v, 0) {
				t.Errorf("%v: state went bad after three steps", eq)
			}
			if pass == 1 && eq == eqs[len(eqs)-1] {
				t.Logf("cycled %d equations twice: stats and state vars stable", len(eqs))
			}
		}
	}
}

// TestWaveDispersionFlag: Params.Dispersion turns the mass term on in Wave,
// which is the whole of what separates it from KleinGordon. Same equation,
// same config, one flag.
func TestWaveDispersionFlag(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 2048
	speed := func(disp bool) float64 {
		ss := wvSim(sz, Wave, 64, 128)
		ss.Params.Dispersion.SetBool(disp)
		ss.Params.Update()
		ss.Init()
		wvStep(ss)
		x0 := wvCtr(sz)
		const n = 100
		for range n {
			wvStep(ss)
		}
		return (wvCtr(sz) - x0) / n / float64(ss.Params.C)
	}
	off, on := speed(false), speed(true)
	if math.Abs(off-1) > 0.03 {
		t.Errorf("Dispersion off: %.4f c, want c", off)
	}
	if off-on < 0.08 {
		t.Errorf("Dispersion on: %.4f c against %.4f c off -- the flag did nothing", on, off)
	}
	t.Logf("wavelength 64: Dispersion off %.4f c, on %.4f c -- the mass costs %.4f c", off, on, off-on)
}
EOF

## `Params.Dispersion`

One flag on `Wave` that turns on the mass term — which is the whole of what separates it from KleinGordon:

```
wavelength 64: Dispersion off 1.0059 c, on 0.7806 c -- the mass costs 0.2253 c
```

Same equation, same config, one toggle, and now you can flip it mid-run and watch the packet slow. The doc on the flag carries the mechanism (Laplacian's restoring force is the *difference* from neighbours and fades with wavelength; the mass is a spring to ground and doesn't — so it's the long waves that slow). Added to `WaveShouldDisplay` along with `ThreeD`, `Mass`, `Wavelength`, `PacketWidth` and `Amplitude`, which weren't exposed before.

## Equation switching

`ConfigSim` now ends with `ss.Config.sim = ss; ss.ConfigEquation()`, and the equation-specific work lives in:

- **`Sim.Reset()`** — clears `StatFuncs`, `initFuncs`, `viewInitFuncs`, `InitFunc`, and rebuilds the stats tree (tensorfs has no delete, so it's rebuilt, not emptied).
- **`Sim.ConfigEquation()`** — Reset, the equation switch, `ConfigState`, `Init`, then caches `curEquation`. Both are `//types:add` so they're callable from a toolbar as a fallback.
- **`Config.Update()`** — reconfigures when `Equation` differs from `curEquation`, setting the cache *before* reconfiguring since that path calls back through here. `Equation` lost its `edit:"-"` so it's now selectable.

`TestEquationSwitch` cycles all ten equations **twice** through the GUI path (set field, call `Update`), and asserts the stat count and state-var count are identical on both passes. That's the failure I was most worried about: a second pass that re-registers stats would silently double every row — the same bug that bit the electroweak stats earlier.

## One design call worth knowing about

**`Reset` deliberately does not touch `Params`.** If it restored defaults you'd lose `ThreeD` on every switch, which would be maddening. But that means the previous equation's `Mass` or `C` would otherwise leak into the next one — so instead **each equation's Config method now declares the params it depends on**. I filled the gaps in `WaveConfig` (C, Mass), `KleinGordonConfig` (C, Mass, Dispersion off) and `WaveCDirConfig` (C); the others already did. The test asserts `ThreeD` survives every switch.

## What I couldn't verify

Two GUI-side things, since I can't see it run:

1. **Does core actually call `Config.Update()` on a field edit?** `Parameters` has an `Update()` and appears to rely on the same mechanism, so it should — but if the dropdown doesn't reconfigure, the method is there to call from a toolbar button.
2. **The view and plot hold references** to the old `ss.Stats` node and to state vars that may no longer exist. `Reset` rebuilds the stats tree, so a plot holding the old one will show stale or empty data until it picks up `ss.Stats` again, and the view's panel vars will point at indices belonging to the previous equation until the new `ViewInit` funcs run. Those probably need a rebuild hook on your side — you'd know better than me where it belongs.

`waves.go`'s `ConfigFunc` also switches on the captured `eqs` rather than `sim.Config.Equation`, so it won't re-apply on a GUI switch. That's fine as-is since `ConfigFunc` isn't re-run — just worth knowing that its size/ThreeD settings are one-time.

<thinking>
I found the actual bug: `VarsListUpdate` has an early-out that skips rebuilding the list if the new variable count matches the old one, so switching between equations with the same number of variables leaves stale entries. It's also compounded by the map being keyed on enum values from the old enum type, so switching enum types like WaveCStates to WaveStates would misalign identities even when the rebuild does happen.

The real fix is checking whether the variable's type actually changed rather than just comparing counts—since enum values compare on type plus value, checking if the first value is already a key in the settings map gives a cheap way to detect a type switch and force a rebuild.

package wavesim

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

func modeSim(eq Equations, wl float32) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = eq
	ss.Config.Size.Set(256, 1, 1)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	if eq == Wave {
		ss.Params.Diffusion.SetBool(true)
	}
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.InitFunc = func(s *Sim) {
		if eq == Wave {
			s.Sine(WavePos, math32.X, wl, 0, 1, 0)
		} else {
			s.Sine(WaveCa, math32.X, wl, 0, 1, 0)
		}
	}
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

func TestScratchDiff(t *testing.T) {
	const wl float32 = 32
	k := 2 * math.Pi / float64(wl)
	kh2 := 4 * math.Sin(k/2) * math.Sin(k/2)

	// diffusion: the mode decays
	d := modeSim(Wave, wl)
	D := float64(d.Params.CSq)
	at := func(ss *Sim, v int) float64 {
		return float64(State.Value(1, 1, 9, v, int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
	}
	a0 := at(d, int(WavePos))
	const n = 60
	for range n {
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		ctx.StepInc()
		RunWaveKernel(int(ctx.Size.X))
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	rate := -math.Log(at(d, int(WavePos))/a0) / n
	fmt.Printf("diffusion: D=%.4f, decay %.6f per step   (D khat^2 = %.6f)\n", D, rate, D*kh2)

	// WaveC: the same mode rotates
	w := modeSim(WaveC, wl)
	Dc := float64(w.Params.C)
	prev := at(w, int(WaveCa))
	var first, last, cnt int
	for i := range 2000 {
		w.RunWaveC(int(GetCtx(0).Size.X))
		GetCtx(0).StepInc()
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(GetCtx(0).EdgesN()))
		v := at(w, int(WaveCa))
		if prev > 0 && v <= 0 {
			if cnt == 0 {
				first = i
			}
			last, cnt = i, cnt+1
		}
		prev = v
	}
	if cnt >= 2 {
		per := float64(last-first) / float64(cnt-1)
		fmt.Printf("WaveC:     C=%.4f, rotates %.6f per step (2pi/%.1f)  (C khat^2 = %.6f)\n",
			Dc, 2*math.Pi/per, per, Dc*kh2)
		fmt.Printf("ratio rotation/decay = %.4f\n", (2*math.Pi/per)/rate)
	} else {
		fmt.Printf("WaveC: only %d crossings\n", cnt)
	}
}
EOF

// wvMode puts a single pure sine mode of the given wavelength into an
// equation, in 1D with wrapped edges, so its one lattice wavenumber can be
// watched on its own.
func wvMode(eq Equations, wl float32) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = eq
	ss.Config.Size.Set(256, 1, 1)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesWrap
	if eq == Wave {
		ss.Params.Diffusion.SetBool(true)
	}
	ss.Params.Update()
	ss.InitFunc = func(s *Sim) {
		if eq == Wave {
			s.Sine(WavePos, math32.X, wl, 0, 1, 0)
		} else {
			s.Sine(WaveCa, math32.X, wl, 0, 1, 0)
		}
	}
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

// TestDiffusion is the last corner of the picture, and the one that says what
// the i in a quantum wave is for.
//
// Params.Diffusion moves the Laplacian from the acceleration to the velocity
// and nothing else: same term, same C^2. WaveC is that same first-order
// equation with an i in front. So a mode of wavenumber k DECAYS at C^2 khat^2
// under diffusion and ROTATES at C^2 khat^2 under WaveC -- the same rate, and
// the i is the entire difference between heat spreading out and a wave
// propagating.
func TestDiffusion(t *testing.T) {
	const wl float32 = 32
	k := 2 * math.Pi / float64(wl)
	kh2 := 4 * math.Sin(k/2) * math.Sin(k/2) // the 1D lattice khat^2
	at := func(v int) float64 {
		return float64(State.Value(1, 1, 9, v, int(GetCtx(0).CurState)))
	}

	d := wvMode(Wave, wl)
	want := float64(d.Params.CSq) * kh2
	a0 := at(int(WavePos))
	const n = 60
	for range n {
		ctx := GetCtx(0)
		ctx.StepInc()
		RunWaveKernel(int(ctx.Size.X))
		RunEdgesWrapKernel(int(ctx.EdgesN()))
	}
	a1 := at(int(WavePos))
	if a1 >= a0 {
		t.Fatalf("with Diffusion on the mode should decay, went %.4f -> %.4f", a0, a1)
	}
	decay := -math.Log(a1/a0) / n

	w := wvMode(WaveC, wl)
	if math.Abs(float64(w.Params.C)-float64(d.Params.CSq)) > 1e-6 {
		t.Fatalf("the two coefficients must match to compare rates: %v vs %v", w.Params.C, d.Params.CSq)
	}
	prev := at(int(WaveCa))
	var first, last, cnt int
	for i := range 2000 {
		w.RunWaveC(int(GetCtx(0).Size.X))
		GetCtx(0).StepInc()

		v := at(int(WaveCa))

				first = i
			}
			last, cnt = i, cnt+1

		prev = v
	}

## `Params.Diffusion`

The Laplacian drives the **velocity** instead of the acceleration. Same term, same C², one derivative earlier:

```go
if Params[0].Diffusion.IsTrue() {
    vel = Params[0].CSq * force
} else {
    vel = pvel + Params[0].CSq*force
}
```

And it turns out to complete the picture more precisely than I expected, because **C² at the default C = 0.5 is exactly 0.25, which is `WaveCC`**. So the two are the same equation with the same coefficient, differing only by the i — and that's measurable:

```
same mode, same coefficient: diffusion decays at 0.009654 per step,
WaveC rotates at 0.009607 (C^2 khat^2 = 0.009607) -- the i is the only difference
```

Both land on C²k̂² to within 0.5%. One decays at that rate, the other turns at it. That's your "half-way to the diffusion equation except that it rotates", as a number.

Which fills the grid:

| Laplacian drives | real field | complex field |
|---|---|---|
| acceleration | **Wave** — oscillates, ω = ck | — |
| velocity | **Wave + Diffusion** — decays at C²k̂² | **WaveC** — rotates at C²k̂² |

I dropped the mass-term flag entirely, as you said — switch to KG for that. `TestWaveDispersion` still covers the mass/dispersion point using the real KG.

## View rebuild

You were right that it wasn't anticipated, and there were two separate problems.

**`VarsListUpdate` early-outs on variable *count*.** Two equations with the same number of variables would keep the old settings map entirely. Since enum keys carry their type, checking whether `vals[0]` is already a key is a reliable identity test, so it now rebuilds whenever the *set* changes rather than just the size.

**Nothing re-pointed the live View.** New `Sim.ViewRebuild()`, called at the end of `ConfigEquation`: resets `Size` and `Start`, calls `SetVar(vals[0], -1)` to rebuild the settings map and refill every panel with a variable of the *new* equation, then re-runs the view init funcs and updates. It no-ops when there's no GUI, so the tests and headless runs are unaffected.

One thing to check on your end: I use `ss.StateVars.Values()[0]` rather than `ss.StateVars` itself, because `StateVars` is the count sentinel (`WaveStatesN`), not a real variable. For the enums layered on `EMStatesN` that should give a valid first value, but you'll see immediately in the GUI if any equation comes up pointing somewhere odd before its `ViewInit` fires.

I also can't verify the panel *count* — if an equation's `ViewAll` set `NPanels = PanelsFour` and the next one only wants one, `ViewRebuild` fills all four with the new equation's first variable but leaves `NPanels` at four. That may be what you want; if not, resetting `NPanels` in `ViewRebuild` is a one-liner.

# --- generic open (outflow) halo, for the FIRST-ORDER equations ---
p=base+'wavesim/edges.goal'; s=open(p).read()
anchor = "// EdgesWrapKernel"
blk = '''// EdgesOpenKernel is the damping boundary for the FIRST-ORDER equations, and
// it works differently from the Sommerfeld one the second-order kernels use.
//
// Sommerfeld damping applies the force as a velocity instead of an
// acceleration, which needs there to BE an acceleration to leave out. A
// first-order equation has none: its whole update is already a velocity. What
// it has instead is a halo that the interior stencil reads, and the job is to
// fill that halo with the value an outgoing wave would have put there.
//
// This writes the nearest interior value, which makes the interior's centered
// difference at the boundary one-sided and lets a wave leave rather than
// bounce. It is the standard cheap open boundary. It is NOT transparent: what
// survives is reflection of whatever does not look locally like a plane wave
// going straight out, which for a dispersive equation is a good deal. See
// TestEdgesOpen for how much comes back in each case.
func EdgesOpenKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	face := ctx.EdgeCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if face < 0 {
		return
	}
	// step one cell inward along this face's normal
	sx, sy, sz := x, y, z
	p := ctx.SizePlus1()
	if x == 0 {
		sx = 1
	} else if x == p.X {
		sx = p.X - 1
	}
	if y == 0 {
		sy = 1
	} else if y == p.Y {
		sy = p.Y - 1
	}
	if z == 0 {
		sz = 1
	} else if z == p.Z {
		sz = p.Z - 1
	}
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	nvars := ctx.NVars
	for vi := range nvars {
		State[z, y, x, vi, cur] = State[sz, sy, sx, vi, cur]
		State[z, y, x, vi, prv] = State[sz, sy, sx, vi, prv]
	}
}

'''

// whatever is arriving carry on out at c", and both of those would fight it.
func DiracDampKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	face := ctx.EdgeCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if face < 0 {

	}

		State[z, y, x, vr+int32(Dirac1Av)-int32(Dirac1As), cur] = v
		State[z, y, x, vr, cur] = pp + v
	}
}'''

package wavesim

import (
	"fmt"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

func dampSim(eq Equations, sz int32, init func(*Sim)) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = eq
	ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, sz, sz)
	ss.Config.Wavelength = 8
	ss.Config.PacketWidth = 6
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesDamp
	ss.Params.Update()
	if init != nil {
		ss.InitFunc = init
	}
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

// total energy-ish: sum of squares over every state variable in the interior
func dampTot(ss *Sim) float64 {
	var s float64
	c := GetCtx(0)
	cur := int(c.CurState)
	nv := int(ss.StateVars.Int64())
	for z := int32(1); z <= c.Size.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= c.Size.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= c.Size.X; x++ {
				for v := range nv {
					f := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), v, cur))
					s += f * f
				}
			}
		}
	}
	return s
}

func TestScratchDamp(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 32
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		eq   Equations
		name string
		init func(*Sim)
	}{
		{Wave, "Wave (Sommerfeld)", nil},
		{KleinGordonC, "KGComplex (Sommerfeld)", ChargedPacket},
		{Dirac, "Dirac (Sommerfeld, new)", func(s *Sim) {
			s.MovingWavePacketConfig(Dirac1As, Dirac1Av, math32.X, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), 1, 0, 1)
		}},
		{WaveCDir, "WaveCDir (open, new)", nil},
		{WaveC, "WaveC (open, new)", nil},
		{Weyl, "Weyl (open, new)", nil},
	} {
		ss := dampSim(tc.eq, sz, tc.init)
		ss.StepRun()
		t0 := dampTot(ss)
		for range 200 {
			ss.StepRun()
		}
		t1 := dampTot(ss)
		fmt.Printf("%-26s remaining %7.3f%% of initial\n", tc.name, 100*t1/t0)
	}
}
EOF

const (

	EdgeDampMax   float32 = 0.06

// EdgeDampFactor returns the per-step attenuation for a cell: 1 through the
// bulk, easing down to 1 - EdgeDampMax at the boundary over EdgeDampWidth
// cells. The first-order kernels multiply their output by it when Edges is
// EdgesDamp, which is how a wave leaves the box instead of bouncing.
//

// dispersive one has no single speed to be transparent to, so neither can do
// it in one cell. They absorb over a layer instead.

// Dimensions of size 1 are skipped: a 1D run is not near a boundary in Y.
func EdgeDampFactor(x, y, z int32, sz math32.Vector3i) float32 {

		}

		if float32(sz.Z+1-z) < dz {
			dz = float32(sz.Z + 1 - z)
		}
		if dz < d {
			d = dz
		}
	}
	if d >= EdgeDampWidth {
		return 1
	}
	f := (EdgeDampWidth - d) / EdgeDampWidth
	return 1 - EdgeDampMax*f*f
}

	ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, sz, sz)
	ss.Config.Wavelength = 8
	ss.Config.PacketWidth = 6
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Params.ThreeD.SetBool(true)
	ss.Params.Edges = EdgesDamp
	ss.Params.Update()
	if init != nil {
		ss.InitFunc = init
	}
	ss.Init()
	return ss
}

// dampTot is the sum of squares over every state variable in the interior:
// how much wave is still in the box, whatever the equation calls it.
func dampTot(ss *Sim) float64 {
	var s float64
	c := GetCtx(0)
	cur := int(c.CurState)
	nv := int(ss.StateVars.Int64())
	for z := int32(1); z <= c.Size.Z; z++ {
		for y := int32(1); y <= c.Size.Y; y++ {
			for x := int32(1); x <= c.Size.X; x++ {
				for v := range nv {
					f := float64(State.Value(int(z), int(y), int(x), v, cur))
					s += f * f
				}
			}
		}
	}
	return s
}

// TestEdgesDamp sends a packet into the boundary in every equation that damps
// and measures what comes back, which is the only thing a damping boundary is
// for.
//
// Two mechanisms are being checked. The second-order equations use Sommerfeld
// damping in the boundary cell, where the force sets the velocity instead of
// adding to it. The first-order ones cannot: they have no acceleration to
// leave out, so they use an open halo plus [EdgeDampFactor], an absorbing
// layer several cells deep. On its own the open halo leaves nearly half a
// Weyl packet in the box, so the layer is doing most of the work.
func TestEdgesDamp(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 48
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		eq   Equations
		name string
		init func(*Sim)
	}{
		{Wave, "Wave", nil},
		{KleinGordonC, "KleinGordonC", ChargedPacket},
		{Dirac, "Dirac", func(s *Sim) {
			s.MovingWavePacketConfig(Dirac1As, Dirac1Av, math32.X, math32.Vec3(-1, -1, -1), 1, 0, 1)
		}},
		{WaveCDir, "WaveCDir", nil},
		{WaveC, "WaveC", nil},
		{Weyl, "Weyl", nil},
	} {
		ss := dampSim(tc.eq, sz, tc.init)
		ss.StepRun()
		t0 := dampTot(ss)
		if t0 <= 0 {
			t.Errorf("%s: nothing in the box to damp", tc.name)
			continue
		}
		for range 300 {
			ss.StepRun()
		}
		left := dampTot(ss) / t0
		if left > 0.01 {
			t.Errorf("%s: %.3f%% of the wave is still in the box after 300 steps -- it is reflecting",
				tc.name, 100*left)
		}
		t.Logf("%-13s %.3f%% left after 300 steps", tc.name, 100*left)
	}
}
EOF

## Two mechanisms, because one doesn't fit

**`DiracDampKernel`** follows the house pattern exactly — Sommerfeld damping in the boundary cell, force setting the velocity instead of adding to it, over four components. Mass and spin term both dropped at the boundary, as `KleinGordonCDampKernel` already does with its mass: the only question there is "let whatever's arriving carry on out at c", and both of those fight it. It came out best of the lot at 0.004%.

**The first-order three can't use that** — Sommerfeld needs an acceleration to leave out, and their whole update is already a velocity. So they get a different thing, in two parts:

- **`EdgesOpenKernel`** (generic, in `edges.goal`): writes the nearest interior value into the halo so the boundary isn't a wall.
- **`EdgeDampFactor`** (in `funcs.goal`): an absorbing layer 8 cells deep that the kernels apply to their own output when `Edges == EdgesDamp`.

## Worth knowing: the open halo alone is nearly useless

My first version was just the halo fix, and it reflected badly — **47% of a WaveCDir packet and 56% of a Weyl one came back.** One cell cannot absorb a wave. I tried proper linear extrapolation instead of copying, expecting the full one-sided difference to help, and it was *worse* (Weyl went to 77%) — I assume the leapfrog's parasitic mode converting at the boundary, though I didn't chase it.

The layer is what actually does the work, and its strength is not monotonic. Measured on a Weyl packet into 48³:

| `EdgeDampMax` | reflected |
|---|---|
| 0.03 | 10.6% |
| 0.06 | 3.9% |
| 0.12 | 0.69% |
| 0.2 | 0.12% |
| 0.3 | 0.11% |
| 0.5 | 0.26% ← rising again |

Too gentle and the wave crosses the layer and hits the far wall; too fierce and **the layer's own edge becomes a wall**. 0.25 sits near the bottom. Those numbers are in the constant's doc comment so the next person doesn't have to rediscover the curve.

`TestEdgesDamp` fires a packet into the boundary in all six equations and fails any that keeps more than 1%.

One behaviour change to be aware of: `Dirac` with `EdgesDamp` previously ran only `MaxwellDampKernel`, leaving the Dirac variables' halo at zero — a hard wall. It now damps properly, so `DiracHydrogen` and `SpinInPotential` will lose their outer tails rather than reflecting them. All their tests still pass, but the numbers may shift slightly from what you had.

## Schrödinger needed both, and the open kernel alone wasn't enough

The open halo you wired in was right but only half of it:

```
Schrodinger, open halo only:      9.242% left after 300 steps
WaveC, open halo + layer:         0.053%
```

Which is decisive, because **`WaveC` *is* Schrödinger** — same Laplacian-driving-velocity on a complex field, same Visscher two-kernel integration, differing only in whether the coefficient is called `C` or `ħ/2m`. Before I added the layer, WaveC measured 7.8%; Schrödinger's 9.2% is the same number. There's no mechanism by which one would need the layer and the other wouldn't.

So it gets the layer too, in `SchrodingerBKernel` — the b pass, because that's where both halves are in hand. Also damps `CabAv`, which `WaveC` doesn't have to worry about since it has no velocity variables:

```
Schrodinger   0.064% left after 300 steps
```

Right alongside WaveC. `Schrodinger` is now in `TestEdgesDamp` with the rest, so it can't regress.

## A footgun the failure exposed

`TestSchrodingerGroupVel` broke, and it was worth breaking. `FreePacket` runs in a 48³ box with an 8-cell layer on each side — so a third of the domain is absorbing, and the packet's tails were sitting in it from step one, getting eaten asymmetrically and dragging the centroid (0.318 measured against 0.354 predicted).

Two fixes:

- **`EdgeDampFactor` now caps the layer at a quarter of the smallest active dimension.** Eight cells is a sensible layer in a big box and the *entirety* of a small one — a 16³ box would have been absorbing everywhere. No effect at 48³ or above, so the reflection numbers are unchanged.
- The group-velocity test moved to 96³ so the packet stays clear of the layer. It reads **0.35151 against 0.35355 predicted** — 0.6%, better than the 0.34769 it managed before, since the bigger box also cuts the wrap contamination.

Worth knowing generally: any measurement near a damped boundary is now measuring the layer as much as the physics.

I left that one alone — it's a harder question than the others and I didn't want to guess. Two reasons it isn't just another `MaxwellDampKernel` call:

`ElectroweakKernel` writes `A0s..AZs` itself as the weak-mixing rotation of W³ and B, which is why `StepRun` doesn't run `MaxwellKernel` for it — damping those directly would fight the same way.

Every damping scheme here attenuates toward zero, which at an electroweak boundary means driving the field to the symmetric point and creating a domain wall right where you wanted quiet. A real EW absorber would have to damp the gauge fields toward zero but the Higgs toward *v*, and above T_c those are the same thing while below they aren't.

p='/Users/oreilly/wavereality/waves/wavesim/electroweak.goal'; s=open(p).read()
old = "//gosl:end"
new = '''// ElectroweakDampKernel is Sommerfeld damping on the boundary shell, with one
// twist the other equations do not need: the Higgs does not damp to zero.
//
// Everything else here damps toward nothing, because nothing is what those
// fields are in the vacuum. The Higgs is not: below the critical temperature
// its vacuum is |Phi| = HiggsV, and a boundary that pulled it to zero would
// build a wall of restored symmetry right where the box was supposed to go
// quiet -- and a domain wall radiates, which is the opposite of damping.
//
// So the doublet gets two treatments. The wave part damps as everything else
// does, force setting the velocity rather than adding to it. Then its
// MAGNITUDE is relaxed toward HiggsV while its direction is left alone. The
// direction matters: which way the doublet points in SU(2) is a gauge choice,
// and pinning it at the boundary would be a gauge transformation with a
// gradient, which is a current. Relaxing only the magnitude is blind to that.
//
// Above TempCrit the thermal mass drives HiggsV to zero on its own, and this
// becomes ordinary damping to nothing without any special case.
func ElectroweakDampKernel(i uint32) { //gosl:kernel
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	var x, y, z int32
	face := ctx.EdgeCoords(i, &x, &y, &z)
	if face < 0 {
		return
	}
	sz := ctx.SizePlus1() // exclude updating on edges
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	csq := Params[0].CSq

	// the gauge fields: B, W1, W2, W3, each four potentials then four
	// velocities, all damping toward zero as Maxwell's do
	for g := range 4 {
		base := int32(EWB0s) + int32(g)*8
		for k := range 4 {
			vr := base + int32(k)
			pp := State[z, y, x, vr, prv]
			f := LaplacianEdge19(x, y, z, sz.X, sz.Y, sz.Z, vr, prv, pp)
			v := csq * f // key damp: no +=
			State[z, y, x, vr+4, cur] = v
			State[z, y, x, vr, cur] = pp + v
		}
	}

	// the Higgs doublet: same damping of the wave part
	var hs [4]float32
	for k := range 4 {
		vr := int32(EWHsCa) + int32(k)
		pp := State[z, y, x, vr, prv]
		f := LaplacianEdge19(x, y, z, sz.X, sz.Y, sz.Z, vr, prv, pp)
		v := csq * f
		State[z, y, x, vr+4, cur] = v
		hs[k] = pp + v
	}
	// then pull the MAGNITUDE toward the vacuum, leaving the direction be
	m2 := hs[0]*hs[0] + hs[1]*hs[1] + hs[2]*hs[2] + hs[3]*hs[3]
	if m2 > 0 {
		m := math32.Sqrt(m2)
		want := m + EdgeDampMax*(Params[0].HiggsV-m)
		sc := want / m
		hs[0] *= sc
		hs[1] *= sc
		hs[2] *= sc
		hs[3] *= sc
		m2 = want * want
	}
	for k := range 4 {
		State[z, y, x, int32(EWHsCa)+int32(k), cur] = hs[k]
	}
	State[z, y, x, EWHmag, cur] = m2
}

//gosl:end'''

func ewDampSim(sz int32, init func(*Sim), damp bool) *Sim {

	ss.Config = &Config{}

func ewGauge(ss *Sim) float64 {
	var s float64

	cur := int(c.CurState)
	for z := int32(1); z <= c.Size.Z; z++ {

	}

}

// without disturbing the Higgs, which is the one equation here whose vacuum is
// not zero.

// Damping the Higgs toward zero would lay a wall of restored symmetry along
// the boundary, and a domain wall radiates. So it is copied from the interior
// instead, which preserves its magnitude AND the SU(2) direction it happens to
// be pointing -- that direction is a gauge choice, and pinning it would be a
// gauge transformation with a gradient, which is a current.
func TestElectroweakDamp(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 24
	for _, edges := range []Edges{EdgesWrap, EdgesDamp} {
		ss := ewDampSim(sz, edges, HiggsBroken)
		v := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
		var lo, hi = math.Inf(1), 0.0
		for range 100 {
			ss.StepRun()
			c := GetCtx(0)
			for _, p := range [][3]int{{1, 1, 1}, {sz / 2, sz / 2, sz / 2}, {sz, sz, sz}} {
				m := math.Sqrt(float64(State.Value(p[2], p[1], p[0], int(EWHmag), int(c.CurState))))
				lo, hi = math.Min(lo, m), math.Max(hi, m)
			}
		}
		off := math.Max(math.Abs(lo-v), math.Abs(hi-v)) / v
		if off > 0.01 {
			t.Errorf("%v: the broken vacuum wandered to %.5f..%.5f against v = %.5f", edges, lo, hi, v)
		}
		t.Logf("%v: |Phi| holds at %.5f..%.5f, v = %.5f", edges, lo, hi, v)
	}

	ss := ewDampSim(48, EdgesDamp, PhotonPulse)
	ss.StepRun()
	g0 := ewGaugeSum()
	for range 300 {
		ss.StepRun()
	}
	left := ewGaugeSum() / g0
	if left > 0.05 {
		t.Errorf("photon pulse: %.2f%% of the gauge field is still in the box", 100*left)
	}
	t.Logf("photon pulse: %.3f%% of the gauge field left after 300 steps", 100*left)
}

## The Higgs is copied, not pushed to *v*

I tried what you said first — Sommerfeld-damp the wave part, then relax |Φ| toward `HiggsV`. It destroyed the vacuum: |Φ| swung between 0.0005 and 0.47 against v = 0.123, **including at the box centre**.

What works is simpler: **copy the Higgs from the nearest interior cell.** That gets the magnitude right for free, and it also leaves the SU(2) *direction* alone — which matters, because which way the doublet points is a gauge choice, and pinning a direction at the boundary is a gauge transformation with a gradient, i.e. a current. Copying is blind to both. Above T_c, where `HiggsV` falls to zero, it damps to zero on its own with no special case.

The gauge fields get ordinary Sommerfeld damping, and the derived views (`A0s`, `EWZ0`, `EWWPr0`) follow automatically since the kernel recomputes them from the gauge basis each step.

## A real bug underneath it, affecting every equation

Neither version worked at first, and the reason wasn't the Higgs treatment at all.

**`Init` only seeded the halo when edges wrap.** `RunWrapEdges` returns immediately unless `EdgesWrap`, and `Init` zeroes everything and then fills only the *interior* — so with damped edges the halo started at **zero against an interior at v**. A full-VEV step discontinuity along the entire boundary on step one. For the Higgs that's the top of the Mexican hat laid along the whole wall; it rolls off and rings the whole box, which is exactly what I was seeing.

New `Sim.RunEdgesHalo()` handles both modes, and `Init` calls it. This was latent for *any* config with damped edges and a nonzero background, not just electroweak.

I also pointed the Visscher inter-pass refresh at it — `RunSchrodinger` and `RunWaveC` were calling `RunWrapEdges`, so their second pass read a stale halo whenever edges were damped rather than wrapped. Same class of bug as the one we fixed for wrap.

## Why the test measures variance

My first absorption number was 15.3%, which looked like a failed boundary. It wasn't. The residual sat in `BYs` and `W3Ys` in exactly the pulse's original 3.48:1 ratio, and rms 0.1763 against |mean| 0.1729 — **98% of it was a uniform DC offset**.

A k=0 mode has zero group velocity. It cannot propagate to the boundary, so *no* boundary condition can absorb it, and `PhotonPulse` leaves a small one because a gaussian times a cosine doesn't integrate to zero. Counting it made a working boundary look broken. `ewGaugeWave` measures the variance about each variable's mean instead, and the answer is **0.600%**.

That's also why the earlier 1.41% figure was wrong in the other direction — the discontinuity was inflating the baseline it was divided by.

What survives is the transpose term, sourcing the **longitudinal** $W^3_z$ (physical for a massive vector: it's the eaten Goldstone).

**It really is the collision.** W³ rises monotonically rather than peaking, which looked like a runaway. The control settles it: a single packet generates **exactly zero**. The rise is accumulation over repeated wrap-around passes.

**`Higgs Symmetric` needed `A0NoWave`.** It blew up to `NaN` — not the Higgs, which broke correctly, but `W10` and `B0` growing 5000×. That's the secular gauge branch from the degenerate eigenvalue we hit earlier. Your `MaxwellKernel` already had the cure, so I wired `Params.A0NoWave` into the electroweak kernel: for the $\nu=0$ components, drive the potential from the force instead of accumulating a velocity. On by default; bounded ever since.

Also switched the seed from white noise to a sum of six long-wavelength modes — white noise puts power at the lattice cutoff, which is both unphysical and the quickest way to destabilise a nonlinear solver, and non-periodic seeds fight wrapped edges.

One caveat on the two massive configs: they call `ewDemoScale` to raise `HiggsMu` to 0.388. At the Standard Model scale the boson Compton wavelengths are ~22 cubes, so a visible packet is far above threshold and the Z would travel at 0.97c — nothing you could see. `g` and `g'` are untouched, so the mixing angle and $m_W/m_Z$ stay physical. It's noted in the Doc strings that surface in the GUI.

Three small things I fixed on top of it:

**`config_test.go` needed the wrap too.** `cfgSim` drives the pieces directly rather than going through `Init()`, so once `ewWrapEdges` came out of the config funcs, nothing wrapped the edges before the first step — step 1 read zero edge planes. Added `WrapEdges()` to the helper so the test path mirrors `Init()`. No measurable change (`ewStep` wraps every step anyway, so it was a one-step boundary transient), but the test should exercise the same initial state the GUI does.

**Regenerated the yaegi bindings.** `WrapEdges` is a new exported package-level func and wasn't in `github_com-WaveReality-waves-wavesim.go` — the extract must have run just before you added it. Now bound, and `go build ./yaegiwaves/` passes. `SlabPacket`/`SlabPacketConfig` need nothing there; yaegi doesn't bind methods on `Sim` individually.

Two observations on the new structure, neither blocking:

`HiggsBroken` still calls `RunEdgesWrapKernel` inline, which the `Init()` change makes redundant. Left it — harmless, and it's your code.

The bigger one: the three packet configs do `ss.Config.Wavelength = wl` before calling `SlabPacketConfig`, so `Init()` overwrites whatever the user typed into the form. Editing Wavelength in the GUI has no effect for these. If you want the Config to actually drive them, it's `wl := ss.Config.Wavelength` and feed that to `ewFreq` as well — the carrier frequency has to track `k` or the packet splits into two counter-propagating halves. I left it alone because a config arguably *should* set up its own scenario, and it's your edit to make; say the word and it's a three-line change. Worth knowing the defaults are `Wavelength = 8, PacketWidth = 8`, i.e. a single cycle under the envelope, which disperses fast enough that the speed measurement gets mushy — the demos would want better defaults from somewhere if Config becomes the source of truth.

// how separated are the two packets at t=0, and how much W^3 do they make?
func TestZZWCollGeom(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 100
	for _, tc := range []struct{ wl, wid float32 }{
		{16, 24}, {16, 19.2}, {16, 12}, {8, 12}, {8, 8},
	} {

			WCollision(s)
		})

		// midpoint amplitude of one packet relative to its own peak
		half := 0.4 * sz / 2
		rel := math.Exp(-float64(half/tc.wid) * float64(half/tc.wid))
		peak, at := 0.0, 0
		w3 := func() float64 {
			tot := 0.0

func TestZZWCollSep(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 100
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		wid, frac, amp float32
	}{
		{24, 0.3, 0.1}, {24, 0.25, 0.1}, {12, 0.25, 0.1}, {12, 0.25, 0.3}, {8, 0.25, 0.3},

			HiggsBroken(s)
			p := s.Params
			s.Config.PacketWidth = tc.wid
			om := ewFreq(s, s.Config.Wavelength, p.MW)
			a := tc.amp * p.HiggsV
			s.SlabPacketConfig(EWW1Xs, EWW1Xv, sz*tc.frac, a, 1, om)
			s.SlabPacketConfig(EWW2Xs, EWW2Xv, sz*(1-tc.frac), a, -1, om)
		})
		_ = ss
		half := float32(sz) * (0.5 - tc.frac) / 1 // half the SHORT separation
		if tc.frac == 0.3 {

		} else {
			half = float32(sz) * 0.5 / 2
		}

			tot := 0.0

				tot += cfgSumSq(sz, int32(EWW30s)+c)
			}
			return tot
		}

			}

			tc.wid, tc.frac, tc.amp, math.Exp(-r*r), peak, at)
	}
}

p='electroweak.goal'
s=open(p).read()

old = """// A single packet on its own generates exactly zero, so what appears really is
// the two fields coupling and not one of them self-interacting. With wrapped
// edges the pair re-collides every lap, so the signal accumulates rather than
// peaking once.
//
// The amplitude is deliberately large, a tenth of the vacuum value, because the
// effect is quadratic in W and vanishes for small packets.
func WCollision(ss *Sim) {
	ewDemoScale(ss, 0.388)
	HiggsBroken(ss)
	p := ss.Params
	wl := ss.Config.Wavelength
	om := ewFreq(ss, wl, p.MW)
	amp := 0.1 * p.HiggsV
	zl := float32(ss.Config.Size.Z)

	ss.SlabPacketConfig(EWW1Xs, EWW1Xv, zl*0.3, amp, 1, om)
	ss.SlabPacketConfig(EWW2Xs, EWW2Xv, zl*0.7, amp, -1, om)
}"""

new = """// A single packet on its own generates exactly zero, so what appears really is
// the two fields coupling and not one of them self-interacting. With wrapped
// edges the pair re-collides every lap, so the signal accumulates rather than
// peaking once.
//
// This one sets its own envelope width rather than taking Config.PacketWidth,
// because the shared default of 1.5 wavelengths is too wide here. The packets
// start 40% of the box apart, so at 1.5 wl the two Gaussians already overlap at
// half their peak amplitude before the first step -- one broad blob, not two
// packets that meet. Measured on a 100-deep box: width 1.5 wl leaves 50% overlap
// at t=0, 1.2 wl leaves 34%, and 0.75 wl leaves 6%, which is the first value
// that looks like a collision.
//
// The amplitude is deliberately large, a quarter of the vacuum value, because
// the source is quadratic in W and vanishes for small packets. Amplitude, not
// overlap, is what sets the signal: narrowing the envelope from 1.5 wl to
// 0.75 wl costs a factor of 260, and raising the amplitude from 0.1 v to 0.25 v
// wins back a factor of 6 for free, since the effect goes as amp^2.
func WCollision(ss *Sim) {
	ewDemoScale(ss, 0.388)
	HiggsBroken(ss)
	p := ss.Params
	wl := ss.Config.Wavelength
	om := ewFreq(ss, wl, p.MW)
	amp := 0.25 * p.HiggsV
	zl := float32(ss.Config.Size.Z)
	ss.SlabPacket(EWW1Xs, EWW1Xv, zl*0.3, wl, 0.75*wl, amp, 1, om)
	ss.SlabPacket(EWW2Xs, EWW2Xv, zl*0.7, wl, 0.75*wl, amp, -1, om)
}"""
assert old in s
open(p,'w').write(s.replace(old, new))

Yes — `yaegiwaves/make` is what `go generate ./...` runs there, and I'd run it before your message; ran it again just now and it's clean (nothing new to bind — `SmoothNoise` and `SlabPacket` are methods on `Sim`, which yaegi doesn't extract individually; only package-level symbols like `WrapEdges` show up). I noted that in memory so I stop rediscovering it.

**`Sim.Init()` in `config_test` — right call, and it caught a real bug.** No reason not to, and it's strictly better: the test now goes down the same path the GUI does instead of a parallel reimplementation that drifts. It immediately earned its keep — `TestHiggsVacuumStatic` started failing:

```
after 500 steps: hs0a drift = 2.903e-01, velocity = 1.918e-02
```

`HiggsBroken` lost its internal `RunEdgesWrapKernel` when `Init()` took that over — correct for anything going through `Init()`, but `electroweak_test.go`'s `ewSim` drives the kernels directly and doesn't. So the VEV fill left the edge ring at zero, `Laplacian19` saw a cliff at the boundary, and the "exact fixed point" drifted by 0.29. Fixed `ewSim` to call `WrapEdges()`, and folded the local `ewWrap()` helper into it since they're now the same function. Also dropped the `ss.Params = &Params[0] // ConfigVars early-returns...` line — that comment stopped being true when you removed the early return, and `ConfigVars` sets it anyway.

All 22 pass.

**Config.Wavelength fix works.** I dropped the hardcoded `wl: 16` from the speed test so it reads `ss.Config.Wavelength` — the prediction now tracks whatever `ElectroweakConfig` chooses instead of silently agreeing with it. Same numbers: photon 0.9325 c, Z 0.6904 c.

## Your `// todo: can this be 1.5 ok?`

Measured it rather than guessing. On a 100-deep box, the two packets start 40% of the box apart, so the question is how much of each Gaussian is already sitting on the other at t=0:

| envelope width | overlap at midpoint | W³ generated |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 wl (24) | **0.499** | 8.58e-1 |
| 1.2 wl (19.2) | 0.338 | 1.39e-1 |
| 0.75 wl (12) | 0.062 | 3.33e-3 |

So: no, 1.5 isn't ok, and 1.2 wasn't really either. At 1.5 the packets overlap at **half their peak amplitude before the first step** — it's one broad blob, and the large W³ is mostly "two fields that were already on top of each other," not two packets meeting. That's also why the signal only ever accumulates.

But the fix is cheap, because **amplitude is what sets the signal, not overlap** — the source is quadratic in W. Narrowing to 0.75 wl costs 260×; going from 0.1 v to 0.25 v wins back 6×, and the encounter is now a real event. Net result is *better* than before:

```
YangMills=false  peak sum(W^3^2) = 9.3413e-11
YangMills=true   peak sum(W^3^2) = 1.6572e+01     (was 5.85)
```

I made that change — `WCollision` now calls `SlabPacket` directly with `0.75*wl` instead of `SlabPacketConfig`, since the shared `Config.PacketWidth` genuinely is wrong for this one config and 1.5 wl is right for the two pulse demos. Reasoning is in the doc comment. If you'd rather it stay uniformly Config-driven, the alternative is letting this config write `Config.PacketWidth` — which reopens exactly the clobbering you just closed, so I went the other way.

One thing worth knowing regardless: with wrapped edges, two packets can never be more than half a box apart, so centers at 0.3/0.7 are separated by 40% the short way, not 40%... and 0.25/0.75 is the true maximum. Doesn't matter at width 12 (6% overlap either way), but it caps how clean this can ever get at wide envelopes.

new = """// SliceDim returns the state dimension held fixed by the current view: the
// one that is neither horizontal (always X) nor [View.Depth].
func (vw *View) SliceDim() math32.Dims {
	if vw.Depth == math32.Z {
		return math32.Y
	}
	return math32.Z
}

// DepthSize returns the number of state cells drawn going back into the screen.
func (vw *View) DepthSize() int32 {
	return vw.Size.Dim(vw.Depth)
}

// StateCoord returns the state coordinate sampled by the display cell xi
// across and di back into the screen, given the already offset start corner.
func (vw *View) StateCoord(st math32.Vector3i, xi, di int32) math32.Vector3i {
	c := st
	c.X = st.X + xi
	c.SetDim(vw.Depth, st.Dim(vw.Depth)+di)
	return c
}

func (vw *View) ZoomInSize(n int32) {
	if vw.Size.X <= 4 {
		return
	}
	dd := vw.Depth
	n = min(n, vw.Size.X-4)
	vw.Size.X -= 2 * n
	vw.Start.X += n
	if vw.Size.Dim(dd) > 4 {
		vw.Size.SetDim(dd, vw.Size.Dim(dd)-2*n)
		vw.Start.SetDim(dd, vw.Start.Dim(dd)+n)
	}
	vw.UpdateView()
}"""

	ctx := GetCtx(0)

	fs := ctx.SizeFull()

		if vw.Start.Z < 0 {

		} else if vw.Start.Z > sz.Z+1 {

		vw.Start.X = (fs.X - 1) - vw.Size.X
	}
	if vw.Start.Y+vw.Size.Y >= fs.Y {
		vw.Start.Y = (fs.Y - 1) - vw.Size.Y
	}
	vw.UpdateView()
}"""
new = """// MoveSlice moves the slice plane by n along [View.SliceDim]: the one state
// dimension that is not on screen.
func (vw *View) MoveSlice(n int32) {
	sd := vw.SliceDim()
	sz := GetCtx(0).Size
	p := vw.Start.Dim(sd) + n
	p = max(p, 0)
	p = min(p, sz.Dim(sd)+1)
	vw.Start.SetDim(sd, p)
	vw.UpdateView()
}

// MoveStart moves the displayed region within the slice plane, by mv.X across
// and mv.Y back into the screen. Use [View.MoveSlice] to change which slice.
func (vw *View) MoveStart(mv math32.Vector3i) {
	fs := GetCtx(0).SizeFull()
	dd := vw.Depth
	vw.Start.X += mv.X
	vw.Start.SetDim(dd, vw.Start.Dim(dd)+mv.Y)
	if vw.Start.X < 0 {
		vw.Start.X = 0
	}
	if vw.Start.Dim(dd) < 0 {
		vw.Start.SetDim(dd, 0)
	}
	if vw.Start.X+vw.Size.X >= fs.X {
		vw.Start.X = (fs.X - 1) - vw.Size.X
	}
	if vw.Start.Dim(dd)+vw.Size.Dim(dd) >= fs.Dim(dd) {
		vw.Start.SetDim(dd, (fs.Dim(dd)-1)-vw.Size.Dim(dd))
	}
	vw.UpdateView()
}"""

// across, Y is up and Z goes back into the screen. In an X-Z view the two
// already agree; in an X-Y view the state Y and Z components swap, so that a
// vector always points along the axis its own dimension is drawn on.

	if vw.Depth == math32.Z {

	}
	return math32.Vec3(v.X, v.Z, v.Y)

new = """// SetDepth sets the state dimension drawn going back into the screen, which
// selects the display plane, and re-centers the slice level on the dimension
// that is now off screen. Only [math32.Y] and [math32.Z] are meaningful:
// the horizontal axis is always state X.
func (vw *View) SetDepth(dim math32.Dims) {
	if dim != math32.Y && dim != math32.Z {
		return
	}
	vw.Depth = dim
	fs := GetCtx(0).SizeFull()
	sd := vw.SliceDim()
	vw.Start.SetDim(dim, 1)
	vw.Start.SetDim(sd, max(fs.Dim(sd)/2, 1))
	// the depth extent changes, so the mesh has to be rebuilt, not just redrawn
	vw.RebuildView()
}

old = """// SlabPacket adds a ONE-WAY travelling wave packet to a gauge potential and
// its velocity: a cosine carrier under a Gaussian envelope along Z, uniform
// across X and Y. A slab rather than a blob, so it does not diffract and the
// propagation speed stays unambiguous to the eye.
//
// The velocity is the point. For psi = env(z) cos(k z - om t) the initial time
// derivative is om env sin(k z), and dir flips it for the other direction.
// Setting only the position would split the packet into two halves running
// opposite ways at half amplitude each.
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacket(pos, vel EWStates, ctrZ, wavelength, width, amp, dir, om float32) {
	pi := int(pos.Int64())
	vi := int(vel.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		dz := float32(c.Z) - ctrZ
		g := dz / width
		env := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
		pv := env * math32.Cos(k*dz)
		vv := dir * om * env * math32.Sin(k*dz)
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, cur] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, prv] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, cur] += vv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, prv] += vv
			}
		}
	}
}

// SlabPacketConfig is a version of [SlabPacket] that takes its
// wavelength and width variables from [Config]
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel EWStates, ctrZ, amp, dir, om float32) {
	ss.SlabPacket(pos, vel, ctrZ, ss.Config.Wavelength, ss.Config.PacketWidth, amp, dir, om)
}"""

new = """// SlabPacket adds a ONE-WAY travelling wave packet to a gauge potential and
// its velocity: a cosine carrier under a Gaussian envelope along dim, centered
// at ctr and uniform across the other two dimensions. A slab rather than a
// blob, so it does not diffract and the propagation speed stays unambiguous to
// the eye.
//
// The velocity is the point. For psi = env(d) cos(k d - om t) the initial time
// derivative is om env sin(k d), and dir flips it for the other direction.
// Setting only the position would split the packet into two halves running
// opposite ways at half amplitude each.
//
// dim is normally [math32.X], since X is the horizontal display axis in every
// view, so the packet then runs across the screen. pos should be a component
// TRANSVERSE to dim, which for an X-Z view means the Y component: [View]
// draws state Y along the vertical, so a Y-polarized wave travelling along X
// is the textbook transverse picture.
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacket(pos, vel EWStates, dim math32.Dims, ctr, wavelength, width, amp, dir, om float32) {
	pi := int(pos.Int64())
	vi := int(vel.Int64())
	ctx := GetCtx(0)
	cur := ctx.CurState
	prv := ctx.PrevState()
	sz := ss.Config.Size
	k := TwoPi / wavelength
	var c math32.Vector3i
	for c.Z = range sz.Z {
		for c.Y = range sz.Y {
			for c.X = range sz.X {
				d := float32(c.Dim(dim)) - ctr
				g := d / width
				env := amp * math32.FastExp(-g*g)
				pv := env * math32.Cos(k*d)
				vv := dir * om * env * math32.Sin(k*d)
				f := c.AddScalar(1)
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, cur] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, pi, prv] += pv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, cur] += vv
				State[f.Z, f.Y, f.X, vi, prv] += vv
			}
		}
	}
}

// SlabPacketConfig is a version of [SlabPacket] that takes its
// wavelength and width variables from [Config]
func (ss *Sim) SlabPacketConfig(pos, vel EWStates, dim math32.Dims, ctr, amp, dir, om float32) {
	ss.SlabPacket(pos, vel, dim, ctr, ss.Config.Wavelength, ss.Config.PacketWidth, amp, dir, om)
}"""

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/colors/colormap"
	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

// vwSim builds a state tensor of the given interior size and fills the chosen
// variable with a value that encodes its own coordinates, so that any sampling
// mistake shows up as the wrong cell rather than the wrong number.
func vwSim(size math32.Vector3i, vr EWStates) *Sim {
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU = false
	ss.Config.GUI = false
	ss.Config.Equation = Electroweak
	ss.Config.Size = size
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.StateVars = EWStatesN
	ss.ConfigState()
	GetCtx(0).Init()
	State.SetZeros()
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	for z := int32(0); z < size.Z+2; z++ {
		for y := int32(0); y < size.Y+2; y++ {
			for x := int32(0); x < size.X+2; x++ {
				State.Set(vwCode(x, y, z), int(z), int(y), int(x), int(vr.Int64()), cur)
			}
		}
	}
	return ss
}

// vwCode packs a coordinate into one value, small enough that ValColor's
// fallback (clamp to +-1) leaves it untouched.
func vwCode(x, y, z int32) float32 {
	return 0.001*float32(x) + 0.00001*float32(y) + 0.0000001*float32(z)
}

func vwView(ss *Sim, vr EWStates, depth math32.Dims, slice int32) *View {
	vw := &View{}
	vw.sim = ss
	vw.Settings.Defaults()
	vw.colorMap = colormap.AvailableMaps[string(vw.Settings.ColorMap)]
	vw.Size = ss.Config.Size
	vw.Depth = depth
	vw.Panels[0].Var = vr
	vw.Panels[0].Mode = Plane
	vw.Panels[0].CurPrev = Current
	vw.Start.X = 1
	vw.Start.SetDim(depth, 1)
	vw.Start.SetDim(vw.SliceDim(), slice)
	return vw
}

// TestViewSliceMapping renders the height field directly and checks that every
// vertex carries the value of the state cell it is supposed to: display X is
// always state X, display depth is View.Depth, and the remaining dimension is
// pinned at the slice level.
func TestViewSliceMapping(t *testing.T) {
	// deliberately unequal, so a swapped axis cannot pass by coincidence
	size := math32.Vec3i(7, 5, 3)
	ss := vwSim(size, EWHs0a)
	_ = ss

	for _, tc := range []struct {
		depth math32.Dims
		slice int32
	}{
		{math32.Z, 2}, // X-Z plane at a Y level
		{math32.Y, 2}, // X-Y plane at a Z level
	} {
		vw := vwView(ss, EWHs0a, tc.depth, tc.slice)
		nx := int(vw.Size.X)
		nz := int(vw.DepthSize())
		if nz < 2 {
			t.Fatalf("depth %v gives only %d cells", tc.depth, nz)
		}
		pm := &PlaneMesh{view: vw, panelNo: 0}
		nVtx, nIndex, _ := pm.MeshSize()
		if nVtx != nz*nx {
			t.Errorf("depth %v: MeshSize gave %d vertices, want %d", tc.depth, nVtx, nz*nx)
		}
		vtx := make(math32.ArrayF32, 3*nVtx)
		norm := make(math32.ArrayF32, 3*nVtx)
		tex := make(math32.ArrayF32, 2*nVtx)
		clr := make(math32.ArrayF32, 4*nVtx)
		idx := make(math32.ArrayU32, nIndex)
		pm.SetPlane(vtx, norm, tex, clr, idx)

		for zi := 0; zi < nz; zi++ {
			for xi := 0; xi < nx; xi++ {
				vi := (nz-1-zi)*nx + xi
				var v math32.Vector3
				vtx.GetVector3(vi*3, &v)
				// the plane is laid out with X across and -Z going back
				if int(v.X) != xi || int(-v.Z) != zi {
					t.Fatalf("depth %v: vertex %d at display (%d,%d) placed at (%g,%g)",
						tc.depth, vi, xi, zi, v.X, -v.Z)
				}
				want := vw.StateCoord(vw.Start, int32(xi), int32(zi))
				if want.Dim(vw.SliceDim()) != tc.slice {
					t.Fatalf("slice dim drifted: %v", want)
				}
				if got := 0.5 * vwCode(want.X, want.Y, want.Z); math.Abs(float64(v.Y-got)) > 1e-9 {
					t.Errorf("depth %v display (%d,%d): height %g, want %g for state %v",
						tc.depth, xi, zi, v.Y, got, want)
				}
			}
		}
		t.Logf("depth %v: %d x %d cells, slice %v = %d, all vertices map to the right state cell",
			tc.depth, nx, nz, vw.SliceDim(), tc.slice)
	}
}

// TestViewDisplayVector: a state vector must point along the axis its own
// dimension is drawn on, in either view.
func TestViewDisplayVector(t *testing.T) {
	v := math32.Vec3(1, 2, 3)
	xz := (&View{Depth: math32.Z}).DisplayVector(v)
	if xz != v {
		t.Errorf("X-Z view should pass a vector through unchanged: got %v", xz)
	}
	xy := (&View{Depth: math32.Y}).DisplayVector(v)
	// state Y is drawn going back into the screen (display Z), state Z is up
	if xy != math32.Vec3(1, 3, 2) {
		t.Errorf("X-Y view should swap Y and Z: got %v", xy)
	}
}

// TestViewMoveSlice: the slice level moves within bounds and nothing else does.
func TestViewMoveSlice(t *testing.T) {
	size := math32.Vec3i(7, 5, 3)
	ss := vwSim(size, EWHs0a)
	_ = ss
	vw := vwView(ss, EWHs0a, math32.Z, 2)
	sd := vw.SliceDim()
	if sd != math32.Y {
		t.Fatalf("X-Z view should slice in Y, got %v", sd)
	}
	before := vw.Start
	vw.MoveSlice(1)
	if vw.Start.Dim(sd) != before.Dim(sd)+1 {
		t.Errorf("slice did not move: %v -> %v", before, vw.Start)
	}
	if vw.Start.X != before.X || vw.Start.Dim(vw.Depth) != before.Dim(vw.Depth) {
		t.Errorf("in-plane corner moved: %v -> %v", before, vw.Start)
	}
	for range 100 { // must clamp, not run off the end
		vw.MoveSlice(1)
	}
	if got, mx := vw.Start.Dim(sd), size.Dim(sd)+1; got != mx {
		t.Errorf("slice clamped to %d, want %d", got, mx)
	}
	for range 100 {
		vw.MoveSlice(-1)
	}
	if got := vw.Start.Dim(sd); got != 0 {
		t.Errorf("slice clamped to %d, want 0", got)
	}
}

Took the stab. Right that I can't see the GUI — but the sampling logic is testable without one, so I wrote tests that drive `PlaneMesh.SetPlane` directly and check every vertex lands on the state cell it should. 25 tests pass.

## What I did

Rather than hardwire XZ, I made the axis mapping explicit, because a blanket switch breaks your 2D sims: they're `Size.Set(100, 100, 1)`, so an XZ slice would be one cell deep and render nothing.

New `View.Depth math32.Dims` — the state dimension drawn going back into the screen. Horizontal is always state X, height is always the value, so `Depth` alone picks the plane, and `SliceDim()` is whatever's left over. Four helpers carry it: `SliceDim`, `DepthSize`, `StateCoord`, `DisplayVector`. Everything that used to hardcode "depth is Y, slice is Z" now goes through those — `planemesh.go` (all three render modes plus `MeshSize`), `ZoomInSize`/`ZoomOutSize`, `MoveStart`, click-picking in `events.go`, `planeScale` and the corner label in `planeobj.go`.

Default in `ConfigGUI`: `Depth = Z` (XZ plane, sliced in Y), falling back to `Y` when `Size.Z <= 1`. So 2D and 1D behave exactly as before, 3D gets what you want. There's a chooser in the viewbar to flip live — it calls `SetDepth`, which re-centers the new slice and rebuilds the mesh, since the depth extent changes.

`MoveStart` was overloaded: `mv.Z != 0` meant "change slice," anything else meant "pan in plane." Split into `MoveSlice(n)` and a `MoveStart` that pans in display terms (X across, Y into the screen). The up/down toolbar buttons now call `MoveSlice`.

## Two things you should look at

**I changed vector-mode rendering.** `SetVectors` drew arrows as `Vec3(vx, vy, vz)` in display space while positioning cells by state X and Y — so a vector's Y component pointed *up* while its Y *position* ran into the screen. Inconsistent either way, but under XZ the naive mapping happens to be correct, and under XY it needs Y and Z swapped. `DisplayVector` does that. This changes how existing 2D vector displays look — a 2D E-field pointing +Y now points into the screen instead of up. Correct, I think, but it's a visible change to something you didn't ask about, so revert it if you preferred the old look.

**`planeScale` has a latent bug I left alone.** It computes `nsc.Z` and, for >2 panels, doubles `sz.Z` — but the mesh scale is `Pose.Scale.Set(nsc.X, ht, nsc.Y)`, so `nsc.Z` feeds nothing and 4-panel layouts never shrink in depth. I set `sz.Y = DepthSize()` and left the rest, so behavior is identical to today. Fixing it would change your 4-panel layout, which you may have tuned by eye.

## Packets now travel along X

Needed either way, as you said. `SlabPacket`/`SlabPacketConfig` take a `math32.Dims` now, matching `MovingWavePacket`'s idiom, and the three configs pass `math32.X` and polarize along **Y** — which `DisplayVector` maps to display-up in an XZ view, so a transverse wave actually looks like the textbook picture.

Speeds are unchanged to five digits, which is a decent isotropy check on the whole kernel:

```
photon  v = 0.46625  want 0.49039  (v/c = 0.9325)
Z       v = 0.34519  want 0.34235  (v/c = 0.6904)
W collision: 1.6573e+01 with Yang-Mills vs 1.8413e-10 without
```

Watch vars moved with them: `AYs`, `EWZY`, and for the collision `EWW3Xs` — the generated mode is longitudinal, so it follows the propagation axis.

One loose end: `ElectroweakViewAll` puts `A0s` in panel 1, which is identically zero for a transverse pulse. `AYs` would make Photon Pulse visible the moment you pick it. Didn't change it since the Higgs configs may be why A0s is there.

**Panel 1 → `AYs`.** Photon Pulse now shows the packet the moment you pick it.

**`Depth` defaults to `Z` unconditionally.** No more size sniffing — the X-Z plane sliced at a Y level is the standard orientation, full stop. The one thing that now differs from before: if a sim ever runs with the bare `Config.Defaults()` size `(100,100,1)` and no per-equation override, Plane mode gets a 1-cell depth and draws nothing until you flip the chooser. What it did buy, beyond the switch itself, is that the axis assumption is now stated in one place instead of being spread across four files as repeated `Size.Y` / `Start.Z` references — which is what made the vector-arrow inconsistency visible in the first place.

func TestPulseCondensateBackReaction(t *testing.T) {

		name  string
		init  func(*Sim)
		probe int
		min   float64 // lowest fraction of vacuum |Phi|^2 allowed

				h := float64(State.Value(2, 2, int(x), int(EWHmag), cur))
				num += a * a * h
				den += a * a
			}
			if den > 0 {
				lo = math.Min(lo, num/den)
			}
		}
		frac := lo / v2
		t.Logf("%-7s lowest |Phi|^2 under the packet %.5f of vacuum %.5f -> %.0f%%",

		}
	}
}"""

Fixed — 26 tests pass. But it wasn't a tolerance problem, it was real physics, and I think you'll want to know about it.

## What amplitude 1 actually does

Only the Z broke. At amp 1 it runs at **0.755 c** against a tree-level prediction of 0.685. I traced it by measuring the condensate the packet is sitting in:

```
amp=0.02  |Phi|^2 in packet = 100% of vacuum   v=0.34519   tree +0.8%
amp=0.10                      100%             v=0.34551   tree +0.9%
amp=0.30                       98%             v=0.34827   tree +1.7%
amp=0.60                       91%             v=0.35812   tree +4.6%
amp=1.00                       49%             v=0.37734   tree +10.2%
```

At amp 1 the Z packet is comparable to `v` (0.93 v at the demo scale), so it's not a perturbation on the vacuum — **it partially melts the condensate it's travelling through**, down to 33% at the instantaneous minimum. Less condensate means less mass means a faster Z. The tree-level formula assumes a linear wave on an undisturbed vacuum, so it simply doesn't apply there.

The flip side is the nicest number in this session:

```
photon  lowest |Phi|^2 under the packet = 0.01513 of vacuum 0.01513 -> 100%
Z       lowest |Phi|^2 under the packet = 0.38107 of vacuum 1.16610 ->  33%
```

The photon packet at amp 1 is about **66× the VEV** and leaves `|Phi|^2` unmoved in the fifth decimal. That's exact masslessness demonstrated directly rather than inferred from a speed — Q annihilates ⟨Φ⟩, so the photon direction is flat no matter how far you push along it. Its speed is also bit-identical to the amp 0.02 run.

## The fix

`TestConfigPulseSpeeds` keeps the tight 8% tree-level check on the photon and gives the Z 15%, with the reason written down rather than the number quietly widened. I added the assertion that actually carries the demo's claim and doesn't depend on the packet being small: the Z lags the photon by a clear margin.

New `TestPulseCondensateBackReaction` pins the mechanism — photon must leave the condensate within 1% of vacuum, Z must drive it below 70%. That's what makes the loosened Z tolerance honest: the deviation is explained and measured, not absorbed.

Updated `ZPulse`'s doc to say ~0.75 c and why, since it claimed 0.70.

Worth deciding: the Z demo is now showing a strongly nonlinear excitation that locally restores electroweak symmetry, not a Z boson propagating on the vacuum. Still visibly subluminal, so the demo's point survives — and arguably "watch the Z melt the Higgs as it goes" is the better demo. If you'd rather it be the clean linear case, **amp 0.6 keeps 91% of the condensate and sits within 4.6%**, while still filling most of the display range.

new = '''// cfgSpeed runs one of the pulse configs at a given Config.Amplitude and
// returns the packet speed in units of c, plus the lowest fraction of the
// vacuum |Phi|^2 found under the packet along the way.
func cfgSpeed(sz int32, init func(*Sim), probe int, amp float32, nst int) (vc, hfrac float64) {
	ss := cfgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {
		s.Config.Amplitude = amp
		init(s)
	})
	v2 := float64(ss.Params.HiggsV) * float64(ss.Params.HiggsV)
	hfrac = math.Inf(1)
	// the probe variables are written BY the kernel, so they are still zero
	// before the first step: take the baseline after one step, not before.
	ewStep(ss)
	c0 := cfgCentroid(sz, int32(probe))
	for range nst {
		ewStep(ss)
		// |Phi|^2 weighted by the local packet intensity: what the packet
		// itself sits in, not the box average.
		var num, den float64
		cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
		for x := int32(1); x <= sz; x++ {
			a := float64(State.Value(2, 2, int(x), probe, cur))
			h := float64(State.Value(2, 2, int(x), int(EWHmag), cur))
			num += a * a * h
			den += a * a
		}
		if den > 0 {
			hfrac = math.Min(hfrac, num/den/v2)
		}
	}
	c1 := cfgCentroid(sz, int32(probe))
	return (c1 - c0) / float64(nst) / float64(ss.Params.C), hfrac
}

// cfgGroupVel is the lattice group velocity in units of c, for a carrier of
// the given wavelength and a field of the given mass. omega = c sqrt(khat^2 +
// m^2) with khat = 2 sin(k/2), so dom/dk = c khat cos(k/2) / sqrt(khat^2+m^2).
// The cos(k/2) is why even a massless packet comes out slightly subluminal.
func cfgGroupVel(wavelength, mass float64) float64 {
	k := 2 * math.Pi / wavelength
	kh := 2 * math.Sin(k/2)
	return kh * math.Cos(k/2) / math.Sqrt(kh*kh+mass*mass)
}

// TestConfigPulseSpeeds: the photon packet must travel at c and the Z packet
// measurably slower, at its group velocity.
//
// This runs at a small Config.Amplitude, because the tree-level group velocity
// is a statement about a LINEAR wave on an undisturbed vacuum. The configs
// themselves default to amplitude 1 so they read at the GUI's display scale,
// and there the Z is large enough to move the condensate it travels through;
// TestPulseCondensateBackReaction covers that regime.
func TestConfigPulseSpeeds(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 96
	const amp = 0.02
	var speed [2]float64
	for ti, tc := range []struct {
		name  string
		init  func(*Sim)
		probe int
		mass  func(p *Parameters) float64
	}{
		{"photon", PhotonPulse, int(AYs), func(p *Parameters) float64 { return 0 }},
		{"Z", ZPulse, int(EWZY), func(p *Parameters) float64 { return float64(p.MZ) }},
	} {
		// the carrier comes from Config, which ElectroweakConfig sets, so the
		// prediction tracks whatever the config chooses rather than a literal.
		ss := cfgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) {})
		wl := float64(ss.Config.Wavelength)
		m := tc.mass(ss.Params)
		if tc.name == "Z" { // ZPulse raises the scale, so take m_Z from there
			ss = cfgSim(sz, func(s *Sim) { ewDemoScale(s, 0.388) })
			m = tc.mass(ss.Params)
		}
		wantV := cfgGroupVel(wl, m)

		got, hfrac := cfgSpeed(sz, tc.init, tc.probe, amp, 100)
		speed[ti] = got
		t.Logf("%-7s amp %.2f: v = %.5f c, want %.5f c (%+.1f%%), condensate %.0f%% of vacuum",
			tc.name, amp, got, wantV, 100*(got/wantV-1), 100*hfrac)
		if math.Abs(got/wantV-1) > 0.08 {
			t.Errorf("%s speed %g c, want %g c", tc.name, got, wantV)
		}
		// The lattice already puts a massless packet at cos(k/2) = 0.98 c, and
		// the finite packet loses a few percent more to dispersion; the point
		// is that it is near c and far above the Z.
		if m == 0 && got < 0.9 {
			t.Errorf("photon should move at essentially c: %g c", got)
		}
		if m > 0 && got > 0.85 {
			t.Errorf("Z should be visibly subluminal, got %g c", got)
		}
	}
	// the claim the demo makes, and the one that holds at any amplitude
	if speed[1] > speed[0]-0.1 {
		t.Errorf("Z at %.4f c should lag the photon at %.4f c by a clear margin",
			speed[1], speed[0])
	}
}

// TestPulseCondensateBackReaction measures what the pulses do to the Higgs
// condensate they travel through, which at the default amplitude is the
// difference between a linear wave and a strongly nonlinear one.
//
// The photon direction is the combination that Q = T^3 + Y annihilates, so it
// costs the condensate nothing no matter how large it gets -- at amplitude 1
// the packet is many times v and |Phi|^2 does not move, and its speed is the
// same as in the linear regime. That is exact masslessness shown directly,
// rather than inferred from a propagation speed.
//
// The Z direction does not annihilate the vacuum, so a packet comparable to v
// partially restores the symmetry underneath itself. The local mass falls with
// the condensate and the packet speeds up, which is why the tree-level group
// velocity only applies to a small Z.
func TestPulseCondensateBackReaction(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 96
	for _, tc := range []struct {
		name    string
		init    func(*Sim)
		probe   int
		minDrop float64 // how far below vacuum the condensate must go at amp 1
		maxDrop float64
	}{
		{"photon", PhotonPulse, int(AYs), 0.99, 1.01},
		{"Z", ZPulse, int(EWZY), 0.0, 0.70},
	} {
		vLin, hLin := cfgSpeed(sz, tc.init, tc.probe, 0.02, 100)
		vBig, hBig := cfgSpeed(sz, tc.init, tc.probe, 1, 100)
		t.Logf("%-7s amp 0.02: v = %.5f c, condensate %3.0f%%   |   amp 1: v = %.5f c, condensate %3.0f%%  (%+.1f%% faster)",
			tc.name, vLin, 100*hLin, vBig, 100*hBig, 100*(vBig/vLin-1))
		if hBig < tc.minDrop || hBig > tc.maxDrop {
			t.Errorf("%s left the condensate at %.0f%% of vacuum, want %.0f-%.0f%%",
				tc.name, 100*hBig, 100*tc.minDrop, 100*tc.maxDrop)
		}
		if tc.name == "photon" && math.Abs(vBig/vLin-1) > 0.01 {
			t.Errorf("photon speed moved %.1f%% between amplitudes: it should not "+
				"care, since it does not couple to the condensate", 100*(vBig/vLin-1))
		}
		if tc.name == "Z" && vBig <= vLin {
			t.Errorf("Z at amplitude 1 (%g c) should outrun the linear Z (%g c): "+
				"it has melted its own mass down", vBig, vLin)
		}
	}
}
