That state calculation is computing a staggered product of new and old wavefunction components, similar to a Visscher staggered norm, meaning it's ψ(t)·ψ(t+1) rather than |ψ|²—so it can go locally negative even though the total sum is conserved. That means the intensity weight itself can be negative, which I need to account for when computing a robust width.

I decide the honest fix is to clamp negative weights to zero for both centroid and width, since those negative bits are just a staggering artifact and small relative to the peak. There's a slight risk it shifts existing group-velocity results, but I'll implement the clamp, verify existing tests still pass, and reconsider if velocities move materially—also confirming that with clamping in place, the ratio r can't exceed 1 except by tiny roundoff, which is fine for near-delta distributions.

package wavesim

import (
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/enums"
	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

func TestScratchTable(t *testing.T) {
	mean := func(v []float64) float64 {
		if len(v) <= StatGroupVelWindow {
			return 0
		}
		v = v[StatGroupVelWindow:]
		tot := 0.0
		for _, x := range v {
			tot += x
		}
		return tot / float64(len(v))
	}
	cases := []struct {
		name  string
		eq    Equations
		probe enums.Enum
		init  func(*Sim)
	}{
		{"Wave", Wave, WavePos, nil},
		{"KleinGordon", KleinGordon, WavePos, nil},
		{"WaveCDir", WaveCDir, WaveCMag, nil},
		{"WaveC", WaveC, WaveCMag, nil},
		{"Schrodinger", Schrodinger, CabMag, nil},
		{"KleinGordonC", KleinGordonC, CabAs, nil},
		{"Weyl-nu", Weyl, WeylLMag, NeutrinoPacket},
		{"Weyl-e", Weyl, WeylLMag, ElectronPacket},
		{"Dirac", Dirac, DiracMag, nil},
	}
	for _, tc := range cases {
		ss := &Sim{}
		ss.Config = &Config{}
		ss.Config.Defaults()
		ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
		ss.Config.Equation = tc.eq
		ss.Config.Size.Set(512, 8, 8)
		ss.Config.Wavelength = 32
		ss.Config.PacketWidth = 12
		ss.ConfigSim()
		if tc.init != nil {
			ss.InitFunc = tc.init
			ss.Init()
		}
		for range 100 {
			ss.StepRun()
		}
		wd := ss.StatVals(StatWidthName(tc.probe, math32.X))
		vg := ss.StatVals(StatGroupVelName(tc.probe, math32.X))
		vd := ss.StatVals(StatDispersionName(tc.probe, math32.X))
		t.Logf("%-13s wid %6.3f -> %6.3f  Vg %+.4f  Vd %+.5f  (C %.3f Mass %.3f)",
			tc.name, wd[0], wd[len(wd)-1], mean(vg), mean(vd), ss.Params.C, ss.Params.Mass)
	}
}
EOF

// Copyright (c) 2026, The WaveReality Authors. All rights reserved.
// Use of this source code is governed by a BSD-style
// license that can be found in the LICENSE file.

package wavesim

import (
	"math"
	"testing"

	"cogentcore.org/core/enums"
	"cogentcore.org/core/math32"
)

// dispMean is the mean of a rate stat, skipping the leading samples that read
// zero while the [StatGroupVelWindow] window fills.
func dispMean(vals []float64) float64 {
	if len(vals) <= StatGroupVelWindow {
		return 0
	}
	vals = vals[StatGroupVelWindow:]
	tot := 0.0
	for _, v := range vals {
		tot += v
	}
	return tot / float64(len(vals))
}

// TestStatWidth checks the width measurement itself against gaussians of known
// sigma written straight into the state, before any equation is involved.
//
// The case that matters is the one centred on zero: half the packet sits at
// each end of the axis, and a plain second moment would call that nearly the
// width of the box. The circular form in [CircularWidth] does not care where
// the packet sits.
func TestStatWidth(t *testing.T) {
	const ln = 128
	ss := &Sim{}
	ss.Config = &Config{}
	ss.Config.Defaults()
	ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
	ss.Config.Equation = Wave
	ss.Config.Size.Set(ln, 1, 1)
	ss.ConfigSim()
	ss.Init()

	vr := WaveVel
	vri := int(vr.Int64())
	cur := int(GetCtx(0).CurState)
	vrs := []enums.Enum{vr}
	ctrs, wids, wts := make([]float64, 1), make([]float64, 1), make([]float64, 1)

	// a gaussian of known sigma, wrapped, at a known centre
	set := func(sigma, ctr float64) {
		State.SetZeros()
		for x := range ln {
			d := float64(x) - ctr
			for d > ln/2 {
				d -= ln
			}
			for d < -ln/2 {
				d += ln
			}
			State.Set(float32(math.Exp(-d*d/(2*sigma*sigma))), 1, 1, x+1, vri, cur)
		}
	}
	for _, sigma := range []float64{2, 4, 8, 16} {
		for _, ctr := range []float64{ln / 2, 0} {
			set(sigma, ctr)
			StateMoments(ss.Config.Size, math32.X, int32(cur), false, vrs, ctrs, wids, wts)
			err := wids[0]/sigma - 1
			where := "centred"
			if ctr == 0 {
				where = "straddling the wrap"
			}
			t.Logf("sigma %4.0f %-19s: measured %7.4f (%+.3f%%), centroid %6.2f",
				sigma, where, wids[0], 100*err, ctrs[0])
			if math.Abs(err) > 0.01 {
				t.Errorf("sigma %g %s: measured %g, off by %.2f%%", sigma, where, wids[0], 100*err)
			}
		}
	}
	// filling the box is the most spread a distribution can be, and the width
	// must report that rather than running away
	State.SetZeros()
	for x := range ln {
		State.Set(1, 1, 1, x+1, vri, cur)
	}
	StateMoments(ss.Config.Size, math32.X, int32(cur), false, vrs, ctrs, wids, wts)
	want := CircularWidthMax * ln
	t.Logf("uniform: measured %.4f, saturates at L/sqrt(12) = %.4f", wids[0], want)
	if math.Abs(wids[0]-want) > 1.0e-6 {
		t.Errorf("uniform width %g, want the saturation value %g", wids[0], want)
	}
}

// dispCase is one equation and the packet to measure it with.
type dispCase struct {
	name  string
	eq    Equations
	probe enums.Enum
	init  func(*Sim) // nil for the equation's own default
	rest  bool       // started at rest, so there is nothing to compare Vg to
	maxVd float64    // 0 means no bound: logged but not asserted
}

// TestDispersion is the cross-equation comparison: the same packet, the same
// box and the same measurement under every wave equation, so the numbers mean
// something against each other.
//
// The split it asserts is the structural one. An equation whose spatial
// operator is a GRADIENT -- WaveCDir, and Weyl with no mass -- carries a packet
// without changing its shape at all, because every k in it moves at the same
// speed. An equation whose operator is a LAPLACIAN does not, and neither does
// one with a mass term: those have a curved omega(k), so the packet's own
// spread of wavenumbers spreads the packet.
//
// The second-order equations pick up a further contribution from the lattice
// alone, which is why Wave is not at zero either despite being non-dispersive
// in the continuum.
func TestDispersion(t *testing.T) {
	const sz = 384
	const nst = 150
	// a packet several wavelengths wide, so it is narrow in k and the lattice
	// curvature is not what is being measured
	const wl, pw = 16, 32
	for _, tc := range []dispCase{
		{name: "Wave", eq: Wave, probe: WavePos},
		{name: "KleinGordon", eq: KleinGordon, probe: WavePos},
		{name: "Maxwell photon", eq: Maxwell, probe: AZs, init: PolarizedPhoton},
		{name: "WaveC", eq: WaveC, probe: WaveCMag},
		{name: "WaveCDir", eq: WaveCDir, probe: WaveCMag, maxVd: 0.005},
		{name: "Schrodinger", eq: Schrodinger, probe: CabMag, init: FreePacket},
		{name: "KleinGordonC", eq: KleinGordonC, probe: CabMag, init: ChargedPacket},
		{name: "Weyl neutrino", eq: Weyl, probe: WeylLMag, init: NeutrinoPacket, maxVd: 0.005},
		{name: "Weyl electron", eq: Weyl, probe: WeylLMag, init: ElectronPacket},
		{name: "Dirac at rest", eq: Dirac, probe: DiracMag, init: SpinAtRest, rest: true},
	} {
		ss := &Sim{}
		ss.Config = &Config{}
		ss.Config.Defaults()
		ss.Config.GPU, ss.Config.GUI = false, false
		ss.Config.Equation = tc.eq
		ss.Config.Size.Set(sz, 4, 4)
		ss.Config.Wavelength, ss.Config.PacketWidth = wl, pw
		ss.ConfigSim()
		if tc.init != nil {
			ss.InitFunc = tc.init
			ss.Init()
		}
		for range nst {
			ss.StepRun()
		}
		wd := ss.StatVals(StatWidthName(tc.probe, math32.X))
		if len(wd) == 0 {
			t.Errorf("%s: no width stat recorded", tc.name)
			continue
		}
		vg := dispMean(ss.StatVals(StatGroupVelName(tc.probe, math32.X)))
		vd := dispMean(ss.StatVals(StatDispersionName(tc.probe, math32.X)))
		grow := wd[len(wd)-1]/wd[0] - 1
		at := ""
		if tc.rest {
			at = "  (at rest)"
		}
		t.Logf("%-14s Vg %+.4f  Vd %+.5f   width %6.3f -> %6.3f (%+.1f%%)%s",
			tc.name, vg, vd, wd[0], wd[len(wd)-1], 100*grow, at)
		if math.IsNaN(vd) {
			t.Errorf("%s: dispersion went bad", tc.name)
		}
		if tc.maxVd > 0 && math.Abs(vd) > tc.maxVd {
			t.Errorf("%s: a gradient operator carries every k at the same speed, so it "+
				"should not spread: Vd = %g, want under %g", tc.name, vd, tc.maxVd)
		}
	}
}
EOF

  ```
  // CircularWidthMax is the standard deviation of a uniform distribution over a
  // span of 1: the largest width [CircularWidth] can report.
  const CircularWidthMax = 0.28867513459481288225 // 1/sqrt(12)
  
  // CircularWidth returns the standard deviation of a distribution on a ring of
  // circumference ln, given the intensity-weighted mean cosine and sine of its
  // angle. It is exact for a wrapped Gaussian, and saturates at the uniform
  // value rather than diverging as the distribution fills the ring.
  func CircularWidth(mc, ms float64, ln int) float64 {
  	l := float64(ln)
  	mx := CircularWidthMax * l
  	r := math.Sqrt(mc*mc + ms*ms)
  	if r <= 0 {
  		return mx
  	}
  	if r >= 1 {
  		return 0
  	}
  	return min(l/(2*math.Pi)*math.Sqrt(-2*math.Log(r)), mx)
  }
  ```

The stat is in and validated. Waiting on the full suite; here's where things stand.

**`Wid` and `Vd`, recorded by the same code path everywhere.** Rather than a new per-equation stat, I folded two more series into the existing packet stat, so every equation that already reports `Vg` now reports dispersion in the same units with no per-equation code:

- `Wid<Var><Dim>` — the rms width of the intensity, in cubes
- `Vd<Var><Dim>` — how fast that width grows, **in units of C, the same scale as `Vg`**

That shared scale is the point: one plot now says how far a packet gets before it smears out. `Vg` and `Vd` are on by default; the centroid and the raw width are recorded but off.

Dirac had no packet stat at all, so I added one — it's the equation where the answer is most dramatic.

## Two things had to be fixed before the number meant anything

**A linear second moment is wrong under wrap.** A packet straddling the boundary is half at each end of the axis, and a plain Σw·d² calls that nearly the width of the box. I used the circular standard deviation instead — the spread on a ring, from the intensity-weighted mean cosine and sine. It's exact for a wrapped Gaussian, costs one extra pass-free accumulation, and saturates at the uniform value L/√12 instead of diverging.

**`WeylLMag` goes negative.** It's written as a *staggered* product, ψ(t)·ψ(t+1), so it's conserved in the sum but carries small negative lobes locally. With those left in, the total can fall below the partial sums, `r` exceeded 1, and the width read exactly 0.000 from step 40 onward while `Vg` kept reporting a perfectly sensible 0.82. An unsquared weight is now clamped at zero. This was silently corrupting the existing centroid too.

## The measurement, checked against analytic Gaussians

```
sigma    2 centred            : measured  2.0000 (-0.000%)
sigma    2 straddling the wrap: measured  2.0000 (-0.000%)
sigma   16 centred            : measured 15.9962 (-0.024%)
sigma   16 straddling the wrap: measured 15.9962 (-0.024%)
uniform: measured 36.9504, saturates at L/sqrt(12) = 36.9504
```

Straddling the wrap is bit-identical to centred.

## The cross-equation table

Same box, same packet (384×4×4, wavelength 16, width 32 — several wavelengths, so this measures the equation and not the lattice), 150 steps:

```
Wave           Vg +0.9801  Vd +0.01960   width 16.008 -> 17.324 (+8.2%)
KleinGordon    Vg +0.9674  Vd +0.01909   width 16.008 -> 17.300 (+8.1%)
Maxwell photon Vg +0.9805  Vd +0.01960   width 16.008 -> 17.324 (+8.2%)
WaveC          Vg +0.7650  Vd +0.00415   width 16.000 -> 16.154 (+1.0%)
WaveCDir       Vg +0.9349  Vd +0.00272   width 15.986 -> 16.012 (+0.2%)
Schrodinger    Vg +0.3825  Vd +0.00208   width 16.000 -> 16.154 (+1.0%)
KleinGordonC   Vg +0.9674  Vd +0.01909   width 16.008 -> 17.300 (+8.1%)
Weyl neutrino  Vg +0.9297  Vd +0.00011   width 15.993 -> 15.985 (-0.1%)
Weyl electron  Vg +0.4784  Vd -0.02016   width 15.995 -> 15.179 (-5.1%)
Dirac at rest  Vg -0.0000  Vd +0.24284   width 16.000 -> 33.397 (+108.7%)
```

The split is structural, and it's the one your Weyl argument predicts: **a gradient operator holds the packet's shape exactly** — the massless Weyl reads 0.00011, 180× cleaner than the second-order wave — because every k moves at the same speed. A Laplacian doesn't, and neither does a mass.

Three cross-checks fell out that I didn't set up: Maxwell's photon matches Wave to five digits, and `KleinGordonC` matches real `KleinGordon` to five digits — same operator, same number. And `Schrodinger`'s `Vd` is *exactly half* `WaveC`'s, with `Vg` exactly half too — identical dynamics, read against a C that differs by a factor of two. That's your Wave:KG = WaveC:Schrödinger point falling out of the instrumentation.

Two readings need their caveat stated. The massive Weyl's `Vd` is **negative** because the probe is the left-handed half alone, which the mass is draining into the right-handed one — a component leaving, not a packet coming apart. And `Wave` sits at 0.0196 rather than zero: that's lattice dispersion, not the continuum equation.

I'll confirm when the suite finishes — `goal build`, `go generate`, and the yaegi regen are all clean so far.

Fixed and re-verified the three affected tests. Full suite re-running.

The clamp was wrong for the centroid, and `TestWeylNeutrino` caught it precisely: the stat read 0.2385 against the packet's actual 0.2875.

The reason is worth recording. Those negative lobes in a staggered `Mag` sit at a **fixed carrier phase**, not a fixed place in the envelope. Dropping them ties the centroid to the *phase* velocity rather than the group velocity — which is exactly the 17% slow reading. So the clamp now applies to the width and only the width, which needs a genuine density to be meaningful; the centroid keeps the signed weight and behaves exactly as it did before I touched it.

Corrected numbers where the centroid change moved them — `Vd` is unaffected throughout:


The massless Weyl packet is 180× cleaner than the second-order wave — a gradient operator moves every k at one speed, so the shape is simply preserved. That is the quantitative version of the argument you'd been building toward.

Two caveats I'd keep attached to these numbers. `Wave` sits at 0.0196 rather than zero because of lattice dispersion, not the continuum equation. And the massive Weyl reads negative because the probe is the left-handed half alone, which the mass is draining into the right-handed one — a component leaving, not a packet coming apart. If you want a true dispersion number for the electron you'd need a total-magnitude variable; Weyl doesn't currently have one.

	ss.AddStat(ss.StatGroupVelMag(math32.X, WeylMag, WeylLMag, WeylRMag))"""

`WeylMag` is in and the Weyl tests pass. Full suite running; one thing to flag now, because it changes the conclusion I gave you last message.

## The variable

[weyl.goal](wavesim/weyl.goal) — `WeylMag` = `|ψ_L|² + |ψ_R|²`, placed before `WeylLMag`/`WeylRMag` to match Dirac's total-then-parts order. The kernel computes both halves into locals and writes all three, so it stays the same staggered product as the others. `WeylStats` now sums it and probes it first in the group-velocity call, ahead of the two chiralities.

I left `WeylViewAll` alone — you set those four panels to the components deliberately.

## I was wrong about why the electron read negative

I told you the -0.020 was the mass draining L into R, and that a total-magnitude variable would fix it. It doesn't. `WeylMag` reads **-0.02014** against `WeylLMag`'s -0.02016 — the same number.

The width trace shows what's actually happening:

```
neutrino Mag: 15.99 15.95 15.79 15.59 15.54 15.61 15.72 15.83 15.91 15.96
electron Mag: 16.00 15.95 15.70 15.39 15.10 14.90 14.83 14.82 14.90 15.01
```

Both **breathe**. A slab with a carrier on it isn't an eigenstate of the lattice equation, so the width dips and recovers — 3% for the neutrino, 7% for the electron, over something longer than a 150-step run. The neutrino's window mean landed near zero by luck, covering roughly equal up and down; the electron's landed on the descending half. Nothing was being drained.

So `Vd` is a sound instantaneous rate but a finite-run mean of it is only meaningful for a packet that's genuinely spreading — `Dirac at rest` at +0.243 growing monotonically to +108.7% is the real thing. I've put that caveat in the test doc.

## The bug that cost the detour

Adding the enum member broke four Weyl tests — chirality conservation drifted 6.3%, the at-rest L/R ratio left 1.000000, hydrogen went NaN. Not the new code: `WeylStatesN` lives in the generated `enumgen.go`, and I'd run only `goal build`. The state tensor was one variable short, so the last one wrote over its neighbour.

Your memory file already warned me about exactly this, with `EWStatesN`. I've added the diagnostic signature to it, because it sent me down a wrong path: *inserting* mid-enum corrupts the physics, *appending* looks fine — since the variable that falls off the end is then the unused new one. That reads like index-sensitive code and isn't.

`WeylStatesN` is now 30 and all eight Weyl tests pass, including the gauge-invariance one back at -1.91%.
